item.title: [Invest Like The Best] The Hidden Capital Crunch Behind Silicon Valley’s AI Boom
item.dc:creator: Invest Like The Best
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个反直觉的发现：Anthropic 已经不是"创业公司"，而是一家"主权实体"

$1400 亿募集、$100 亿支出、$1320 亿静静躺在资产负债表上——这不是一张初创公司的财务表，这是一张战略储备国家的表。它的现金余额比瑞士 2000 年的外汇储备还大。真正值得注意的不是"烧钱有多快"，而是烧钱有多慢——它在做的事情，本质上是把美元换成"未来算力的看涨期权"，就像冷战时期美国囤积战略石油储备、或中国央行囤积黄金一样。这重新定义了 Ramp 描述的"神经病式恐慌性购买算力"：它不是在购买生产资料，它是在执行货币政策。这意味着未来 18 个月最该观察的不是 Anthropic 的收入增长，而是它的"储备释放节奏"——因为那决定了整个算力市场的利率曲线。

"Cuck Tranche"：一个金融结构背后真正的是社会心理学

Ramp 轻描淡写地把它说成"资本密集型公司的必需"，但把它放回更大的图景：这是硅谷第一次发明出一个"用金钱购买尊严"的金融工具。常规的二级市场买入是信息套利；而 cuck 轮次是身份套利——VC 支付 3-5 倍溢价，不是为了回报，而是为了购买"我们没有错过这一轮"这个叙事。行为经济学里有个远亲叫"沉没尊严成本"（sunk dignity cost），但更精准的类比是奢侈品行业的限量款机制：价格越高、排队越激烈，因为稀缺本身就是最强信号。硅谷正在把"输掉的 deal"重新定义为"可以赎回的损失"——这是一个会写进未来 MBA 教材的结构性创新。注意 Ramp 用的那个词："完全全部"的人都 cuck 过——他把这个结构命名成了一种集体羞耻，而羞耻恰恰是让这种定价机制自我延续的燃料。

真正的隐藏模式：VC 市场变成了一台"反身性机器"，而硅谷的真正护城河是威尼斯式的

Ramp 不经意间说出了全场最关键的一句话：价格区间现在动辄 4 倍。这意味着 VC 定价已经失去了"发现价格"的功能——它不再反映公司内在价值，而变成了叙事验证的仪式。这完美对应索罗斯反身性理论的升级版：定价（感知）直接改变基本面（因为更高估值吸引更好的人才、更多的算力、更大的客户），然后又反过来验证最初的定价。

但让我真正意外的，是另一个层次的连接：这与 Jane Jacobs 关于城市密度的理论惊人一致。硅谷能撑起这个体系，不是因为钱多，而是因为个人天使投资者的密度——Ramp 说"比全球任何地方高 100 倍以上"。Ramp 把它当"好事"，但隐藏的含义更深：这个密度构成了一层社会性的流动性缓冲。当机构 LP 开始谨慎（他们已经是——80% 的流动性集中在 SpaceX / Anthropic / OpenAI / Databricks 四家），这些账户上躺着上千万美金的个人继续为长尾公司提供血液。

所以硅谷不是一个金融市场，它是一个由个人关系网络支撑的流动性生态——它最接近的历史原型，不是伦敦城、不是华尔街，而是威尼斯共和国：一个靠家族信任链、世代通婚、物理相邻的高密度网络，以极低的交易摩擦撬动全球资本流动的城邦。这解释了为什么复制硅谷从来没有成功——你可以复制钱、复制税收政策、复制气候，但你没法在 5 年里长出 500 年的社交密度。

两个被忽视的弱信号

  • Neolabs 用 benchmark 作弊的现象，是学术界 p-hacking 和医药研究复制危机的完美镜像。我们正在创造一整层"在测试集上最优但在真实世界可能毫无价值"的技术。这意味着下一波"AI 失败叙事"可能不来自技术本身，而来自"基准指标与商业价值的脱钩"——而这是一个几乎没人在定价的风险。

  • VC 开始用算力代替现金进行投资——这个创新在金融史上有一个古老的镜像：中世纪意大利银行用粮食和盐作为抵押品，当货币体系跟不上实体经济的流动速度时，实物成为新货币。GPU 正在成为硅谷的"新粮食"，而当实物成为货币，通常意味着法定货币系统已经不足以承载真实的交换——这是一个值得警惕的宏观信号。

  • Ramp 自曝："我犯的最大错误是每一支基金都募小了。" 这句话被他当作商业复盘，但其实它在揭示一个更深的结构性事实：整个 VC 行业都在系统性低估自己的最佳 deal 的吸纳能力。这是一个"最成功的 VC 都承认自己过度保守"的时代——这本身就是一个顶级泡沫信号，因为它会在未来 24 个月驱动下一轮基金规模的系统性膨胀。

📝 转录文本

The Hidden Capital Crunch Behind Silicon Valley's AI Boom

Cold Open: The Moving Goalpost

Every few years in Silicon Valley, the goalpost moves for what terminal outcomes can actually be. So when I got started in early stage investing in 2016, people looked at every company from the lens of: "in a best case scenario, this could be a $10 billion outcome." And then everybody started looking at companies from the lens of: "in a best case scenario, this company can be worth $100 billion." And then now we're at a new goalpost of: "in a best case scenario, this company could have a trillion dollar outcome."

And now between SpaceX, Anthropic, and OpenAI, you have three trillion dollar companies. My bet is there might be two to three more — and not 40 more.

State of the Deal Market: Pace, Trunches, and the "Cuck Tranche"

Host: One of our mutual LPs describes you as the person from whom he learns the most per minute about what's going on in venture markets. We did the big picture last time — today let's zoom in on this moment. How would you describe the state of things right now at the deal level around San Francisco?

It's very fast-paced. Insanely fast-paced, in the sense that rounds are happening quicker than ever. Follow-on rounds are happening quicker than ever. There are certain companies that just get a lot of attention very early in their life cycle and they get a lot of demand for their financing — whether it's their seed or their Series A or their Series B — and there's a handful of firms that those founders want to raise capital from, and those guys get preferential pricing. That's really trunch number one.

Then there's a bunch of VC firms that lose that deal. Historically those firms would say: "Okay, we'll maintain a relationship, we'll put in a small check to maintain that relationship, and as the thing performs, we'll do the next round." And in 2021 you had the "fast follow" — a couple weeks later they'd raise at 2x the valuation from one of the people that lost that financing.

But in this market it's: "Okay, we lost this round, but we don't want to wait for the next round. What do we need to pay to get into this financing today?" And it's usually not 2x. It's usually 3 to 4 to 5x, happening in tandem with the primary. That's the secondary trunch — which has become known elegantly in Silicon Valley as the "cuck trunch."

The thing that's interesting is these companies are so capital-intensive that they actually need that level of capital, and they don't want to raise all of it in the primary. So I don't think the trunching is an unhealthy sign of the market — I think it's a necessity of these types of companies and this environment. Sometimes you get into the early trunch, and other people get into the second trunch, and sometimes you're the one getting cucked. Anybody who tells you they've never gotten cucked is lying. Everyone's gotten cucked once or twice at least.

You're also having people running around like chickens with their heads cut off trying to keep up with the market, throwing out offers very quickly. And you're seeing some bad behavior — people changing or pulling offers after the fact. A lot of this is reminiscent of 2021.

The pace makes everyone feel like they need to do something to stay ahead of the curve. In this market, getting markups is the bare minimum requirement to keep up. Markups don't even feel good anymore — they just feel like pacing. Once every three weeks something happens in your portfolio and you feel pretty good; the next three weeks you see things happening to companies you're not in, and you're like, "Holy sh**, I'm falling behind again."

The Revenue Narrative: What's Misleading About This Market

The pace isn't unprecedented — 2021 had a similar pace. But today the pace is healthier because there's real value creation. These companies are doing truly amazing things, growing at unprecedented rates.

What's a little misleading, though, is the story behind the revenue. You have companies growing 10, 15, 20x year-over-year — but any company growing at that rate has something interesting about their revenue. It's not clean, pure-play SaaS revenue, 90%+ gross margins, annualized recurring contracts. They all have something:

  • Ridiculously high growth but very low or negative margins
  • Really fast growth but very high customer concentration
  • "Annualized" revenue because they're selling data — whatever revenue was last month, multiplied by 12
  • Consumer-based rather than enterprise-based
  • Usage-based rather than contractual

This can be discouraging to founders whose companies aren't growing that fast. But if you peel the layers back, you need to compare your revenue growth to companies within your style — not to absolute topline figures.

You have data labeling companies growing at insane rates, but margins of 15–20% because getting that data is expensive. You have other companies reliant on foundation model providers, where all the margin goes to the foundation model companies.

The Margin Story Is Actually Improving

But the cool thing is that margins are improving at a rapid clip.

Host: Anthropic's were 85% in the first half of this year, they said.

Yeah. And we have companies in our portfolio that are going to grow 200–700% this year, but their margin profiles are going from –15% to +35%. Massive revenue growth and margin growth simultaneously.

Then you have vertical SaaS businesses getting 100x revenue multiples. People ask: how do you compare that to public markets where SaaS multiples are 13x revenue? And you look at them and go: are these actually SaaS businesses, or are these labor-replacement businesses?

Some people don't buy the labor-replacement thesis. The way you have to believe in it: these companies are still growing 5, 7, 10x year-over-year even at massive scale. I haven't actually seen them replace labor yet, but at this pace — look at companies selling to law firms. If you look at how much law firms spend on software, you'd say "these companies can't be that big." But look at how much they spend on paralegals — that's a really big number. Capture 20% of that, and the math really works.

This Market vs. 2021: Similarities and Differences

Host: Compared to 2021 — two very euphoric, frothy-seeming markets — what are the most notable similarities and differences?

In 2021, the companies weren't that interesting when you really looked at them. We just didn't have anything else to compare them to. SaaS companies growing 5x, 3x, 3x, 2x — everyone said "best in class." Companies with $8M of SaaS revenue raising at billion-dollar valuations, with very constrained TAMs, on seven-year paths to $100M ARR. That was "venture" back then.

Today, you look at those and go: I can't believe we even got out of bed for those opportunities.

Similar today: round structures, deal volume, the feeling of needing to keep up. In 2021 there was a six-month window where VCs were just ripping checks — ask any of them to look back at that portfolio and they'll scratch their heads: "What were we thinking?" We could be in 2019, not 2021 — but some signs are back. Public market investors aggressively coming into venture. Frantic deal-making. Term sheets getting pulled, reneged, renegotiated. In the last 6–8 weeks, I've seen more deals get renegotiated after being offered than at any point since 2021.

Dissimilar today: the enthusiasm around the companies. Nobody in 2021 was investing thinking companies would be category-defining or global-scale within 18–24 months. That's playing out in this market. Companies are finding product-market fit faster than ever. I can't think of anything I invested in in 2021 that I was using personally — now I'm actually seeing how much value these things drive. I have family members, non-early adopters, using these products as parts of their daily life. There's a huge paradigm shift. People truly believe: if there's ever a window where you can't afford to sit on the sidelines, it's now.

The LP Side: Deployment Velocity and the Liquidity Problem

Host: Can you drill down to the LP side — the funds being raised? At some point the sources of capital themselves start asking deeper questions.

When a VC fund raises, they're raising for an 18–24 month initial deployment window. In the last 18–24 months, the mega platform funds have probably raised two to three times in that same window. Deployment periods are about 3x faster than planned.

VC firms have their pulse on the market better than anyone. They raise capital to support their portfolio construction model — X bets, X ownership, over X time. Every single mega firm has dramatically underestimated how much capital they need to get target ownership. More companies they want in, higher prices, more capital required for the same ownership. That's why they're back sooner, for larger sums.

LPs are realizing there are two outcomes: 1. Maintain ownership → way fewer shots on goal. (Shots on goal are your hedge against bad picking. Lose them, and your upside is capped.) 2. Maintain shots on goal → way less ownership per company.

The alternative — "we need our ownership, we'll invest in fewer companies" — only works if you're a better picker. You can still produce outsized returns, but only on your core positions.

The Liquidity Concentration Problem

LPs expected dramatically more liquidity at this point in the cycle. Here's the funny thing: LPs with 35–50% of exposure in venture capital — if you peel the layer back, it's not 30–40% of AUM in venture broadly, it's 30–50% of AUM in three or four companies. SpaceX, Anthropic, OpenAI, Databricks, a handful more. Those are the names that need to generate liquidity to get exposure down.

If you weren't in a fund with SpaceX exposure, you haven't gotten any liquidity. So the LPs generating meaningful liquidity are the ones in funds with exposure to those specific companies. Outside of them, LPs aren't getting much back. That puts funds without those LPs in a position where they're trying to extract new capital sources — because traditional LPs are limited on cash.

Concrete Examples of Deployment Velocity

Host: Could you give an example — no names, rough numbers — of the accelerated pace?

  • One fund raised $2.5B, started deploying in July, told me they're back in market in January.
  • Another: $3B nine months ago, now back looking for $5B.

They'll get it — they're great managers. But that's the intensity.

The ripple effect: VCs are now giving term sheets saying, "We want to put $150M in your company — is it okay if we fund in mid-January, three months from now?" Founders go: "Wait, you need three months to fund?" And it's: "No, no, we're good for it — but all the money in our current fund is committed to existing companies, we're closing a new fund, docs, onboarding, capital call facility — it'll be mid-January."

Another company got a $50M term sheet, the VC wiring 40 of the 50 — wired $5M at close and told them another 8–10 weeks for the rest. They'll get the money, but it draws attention to the pace.

The Anthropic S1 and the Compute-as-Capital Question

Host: This seems furious and unsustainable — and maybe understandable, given it's funding the most interesting technology buildout in human history. But Anthropic's S1 came out which makes an interesting day to have this discussion.

The most glaring stat in that thing: they've raised $140 billion, spent $10 billion of that, and have $132 billion on the balance sheet. $10 billion of cash to get to the revenue numbers they're at with 85% gross margins — unbelievable.

Host: Does all this make you wonder if we need innovation in financial products? When you boil down why everyone needs all this stuff, the answer is always compute. Are we trying to solve a very modern problem with what's become an antiquated instrument?

Yes and no. There's no shortage of new debt vehicles to finance growth. GC has their customer value fund — "if you can prove that for every $10M it unlocks $30M of revenue, we'll finance it."

Compute as a Capital Instrument

There are VC firms financing companies with compute instead of cash. For a lot of founders, that's more attractive: "You guaranteed your allocation this round, because we're going to spend this money on compute regardless." But the complexities: you have to secure the compute, get good pricing. Do you give it in perpetuity? For one training run? How many times can you recycle the same compute?

Getting new capital structures widely adopted in Silicon Valley is hard. VCs default to clean equity without unique covenants. Founders rely on VCs for opinions on capital, and VCs historically don't like venture debt products — they give you a million reasons not to. GC's value creation fund is doing great now, but for the early couple years, it required significant education.

So yes, there's always room for innovation. Billions of dollars in equity capital to spend entirely on compute may not be the best use of equity capital.

The Neocloud Market and the Compute Paradox

Host: You've got Elon saying there's going to be all this stranded capacity, Neocloud having a tough week in the markets, and at the same time literally nobody can seem to get a prior-generation — let alone Vera Rubin — allocation from Nvidia. The price of GPUs just looks unidirectional.

In our portfolio, we're routinely helping companies find compute, because finding it isn't easy. A lot of the largest Neoclouds aren't really interested in engaging with sub-$200M deals. Companies without that scale lease capacity here and there. But on a relative basis, those aren't what's moving the needle.

What moves the needle: hyperscalers, frontier model labs, and private neolabs raising $1B+ seed valuations.

The only thing that limits demand over time is if compute needs diminish, or if these companies have a harder time raising. The best assets will keep raising and have all the compute they need.

The most interesting segment: the neolab segment. People thought there'd be two or three great ones — now there are probably 80 or 90 neolabs that have raised $1–5B each. The funny thing: it's very hard to underwrite how well they're doing. You basically underwrite them based on how much money they're raising.

We met a neolab a couple weeks ago raising $1B (second round) that would spend the entire billion next year on compute for one training run — and said they'd probably need to raise another $5B throughout the year. Often they launch something impressive, but it's hard to discern whether it's truly generalizable or benchmark-maxed to perform well on specific tests.

The Real Constraint: Debt, Not Equity

Host: Could capital be the actual constraint — if capital markets dry up, that changes the compute story?

Potentially. And I think it's more on the debt side than the equity side. A lot of these guys need debt in excess of 5–10x the equity they raised. Given what's happened in public markets with some Neoclouds, their cost of debt is going to increase. So it's less about equity for compute, and more about whether they can raise the debt at terms that make business viability work — for the show to go on.

Seed in a Trillion-Dollar Imagination

Host: What about seed as a concept? Some seed deals get done at crazy prices — seed risk for Series D pricing. How do you feel about seed?

Every few years the goalpost moves for terminal outcomes. 2016: "best case $10B." 2021: "best case $100B" — because Stripe, Databricks, Airbnb, DoorDash were approaching it. Turns out that only two or three companies beyond those actually ended up as $100B companies, but everyone got priced as if they might. Today: "best case $1T." Between SpaceX, Anthropic, OpenAI, you have three. My bet: two or three more, not 40.

So now what's a $1B entry valuation for a $1T outcome? That's what shifts the dynamic.

Reactive vs. Proactive Investing

At every stage, there are opportunities for good pricing on great companies. The investors who do badly in bad vintages are the ones deploying the majority of their capital into the most obvious thing. In 2021, VCs doing 100x revenue multiple SaaS deals with the bulk of their portfolio are now bottom quartile — or bottom 75% — for that vintage.

Two ways to make returns in venture: - Reactive, done well: top quartile. - Proactive: top 5%.

Proactive means backing great founders working on markets that aren't yet obvious. If the idea isn't obvious yet, you won't get a lot of competition. You can price accordingly.

Case Studies: Conduit and Etched

Conduit (BCI — brain-computer interface). We seeded them nine months ago. Anyone who met the founders would've told you they were brilliant — but nine months ago, nobody in the Valley cared about BCI as a category. Neuralink implants chips in your brain for perfect readouts; Conduit extracts brain information via a product you wear on top of your head. When I met them, they had a small amount of human training data showing scaling behavior — the more data, the more accurate — and already with 80% accuracy they could decode what someone was thinking before they typed it.

Now they have 30,000 hours of human training data. In the last 8–10 weeks, BCI became a popular category. Conduit raised a large oversubscribed round — 13 term sheets. If they succeed, in 5–10 years you and I might wear a little device over our ear that understands our thoughts, communicates with our agent, and distinguishes actionable from non-actionable thoughts. Your agent just runs in the back-end for everything you think. You become the most efficient human in the world. Now people are saying: "Wait, someone could build a $1T outcome in BCI" — and Conduit's latest round prices that in.

Etched (AI chip fabrication) — Gavin Uberti. Gavin met every great investor in Silicon Valley. Not a single VC walked away not thinking he was brilliant. But everyone assumed a startup can't out-compete incumbents on AI chip fab — it's just never going to happen. It wasn't until Sequoia blessed him with a $10B valuation that everyone said: "Oh wait, startups could totally run circles around incumbents here." Every other chip company then raised at astronomical valuations.

The market was obvious to these founders before it was obvious to the market.

The Right Number of Term Sheets

Host: If I had to shrink that into one metric — is it something like the ideal number of term sheets? You don't want 50, you want a handful?

If a company gets 15 term sheets, it's going to get very expensive. 2–3 term sheets → reasonable pricing, less competition. If a great investor can convince the founder to take their money, that's a core position.

But more importantly: lots of meetings mean the founder is impressive — people vouch for them. If the company gets many meetings but few conversions, it's usually not because the founder was bad — it's because people walked away thinking it wasn't that interesting of an opportunity. And the default in venture is: it's not that interesting. In a few cases, it actually is — but most VCs are reactive, not proactive, and nobody wanted to be proactive about learning what this exceptional person has decided to dedicate the next decade to.

The Current Landscape: 4x Pricing Dispersion

Host: Anything especially unusual about this period versus your whole history?

Valuations now require a really big imagination to justify. It's getting harder — even for people who actually know the market — to understand where something will clear. In a normalized market, I can tell a founder: "If we go out with term sheets and leverage, we can probably get this valuation from a high-quality partner."

Today I'm saying: "You can get a term sheet as low as here and as high as here" — a 4x difference. I'm not on the money, because the market is so erratic. Someone may come in and do something irrational to not lose the deal — triple what the second-highest bidder is willing to pay.

Why? Every founder has an expectation pegged to a friend's comparable round. But that friend's valuation may have come from one person paying 3x the second-highest bidder. So you give a founder an offer you think is generous, and they're offended — they can point to a comparable at 3–4x your price.

The Other-End-of-the-Spectrum Strategy

Host: Is the rational thing to do the opposite — go to businesses where you can really investigate them? Databricks or Stripe-type companies?

Less competition there. You can deploy large sums as a passive investor, with exposure to great companies. The question: is it 2019 or 2021? In 2021 you could've invested in Stripe at $100B — still a great company. Today it's $179B. That's an 11–12% IRR over 5 years. Still better than the bottom 75% of ventures.

You can secure a top-quartile position in venture by backing the best companies at the highest prices, because great companies tend to keep being great — they compound.

But my concern: how consensus this approach has become. I've seen a record number of VC firms in the last 18 months land on the same idea — there's a handful of obviously great companies that can absorb huge capital, and if you can show access, you can raise large funds and passively deploy. It's become a consensus strategy.

I can't really think of many times in history where an easy strategy turned out to be a good long-term strategy. Some strategies have been considered easy money — but not at this scale. If everybody believes it's easy, it's probably not a great way to make money.

The Data Companies Conundrum

Host: For years the narrative was that data companies are more a trade than a business. Has the narrative shifted?

Data companies are a conundrum. The old belief: no long-term sustainability, because eventually the people buying data get all they need. But people dramatically underestimated the data needs of model builders — they only keep increasing. Certain companies are ahead of the curve on knowing what data is needed, can deliver at quality, and go collect it.

Two types of data companies in robotics:

  1. "Data is a giant forever business" — can sell data for 10, 15, 20 years, collect tens of billions in revenue. Some VCs believe this and want to invest in many data provider companies.
  2. "Data is a means to an end" — eventually the market will be saturated, but selling data is a great way to finance our own robotics research. We know the market better than anyone, we can collect data, we can raise equity and self-finance through data sales.

Two camps, both deeply versed in the category, two very different perspectives on the ultimate outcome.

The Angel Investor Flywheel

Host: What about the newest influx of angel investors — people getting incredibly wealthy from the big three going public? Employee balance sheets the size of huge seed funds.

It just continues making Silicon Valley the best place in the world to start a company. The reason no other ecosystem has ever taken off the way Silicon Valley has: Silicon Valley has the largest density — by an order of magnitude, probably 100x or greater — of individuals running around writing $100K to $1M personal checks off their balance sheet to help with companies before they're institutional.

People who'll write a $1M check, and if they lose it, they don't care. That's the mentality here. It's probably good for innovation — more of them → more startup innovation.

Abstract's Evolution: From $100M to $800M

Host: Do you want Abstract to stay a pure-play seed firm, or evolve?

We've evolved. In recent years we've dabbled at venture stage (Series A–C) — led Series B financings in Socket, Doctronic, Dust. Made passive growth investments in Crusoe. Put about 15% of our 2023 vintage into the formation round of xAI. Were a big investor in the Series B of Polymarket.

Our first fund was $100M. The latest is $800M.

Then vs. now LP sentiment: When I raised a $100M seed fund in 2018, I got so much from LPs saying it was too big for a fund one. This vintage, I went out for $800M and got LPs commending me on my discipline for staying so small. $100M was a large fund in 2018; $800M is a small fund in 2026.

Looking back at our best-returning deals, we were almost never allocation constrained — we were capital constrained. Great relationships, great conviction, but our fund size didn't give us permission to be lead. A founder who trusts you, whom you've known early, showing up outside a traditional financing process with a number they don't feel they need to shop and enough of the round that they don't have to go to other investors for pro rata — that's the easiest way to keep piling capital into your value-driving positions.

Philosophy on Fund Sizing

Most managers get overly fixated on what their fund looks like in the future, not fixated enough on what their current fund can be. Deploy the current capital as well as possible, and when you go to raise next, you'll have more optionality than otherwise.

Every raise, I ask: do we believe we can deploy more capital into the same or greater quality of companies than the previous vintage? Can we raise a larger fund without compromising the return profile? If yes → we raise accordingly.

The Biggest Mistake

Someone asked me the biggest mistake I've made since building Abstract. The answer: we've always raised our funds too small. In every single fund, I could have maintained an identical return profile with probably 2x the capital. LPs would've gotten the same return quality. From our side, we could have led more frequently rather than co-invested, improved our position within those companies, and built our name as a firm that leads later-stage financings too. The model going forward: do the best you can with the money you have, evaluate your position, raise accordingly next vintage.

Three Closing Questions

Host: Three recurring questions to end on: 1. Opportunity set 1–10 vs. your own history 2. Frothiness 1–10 3. Bellwether companies to watch

1. Opportunity Set: 10

Relative to my 10 years in venture — 10. It's not that people are funding all the best companies with huge capital — it's that people want to fund so many companies. The largest number of companies we've found we want to be investors in, relative to any vintage.

2. Frothiness: ~6.5–7

I'd call 2021 a 10. Today is maybe 6.5–7. The frothiness is there, but there's a lot to justify it — the rate of growth, adoption, and product-market fit is unprecedented, and that warrants frothiness.

3. Bellwether Companies (beyond the obvious IPO candidates)

Looking 5 years out, companies you'd want exposure to in this vintage:

  • Neuralink and Chai Discovery — very high up
  • Isomorphic — very high up (Bio: AI-native next-gen biotech — $500B to $1T+ market opportunities if they execute. Best teams, best investors, access to capital.)
  • Applied Compute — probably the pioneer and leader in the category of owning your own data, knowledge, intelligence
  • Prediction markets — the rate at which these companies are growing is insane. And they're not even AI companies — they're true consumer businesses.
  • Physical Intelligence — could be a multi-hundred-billion, trillion-dollar company. Exceptional team, huge magnet for talent, huge ability to retain talent.

What I always look for: retention of top talent. There's no shortage of talent in Silicon Valley — but retaining the highest quality is the single hardest thing. The best people at your company can get a job anywhere, probably at a higher comp and equity package. Whenever I see companies with high density of that talent and the ability to retain it, I get extra bullish.

Host: Fun three questions to end with. It'll be fun to compare in future episodes. Rampton, thanks so much.

Guest: Of course, man.

## 一个反直觉的发现：Anthropic 已经不是"创业公司"，而是一家"主权实体"
$1400 亿募集、$100 亿支出、$1320 亿静静躺在资产负债表上——这不是一张初创公司的财务表，这是一张**战略储备国家**的表。它的现金余额比瑞士 2000 年的外汇储备还大。真正值得注意的不是"烧钱有多快"，而是**烧钱有多慢**——它在做的事情，本质上是把美元换成"未来算力的看涨期权"，就像冷战时期美国囤积战略石油储备、或中国央行囤积黄金一样。这重新定义了 Ramp 描述的"神经病式恐慌性购买算力"：它不是在购买生产资料，它是**在执行货币政策**。这意味着未来 18 个月最该观察的不是 Anthropic 的收入增长，而是它的"储备释放节奏"——因为那决定了整个算力市场的利率曲线。
## "Cuck Tranche"：一个金融结构背后真正的是社会心理学
Ramp 轻描淡写地把它说成"资本密集型公司的必需"，但把它放回更大的图景：这是硅谷第一次发明出一个**"用金钱购买尊严"的金融工具**。常规的二级市场买入是信息套利；而 cuck 轮次是**身份套利**——VC 支付 3-5

item.title: [Bits + Bips] Why ICE Wants to Run Hyperliquid-Based Perps in the US
item.dc:creator: Bits + Bips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、创始人的"不安全感"：为什么 ICE 比 CME 跑得更快

Chris Perkins 不经意间说出了整个华尔街最被低估的一条规律：由创始人掌舵的交易所，天然带有"被颠覆者的创伤记忆"。Jeff Sprecher 二十多年前是用电子化颠覆了场内公开喊价的那个人——他亲手把 NYSE 吞下去，而不是被 NYSE 吞下去。所以当 Hyperliquid 冒出来时，他的本能不是起诉，而是入股。

而 CME 是一家职业经理人公司。它的 DNA 是"守成"，不是"再造"。你能看到结果：Bloomberg 报道 CME 和 ICE 两周前还联合游说监管层去查 Hyperliquid，但 ICE 一边举报一边谈股权——这不是矛盾，这是创始人式的双轨对冲。CME 则只会做前者。

一个让读者意外的推论：未来十年金融基础设施的赢家名单，会和哪家公司"还有活着的创始人"高度相关。看看纳斯达克、伦交所、港交所——没有一个是创始人在位。ICE 是西方主流交易所里唯一的例外。这不是巧合，这是幸存者偏差尚未显化的半衰期。

二、跨领域连接：ICE 正在走"迪士尼 1995"的路

大家都在把 ICE 比作交易所，但更精准的类比在娱乐业——ICE 正在复刻迈克尔·艾斯纳时代迪士尼的"全渠道收购"剧本：Polymarket（预测市场）+ OKX（加密现货）+ Trade XYZ/Hyperliquid（永续）+ NYSE（股票）+ ICE Futures（商品）。迪士尼当年买 ABC、买 ESPN、买 Pixar，不是为了"更多内容"，而是为了让同一个 IP 在不同通道里循环变现。

ICE 正在构建的不是"更大的交易所"，而是风险敞口的多模态分发网络。同一个人对特斯拉的看法，可以在 NYSE 买股票、在 ICE Futures 买期货、在 Trade XYZ 开永续、在 Polymarket 下注马斯克明年是否被罢免。四个产品，四种延迟，四种杠杆，四种税务处理——但都是同一份"观点"的原材料。

Austin 提到的那个点非常关键但没展开：OTC 市场是 ICE 唯一没拿下的大陆。而 OTC 恰恰是机构的主战场。所以真正的终局拼图，可能是 ICE 接下来会收购或入股某家做链上 RFQ 的协议——这才是"全渠道闭环"的最后一块。

三、最反直觉的洞察：永续合约是"零日期权"的终极形态

Austin 几乎说到了但没有点破：散户不是在交易期权，散户是在购买杠杆。零日期权（0DTE）在美国爆炸式增长的真相，不是因为散户突然理解了 Gamma 曲面，而是因为那是他们能合法拿到的最高杠杆。

那么从第一性原理看：永续合约是"零日期权"进化链条的终点。 - 周期权 → 日期权 → 零日期权 → 永续合约 - 每一步都在剥离"时间"这个变量，让杠杆更纯粹 - 零日期权还有 Theta 这个噪声；永续只有资金费率，而且是对称的

这意味着什么？美国的零日期权市场（CBOE 的现金牛）正站在一个结构性萎缩的悬崖边。CBOE 的 SPX 0DTE 已经占全市场期权交易量的 50%+，一旦 ICE 把 SPX 永续带到美国本土，那部分需求会以惊人的速度迁移——因为永续在"纯杠杆表达"上的用户体验优势是碾压级的。

这是为什么 CME 那么慌。 这也可能是为什么 CBOE 在这则新闻里诡异地沉默。它才是真正要被颠覆的那个，不是 CME。

四、一个被所有人忽视的伏笔

Perkins 讲了一段"商品归联邦管，证券归州管，但证券衍生品归联邦管"——听起来像枯燥的监管知识，其实埋了个巨大的套利窗口：

如果股票的永续合约（equity perps）被归类为"证券衍生品"，它就落在 CFTC 管辖下，而不是 SEC。 这意味着 ICE 可以绕开 SEC 那套为 20 世纪设计的披露框架，直接用 CFTC 更灵活的衍生品规则来运行一个事实上的"链上股票市场"。

这是一次监管套利，但是合法的——因为它本来就在法律的字面规定里。如果这条路跑通，未来美国散户买特斯拉"永续"的体验，会比买特斯拉股票更顺滑、更便宜、更快。当这件事发生时，NYSE 的现货交易量会从哪里来？

Perkins 那句"NYSE 应该被称为 ICE 旗下的 NYSE"——那不是炫技，那是预言。

📝 转录文本

Why ICE Wants to Run Hyperliquid-Based Perps in the US

开场：交易所世界的大新闻

So, ICE, the owner ICE, is taking a minority stake in Trade XYZ and will be the exclusive operator of a planned US market for 24/7 hyper liquid based perpetual futures. Stan Druckenmiller is also investing. He tweeted, "It is the clearest sign yet that on-chain perps are heading up like here in the United States."

So, what's the deal? ICE takes a minority stake. It becomes the exclusive operator of the US venue. It needs regulatory approvals. The contracts are allegedly planned across equities, indices, commodities, FX, crypto. And those markets, by the way, have already done 650 billion in volume in just over a year.

Uh Jeff Sprecher said, "We see perps markets as additive to our futures markets, not a replacement for them." Having called hyper liquid, quote, "Bigger than Nasdaq." Good shade. Uh about 2 weeks after Bloomberg reported ICE and CME urged regulators to probe it.

Um So, Stan Druckenmiller plans to use the product himself, quote, "To enhance my investment process." Uh Tim Worrall noted that Trade XYZ is 90% of all of the open interest for these types of contracts. And the bull case, Matt Hougan, said 99.9% of Americans do not even know it exists. We're just getting started.

Chris Perkins：美国终于把创新搬回岸上

So, Chris, you've been a long-time proponent of derivatives. You've been a long-time practitioner in the space. Let me start with you. American perpetuals, ICE, what does this mean?

Yeah, USA, USA. Been waiting for this for a very very long time. I testified in Congress a long time ago. I said, "We got to bring this onshore. Like, why is all the innovation happening offshore?" Finally, you're starting to see it really happening.

And so, um hat tip to the CFTC, the hard-working public servants there. Um this stuff is not easy. They're working within a defined legal framework called the Commodities and Exchange Act. They're taking leadership. See Chairman Selig out there every day. Really and I and I know the chairman quite well. This is a guy who's really focused on responsible innovation. Nobody wants to do anything that's irresponsible. But we're finally seeing innovation come on shore for the first time in decades, frankly. Prediction markets and perpetuals. Um I don't know what what I would say the last like time we've seen this amount of innovation.

颠覆性技术面前的两种选择

Um So what's interesting about it is that you're seeing partnerships. Now when you're confronted with a very disruptive technology, you can do a couple things. You can fight it—and we've seen this over and over again. Um or you can find a way to build it or partner with it.

If you look at ICE's portfolio right now, it's actually pretty interesting. They've got um Polymarket. They have the deal with OKX. And now they have the deal uh with Trade XYZ / Hyperliquid.

Jeff Sprecher 的创始人基因

So Jeff Sprecher—and I think one of the things that sets him apart is—he's a founder-led company. He founded ICE. And when you're a founder, I feel like you have um, you know, for those of us who've founded things, you have this like embedded sense of insecurity at times. It's a very positive thing because you were the disruptor once and you don't want to be disrupted.

And so I commend ICE, you know, all the team over there, Michael Tribue, um Jeff. Like they're leaning in and it's a lot of hard work. It's um it's not easy integrating big personalities, um big capabilities, but the dream is convergence.

And we've seen Hyperliquid, Trade XYZ create product market fit. Why? Because they've created interesting and really galvanized communities. Uh they've created the right incentivization mechanisms with their token. And they've also um found product market fit with markets that maybe people wouldn't touch.

And so like I love seeing this convergence. I think it's great for the rest of the space. Um you saw something similar happen with like Robinhood. It's partnering, you know, with with Lighter. So, like I love when these marriages happen, these dance partners are being picked. And uh I just think it's very very healthy for the space. Um, and for those who don't have dance partners, I think it's going to accelerate their focus on seeing who doesn't have a dance partner yet.

冷静声音：Stan 买了不代表你该买

Yeah, I like Jeff Sprecher a lot. He's an incredible CEO founder. ICE is one of the best businesses in the world. It's a great moat, great asset.

Uh a few observations. One is: because Stan Druckenmiller bought something doesn't mean you should. You know, one of the themes we liked this year that we've talked about has been hyper liquid. It's like one of the most obvious opportunities in digital assets. Uh this is now a moment where that's becoming recognized and mainstream with someone like Stan Druckenmiller buying it. It sold off like 12 points today.

Uh the other is, you know, Stan owned like Palantir. It was like a 0.1% position. He's friends with Joe Lonsdale. I met them both at an event one night. These are just like window dressing things. When Stan says something, it doesn't mean that he's endorsing an asset and you should go buy it. You know, keep your wits about you when you see these headlines. There's a story behind the story somewhere. I don't know what that story is. But um I don't think anyone of us knows that story except for Stan Druckenmiller.

Austin 追问：ICE 正在搭建"全栈市场"

I'm in. One thing I'm super interested in here though, and you guys have sort of pointed at it, is ICE going along and accumulating all of these different components of market innovation, right? You've got a spot exchange, you've got a regular way derivatives exchange, you're working with a crypto exchange, you're working with predictions markets, now you're working with a perpetual futures exchange.

Right? There are not a lot of things that are not within that stack. And most of what you're missing is now stuff that trades OTC—and I don't... over the counter for those who are not like trading people. And I don't know how sort of investable as a platform business that side of market will ever be.

And so it seems to me like what ICE is putting together here is call it the all-everything stack, as they're trying to pick all these different individual pieces up.

现货 vs 期货的核心问题

What I'm watching for is how much of market's volume moves from spot markets into futures markets. Because Chris, as you know, in derivatives world as we've seen in crypto, spot volumes and futures volumes are not the same thing, right? Like the futures actually sometimes dominate here. So, what are you expecting as this happens in US equity markets?

Perkins：衍生品才是真正统治世界的生意

First thing I find is so ironic is like every time someone talks about um ICE, they say "ICE, it's the owner of NYSE." But guys, there's like a real reason why ICE bought NYSE and not the other way around, right? It should be like, you know, "NYSE which is owned by ICE" or something. Like we should really highlight ICE because derivatives rule the world.

Um they're the most lucrative, most... um cash markets. They get squeezed is like zero when it comes to revenue across the various providers. That's very very difficult. Um you know, unless you're doing incredible volumes, that's why you're seeing that. Derivatives remain probably the most lucrative business model when it comes to any type of product. So that's a big deal.

衍生品的神圣功能：风险转移

And um yes, derivatives tend to be multiples of spot market in notional volume. Um derivatives perform a very sacred function of something called risk transfer. Um they provide foundational risk management for the markets to function because people are able to lay off risk.

They started in like uh—I'm going to get this wrong—I want to say 18th century Japan uh with rice futures. They originally started helping farmers really hedge the risk of their crops and help with pricing. You have hedgers and speculators. These markets really are foundational.

美国监管的一个关键细节

One of the issues we've had in crypto markets to date is that we've had very very few futures because, we in the US, we only have futures on commodities. Now let's just step back cuz like this is important—and because everyone's like "Clariac, oh my god, what happened, what didn't happen?"

Today, securities are regulated at the federal level. Um commodities are regulated at the state level, but derivatives on commodities are at the federal level. Those markets are so important, they make the world go round.

Austin：如果股票永续真的来了，融资市场会怎样？

So, let me volley back in another way then as we've talked about this. If we start having significant futures interest in equities, what is that going to do to transform funding markets for American companies, right? Because we're going to have sort of the similarity of the crypto where now the interest in futures probably leads the interest in spot. And you're going to have funding disparities.

零日期权的真相：散户只是想要杠杆

The reason I look at that one is: if you look at retail trading activity in the United States and you contrast call it 2002 to today, there's already significantly more zero-day options volume than there's ever been, and volatility has been driving a lot of markets.

My personal view is that for retail in particular, that's just demand for leverage. Right? I don't think they're literally trying to trade like Vega and Gamma and Theta, right? Like they're just looking for leverage.

And futures, like perpetual futures, honestly are a cleaner way to express the leverage preference because you don't have all those time decay type variables that are occurring inside of an option structure.

So, Chris, I'm curious: are we going to see options volumes move to perps? Are we going to see spot volumes move to perps? What do you expect?

Perkins：水涨船高，不是谁取代谁

Honestly, I don't think... um yeah, some people say, "Oh, perps are easier because, to your point, they are just easier to understand than all of the different Greeks that you have with options for retail." Um I don't buy that. I think that the ship's going to rise with—like all ships are going to rise with the tide.

Retail's getting much more sophisticated. I think to your point, they love the idea of leverage uh with perps and the leverage that they can get. It wasn't necessarily that easy for retail to get scalable leverage, you know, previously. But the more... retail loves yields, they love leverage. That's just what they love, right?

Um, but I also think we're seeing some projects, some options projects, even now picking up. Because retail's getting more sophisticated and I think derivatives will continue to grow. I mean, when I was in TradFi 6 years ago, like one of the... and to this day it was the sophistication of the retail markets that was one of the fastest growing demographics across markets. It remains so. It remains very exciting.

这场游戏里有输家吗？

Um, is there somebody who loses in this game? Is there a product that loses in this game? Some folks say, "Ah, it's futures because they're paying and you got to roll them all the time." I don't know. I don't know if I'd buy that. I think different strokes for different folks, different products for different um hedging strategies or even strategies around speculation, which is fine, an important part of futures markets.

I just think it's great that you're going to have more choice. Um, and I think the important thing is that the CFTC will do this. They'll make sure there's sufficient disclosures. AI also helps. "Hey, how does this product work? Can you explain it to me like I'm a fourth grader?" And you can get that output so that you can better identify. So, I just think it's good for markets—and let the markets decide. I think the CFTC will be thoughtful about how crazy you can get um and I think that they will make sure that innovation stays responsible.

节目尾声

If you liked this segment, please like, subscribe, and tune in every Monday at 4:30 p.m. Eastern time. I'm Austin Campbell, the host of Bips and Bips, along with my friends Romil Walia and Chris Perkins, and our slate of exceptional guests. Every week we're going to discuss macro, crypto, and the collision of worlds covering topics that move markets and shape the financial landscape.

One more thing, we've got a listener survey open. It takes just a few minutes, it's anonymous, and it changes what we make next. Use the QR code on screen or go to unchainedcrypto.com/survey. The link is in the show notes.

What if your crypto could do more than just sit in your wallet? Nexo is a digital assets wealth platform where you can generate daily interest on your crypto or borrow funds against your assets. Today, Nexo serves more than 10 million clients. Find out more at nexo.com.
