item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] Why Robert Caro’s Books Are So Long
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、关于那个被回避的问题

采访者问：如果回到1975年告诉年轻的卡罗这套书要花40年，他会作何反应？——卡罗根本没有回答这个问题。他立刻转向谈"被剪掉的内容"。

这个回避本身比任何回答都更有启示：卡罗的内在时间不是用"年"计量的，而是用"被迫删除的字数"计量的。对他而言，"40年"是一个空洞的外部单位，而"35万字"才是真实的创伤刻度。当一个人的心理时钟运行在"遗漏物"而非"流逝物"上时，他谈论人生的方式就必然是谈论墓地——而不是地图。

二、"影子书"：被剪掉的部分才是真正的本体

这里藏着一个让人意外的结构反转：我们以为《权力经纪人》是一本1300页的巨著；但卡罗告诉我们，这1300页只是从超过200万字的手稿里切下的一个切片。那些"没进书里的90%"并没有消失——它们在纽约历史学会的档案柜里，安静地等待被激活。

换句话说，卡罗同时在写两本书：一本是出版的书，一本是档案的书。

这让我想到一个跨领域的类比——软件工程里"源代码"和"编译后的二进制"的关系。出版的书是deployed binary，档案是source code。未来的学者可以用同一份"源代码"重新编译出不同的书：一本萨姆·雷伯恩的传记、一本更详尽的纽约城市史、一本关于参议员心理学的著作。卡罗实际上在搭建的不是一本书，而是一个可再编译的知识基础设施。

三、最隐秘的洞察：他无法不写要被剪的内容

卡罗说了一句极其关键却容易被忽略的话：

"I don't seem to have the ability not to write the stuff that I think should be written, even though I know so much of it is going to have to be cut."

明知道要被剪，却依然写下来——这不是浪费，这是他的认知机制本身。

常识认为"研究是输入，写作是输出"。但卡罗颠倒了这个顺序：写作本身就是思考发生的地方，不是思考完成之后的报告。那35万字被剪的内容，不是没用的边角料，而是让剩下那70万字能够"立住"的暗物质——像物理学里不可见的质量，却决定了可见部分的引力结构。

这解释了为什么他的书读起来有一种奇特的"厚度感"：读者感受到的，其实是他没写进去的那些东西留下的引力。

四、经济学上的反直觉决定

卡罗为了让档案留在纽约、方便人查阅，主动少拿了一大笔钱。 在一个把知识产权视为资产的时代，这是近乎异端的。他把档案当成公共基础设施——像地铁、像公园——而不是私有财产。他给出去的不是"卡罗的遗产"，而是一个开放端口，让未来的学者（他永远见不到的人）可以用他一辈子的采访稿去写他来不及写的书。

他提到雷伯恩那一刻特别动人： 他知道有一本伟大的雷伯恩传记永远不会由他来写——但他也知道，他留下的档案盒里躺着那本书的可能性。这是一种对自己有限生命的清醒接受——用档案预约未来的传记作者。

那700次采访里的人大多已不在人世。所以卡罗的档案柜里住着的不仅是他的作品，更是那些声音的来世。他不是在保存自己的工作，他是在给死者续命。

📝 转录文本

开场：一个被回避的问题

Dwarkesh： If we were able to time travel back to '75 and I could tell Robert Caro then that this new three volumes on Lyndon Johnson he's about to embark on will take more than 40 years — how do you think 40-something-year-old Robert Caro would have reacted to that? Would he have been happy? Would he have been afraid?

Caro： He asked terrific questions. Well, you know, the realization came to me when I was thinking about Johnson.

被剪掉的《权力经纪人》

You know, the power — I'll give you a long answer, but this is the accurate answer. I had to cut so much out of The Power Broker. And I cut out so much stuff that shouldn't have been cut out that I didn't like. I gave Bob Gottlieb, my editor, a manuscript that was 1,050,000 words long, and the most they could fit in — and he really worked at this — into one volume, because I was determined that it would only be one volume, was 700 pages, or about 700,000 words, instead of 1,050,000 words. Which meant we had to cut 350,000 words.

And he has said I cut a lot of the best stuff I ever read. And I felt a lot of the stuff that I cut out — it's tragic that no one knows it. To this day people ask me about things. I said, "Oh, I wrote that." Then they said, "Well, no one ever read it."

But the way I am, I don't know that I would have changed anything. Because as I'm writing the book, I'm saying, "Oh, this is too long. This is going to be too long. I'm going to have to cut so much." But I don't seem to have the ability not to write the stuff that I think should be written, even though I know so much of it is going to have to be cut.

档案柜里的另一本书

Dwarkesh： Well, speaking of which, you have in the other room here cabinets and cabinets of notes on interviews, notes as you're working, things which have never been published before. Eventually historians, other historians will be able to study those notes and those documents that you have compiled over your career.

Caro： Yes.

Dwarkesh： What is it that you hope they do with it? What kind of scholarship do you hope —

Caro： You know, I cut out so much stuff from the books that I wish people knew. Okay? I mean, sometimes you're reading something and you're saying, "Oh, if I had written about that, the newspapers wouldn't be covering it the same way — there'd be a different understanding of it."

以萨姆·雷伯恩为例

I'll give you an easy example: Sam Rayburn.

Now, I have a brief chapter on Rayburn in my books, but Rayburn is a great figure in American history. There's no good biography of Sam Rayburn. Yet he controlled — he ran the House of Representatives. He passed so many of Roosevelt's bills and other bills. He did so much for America that it's a tragedy for me that nobody knows it. And the material to know it is in those cabinets.

Okay? And there happened to be a lot of examples of things I said "whoa" — that didn't make it into the books, but they're there. Like, I have hundreds of interviews. You know, I think I have 700 interviews for The Power Broker alone. The notes for those interviews are in the file cabinets — detailed, you know, the detailed typed-up notes. So the material there — there's a lot there that I think would help people understand how New York evolved the way it did.

为什么是纽约历史学会

And with Johnson — a lot, well, I'm writing about it now — things that happened under his presidency, there's more understanding of it, and it's not going to make its way into my books, but they're going to be there. That's why I gave my archive to the New York Historical Society.

Now, I have to say: I was offered a lot more money by other places. Okay? I took a lot less money — a great deal less money, an amount that mattered a lot to me — because I wanted them to be easily accessible. I wanted them to be in New York, you know. I didn't want them to be at the University of Texas where you have to fly down there. I wanted them to be in New York.

The material is there for a lot of stuff that I never got to put in my books, but it's there if somebody wants it.

留给后来者

I'll give you an example. Uh, I wrote so much more — and I have so much — I interviewed so many senators, so many assistants to senators, to try and write about the Senate. And then I had to cut out, or not write even, go into the vast — I want to say 90%, but I don't really know what percent — of what I learned is not in the books, but they are in the file cabinets. So they're there for someone to look at. That's why my archives are in New York.

Dwarkesh： It's great to know that that research will pay dividends —

Caro： Well —

Dwarkesh： — through many generations of scholars, because obviously it will not be possible to interview the folks you interviewed in the '70s and '80s and '60s again.

Caro： Yes.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一、关于那个被回避的问题
采访者问：如果回到1975年告诉年轻的卡罗这套书要花40年，他会作何反应？——**卡罗根本没有回答这个问题**。他立刻转向谈"被剪掉的内容"。
这个回避本身比任何回答都更有启示：**卡罗的内在时间不是用"年"计量的，而是用"被迫删除的字数"计量的**。对他而言，"40年"是一个空洞的外部单位，而"35万字"才是真实的创伤刻度。当一个人的心理时钟运行在"遗漏物"而非"流逝物"上时，他谈论人生的方式就必然是谈论墓地——而不是地图。
## 二、"影子书"：被剪掉的部分才是真正的本体
这里藏着一个让人意外的结构反转：我们以为《权力经纪人》是一本1300页的巨著；但卡罗告诉我们，这1300页只是从**超过200万字的手稿里切下的一个切片**。那些"没进书里的90%"并没有消失——它们在纽约历史学会的档案柜里，安静地等待被激活。
**换句话说，卡罗同时在写两本书：一本是出版的书，一本是档案的书。**
这让我想到一个跨领域的类比——**软件工程里"源代码"和"编译后的二进制"的关系**。出版的书是deployed binary，档案是source code

item.title: [YC Root Access] The Observability Layer for the Physical World
item.dc:creator: YC Root Access
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、AI 的"非对称冲击"揭露了企业销售的一个隐秘真相

Eagle 轻描淡写地提到一个事实，但它藏着整个 AI 时代最被忽视的信号：工程师生产力提升了 100–1000 倍，而销售只提升了 30%。

大多数人把这解释成"销售工具还没成熟"。错。真正的原因是：企业采购的本质不是执行效率，而是信任交付。AI 能压缩代码、压缩分析、压缩决策推理，但它压缩不了"一个人肯把自己 100 件最贵的设备交给陌生人管"这种信任。Traction 一年飞 2500 次现场拜访，恰恰因为信任带宽的瓶颈不在"告知"，而在"在场"。

这里有一个跨领域的映射：这与医疗咨询行业拒绝被远程医疗完全替代是同一结构。两个领域共同的特征是——一旦出错，损失是非线性且不可逆的。在这种市场里，谁能把"人在场"这件事做得比竞争对手便宜，谁就赢了。Eagle 在董事会上反复论证"现场销售其实比 Google inbound 便宜"，这不是反直觉，这是信任密集型市场的一级规律。

二、两位创始人的父辈，暴露了"深度工业 AI"的一个隐藏选拔机制

Eagle 的父亲是意大利造纸厂厂长，Gabriel 的父亲在印度/英国水泥厂做了 35 年。这不是温情故事——这是一个尚未被 YC 公开的选拔算法。

一般的工业 SaaS 创业者会在产品打磨阶段崩溃。Traction 花了两年才拿到第一个客户、三年做出"minimum awesome product"——不是 MVP 而是 MAP。能撑过这两年的人，必须带着一种代际耻感或代际荣誉：你不是在解决一个市场问题，你是在修复你爸爸那一代人的不公。

这里有个非常锋利的推论：工业 AI、前沿制造 AI、能源 AI——这些需要 3+ 年才能验证 PMF 的领域——可能根本无法用"典型创业者画像"筛选。它们需要筛选"继承性动机"。这是 VC 尽调时几乎从不问的问题：你解决这个问题的个人债务是什么？Eagle 的例子说明，没有这种债务的人，大概率在第 18 个月就放弃了。

三、Nemotron + 领域本体 碾压 Fable 5，暗示了 Scaling Law 的一条隐藏裂缝

这是整场对话里最被低估、也最重要的技术信号：Traction 用 Nvidia 开源的小模型 Nemotron，叠加自己的 350,000 资产本体做 post-training，用 1/20 到 1/100 的 token 成本达到比 Fable 5 更好的结果。

主流叙事是"The Bitter Lesson"——通用计算永远赢过结构化知识。但 Eagle 无意中提供了一个反例证据：在边界清晰、本体丰富的垂直域内，Bitter Lesson 存在一个反转窗口。当一个领域积累到一定规模的结构化数据（在 Traction 这里是数百亿个传感器文件 + OEM 手册 + 服务工单），小模型 + 领域结构就能赢。

跨领域连接：这与音乐信息检索（MIR）领域的经验惊人一致。Shazam 本身就是用极小的声纹指纹 + 精心设计的匹配算法打败所有"端到端深度学习音频识别"方案的。Eagle 用 Shazam 作比喻并非偶然——他直觉上触到了同一个原则：当问题空间的"自然语法"足够清晰时，智能应该嵌入结构，而不是嵌入参数。

对投资人的启示很刺耳：如果你今天 All-in 前沿 LLM，你押的是一个赛道；但很多万亿级垂直市场的最终赢家，可能是用开源小模型+私有本体建护城河的"域内暴君"。Traction 正在变成其中一个。

四、一个几乎没人说破的二阶洞察：Traction 在"做客户的第一次 AI 体验"

Eagle 顺口提了一句"我的客户第一次接触 AI，就是通过我们的产品"。这句话值得单独拆开看。

对程序员来说，Cursor 带来的是"AI 魔法"叠加"编程能力放大"的双重奇观。Traction 对工厂厂长做的是同样的事：他第一次感受到 AI 的那一刻，也是他 50 年没解决的停机问题被解决的那一刻。

这是一种复利型的归因效应：客户会把"整个 AI 革命的震撼"都归功于你的产品。这是所有 AI-for-traditional-industry 公司的隐藏结构性优势，但只有少数人意识到它，并刻意去利用它——比如 Traction 的现场销售节奏，本质上就是在"主持仪式"而不是"讲产品"。

类比：这与 1990 年代末企业第一次接触互联网时，谁先让他们"看到网页"，谁就成了他们心中"互联网=你"的锚点。亚马逊、Salesforce、Google 都吃到了这一代红利。物理世界的 AI，现在正在打开同一个窗口。

📝 转录文本

开场

[music] Today I'm excited to be joined here by Eagle Marinelli, co-founder and CEO of Traction. Traction builds physical AI for asset-heavy industries and works with some of the biggest enterprises in the world like Eli Lilly and McKesson. Today they're announcing their Series D, which values them at $1.4 billion, and they've crossed over $100 million in ARR. So congratulations, Eagle.

Thank you.

Cool. Well, why don't we just start — give us a sense of: what exactly does Traction do? What's the product? How does it work? Just tell us a little bit about that.

Traction 做什么：物理世界的可观测性层

Yeah, for sure. We're tackling essentially the trillion dollar problem, which is machine downtime. So think about a data center, right? Everybody's talking about GPUs right now and capacity, but have you ever seen a data center, you know, I guess from a distance where you can see all this wrapper — which is, you know, from the moment that the energy is coming in, it's coming to a transformer and then getting distributed to battery packs or mega packs, and then going through chillers and then evaporators and diesel generators. So we are essentially the key monitoring infrastructure for critical assets, and we do hardware and software solutions and AI to tackle those.

By the way, if I'm building software I have observability tools, so I know kind of like if they're in the logs, if something's crashing, or if someone's visiting my website. You guys are that for the physical world.

Exactly. So within the 500 largest industrial operations today, it's sort of estimated that 11% of their revenue is blocked. So it's the cost of opportunity — which is $1.4 trillion in industrial GDP — that is essentially blocked because assets like chillers, HVAC… think about what's cooling this room right now. It's probably somewhere in the ceiling here. This could also be monitored by Traction. And so what we do essentially: we guarantee 100% capacity and availability for that physical asset.

And what exactly is the product? Is it hardware? Is it software? Just help us understand kind of what exactly…

产品的三层：硬件、AI、LLM 上下文

So I like to think — you've mentioned two of our customers. Think about Mounjaro for a second, which is this miraculous drug. The moment that Mounjaro is being manufactured — apart from Mounjaro's raw formula, which is sort of trade secret — it needs compressed air to be manufactured, it needs palletizer robotic arms to continue along the journey of the line. So you think about these pieces, and the reason why they fail is essentially three main things.

It is a mechanical reason — the robotic arm couldn't actually work properly, and then it caused downtime because one of the joints was not lubricated correctly. So we've identified that.

But it could also be the second reason, which is electrical — there was a discharge or a surcharge that essentially led to one of the electrical components to burn out. So we also identify that before it happens.

Or it could be an operational reason — an operator went there and kicked the thing, kicked the box, and now the palletizer is not doing its thing properly. And we also have ways to identify these.

So it starts with proprietary hardware essentially — we have vibration, ultrasound, magnetic field, current sensors that are beautifully designed and non-invasive, but they are there for the purpose of collecting that data. And then that data gets transferred to our AI, which has a bunch of deterministic properties like Shazam. We are decompounding this analog data and assessing what is the actual condition that is happening with this asset — just like Shazam is trying to assess if you're hearing Metallica or Guns N' Roses.

And then later on, other models are going to try to assess, based on the music that's playing, what is the volume — is it critical, should I go there right now, can it wait? And that is the moment that we make the use of course of post-trained LLM, because then you need context: you need the manual data sheet of that asset, you need the PDF from the OEM (the Original Equipment Manufacturer), you need a layer of memory. Because what's critical for you may not be critical for another type of factory or another type of user.

And presumably every factory is almost like it's its own system. So it's probably got its own history and environment and context that's specific to that factory or plant.

It's very, very, very sophisticated, but in its nature it's doing a very simple thing: providing information for our key users. Information ahead of time. And you need all of this stuff in order to make that happen.

回到 2021：YC 时期的原始形态

Cool. Well, you're doing it at significant scale now. These are some of the biggest plants and physical locations in the world, and you're doing it at more scale than anybody else at the moment. But if we rewind a little bit — when you went through YC in 2021, what was the original idea? Where did it all begin?

Yeah. So first we applied and I think we were — oh no — we were zero in revenue. For those that don't know, I believe in winter of '21 was our second application.

Okay. It's the first one I saw.

Yes. And in reality, it's the first application. In order to sum up all those parts, it really took a lot of time for us just in order to test product market fit. I remember you mentioned to me once — and it's real up until now — like, "Eager, you're not going to be able to deal with an MVP, a minimum viable product. It has to be a minimum awesome product."

Yeah.

Because in order to test that, you're going to have to build your own hardware, and then you're going to have to build your own software, and then you're going to have to build your own AI. So it sort of had always had a high ceiling in order to cross that.

Because it's real machinery, it's real stuff, it's expensive. And yeah, I remember this conversation — you can't have something like, "oh, we missed it," and ever expect to get the trust back with that customer.

Yeah. And with that, it truly came essentially a little bit of the chicken-and-the-egg process in the beginning of sales, especially because in order for the system to work, it has to have a lot of data. In order to have a lot of data, everything has to be ready. And in order for everything to be ready, a customer needs to trust us that like, "okay, I'm going to give you my 100 most precious pieces of equipment, and it's now run by Traction."

So that whole process gave us a lot of gray hair for sure. And YC truly was the first believer, but in order for that to be accomplished, it has taken us like two years since foundation in order to have your "yes."

Right.

And so we were moving every piece that we possibly could to have the product as much ready as possible — and that was generally done by founders because we were all technical founders. When in fact my first hire was actually an SDR — sales development — because we thought, well, we can do all this stuff, we're computer engineers, we're going to figure it out, but we need someone to sell. Because in our industry, one thing has to run in parallel with the other. So we were also generating pipeline from day zero.

创始故事：父亲的工厂

So usually with this type of idea, where the bar to entry is high because the product needs to be quite good on day one, and it can take a couple of years to really perfect it — founders need very high conviction. Certainly higher conviction than something you can sort of board over a weekend and rapidly iterate on. So maybe tell us a little bit about how you came up with this idea? What was the founding story and what gave you such conviction and attachment to solving it?

Yeah. It was a combination of two things. The first one is that I've seen my father struggling with that.

Yeah, tell us more. It was a fascinating story.

Throughout his whole career, he was a plant manager of a paper manufacturing facility. And not only would I not see him very often, he would also complain a lot about the technologies that he was using at that time. And at the same time, my co-founder's father sort of lived the same thing, where he worked like 35 years in this cement factory. So the first thing that's fascinated — from India to England, I think I've talked about this — but yeah, they both… like the only jobs available for immigrants in that era were really machine operators in factories. So my dad worked in the same paint factory for almost 40 years, something like that, and my mom in like a plastics factory putting together components.

Yeah, definitely.

So you know, my family came from Italy, and essentially manufacturing was — and still is — how you build this very structured middle class, which was my upbringing. But that was it. This is sort of where I grew up, seeing his struggles.

And then when we got together — Traction has a very different story than other companies, in a sense that in the day that we started the company, which was September 2019, I remember I bought 40 domains online. So like traction.com, .mx, .de, .jp — didn't buy China.

And who is "we"? That's funny. Who is "we" at this point?

It was me and Gabriel essentially. So that's the thing — we had a problem idea, where we'd seen that machine downtime was a big problem. We couldn't really research a lot of attempts prior to what we were doing. It's not that nobody has ever tried, but nobody has truly ever tried successfully. So it was this huge wide space — and a problem that we were familiar with — and the butterflies in the stomach on day one, and sort of like: okay, from now on we're going to have to figure out what is the proper solution.

So I say it's different in that sense — that truly, on day one, two or three, we were still thinking how are we going to solve this problem. So I visited essentially 88 facilities in the first year. I was just on the road a lot, on the airplane a lot, talking with dozens of —

Customer discovery, basically.

现场销售：2500 次 on-site 的哲学

Exactly. And on-site is still a DNA of our sales culture up to nowadays. Just last year we did 2,500 on-sites — which actually, I've come to the conclusion after fighting in multiple board meetings, that look: it is actually cheaper than marketing. Take a look at the growing cost of inbound coming from Google, and a Hertz car rental and flight and hotel — when you sum it all up, you can move that deal to a point that you've already surprised the customer that you're there, that you're mapping their struggles.

And we do this thing which is a risk assessment. So we are going to do the job for you in mapping your whole facility and say, "hey, here's the opportunity, here's the assets that need observability and this is the asset protection that you're going to need," and so on and so forth.

You basically do a bunch of work up front during the sales process for them.

Exactly.

客户发现：避开"泛化"，深耕"本体"

Cool. Okay, then let's definitely come back to the sales process, because I think you guys have interesting insights there. On the customer discovery front — you're going to these factories and manufacturing plants in person. How are you approaching that? Something I'm always curious about with founders: did you have in mind "I'm going to pitch them on this solution and see how they respond," or were you just observing? What was your process for figuring out the right way to get use out of those visits?

So I've always tried to validate if there are problems in different segments. What are the sort of overlaps that I can find from a pharmaceutical line, to a food and beverage facility, to a paper production facility? So when I was going on this expedition, the thought has always been: I'm teeing up all these problems because you're showing up, right? And I imagine even nowadays, showing up with AI in a very rigid environment — you're sort of showing up as a little bit of, "this guy is going to help us tackle all our problems" — but it's up to you to sort of define the lane of how much are you going to solve.

And we've always tried to avoid generalism in the solution and go as much as in-depth in compounding: if we solve this problem for this person, is it the same domain of that other customer and that other customer? That has always been our approach — to a point that we were resisting adjacencies. So if you think about Traction today, we're very domain-specific in that realm. Which is weird because we're sector-agnostic too, but just because we have the privilege that an HVAC — it's the same equipment for domestic use that it is for industrial use. So the segment array is huge, but we've decided to focus on that specific bay.

第一个客户：液压泵厂

You go in, you're learning about and trying to map the problems between customers. Do you remember who your first customer was? How did you convince them to trust you, and what was the process of getting up and running with them?

I do. I do. They are our customers up to nowadays.

Oh wow. Okay. Cool. What was it?

They are this hydraulic pump manufacturing facility. And I do remember because I've been there multiple times. But what's funny is, I remember at that time I had an SDR that I had already hired, a sales engineer that I had already hired, and an implementation engineer that was with me as well.

So like, how much are you guys investing today? Is it like $500K per company?

At my time, it was like $125K. Right. But I've used every dollar in hiring — every dollar went towards personnel. Because what I've noticed in enterprise sales is that some founders are doing founder-selling for so long, but without any support. You enter their website, there's their Calendly for you to book, and then you talk with them on the first stage, second stage, third stage. But enterprise customers — they want to see that robustness from the get-go. They want to look at your LinkedIn and see that rise in employee count. All of that is kind of important so that you can open that first door.

I think my best application as a founder — I consider myself a solutions engineer. In order to generate demand, there's no surprise. It's scientific at this point. In order for you to generate leads, in order for you to have that first sales call, you're going to follow a script. There are multiple methodologies, but you have to come in in crucial moments where it is truly the verge of sales and product, and there's that gap that you're filling. So I was doing that. It wasn't easy though, even with that sort of army of people of like four people.

In that army.

[laughter]

Did your first customer come through your SDR, or did you find…

We hunt. We went there. We cold-called. Right. So that was from day one. We are still calling, emailing, but it came from our outbound.

And how did you convince them? How do you convince this hydraulic pump company to trust this four-person startup?

付费试点，而不是免费试用

Yeah. So throughout that whole process — which was long, it was tedious — they're trying to also gather social proof. We're talking about the first customer, so you're not —

So bear with me.

But they're like, "that's very interesting. What are the other customers that are also utilizing the solution?"

Yeah.

"And can I talk with them?" So it's that whole dance when you don't have that. Generally the next idea that comes in is a trial. "Since you've lacked a way to provide the social proof, we now need to try the solution." That doesn't happen with me.

Within the way that we've designed our technology — imagine, I've always told my customers: "hey, you've been there for how long? The last 50 years, you're producing the same thing, and you're probably going to produce the same thing for the next 50." So it is not really the trial that moves the needle. You have to gather commitment from one side in order to also move resources on the other side. So I much rather prefer the term pilot — or paid trial — but it has to have commitment from both angles. Because it's not a lack of money on their side; it is truly just: "is this something that will work as intended and is applicable for my situation?"

So we definitely leveraged a lot of those paid pilot programs in the beginning. And that gave us room to breathe on, "look, we're not going to do anything for free. This is expensive, and you also have a huge problem to solve." And that's how we gathered that first.

成功标准：共同行动计划

And it clearly went successfully. But how did you define the conditions for success when you're doing those paid pilot conversations? How specific were you about "this is what we can deliver, and if we do this pilot, will you convert or renew"?

Very specific. You have to have success criteria and sort of like mutual action plans that even the customer can sign off on. It's a shared document between you and them. This is absolutely crucial. Because if you cannot get the answer from them on the questions that you're asking — for example, "hey, we came in here, we're going to start with 30% of your critical assets; if this works, given this performance criteria and SLA condition, and also the look and feel of the platform (it has to be an amazing experience for you) — given these conditions, where are we going to go? Are we now a long-term partner? Are we now going from 30% to 60% to 90% deployment?"

Customers that are unable to answer that — that has always been a yellow flag for me. And reality is, we've let a lot of those go too. And you can't really have this type of customer when you're just starting your company, because it can basically kill your company. Salespeople will say, "oh my god, but you have to hug that pipeline and not let them go."

Yeah.

But you truly have to move a huge bucket to "lost" so that you can focus on those that are giving you commitment. Maybe not as you expected or not ideal, but like, "okay, if this works and so and so, I will commit to going from 30 to 50% deployment." That's something. Otherwise they're just shopping around. They are some sort of sommelier of good enterprise solutions, and you don't need those.

And a real waste of founder time.

Yeah, bad waste of founder time.

AI 的到来：从 autopilot 到 copilot

If we fast-forward — this period you're getting your first customer and growing the business. This was early days, pre-AI, pre-ChatGPT. And then AI came in. It seems to have been a huge boost for your business. Maybe talk us through what changed as these models started taking off, and how did that affect your business, and how did you adapt as a founder?

When GPT more specifically came out, we started thinking: how do we go from a complete deterministic set of artificial intelligence that we had at that time — it was neural network technology, in the same way that radiologists use. We turned our key users from general practitioners to radiologists. They were doing this: "now we can tell what's wrong with the X-ray."

What AI allowed was truly the aha moment. It was always the missing link: "okay, we're that prescriptive, but how do we intake their experience, their context, their feedback, their knowledge of a machine that we don't have into our solution?" So we jumped very quickly on that — almost like, I guess, an idealistic attempt to be the autopilot for our customers — to very quickly shifting to a co-pilot. Essentially going from the position of "we're here for you and this is the amazing stuff that you can do with our technology," and then our customers went on being a part of it to really owning the technology.

自建后训练：Nemotron vs Fable 5

So then quickly we started buying Nvidia GPUs. Yeah, we have a bunch of those. Started doing different tests of pre-training, post-training. Because reality is like, we have this huge ontology which in our case is very valuable and very domain-specific. It's 350,000 assets that we're powering, just ingesting data every single day.

In real time right now, right?

And then the billions of files that we have — from the technical specifications, from this ontology that our customers are uploading, within their service orders, within their different data sheets and applications and digital twins of how is that real operation and how's it working.

I remember seeing a lot of Palantir's technology too. And the insight came when they also started using Nemotron, which was basically Nvidia's open source model. They were a little bit mocked in the beginning — like, "it's kind of not possible that you use such a small model with your ontology and you produce better results than Claude Fable 5." But it's truly fascinating when you get that and you start post-training on your specific ontology for specific tasks within your domain, and what you can do with it.

Let's actually go into that. You're also post-training on top of Nemotron — what are the results you see that your customers couldn't get if they were just calling, or maybe you couldn't get if you were just calling the latest Fable or Astra, one of the frontier models?

Yeah. So the first thing is: if you're trying to do the same thing with the latest state-of-the-art — so get Fable 5 right now — we've run different benchmarks to always try to assess: can they do the same thing, and if yes, at what cost?

Yeah.

So there's two dimensions to this. And reality is Fable 5 is the closest. So it can basically execute 85% of what our models can reach to the same conclusion. But then the token consumption is basically 20 to 100x still, to get to that same conclusion.

Which is huge for you guys, because the whole point is you need to know a second before a machine has any issues — which means you need to be consuming data 24/7, every minute of the day. So cost must be a huge factor.

And then it comes the second portion too, which is — after post-training with the open source models, the harness is very important as well. Because there are different technologies that you can do instead of just reasoning and reasoning and reasoning with tokens. You can use this array of tools, which are still deterministic, right? Because you are looking at something that is within your domain, and you don't need a lot of guessing game just to get to 50% of it.

But what we do then: we also test with humans. Which I think is important. So we always run the test — get the best PhD in mechanical engineering, and they're looking at this asset data, they're looking at this ultrasonic/thermography picture, and everything that's available, that's also available for our model. They're looking at everything and trying to assess what's wrong with the asset. So we do this reverse test as well. And it's sort of like this step: a PhD in mechanical engineering is generally 40–45% right, with all the time in the world, no time expiration. Then a Claude Fable 5 can get to 85% with 100 times the cost. And we can get to 100% essentially.

In the moment that they launch a next model, we're also retraining on a new model of the open source model, and so on so forth. So it is compounding. And I think that's the one piece.

本地部署与数据主权

The second piece is: we also have a lot of customers that are on-premise.

Yeah, they don't want the data leaving their facilities or their cloud.

So it is kind of not popular to say that we deploy on-premise. But on-premise is one of the most beautiful things that's still available for everybody — and it is modern still. Because even if it's in the cloud — so it could be in my cloud, it could be in the customer's cloud, or it could be on-premise, bare metal — the best design for the sort of enterprise application systems. You know, the really traditional SaaS, which is like your data here and it's shared with everybody and so on — it goes just up to a certain point. Enterprise buyers, they want to say, "hey, give me the latest model that you have that you've already trained with everybody's data (which is anonymized etc etc) — but from here on out, I want this to only compound with my own data."

Yeah. Huge companies want to own their own intelligence.

And by the way, we're telling you this as a very cool story right now, but I remember one of the decisions very clearly with our CTO at that time was: this ontology that we're compounding — why are we sending to Anthropic? Why are we sending to OpenAI?

Yeah.

I remember even going to their privacy page and like, "can I really switch off?" And the reality is like, there isn't a way that you can be sure that that PDF that you're sending is not going to be used for their own training and so on so forth. So you also want that domain to stay there.

AI 还缺什么：界面、工人、生产力的非对称

Since you have this really unique position of AI deployed in the real world and real facilities — where do you still see gaps in AI, and where are you excited for it to improve, or for you guys to improve it so you can deliver even more to your customers?

It is changing the way people work. Even our employees — now they have this army of agents doing things for them. Bookkeeping, accounting, and so on. Even tech workers truly — like they were all sort of born and raised already with internet in their hands — are sort of like, "okay, I have all this power in the world, and how do I use it?" And you want to actually measure: "have I truly become more and more productive with that?"

So I think it's the format that this is still embedded. There's a lot of improvements that are still going to happen there. What is the best way to interact with it? Is it a bot with a face of a real person? Is it embedded in the systems? Once we actually solve the medium to which we're delivering this information, things are going to get much more clear.

In the case of our customers, what's interesting about this is: there is labor shortage in our market. In manufacturing in general. It is already extremely hard to hire.

It's not exactly hard to hire for startups the way it is hard to hire for manufacturing. Yeah.

Right. So that thing is coming from them, and it's coming with so much ease, because what this is allowing them to do — they could already not hire. They're also not firing, because those employees are extremely crucial. But now, one employee — I was talking with one of our customers — can this one employee that was just regional to this one facility also control and operate that other facility that he's not locally there? That is the next leap that this technology is allowing them to do.

For our own company, what's interesting is the balance between sales and engineering. I didn't think I would see engineers face the results of their work coming at them more aggressively than salespeople. Everybody thought like, "look, we're now going to buy from these AI bots." It's just not happening. Engineers on a scale of productivity are getting 100 to 1,000 more productive. I don't recall the last time we hired an engineer, because we keep reviewing the headcount plan and keep pushing it forward. But sales — we're still hiring. Then maybe they got 30% more productive, but customers want to buy from people.

Yeah, that makes sense.

And that transaction — the nature of that transaction — is also not changing. But your back office is changing.

机器人与多厂商设备的异构世界

I mean, something else I'm thinking about now — you've just been through this big boost from GPT, transformer models coming out. At YC, it seems to us like there's a lot of excitement around robots. And AI in the real world definitely becomes more exciting. I'm curious — in your world working with asset-heavy industries and customers, as there are more robots in the space and more automation, more smart machinery — how do you see that impacting your business and the opportunities it opens up?

We're very excited with robotics. I think what companies are solving in robotics — in our AI labs we have the Boston Dynamics quadrupeds.

In your own AI lab at Traction you're working on this kind of stuff? That's cool.

Yes, we're working and dispatching them automatically in our own model, controlling their own hardware essentially and what they're going to look at. Again, we have the ontology, so we know exactly what they need to scan in that specific asset. It's very cool.

So this future is happening at a lab scenario already. The only reason it's not happening at the customer — they're just not buying it.

Yeah.

It's the price tag still. We bought the quadrupeds — the Spots — at $100K every dog, and then we put a bunch of instruments on top, which are essentially the Traction gear on top. And then by the time it's a final product, you get to a range of $200K to $300K.

So either there's going to be a more exponential price decrease in the quadruped world, or — which we're also experimenting — drone inspection, which in its nature is cheaper. It can carry just one gear, but at the same time it's nimble, it's fast, and all of a sudden all of those barriers of just transporting the thing are also out. So I think we're very, very bullish on that.

And the thing about operations in general — this has always been happening. You get into any physical plant right now, what you're going to see is an array of different equipment providers. So you're going to have Siemens, Bosch, Schneider, which are not very good at talking to each other, by design. And then you're going to see different robotic arm brands as well. And you're going to see different ages — so you can have an HVAC from 24 years ago, 15 years ago, and five years ago that was manufactured. And all of them, they have different protocols and different things that they carry.

So we've got specialized at homogenizing all of that into one single platform. And hardware is the answer as well for that. Essentially what we do: no matter if you have shadow spots that are not covered, no matter if you have a machine that's partially covered, or a machine that's like, "oh, this is the Ferrari of robots" — but at the same time it needs to be in that same place that you have your other equipment. That is where we believe that we play like a very, very sort of white-card mentality into the space.

护城河：知道"完美运行状态"

When you think about your moats or advantages in this world — is it the fact that you've already got these relationships and your hardware is installed at all of these customers and facilities? Is it the data you've collected from that? It's probably both, but how do you think about that — because physical AI is really just starting to have its moment and take off?

It is that we know the best on how to operate and balance assets in all the genres that's there and available in plants across the world. Our models are that close from operating the asset. Because if you think about what we do essentially — in its nature, it's ensuring capacity in the domain of: if it's a transformer, we're ensuring capacity of electricity; if it's a chiller, we're ensuring capacity of chilled water; if it's an air compressor, of compressed air; if it's a gas compressor, gas.

So what we are ensuring essentially are the consumables that are powering something. Those consumables are then going to cool a GPU — and that is out of our domain. But when they're back, this is within our domain.

Right.

So we're not messing with the GPUs of a data center; that is proprietary technology of someone else. But they need someone for that infrastructure of cooling to go back and forth. For as long as we know what is the perfect operating condition of that, then we can put that on autopilot. And we can do that at scale as well.

And futurally speaking, then dispatch a human, a robot to go there, and correct what's wrong ahead of time, so that there is no unplanned downtime in the foreseeable future essentially.

Yeah, that's interesting. I hadn't thought of it that way actually. You basically start by just logging and monitoring and knowing everything that's going on, but then as the technology improves, it does more than just alert you when something's wrong — it knows what to do, and then in the future it can actually just go in and fix the thing and operate the entire facility. That's kind of exciting.

We know to the level of, in specific air compressors: if you swap a bearing from manufacturer A to manufacturer B, you're going to get more compressed air with the same electricity. So we know to the level of the mechanical design of the asset, to the electrical design, and the operational design.

融资之旅：从 125K 到 Series D

Eagle, congratulations on closing the Series D. That's a huge milestone. LFG.

[laughter] Let's do it.

Something I'm just curious about — so much of the audience here is aspiring founders. How does fundraising change as you go from getting into YC, to raising a seed round, a Series A?

It gets harder.

Yeah, really interesting. Okay, tell us more. What's how does it feel different?

There are so many different angles that you can look at a company. We crossed $100 million of ARR.

Congratulations.

It feels kind of a big number. We've done it in seven years, but new companies now are doing it in weeks.

Annualizing in weeks.

[laughter] Definitely. Jokes apart, we're extremely happy with that — just with the nature of the way we distribute products, the way we get to customers. We have this field sales combined with the way a tech company operates, which makes Traction very unique in that sense.

But fundraising — it goes through a process and a journey. In the beginning, it's about the founders, it's about the market. And execution — you tell me the third thing, this is your specialty essentially. So definitely, I look at my first angel investors and I ask, "what was wrong with you guys?" [laughter] When you look at the first versions of the pitch deck, I would have never invested. "You guys are completely out of your mind." But you were feeling something special about the founder. You were in certain ways also truly fact-checking: can this person walk the talk? Can they hit their milestones? It's sort of a very intuitive journey on an individual level.

Very much.

And then as the company grows, you have to keep reminding investors: "hey, it is still about the people that's here." And that's how we've been getting there and how we'll continue to get there. Otherwise, they would definitely be like spreadsheet investors — which is characteristic of late-stage investors. Spreadsheets after spreadsheets after financial calls. And yes, great numbers tell a story, but we're still building this, and we don't plan to go anywhere. We plan to build this for the next 15 years plus. Which is my mentality. It has always been long-term.

What's characteristic for me, I think, is I've been more of a founder of quality over quantity. Definitely I've always wanted to make sure that quality is in there, but when it's in there, then we double down on that. So it's changing. It's different every time. I think it doesn't compare with the feeling of receiving that $125K. [laughter] Nobody can beat that, right? But it is also special in its own ways.

从 1.4B 到 14B：飞轮已经启动

And so now the company is worth $1.4 billion. What kind of has to happen or what has to be true over the next few years for it to 10x, for it to be worth $14 billion or more?

What is happening right now that we are already seeing: when you get to a certain size, there is an interesting power law that starts happening within the funds that you're bringing and the customers and the company. You have like a flywheel effect essentially. That's what we're feeling right now. We have funds that invest in Traction that also own and operate data centers that we're in — and then it comes back here. So it's that serendipity that ends up happening.

In the beginning, it felt like an overkill. Customers would also say that in different ways — they would quickly recognize, "it didn't take long for them to say, Traction is so far ahead from the nearest competitor." Which in underserved markets tends to be the case. When we have 100 patents and we keep publishing patents, it felt like: is it an overkill? Because we were essentially talking with customers and then building products that we ourselves would like to use — always with that originality of "we can solve problems one way, which is solving it, but then the other way, which is solving it for us if we were there."

So we've always been doing that, and which kind of felt like an overkill. But now as we were also able to establish multi-million-dollar contracts and talking with customers that have that high-tech mentality, now we're seeing: "oh, that's very interesting — because the way that they choose their next technology is not only based on what's available, but based on where they're going, and if you can meet their velocity too."

愿景：压缩时间，让工人 5 点回家

Cool. And then maybe just to close down and bring this full circle — this journey, a lot of it started with your personal story, your father, his experience as a plant manager. When you look forward, if Traction fulfills this vision and it works and it scales, how do the lives and the jobs of your customers change over the future? What becomes new for them?

I think what we're doing — we're compressing time in such a way that: think about this, for the majority of our customers, the first time ever that they're using AI is when they're using our solutions. So think about the magical moment of a programmer looking at Cursor and just like, "wow, what is this?" And so we get to almost double-stack that magic and compress time in a way of: "I had no idea this even existed, and this is what I am capable of doing as an individual."

So there is the individual sense of: they get to come home at 5:00 p.m. — which for me is key for my customers. They have that predictability which my father didn't have. Like weekends at work, burning the midnight oil, all of that. Which is always related to a piece of something that's failing that they didn't have any knowledge of.

And as a bonus as well, we get to save billions of dollars in measurable economic impact for our customers. Like I have in my email signature a savings counter of Traction to customers, which is right now at $1.2 billion.

Wow.

Our dream is to get to $1.4 trillion. It's just 1,000x. [laughter]

So I love the fact that we can measure it so simple. You have all these incentives aligning — from the personal motivation of getting better conditions for frontline workers, to also the economical motivations: this has to produce, and it is producing. Some customers are reporting, for example, one gigawatt of savings in energy, millions of gallons of water that were saved. So it is measurable, but at the same time, at an individual level too, it's very satisfying.

结语

Cool. Okay, well, that's an empowering vision for the future. I think that's all we have time for today. Eagle, thanks so much for being here with us, sharing the story, and congratulations on the round. We're excited to see Traction go from strength to strength.

Thanks for inviting me.

[music]

item.description:
## 一、AI 的"非对称冲击"揭露了企业销售的一个隐秘真相
Eagle 轻描淡写地提到一个事实，但它藏着整个 AI 时代最被忽视的信号：**工程师生产力提升了 100–1000 倍，而销售只提升了 30%**。
大多数人把这解释成"销售工具还没成熟"。错。真正的原因是：**企业采购的本质不是执行效率，而是信任交付**。AI 能压缩代码、压缩分析、压缩决策推理，但它压缩不了"一个人肯把自己 100 件最贵的设备交给陌生人管"这种信任。Traction 一年飞 2500 次现场拜访，恰恰因为信任带宽的瓶颈不在"告知"，而在"在场"。
这里有一个跨领域的映射：这与**医疗咨询行业拒绝被远程医疗完全替代**是同一结构。两个领域共同的特征是——一旦出错，损失是**非线性且不可逆**的。在这种市场里，谁能把"人在场"这件事做得比竞争对手便宜，谁就赢了。Eagle 在董事会上反复论证"现场销售其实比 Google inbound 便宜"，这不是反直觉，这是信任密集型市场的一级规律。
## 二、两位创始人的父辈，暴露了"深度工业 AI"的一个隐藏选拔机制
Eagle 的父亲是意大利造纸厂厂

item.title: [GoldRepublic Global] Why Governments Could Come for Your Gold | Dr. Mark Thornton
item.dc:creator: GoldRepublic Global
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"临时"的永恒——一个被忽略的语言学时间陷阱

Thornton 轻描淡写地丢出一个足以让人脊背发凉的事实：1971 年尼克松关闭黄金窗口，在美国法律文本中至今仍是"临时措施"——55 年的"临时"。这不是官僚的粗心，而是一种精密的语言学机制：用"temporary"这个词冻结社会的决策终结感，与认知心理学中的损失厌恶和锚定效应深度耦合。一旦某状态被框定为临时，社会就停止规划替代方案，而政府得以永久保留该状态。

更令人意外的是：荷兰正在讨论的"对实物黄金课以更高税率、鼓励持有 ETF"的提案，本质上是把 Thaler 与 Sunstein 的助推理论（Nudge Theory）反向武器化——行为经济学原本被用来"温柔地"帮助公民做出更好决策，如今却被用来温柔地把公民赶进一个未来可被按键没收的资产形态。这是行为经济学的黑暗镜像。

二、债券奇点 vs AI 奇点——两条指数曲线共享同一个萎缩的储蓄池

Luke Groman 的"bond singularity before AI singularity"被 Thornton 放大，但对话中隐藏了一个更深层的系统性矛盾：AI 的资本支出与各国国债的滚动再融资，正在竞争同一个被人口老龄化不断萎缩的全球储蓄池。两个资本饥渴的巨兽正在用同一种叙事——"未来生产力"——融资：AI 需要物理基建（数据中心），政府需要金融基建（国债续作）。

这里有个跨领域连接点值得深究：人口学是生物学硬约束，不听金融叙事。婴儿潮一代开始从储蓄池中提取而不是贡献，这个曲线一旦越过交叉点，任何"美联储控制收益率曲线"的叙事都会撞上生物钟。真正的黑天鹅可能不是 AI 泡沫先破或主权债先崩，而是两者在 2027-2030 年间同时触碰到那堵墙。

三、央行讲话的"语义层"——当提示工程成为货币政策

Thornton 顺口提到一个几乎没人在意的细节：Fed 主席候选人 Kevin Warsh 在 Jackson Hole 讲话中反复使用 "hike" 一词，表面是指他在怀俄明山里徒步的双关；但他和特朗普都清楚——算法交易系统会抓取这个词。这个一闪而过的片段揭示了前所未见的金融语言学层级：

在 LLM 驱动的交易系统时代，央行语言不再是对人类的沟通，而是对机器神经网络的提示工程（prompt injection）。

这里产生了一个意想不到的跨领域连接：Lakoff 的框架理论 × 算法交易 × 奥派货币学。贝森特用 89 亿美元"做庄"长期国债的行为，用传统货币学指标看毫无意义（相对于国债存量是沧海一粟），但用语义干预视角看就完全合理——它不是数字够大，而是制造了一个可被算法索引的信号事件。货币政策正在变成一种昂贵的广告学。

四、意外的认识论反转——奥派比凯派更"后现代"

We don't have the resources in the US. We're running low on ammunition. Our military is not very productive. If we got into a real fight, they would need to suck in an enormous amount of resources to carry on something like that, which is almost unimaginable. It is unimaginable for the European economies. Maybe not so much for China. Obviously Russia is ready and able to fight. But the American-European side is not, and they might very well resort to taking the money that's in the ETFs. That would be the simplest, easiest, largest grab of gold.

The Chinese are obviously ready to take that. They have their central bank, their government, their military hoarding gold. They have their insurance companies hoarding gold. They have their population — they've given them the incentive to save their money in gold. So they're ready. I'm not sure if they will be the first to do it, but they are definitely ready. Russia has a bunch of gold.

We certainly wouldn't want to discount the possibility of the US and European countries going after the ETFs — and potentially even individual holdings of gold and silver. In the future it's uncertain. It's going to depend on a lot of other things coming to pass. When I speak of risks, I don't know if any of this stuff is going to come to pass for sure, or when it's going to come, or what the probability of it coming about is going to be. But they are apparent risks — and there are many of them — and they are much more of a short-term orientation to us today than I've ever seen.

Alex: I had a conversation on my German-speaking channel the other day with Dimitri Speck, and he said: well, the moment where the governments are proceeding with confiscation, it's game over. It's the moment where everything will crumble down, because this will be the last gasp for air — seen as an ultra-desperate act, the total loss of confidence in everything.

Mark: We're headed in the direction of hyperinflation. The governments are going to see gold holdings and silver holdings as something to tap into. A bigger hurdle than, for example, tapping into the strategic oil reserves — which has been going on in the Western countries this past year, because they controlled that. But they'll find ways, if necessary, to tap into this. That really brings into question the amount of uncertainty that governments are willing to impose on people, and that people will tolerate. At that point, you're in a very difficult position. You don't have a lot of traditional alternatives to deal with the situation.

Obviously, they've cut off Bitcoin and crypto at the knees. That's not going to be a viable alternative to any great extent, as far as my understanding. And then the stablecoins — they're all wrapped up in government paper money. So, yeah, they know what they're doing. They know what they're working for. And it's not to the great benefit of mankind. It's really to the benefit of politicians, interest groups, and their ideology.

The Netherlands Signal: Taxing Physical Gold, Nudging into ETFs

Alex: We've seen kind of the first signs where it's the opposite — with what I mentioned about the ETF and the physical. Here in the Netherlands, the parliament is looking to reform the way they tax certain assets. One of those assets is obviously physical gold and paper gold. In this new proposal — today's news said that the supervisory entity is looking to see if this proposal is even compliant — they plan to tax physical gold more than ETFs, meaning they want to create a disincentive to own physical gold, pushing people into gold ETFs so that, just as you mentioned, it will be just a snap of a button to be able to confiscate it in a much easier way than actually having physical gold. We're seeing already some premises where one could say, "Oh, this is a very paranoid take on the situation." But considering all the context and the world we're living in, it's pretty plausible that we might see more and more governments taking such actions.

Mark: That's an invitation where they're telling you: you should invest in electronic funds of gold instead of personally held gold — which gives them the option of just confiscating it. Of course, they would never call it confiscation. Like in a European war scenario, they would say: "Well, we're just borrowing the gold right now because our currency is under stress, and if we use the gold now, we won't put as much stress on the currency, so prices won't go up. This is just temporary. It's really going to prevent prices from rising, because if we had to use our currency, borrow and so forth, it would cause higher prices. So we're going to benefit people by borrowing the gold temporarily, and then once we win the war, we'll just buy the gold back and refill your accounts."

Well, going off the gold standard in the United States on August 15th, 1971 — that's still on the books as a temporary measure. Okay? It's still a temporary measure. When Roosevelt stole everybody's gold during the 1930s, they've never gotten their gold back. We've gone through, obviously, a significant demonetization of our system in favor of just paper currency rather than any form of money. They'll come up with a reason. It'll sound plausible. But that doesn't do you any good if the government took your money and you're never going to get it back. If you look it up in the dictionary, that's theft.

Alex: It is. And it makes me think of the Fourth Liberty Loan Bonds, where they promised repayment in gold at a specified standard. Later on, there was also the case of Perry v. United States, where it gave him rights but still did not give him actually the compensation in gold that he was seeking. Instead, the $10,000 loan that he gave to the United States was given back to him in $10,000 — instead of gold — and thereby he actually lost money in the process. He wasn't the only one; it was all the bondholders back then. So there are parallels to what you're saying.

Mark: Yeah. The state does not play fair, because it doesn't need to.

Where to Follow Mark

Alex: Mark, thanks a lot. I think this has been a packed hour of insights. For those who want to follow Mark — you have also the Mises Institute YouTube channel. I guess you also host your podcast on it that can be seen over there. Is there any other means that people can follow your work?

Mark: I'm on Twitter, and I'm all over mises.org. That's all free stuff on mises.org. We give away a new book every month if you go to mises.org/giveaway. We have several podcasts — mine is a 10-minute economic podcast that drops early Saturday morning here in the US. We have a libertarian podcast, a libertarian political podcast. We have a highly academic long-form podcast with Bob Murphy. There's really a lot that you can get, and it's some of the best information — long-term information slash education — that's going to make you better prepared to interpret the world on your own.

Alex: All right. Thanks, Mark. Thanks to the viewers and listeners. Just as a kind reminder — I think 80 to 90% of you do watch our videos, which is of course always welcome, we love the views, but it would also mean a lot to just convert into a subscriber. This way you will make sure that you do not miss any single interview just like the one we had with Mark today, and future guests coming on to the channel. So on this note — thanks, Mark. Thanks to the viewers and listeners for tagging along until now, and I'll see you in the next episode of the Microscopic Podcast.
