## 一、"临时"的永恒——一个被忽略的语言学时间陷阱
Thornton 轻描淡写地丢出一个足以让人脊背发凉的事实：1971 年尼克松关闭黄金窗口，在美国法律文本中**至今仍是"临时措施"**——55 年的"临时"。这不是官僚的粗心，而是一种精密的语言学机制：用"temporary"这个词冻结社会的决策终结感，与认知心理学中的**损失厌恶**和**锚定效应**深度耦合。一旦某状态被框定为临时，社会就停止规划替代方案，而政府得以永久保留该状态。
更令人意外的是：荷兰正在讨论的"对实物黄金课以更高税率、鼓励持有 ETF"的提案，本质上是把 Thaler 与 Sunstein 的**助推理论（Nudge Theory）反向武器化**——行为经济学原本被用来"温柔地"帮助公民做出更好决策，如今却被用来温柔地把公民赶进一个未来可被按键没收的资产形态。这是行为经济学的黑暗镜像。
## 二、债券奇点 vs AI 奇点——两条指数曲线共享同一个萎缩的储蓄池
Luke Groman 的"bond singularity before AI singularity"被 Thornton 放大，但对

item.title: [a16z] How AI Is Turning Figma’s Finance Team Into Builders
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

几个让人意外的观察

1. "Vibe code 一个产品" 正在成为新型尽调工具——而且做的人是财务

最反直觉的一幕：Figma 的 corporate development（并购/投资）团队，背景是财务，现在把"能不能用 Codex 把目标公司的产品重写出来"作为尽调环节之一。这是一个悄悄发生的权力位移——传统上，判断"技术护城河深不深"必须外包给产品/工程部门，财务只能听二手结论、给出估值模型。现在财务团队自己能用一个下午把目标产品复刻出来，他们对"这到底是不是真技术"的话语权第一次超过了他们的建模能力本身。

跨领域连接：这其实是 1990 年代 Bloomberg Terminal 对交易员做的事情的重演——当分析工具下沉到决策者手里，决策者就不再需要"中间翻译层"。只不过那次下沉的是数据，这次下沉的是构建能力本身。

2. "多个AI人格的投委会"——Pier 团队最离谱的发明

他们为每位高管（Pier 自己、Dylan、CRO Sean）训练了AI 人格，内部投资备忘录会先被这些 AI 人格"预审"一遍："这里 Pier 会问什么？Dylan 会质疑哪里？" 这不是效率工具，这是把高管的认知模式商品化、可复用化。

这里藏着一个让人毛骨悚然的二阶效应：当你的思维模式被 LLM 蒸馏成一个可查询的"人格"后，你本人作为 CFO 的不可替代性就开始松动。Pier 在整段对话里谈的"我希望吸引世界最好的财务组织"，和他亲手参与制造的这套系统之间，其实有一条他可能自己都没有完全意识到的张力线。

跨领域连接：这和奥运教练把世界冠军的动作拆成 3D 模型供下一代训练是同一件事——知识从血肉转移到结构。Figma 财务部正在无意中做组织学意义上的"冠军拆解"。

3. 真正被 AI 杀死的不是 Excel，而是"周度节奏"本身

最容易被忽略的一句话是 Ivon 顺口说的——汇报节奏从季度→月度→周度→现在每小时。Pier 说他每天"wake up and rebuild my context"。这不是"更勤奋"，这是时间的粒度崩塌：当信号可以被秒级获取，"等一等再处理"本身就变成一种代价高昂的管理决策。

这里的反直觉洞察是：财务的核心价值正从"报告"滑向"异常探测"。报告是周期性的、被动的；异常探测是连续的、主动的。Pier 的工作越来越像一个系统工程师——他盯着仪表盘，等待 anomaly，然后溯源。

跨领域连接：这是 1980 年代工厂车间从"每日质检"走向"统计过程控制 (SPC)"的翻版。戴明当年把这叫"从检查走向监控"。差别是——那次是制造业花了 30 年完成的转型，这次财务部门在 18 个月内就被按头走了一遍。

4. 隐藏模式：Pier 真正在招的，不是财务，是"产品经理 for internal tools"

通读所有细节——案例研究要求能用 LLM 建模、要能解释敏感性、能沟通、能产品化工作流、未来可能接管 CIO 的一部分职能——他招的其实是一个内部 SaaS 的产品经理，只是披着 CFO 的皮。

他自己也漏嘴了一句关键的话："I don't know if folks are actually treating access to technology as a recruiting vehicle as much as they could or should"——把"能玩到顶级 AI 工具"包装成福利。这意味着财务岗位正在偷偷进入工程师的招聘市场，和工程岗竞争同一批人才。这将在未来 2–3 年引发一场薪酬结构的地震：财务岗的 comp 曲线会向产品/工程靠拢，因为招的人画像在重叠。

一个总结性的"啊哈"：这场对话表面在谈"CFO 怎么用 AI"，底层在谈的是一个古老职能的身份重构。财务从"记录过去"（会计传统）→"预测未来"（FP&A 时代）→现在正在变成"构建系统"（automation-first）。每一次跃迁都不只是工具升级，而是这个职能回答的根本问题变了。下一个问题可能是——当系统自己会构建系统，CFO 回答的问题是什么？Pier 没回答，但他招 VP Finance 的那个案例研究，已经在偷偷测试这件事。

📝 转录文本

开场：吸引世界最好的财务组织

"I think we're going to be able to attract and build the world's best finance organization because so much what people want the ability to learn and feel like they're being invested in and surrounded by people that want to go and become the best at their craft."

— 关于团队招聘的核心观点

"We'd love to hear a little bit about what made someone a great hire on your team, a great person."

"I want folks that feel extremely intellectually curious. You're coming in and trying to solve and try to understand the business really well. You want to use AI as a tool to help you and empower you, but it's really, really critical to still be that thinker."

— 关于 AI 时代的"slop"问题

"We're in an era right now where a lot of slop is being called out. I've heard one CFO talk about how using AI just led to unlimited amount of docs that are being created every day. Anything that you're putting out there that you're asking someone to consume, it's going to take them time, effort, and energy."

"95% of the challenge there is just like getting your data in the right spot."

— 关于未来 12–18 个月

"What do we think changes in the next 12 to 18 months?"

"If our biggest complexity was staying the same, I think we probably wouldn't need the same number of people a year from now."

节目开场与嘉宾介绍

Welcome to the A16Z podcast. I'm CMA Amble. I'm joined here by my partner Ivon Macarov. We recently wrote a piece called You Need a New CFO. Our argument was that AI takes finance to the next level. And the CFO's job increasingly includes building and automation and really designing the systems and the team to do that.

Today we're joined by Pier Milwani, who's the CFO at Figma. We'd love to explore what you have seen over the course of your career and what you and your team are doing now.

"Preier, thanks for joining us."

"Yeah, thanks for having me. Excited."

一、自动化如何改变财务角色

Q：在你们的职业生涯中，自动化如何改变了财务的角色和团队工作？

"You know, I've always felt like the role of a finance individual should be this operational leader. When I joined Figma, none of the automation pieces were in place at all. I felt like in order for me to be effective at the time I had joined, a lot of my work needed to be living in SQL — building the data tables, really understanding how I could orchestrate the financial information to drive the conversations I wanted to then have across the company."

"I continue to go back to those initial days that I had in that seed and what I was doing as the force multiplier — the piece that actually gave me the ability to have the scaled impact across the organization. If anything, I think what I was building way back then is that much more possible and plausible and accessible to individuals by the tools available to them today."

"I hope that more and more folks feel like they can be empowered to take that operational lens to the way that they actually go and position and work with their counterparts across the business. Because I do think that's the magic of shifting this role from what can be viewed as a traffic-cop sort of financey-type function to one that's a business enabler and a true change agent within the organization."

前 AI 时代的自动化：SQL + 一切能用上的工具

Q：具体用什么做自动化？Excel 宏？文档 OCR？

"Yeah, honestly it was like everything under the sun. It started living in SQL — looking at all of our product metric and utilization data, mapping it to all the financial information we had in Stripe. I'd go and create these like 400 or 500 lines of SQL that I'd want to then use to create the golden tables that I'd go and pass off to someone, or then be able to pass to different go-to-market systems that we'd be using."

"I felt like I spent my day living in that query editor."

"— and of course waiting for the query to run for—"

"Totally. Yeah. And you hope you got it right the first time. Eventually I had — we eventually hired data scientists — and I'd go and tap them and say, 'Hey, I have this thing I went and built. Can you go and add it to our ETL process?' So there's a recurring job that I can then use that same information and pass it to Salesforce or Marketo or whatever systems we were using at the time."

"That was the initial sort of unlock for me: oh my gosh, if I can get consistent in our definitions, in the way that we're talking about things — no longer are we ever debating what's true and what's fact. We can just get past that and really focus on how are we actually going to drive the business."

二、时间粒度的崩塌

"I was talking to someone in their early 20s who was complaining about how long a prompt takes to run. And I was explaining to them: you've not lived the pain of hours on hours of waiting for a SQL query to run and then only to come back and be like, it didn't really totally work. It is just an order of magnitude."

"Totally."

— 疫情期间 COVID 相关的使用激增

"The time is really interesting, right? Especially the era that we've lived through. When I was at Webflow and at Figma, we saw for example a huge spike in usage in COVID that I could not believe in the beginning. I thought our data was broken or something else was broken, but it took us weeks to figure it out. Today, I feel like we live in a day where you could figure it out to an hour with some of the spikes, some of the usage, revenue as well. This is very different world we live in. Did you experience that as well?"

"Yeah, I mean our business took off during the early days of the pandemic. That was actually the time where we started to partner with the folks at Indry — right at the early stages over there."

"I wake up every day with the ability to rebuild my context on what's happening. At any moment during the day, the team loves it when I'm — I don't know if they love it, but they know that I'm constantly in there going and taking a look at hourly dashboards or daily metrics on things, to make sure that I'm also sourcing things that I think maybe look like anomalies, or asking the right questions."

"I think they view me similarly to how they view their role within the organization — like a counterpart who has ideas, who wants to come to them and truly build the best business possible, all using and having access to the same data available to each other."

从季度 → 月度 → 周度 → 每日

"What's interesting — when you and I went to college around that time, that was more of a monthly or quarterly cadence. Then it became a weekly cadence. I remember maybe especially with data moving more into the cloud, it became like, let's have a big weekly dashboard. Now what's possible is daily. Has that changed your habits — the way you even just look at, think about data, how often you think about it?"

"Honestly, I view data and having access to it as the key unlock to how I can run my day effectively. Throughout my time at Figma, there would be like 30 people that would sign up for a paid plan in those first few days when I joined, and I'd go through line by line: who are they? Are they personal addresses? Are they business addresses? Are they people we can reach out to? What can I learn from this to help us inform what we eventually built — our organization's product."

"I think early days it's extremely important. Now I understand the repercussions of movement in any one direction. If you catch something before it becomes a big deal, it can actually save the business hundreds, thousands of dollars. But if you catch it in the other direction, you can really put more juice behind it and really seek to unlock in the other way."

"I view this as a daily, if not more than that, rhythm. The goal for me is: how do I empower other folks on my team and across the business to similarly feel the accountability to those same metrics, and truly act as business owners and want to go and triage things — and not say 'hey, I can wait till next week.' You do need to solve it sooner rather than later, because I do think the rhythms here are moving really rapidly."

三、什么样的人是伟大的招聘对象？

Q：在 AI 之前，什么样的人是你团队里的 great hire？

"Honestly a lot of similar things today, but I think you'd apply them slightly differently. I want folks that feel extremely intellectually curious. You're coming in and trying to solve, and trying to understand the business really well, and then seek to problem-solve in a way that is trying to drive the right outcome."

"I don't think that necessarily has changed today. I still very much value that. I do think that you can make a lot of the tedious tasks or the repetitive nature of things feel like they take less and less of your time, so that you can spend more and more of your time really trying to seek how you can find the places of magic within the business that you can go and supercharge."

"So: intellectual curiosity, fluency with data, ability to ask really solid questions, and then structure your thoughts in ways where you can actually make sense of the data that's being given back to you, and then thoughtfully communicate it on the other side of it."

面试一位 VP Finance：Case Study 的神圣性

"Right now I'm hiring for a VP Finance, and the case study part of the process for me is so sacred. I want to test for: how are you using the tools available to you? I fully expect folks to — I don't give them a lot of information as part of this case study. We're a public company, so I get the benefit of a lot of data out there. But how you actually piece those puzzle pieces together in a way that actually makes sense — the model output makes sense, you have the ability not just to create that output but to truly understand how it works."

"I focus the case-study conversation on: have you really understood the structure that you've created? Have you molded it in a way where you've tested — what are the pieces of that model that are the most sensitive to any change? Do you have a strong intuition on how the business is actually working using the tool that you've created?"

"And then, like we were just talking about, can you effectively communicate that? Anyone can go and create a model sitting in — pick your favorite LLM — you can go and do that really easily. But are you using it as an effective tool that actually is enabling you to think? You don't want to outsource your thinking today. You want to use AI as a tool to help you and empower you — but it's really critical to still be that thinker."

"Yeah. A lot of what you're describing applies to a good hire with or without AI. If anything, AI just — you need more of the accountability and thoroughness to know that the thinking is there behind it as you receive a work product."

四、Figma 内部的真实自动化案例

1) 应收账款与 Credit & Collections：Kajal 的自建系统

"Let's drive in a little bit to understand what you've automated."

"They're so broad. I think we've moved really quickly even over the last year to say: how do I go and try to coach people to embrace new tools and new ways of working — to now one where I feel like I'm constantly being hit in the face with a lot of these really cool ideas."

"We do a segment at the company all-hands called FigNation, where we show folks how others have built with AI, and consistently our team shows up as a team that's there."

"Things with — Kajal, our credit and collections team — he's gone and rebuilt his entire workflow: everything from invoice tracking, cash collections, making sure that we can reconcile everything to NetSuite. He's done it in a way where it's a homegrown system tied to the various systems we use. It then is freed him up to say, okay, I can continue to drive down my days-receivable by focusing on the things that really matter, and then focusing on what are the other tedious tasks I can go and build automation for."

"He's then gone and said, well, I can rebuild the way that I want to run our credit checks and I can stitch together the data sets in interesting ways that allow me not to have to manually go into them. It's a singular way where he can now go to anyone and say: hey, go and leverage the tools that I've created to go and really drive change there."

2) Corporate Development：Vibe-coding 作为 Diligence 工具

"On our core dev team, it's been really fun to see how they — can you vibe-code a product is one of the checks that we use in diligence now, which is actually really fun to see. How deep is your moat? How interesting is the technology there?"

"— you'll try to recreate the product? Wow, OK."

"Yeah. Our team's gotten really damn good at some of this, and so you can get through some of the 'is this a real thing or not? How difficult is it or not?' There's obviously nuances to a whole bunch of these ideas, but it gives you a solid intuition there."

"And before, would you have had to go to the product team to do that part of the diligence?"

"Yeah, I mean we still partner with the product team, but you can take a lot more of 'hey, this is what I built, this is what I've seen,' and it builds a lot of credibility there."

"Can I pause? Those are some of the corp dev people, right — not product people? Their finance background, right?"

"Yeah, totally. We're a very document-oriented culture, so they write investment memos, they write M&A memos, whatever it may be. Among them, the end readers are going to be folks on our leadership team or other product leaders. More often than not, there are themes, there are similar questions, there are ways that we all as leaders tend to have a way of looking at problems."

3) "AI 人格"版的投资委员会

"What's been interesting is they've gone and created unique personalities for each of us as leaders — as a set of skills that they can go and run their investment memos by, to actually improve the process."

"Do you have an investment committee that exists — like the interaction between all of them?"

"Throughout — exactly. So that's exactly what they'll end up demoing. They'll sit there kind of going back and forth and saying: okay, this is what Pier would say, and this is what Dylan would say, and this is what Sean would say, our CRO. You kind of get the areas of the document that you either want to plus up, do more diligence on, what are common sets of feedback that I need to go and make sure I ask the questions over. Then it reduces the cycle time that we're all sitting together on."

"There are a lot of these areas where we're both feeling like it's a tool that helps you augment, a tool that helps you go and replace workflow, and then a tool that helps you seek to understand and learn. I'm constantly surprised at how quickly we've been able to riff on things."

"For me, it's actually put me in this really optimistic spot of saying: I think we're going to be able to attract and build the world's best finance organization because so much of what people want is the ability to learn and feel like they're being invested in and surrounded by people that want to become the best at their craft. As much as I can do to effect and enable that change, the better we're going to be able to go at retaining and growing and grooming that talent over time."

4) 构建还是购买？

"Are all those tools — did you build those with the LLM directly, or are you guys also looking at off-the-shelf AI tools that you can partner with? Would you rather build or buy?"

"The ones I was describing — it's a mix. Some of them, folks were sitting in Codex. That's what the team is doing on the corporate development team — they're sitting in Codex and trying to work their way through something."

"We've also seen folks sitting within some of the workflow-automation pieces, building skills around agents using ChatGPT — that's how some of the credit-and-collections pieces were being built."

"We've also started to see folks being able to embrace it and build it on our tooling as well. We have a tool called Figma Make which allows folks to prompt through natural language and create an application, a website — you can then host it, you have a backend behind it. Some of those instances are starting to crop up too. I'm actually excited about that, because then we can flip into this world where we can give product feedback as well — which I know everyone would love."

五、关于 "Slop" 与一致性

"We're in the era right now, the period in the cycle, where a lot of slop is being called out. We went from unlimited tokens to people just calling it slop in meetings. I've heard one CFO talk about how using AI just led to unlimited amounts of docs being created every day — you just can't find anything, because everybody can write a doc now, or 10 docs in a few minutes, where it would take you a week or two."

Q：这自然带出招聘的问题 — 你招更年轻、更会用这些工具的人，还是更资深、知道 world-class 长什么样的人？

"That's what worries me a little bit: that we will forget what world-class looked like, just like in the pre-AI era, where a really good model looks like — especially with some experience and having created models. Where do you think this is going? Have you called 'slop' on some of the stuff that's being created right now with AI, sometimes?"

"Yeah. We've also done a good job internally about building policies around branding — when you've written something with AI. One of the things that's really important, like I was sharing earlier: you should not be outsourcing your thinking."

"Anything you're putting out there that you're asking someone to consume, it's going to take them time, effort, and energy. So you want to make sure you put a similar bar to review, read, summarize, make it simple. You can start in a different place — I'm totally cool with that — but it's on all of us to make sure we're being really thoughtful about how we use each other's time."

"I've been in instances where things look a little bit half-baked and you really poke around and you're like, did you really understand what's going on over here? But I've also been in instances where I'm like, oh my gosh, your speed of iteration here is pretty damn incredible by virtue of how you set up."

T&E 案例：fuzzy match 的魔法

"A couple weeks ago I was sitting in a — we're going through '27 planning, sitting in a T&E review. We're looking at our T&E portfolio and saying, OK, where do we have the opportunity to make changes to policy, or maybe where are we not upholding policy where we should?"

"Our corporate finance team did a really good job of stitching together information that lived in different data sources. We use Navan, we use Zip, we use Ramp. There's a lot of fuzzy match that you have to go through in order to really get that information working. Was someone actually traveling for an off-site? What if they lived in San Francisco and were just visiting? How do you want to tag and treat that data?"

"95% of the challenge there is just getting your data in the right spot. These models are good at making these assumptions for you. I didn't need something 100% perfect. I just wanted something that was directionally in the right vein for where I'm going, that gave me enough information to understand what are the areas I really need to crank the dial on."

"They output a set of suggested changes that we could make. I gave feedback that morning — 30 minutes later on some of the construction of how I actually wanted things to look like — and it was all visualized for me when we got in the meeting. I was like, holy sh**, this is like a really fantastic use case here."

"They did it in a way where I don't think they would have been able to do it by hand. So as much of that slop can happen, I also think some magic can really get unlocked if you use the right tool for the right purpose, and understand what is good enough and what needs to be really, really picture perfect."

六、Agent 浪潮与"自动化先行"的肌肉

"A couple of comments to that. A key unlock is the data. Now with AI you can consume all these sources of data and quickly do the fuzzy match, get a directionally correct or precise reconciliation across these sources — whereas before, you had to run the SQL query, it had to wait, and then you had to be your own BI analyst on top of it."

"The second piece is: there's this muscle that's being developed around automation. Even if there is slop — for example, I was talking to one of our growth-stage CFOs who said in a month or two there have been 40 or 50 agents created by their team, which obviously are not all being used. But it was getting everyone in this motion of: OK, if I'm doing something manual or tedious, I don't have a great tool for it — let me build. A lot of those, maybe 90% of those tools and agents, are not being used anymore, but it got people to think: OK, instead of doing this manually, let me think automation-first around it."

"I 100% agree with you. I also think how you share it, how you get other people to understand what other people are building — then you end up in scenarios where our internal audit team, they spend a ton of time following up with individuals to make sure they're adding information on the tickets, so it could be trackable for our SOX audit. Well, that internal-audit team is not the only team that does that. Our GRC team is doing the same thing as they go through all of our ISO and SOC 2 audits. You have a bunch of this back-and-forth on the AP side when they're going and writing accruals."

"You want to build this motion of triaging, pulling information in, reconciling it — and why not build a singular platform that does that? This is actually where a systems team is really interesting to come in and harmonize some of the things you see are happening, really productize it, so that you don't have all these individuals going and building similar things. I think that is the evolution of what a CIO function should or could be. How do you take a lot of these bottoms-up things that people have crafted and have them rebuilt and repurposed in a way that can live on beyond the creator and the initial builder."

七、谁来 own 这些？"Finance Engineer" 的诞生

"I was also talking to one of our growth-stage companies. The head of customer success was saying every one of his reps had a different dashboard that they had vibe-coded, and they had different numbers."

"There has to be some reconciling function. Which is a great segue — to hear from you around what are people doing in terms of the teams that should be building this, and who is taking the agency? Is it someone initially builds an agent from your team and then you're taking it to an engineering team centrally? We talked a lot about this idea of the finance engineer."

"Having specialists come up with the ideas and iterate — they know what good looks like, they know what they want, they know the process they're trying to make look right. They're fantastic at building these initial prototypes."

"But do I want that same individual to be the one that has to make sure they're checking for all upstream dependencies, making sure if they were ever to leave that this thing is hosted in the right way, and hey, does anyone else across the organization have the same need? Probably not."

"This is where a world-class CIO org can really show some magic. We just had a new CIO join yesterday, a guy named Casper Sorensen who joined over from Coinbase. A lot of what we talked about in the interview process is: how do you create centralized PM-type functions within the CIO organization that can partner with the rest of the business teams, find the things that are really working, and then build foundations that others can build on top of? Not too dissimilar from how a systems organization would have functioned otherwise — but the pace that you can iterate on, and how you can empower others to build on top, is what is changing."

Messy middle

"Is it centralized right now within the company, or do you see that changing?"

"As is all things at Figma, I think we've grown faster than we've built the tools to support it. It's on me to always empower the organization to build, and I don't want to slow people down by creating the infrastructure on top of it. So I think we're chasing a little bit of that right now. With some teams we've done a better job centralizing; with other teams they built far quicker, and we're now in the process of saying, OK, how can we help?"

"We're in the messy middle right now."

"That resonates with a lot of what we're hearing from our companies — whether it's a go-to-market engineer, a talent engineer, this concept of the finance engineer. It's a decentralized set of builders across teams. It could have different profiles. Sometimes it's someone who has an engineering background in finance who's good at thinking about what workflows need to be automated. Other times you borrowed a product engineer from another team to go build. Everyone's in this messy middle right now in terms of what that profile of person looks like."

来自会计背景的 data scientist

"A lot of it reminds me of data-science teams and how they partner with other parts of the organization. As a data-science partner, the deeper you get into understanding the context of the team you're working with, the better you operate as an individual."

"We've got data-science individuals partnering with our product team. They build as much, if not more, product intuition than our product managers and engineers, and they're viewed as part of that core team that can go and help ideate and push change — they're just leveraging a different tool to enable that."

"Similarly, we've got folks on the data-science side supporting our finance organization. The folks that I think have been devoted there actually come from accounting backgrounds, a couple of them. They understand that this stuff has got to be really hard and always correct. They understand the nuances we're describing — checks and balances, what is a refund, what is uncollectible, all that nomenclature. It enables them to be better builders."

"Similarly, I could see that translate to the finance engineer you're describing. You have some shared understanding of what is necessary. You could build that context over time, but it's important to at least build that major, so that you can also go and push other people's frame of thinking as well."

八、谁拥有"定义"？

"Who owns the definitions? The reason I'm asking — especially we see it at an early stage where it could be a team of 20 people and just founders and no finance or business people, and then eventually they bring them on — but they're building definitions of key metrics that serve reporting, that serve investors, and really business decisions. Eventually finance gets hired."

"Where are the definitions? It feels like in the past we used to revisit them maybe every couple of years. Now, because you can access the code or you can access the Stripe logic much easier with AI, has that changed much? How often do you revisit it?"

"My team owns the outputs there. Maybe we're a little bit later than some of those earlier businesses — we have more controls in how we want to talk about it. It's always been really important to me to have consistency in how we talk about our numbers."

"It's one of the things that has always been empowering to how I can show up with our board, with our leadership team, with other folks broadly — they know that what I'm putting out there is the same thing that I would have put out there a month ago. The historicals never change. I'm not trying to hide anything."

"As we grow and as we give ourselves the ability to iterate, we constantly have this conversation on different sets of disclosure as we go through earnings. We want to be consistent, and we want to have the decisions we make be things we can look back on and feel good about, and have longevity further beyond. It's great if it's people finding different ways to think about their business, if it's empowering them to build their business better. But I do think there's some value in consistency as well."

九、团队里谁自动化得最多？

"Who is it on your team that's automated the most? What role?"

"I could say someone, but I assume that someone else is probably coming up with something different really quickly. Honestly, it's individuals who are owning certain parts of our forecast model, all the way through to individuals on our BizOps team that are automating their day-to-day — how they're actually running competitive benchmarking and pricing studies."

"I actually think that it's the one-upping of each other that enables you to create an organization that wants to better one another. I would feel uncomfortable saying there's one individual, because I truly do think this is a team that's trying to do this together."

谁跑得更快？

"Do you think it tends to be people who have more expertise or experience in an area, or is it really across the board? And how much is it coming from you and the role that you've automated yourself?"

"Early days it was helpful for me to go and show folks: hey, if I'm coming and trying to do things in a different way, that should be your signal that my expectation is that you are as well."

"But in large part, the things that are important: have a solid understanding of the data sets that you're trying to pull from. The folks that have been able to move more quickly have an understanding of how these things are stitched together. When you understand how they're architected, you can better think like an architect of: OK, how do I actually bridge these things in a way that's logical? Where do I know where the model is actually making a deterministic decision versus inferring? What tasks is it OK for that to happen? What tasks is it not OK?"

"The rhythm that we've created — the show-and-tell rhythm, the internal hackathons, this ability to bring in other experts — I do a lot of conversations with other finance leaders and I try to bring in some of that intel internally so it can get disseminated. My leaders are also doing that too, which is really cool to see. Everyone right now is trying to learn from one another."

十、Buy vs. Build 与"工作变有趣了"

"One of the common themes coming up in my conversations with CFOs, directors of finance, or even individual contributors is that they're finding it's really fun to be working again. Before, you were reconciling something for 2 or 3 weeks, closing the books for 2 or 3 weeks, or continuously. Now it just feels like people are really turning their eyes towards the business and are able to surface insights."

"There's a lot of excitement around what's possible with AI, what's possible with vertical solutions. One of the things I'm curious — to go back on the buy scenario. I was talking to one of our hyper-growth companies the other day and they said: we just have to buy everything off the shelf, we're moving so fast. Do you ever feel that way? Maybe building is a longer path than just buying one of the solutions out there."

"For the core systems-of-record solutions, the things we just can't mess up — yes, we're going and buying solutions for that."

"The areas where our team is having a lot of fun is the workflow automation — what are the areas where if I think about my day, I'm almost not thinking? How can I augment my day-to-day so I can reorchestrate how I want to spend my time?"

"I fully agree with the sentiment you're sharing. The work has gotten — the work is always going to be interesting, but the work has gotten more fun because you can explore things more quickly. I've had folks on my team come up to me being like, 'holy sh**, I actually am having a ton of fun.' And I actually think that the policies we created and the freedom we've given folks to explore are the reasons why some folks are like, 'I want to stay here. I really like what I'm doing.'"

AI 作为招聘福利

"I don't know if folks are actually treating access to technology as a recruiting vehicle as much as they could or should. I've at least started to do that in the recruiting conversation since I started to hear that from the team — especially when you're trying to pull from folks who are not necessarily in technology. They're like, 'oh my gosh, this is my front entrance into an entirely new world, and if I'm empowered to learn, this is really cool.'"

"Like we talk about perks and benefits — you get X, Y and Z if you come to work here. Your former employer doesn't let you have it available, and now you also get access to all these models or other tools."

"Yeah. And I think it's not just that, but also if you have folks understand what other people are building around them. So much of what you're going to learn is through osmosis of what others have built. If you get this feeling that you're joining an organization that's not just saying they give access to these things, but they're actually building, and you can see it and feel it through the interview process — those are the places I'd gravitate to."

十一、金字塔颠倒：从数据清洗到战略

"In 2020, my partner Angela and I wrote this piece on how CFOs needed modern tools. We had this pyramid diagram in there which was essentially saying that the finance team was spending all their time on this data reconciliation layer, and at the top — which was the smallest amount of time — was being spent on strategic finance, or strategy questions."

"I'm curious if your time — you've actually seen your time and your team's time unlock, not just on doing things they enjoy more, but being more strategic or being able to weigh in on more decisions. How has that changed your role?"

"I feel fortunate that as I've grown within the company, that has taken up more and more of my role. As I then think about what is exciting for others, I also recognize for me to have that, there's benefit in me creating that same space for other people within the organization."

"Yes, there are things we'll have to do as daily rhythms or weekly rhythms. But in the same breath — if I can take our finance organization (which is split in one of the pillars being go-to-market), if I can take the team that's focused on our self-served business and immediately get them out of reconciling last week or last month, and much more focused on what are the experiments we're running, what are the trends we're seeing, what are the additional dollars we should be spending on — that is way more engaging to them."

"They're actually able to do more of that now. Some of the little things here matter so much. How can I automate the creation of a set of materials that I know is going to look and feel the exact same way, and focus my time on the annotation, the discovery, the understanding? We've seen that start to get a lot faster, and the quality of that improve."

"We even had the leader of that team get up and talk about how he had gone and created a set of plugins in Figma to iterate on this stuff really quickly. I would hope that my team is telling me they're spending a growing share of their time on that bucket of things. But you're always going to have to chase the complexity in your business, and manage the complexity with how much time you're able to reserve for the other pieces."

Audit trail 的新含义

"One of the things that we're seeing in the CFO tools we've invested in is the product is moving away from tracking workflow towards providing a result — and then part of the product is the audit trail. Obviously finance needs to make sure everything's correct. You need to be able to track how the product came to a particular reconciliation. But then it's done for you. So it's that balance of both having the audit trail and the result."

"We are definitely seeing our team spend more time doing things like running experiments, and things that used to take a month-long research study. You had to pull in someone from data science, chase down a bunch of people over email, get everyone in a room. Now you can quickly iterate on this because you have agents running in the background."

"It could even be things on the accounting side — like flux analysis. You're spending time as an accountant going through and reviewing the GL accounts for period over period. If you can leverage a tool — and there's a whole bunch of tools out there that give you that initial stab at what has changed, that gives them a set of things they can chase. And maybe it's right right away — I'd love for that to be more and more true — and then they focus their time elsewhere."

"I fully expect that the initial draft, the initial set of expectations, the initial idea of what to pull the thread on, can be surfaced via tools. That's kind of where I was going when I was talking about the T&E piece — it was giving our team sets of threads they can pull, and us enough gut to chase it too."

十二、"Reconciliation" 的词义翻转

"I was thinking how when we grew up the word reconciliation was a very negative word — associated with a lot of bad memories and weeks and months spent on trying to chase something. Now it's just something you do, or maybe it's even a positive word, because you can solve it much easier, quicker with the modern tools and with AI."

"And find — maybe not exactly where the errors are — but just get there so much quicker, and then you still need obviously to go talk to people. FP&A will always continue to be the people discipline."

"Yeah, I under-played how important communication, relationship-building, your ability to influence was to this role. I probably walked in feeling like I could be the smartest person in the room and figure it all out, but then I realized it's a team sport regardless. You can only affect so much change, and you then really do have to get other people to be on the same page with you."

"If you can do that effectively, I think you can be a really effective leader. Those are the true skills. If I can test and get a sense that you have this ability to build really solid followership, you have this ability to build trust with others — that's so invaluable."

十三、未来 12–18 个月：复杂性 vs. 规模

"That's a good segue into what I wanted to chat about next — what do we think changes in the next 12 to 18 months for the team and the role and the function overall?"

"I would love to be in a spot where we're only adding individuals if the complexity of the business is growing faster than the needs to support it. I think we're in a spot now where a lot of the regular business-rhythm pieces — you can start to move in the reverse direction versus needing to add people in order to keep up with it."

"For us, we're going to continue to fight it, because we're adding new products, we're acquiring teams and businesses, we're continuing to evolve what we're doing. In that world, the complexity there is still outpacing where we're able to truly drive complete efficiency. But we're definitely getting more efficient period over period."

Q：这个效率会不会到一个 plateau？

"I would hope that more and more can get completely automated. Maybe I start with the pieces that are truly deterministic — how can I feed it with enough information so that I can feel that the output is completely trustworthy?"

"Getting something to that audit-ready output piece for a system that's truly business-critical is extremely high. It's also going to be an interesting conversation with the auditors on what gets them comfortable."

"I don't take it out of the picture. I do think we'll get there over time. If our business complexity was staying the same, I think we probably wouldn't need the same number of people a year from now. But we only get there because you're doing a better job of finding these places and rhythms where you can build more consistency in the way that you're operating."

十四、Excel 会死吗？

"Is Excel under threat?"

"No. It's like my love language, dude."

"In the same way I was describing how the case study is so important — you use it as a tool. You use it to build intuition. A lot of the output people are still creating is a model. That model could be hosted somewhere, could be something else — but you want this tool to give you this ability to refine your understanding and play with things with your hands."

"It's kind of like the magic that we see with Figma. We can give people the ability to go and have an initial stab in the first draft through prompting and natural language, but sometimes it's so much easier to riff and make changes on your hand."

"Take a color wheel as an example. You've got a screen that you've designed and you're like, hey, I want to change the background. You could sit there in an agent and prompt it — go change the background from red to green — or I could take the color wheel, and you get all different shades of it, and you get the real feel of what's going on. Similarly, I think about that with Excel. It's the way I build trust, the way I build understanding. There may be something better in the future, but for me, it'd be really hard to rip away from me."

"I also grew up in Excel, and I still use Excel to organize my thoughts. If I'm trying to run an analysis — it's even just the spatial organization of it. I think the models aren't quite good enough to create a forecast or a model quite yet, but that organization is still valuable. I don't know if you feel similarly."

"Totally. I also think part of what I've tried to experiment with now is how can I use one of these models to help me better understand the output that a team is putting together? If you give me a 20-tab model, it's going to be really challenging for me to tab through and thumb through everything. But if I can pass that same context through a model to help me understand what are the things that really are the needle-movers, or what are the areas that are more sensitive — it has actually given me a better starting spot to orchestrate and understand things. I've found that really helpful and effective."

大学的 AI 困境

"The world we're living in is also challenging. I was talking to a university professor the other day and I was asking him how do they teach AI at the universities? Well, they don't right now. One of the challenges — they had a course and within the semester they've changed the syllabus several times because new models have dropped. They just have to completely change how they do it, though. So they just sort of give up. They're going back to fundamentals again — teaching people analytical thinking, and Excel, and all of that."

"I imagine you're in a similar world — if you were relying too heavily, you're going to have to redo how you do your earnings."

"A lot has changed, but a lot hasn't changed. I think that's the spirit of where you're going. The core capabilities of what makes a great finance person are still there. How you actually leverage the tools at your disposal to make better decisions is always going to be this moving target for you. The unlock that SQL was for me is now a net-net-new unlock with AI as a tool and capability driver for me. A great finance person has longevity if they continue to adapt."

十五、一位"新型 CFO"的画像

"We wrote this piece — we said it was titled You Need a New CFO. The main point was that there's a mindset shift. Whether the individual actually has changed — it's that they have to think more automation-first, either build or buy the tools depending on what's available and what makes sense. But it's really automation-first."

"I'm curious if you think the profile of a CFO in the next year or two is going to change in any way, or to your point, it's kind of the same dimensions that are important but the mindset continues to evolve."

"If I were to give advice to anyone — hire someone who feels a similar amount of business ownership and operational rigor as the CEO does. They want to win. They want to win no matter which way possible. They have a set of tools that they're going to use, and an understanding of a P&L, to orchestrate that change."

"You truly want a business leader versus — like I was sharing earlier — a traffic cop. That is just not — and yes, there's a lot of things you're going to need to have as commonplace and solid understanding of, like all the accounting fundamentals, your ability to orchestrate a planning process. But the things that make people truly unique in this role — do you understand the business? Can you make change happen? Can you simplify the understanding of how the business model works, so that others are all running in the same direction?"

"It's true whether we're talking about a public company like Figma, or a seed-stage or Series-A startup that's starting to scale their go-to-market and getting traction. That's what the founders and the CEOs really need from finance — that extra opinion on the business, and insights that are easier to get. But also, you still go back to the basics — customers. Do you understand the customers? Do you understand the behaviors? Do you understand the metrics that come from that — inputs, outputs? That will always be the same in what we expect."

一点创意

"Maybe the thing I'd add — creativity is important. Not creative in a sense of 'go create a funky set of metrics,' but how can you actually think about your business in a slightly different light, and use that as the way you go and drive change and be opinionated?"

"I try to do this — I don't know if I'm doing it as much as I could. But if I come up with these ideas, if I can come up with different ways of thinking about things, I actually think some great ideas can come from your finance organization. If you really set them up well and right, they can be this layer within your organization that's just as impactful, and really driving a lot of the internal strategy as well."

"At the investor and board level, we are seeing a much deeper set of analysis come through, or the rapid iteration. Before, it used to be — oh, we have all these questions at the board meeting, and then the team needs to run and cycle through. That process has just short-circuited, and hopefully is less painful on the finance-team side."

十六、收尾：从哪里开始自动化？

"Last question for you, Ivon — as our portfolio companies, or just companies in general, come to you and say, where do I start in terms of automation? What do you give them as advice?"

"I think it's kind of the same place where we always started. You start with the integrity of data. You have to figure out if you actually have good access to data, if you're tracking things. Many times, especially early-stage companies, they don't even track anything. So you have to set that up, and that often goes against the priorities that maybe the first finance hire has — like, 'I've got to close my books sometime, got to send the board update, all of that.'"

"Actually, no — you can't even do that until you're on a solid foundation. You might have to set it, you might have to rebuild it, you might have to change things. We've had a number of people that came in, especially now — very quickly you can realize within several weeks that maybe the revenue is calculated in a way that's not how it should be calculated for that business model."

"More creative ARR at the early stage than I've ever seen before."

"Sure. For sure. It's changing fast too. But it starts with data, and then based on that, you create the reporting rigor, you create the metrics, and then you create the story."

Storytelling 的提前

"One of the things, Pier — especially you've been on that journey as a CFO — storytelling becomes a really important once you have your eyes set on the IPO and you have to be all telling the same story. I feel like that has moved earlier and earlier to earlier stages, because you expect to tell the story now in fundraising for Series A, Series B. Not just the story of what the product vision could be, but the story with the numbers and what the business could really be like."

"That's gotten easier, but it's also gotten harder because a lot of people overthink that with AI. Ivon and I have been hosting these CFO and controller dinners for a couple of years now, and we saw this real market change — I'd say about 9 months ago — when it went from people saying 'oh yeah, I'm generating this tax memo or this onboarding doc with AI' to saying 'OK, yeah, I'm actually doing the core data reconciliation and automating many of the workflows.' And it's really been a step-function change. If anything, the leaders are saying, 'I need to do this, otherwise I'll be perceived within my organization as behind everyone else.'"

"This goes back to your point around winning the hackathons. Finance was never the one that was going to be winning the automation hackathons a couple of years ago, and it's pretty cool to see that's totally changed."

"Yeah, I love this part of it. We have an internal Maker Week — it's our internally branded hackathon. I would always sit there early days and not really know how to participate, and now I'm like, if I had a spare minute, I think I would have a million different ideas. And I'm sure my team feels very similarly."

"Well, Pier, thank you so much for joining us. This was really fun to talk about and understand directly from someone who's gone through this journey of automation over your career. And thanks, Ivon — this was a really fun conversation."

"Yeah, thanks for having me."

"Yeah."

# 几个让人意外的观察
## 1. "Vibe code 一个产品" 正在成为新型尽调工具——而且做的人是财务
最反直觉的一幕：Figma 的 **corporate development（并购/投资）团队**，背景是财务，现在把"能不能用 Codex 把目标公司的产品重写出来"作为尽调环节之一。这是一个悄悄发生的权力位移——传统上，判断"技术护城河深不深"必须外包给产品/工程部门，财务只能听二手结论、给出估值模型。现在财务团队自己能用一个下午把目标产品复刻出来，他们对"这到底是不是真技术"的话语权第一次超过了他们的建模能力本身。
**跨领域连接**：这其实是 1990 年代 Bloomberg Terminal 对交易员做的事情的重演——当分析工具下沉到决策者手里，决策者就不再需要"中间翻译层"。只不过那次下沉的是数据，这次下沉的是**构建能力本身**。
## 2. "多个AI人格的投委会"——Pier 团队最离谱的发明
他们为每位高管（Pier 自己、Dylan、CRO Sean）训练了**AI 人格**，内部投资备忘录会先被这些 AI 人格"预审"一遍："这里 Pie

item.title: [Latent Space] Multicellular Systems - Fabian Theis, Helmholtz Munich
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

当"更小"的叙事被反转：单细胞领域的旗手为什么开始呼吁"更大"

Fabian Theis 作为单细胞基因组学的核心推动者之一，这段话里藏着一个容易被忽略的反直觉信号——他在呼吁离开单细胞。过去十年生物学的主旋律是"向下还原"：从组织到细胞，从细胞到转录组，从转录组到单分子。而他却说：真正有趣的 readout 需要回到多细胞系统。这不是技术偏好的转向，而是一种认知论的反叛——他在暗示：生命的信息并不存在于任何单一细胞里，而只存在于细胞之间的关系中。换句话说，过去十年我们用越来越精细的显微镜看错了地方。还原得越彻底，离"生命"反而越远。

跨领域连接：organoid 是"湿件版 Transformer"，但它跳过了预训练

当 Theis 说迷你大脑"可以计算"时，他碰到的是一条远超生物学的暗线。墨尔本 DishBrain 项目已经让培养皿里的神经元玩 Pong——这意味着神经形态计算（neuromorphic computing）正在被生物组织本身实现。但真正出人意料的类比在这里：Transformer 的"涌现能力"和 organoid 的"自组织节律"，在数学上都是局部规则产生全局功能。两者的关键差别在于——Transformer 需要几千亿 token 的梯度下降才能"学会跳动"；而心脏 organoid 从一簇干细胞开始，几天之内就自发同步跳动。它不需要训练，因为它有几亿年的发育预训练权重封装在 DNA 里。从这个视角看，LLM 并不是"类脑"，LLM 是从零开始的 organoid；而 organoid 则是自带 foundation model 的湿件。

隐藏的系统性真相：组织工程的真正野心是"园艺"，不是"制造"

注意 Theis 的用词——"start connect and do things"（开始连接、开始做事）。他没说"按我们设定的方式做事"。这是一个极其重要的语言滑动。传统生物工程的隐喻是机械（build, assemble, engineer）；而 organoid 的隐喻其实是生态（grow, emerge, settle into）。你不是在组装一颗心脏，你是在创造让心脏愿意出现的条件。

这里有一个跨学科的意外对应：这跟 Stewart Brand 关于"城市像森林一样被养大，而非被规划"的洞见，以及 Christopher Alexander 的 pattern language，在底层逻辑上是同一件事——复杂系统不能被设计，只能被引导着自己长出来。组织工程师、城市规划师、机器学习研究员，正在不自觉地趋同到一种共同的手艺：培育涌现。而这件手艺的核心悖论在于——越试图控制，涌现越不发生；越放手，系统反而越像"活的"。

Theis 短短三句话，其实在宣告一个更大的转变：生物学正在从"分析的科学"变成"培育的科学"，从阅读生命变成与生命协商。

📝 转录文本

为什么要走向多细胞系统

I'm quite convinced that we need to go to multicellular systems to have actually really interesting readouts.

When I first saw that people are able to take essentially cells out of a body of cancer cell and let them then grow into small multicellular systems that actually sort of start connect and do things, I was super super impressed.

两个让人震撼的例子：会计算的迷你大脑，会跳动的心脏类器官

So, you know, people can now for example take some cells, put them in a dish, and then grow little mini brains — essentially set of neurons that essentially really start connecting, talking to each other. And people have shown that they can get those sort of mini brains in a dish to compute.

Similarly, people can take heart cells, grow them into little heart organoids, and actually start beating — like you have beating little heart cell clumps in a dish.
