item.title: [Odds on Open] Welcome to Gas Vegas: Commodities Trading From First Principles With Ex-Goldman Commodities Trader
item.dc:creator: Odds on Open
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、库存即缓冲：被忽略的"价格暴力定理"

John 讲的那个"一行公式"——供给减去需求等于库存变化——表面看像废话，但真正的洞见藏在边界条件里：当库存耗尽或爆满时，价格必须独自承担全部再平衡的任务。这就是为什么 2020 年原油会跌到负 40 美元：不是油突然变成了坏东西，而是缓冲系统失灵后，价格被迫承担起本应由仓储承担的职责。

这个原理远远超出了商品交易。它其实是一切"缓冲-信号"系统的底层律法： - 急诊室没有床位时，分诊医生的决策会变得残酷——因为再没有空间让错误被稀释； - 一个人情绪"库存"耗尽时，一件小事可以引爆剧烈反应——因为心理冗余为零，波动直接传导到行为； - AI 上下文窗口接近爆满时，模型开始丢弃或幻觉——没有空间，Token 就只能通过"价格"（概率权重的畸变）来清算。

库存是文明的减震器。 当你观察一个系统突然变得"疯狂"时，先去看它的缓冲池，而不是去看它的驱动力。

二、Henry Hub 悖论：合约设计打败了地质禀赋

最反直觉的观察是：美国天然气比全世界都便宜，不是因为资本市场、不是因为地质、不是因为管道——而是因为一个 10,000 MMBTU 的实物交割期货合约。

这是个被严重低估的洞察。John 说得很清楚：如果合约是现金结算的（settled on an index），套利就无法发生，价格将脱离物理现实。是"必须真实交割"这一条款，强迫了一百家公司在 Louisiana 的某个点上进行一场"电话亭里的刀战"，而这场刀战的价格发现，拉低了全美天然气的成本。

跨领域的连接让人震撼： - GitHub 的 Pull Request 机制打败了大公司的内部代码审查——因为它强制"真实合并"，不允许只做口头评审； - 司法系统之所以比学术辩论更能产生真理，是因为判决必须"实物交割"（被执行），不能停留在观点层面； - 科学的可重复性本质上就是"实物交割条款"——你的论文必须能被别人物理地复现，否则就是现金结算的废纸。

结论：想改变一个市场的结构，不要去改参与者，去改交割条款。 制度设计者的权力大于参与者的总和。

三、"盘绕的弹簧"：时间可以承载多少错误定价？

最令我震惊的细节：白银市场连续 5 到 8 年处于结构性供给赤字，但价格毫无反应。John 用了一个美妙的意象——"a coiling spring"，盘绕的弹簧。

这颠覆了"市场有效性"的朴素理解。市场不是实时翻译基本面的透明机器，它更像一个有记忆、有心理阻力、有历史心锚的生物。50 美元这个 1980 年 Bunker Hunt 时代的高点，像幽灵一样把白银价格困了四十年。

这个"结构性错位但不爆发"的模式，是识别真正大机会的关键信号。它出现在： - 人际关系：一段婚姻可以在根本性错位中维持十年，然后一周内崩溃； - 公司文化：员工满意度可以连续五年下滑却不出现离职潮，直到某个节点整个团队一夜清空； - 地质断层：张力可以累积几百年而无感知，直到一次 9 级地震释放全部； - 帝国衰落：罗马、唐朝、苏联的崩溃，事后看都是"盘绕"了很久的弹簧。

真正的交易机会不在于发现趋势，而在于识别"赤字已持续但价格未反应"的滞后区。 在那个区间里，时间是你的朋友，波动率是你的礼物。

四、意外收获：个体 > 政策

Aubrey McClendon 这个名字值得单独拿出来思考。John 说他"massively understated"——这个"疯狂钻井工"一个人改变的美国能源版图，比奥巴马的清洁能源政策加起来都多。煤炭被天然气取代不是环保法规的胜利，而是一个痴迷于打井的人把天然气价格打到了比煤还便宜的位置。

这与经济学教科书的"看不见的手"叙事相反——有时市场的转折点是一只非常具体、非常疯狂、有名有姓的手。Linus 之于 Linux、Steve Jobs 之于智能手机、中本聪之于比特币，都是这个范式。

启示：在分析市场时，不要只看"行业趋势"，要寻找那些单枪匹马改变赔率的疯子。 他们通常不在行业报告里，他们在被嘲笑的新闻头条里。

📝 转录文本

开场：供需与库存的第一性方程

There's one equation that you need to be thinking about as a commodities trader, and it's really really simple: supply minus demand equals the change in inventory.

And so when you get to these edge cases where storage is either full or empty, the only thing that you can do is move the price, because there there is no inventory to either draw from or no place to put the excess. So the price does all of the balancing.

And when I think about markets, I think back to 2020 when the crude market went to minus $40. At that time, it seemed, "wow, this is crazy. Crude oil shouldn't be minus $40." But there was basically nowhere to put it. And it made perfect sense to me.

欢迎与介绍

Hey, welcome back to Odds on Open. Today we're going to be having John Noring who used to had natural gas trading at Goldman, and he's going to be giving a lecture on commodities trading from first principles. I hope you enjoy.

Special thanks to Ethan Co for inviting me back to the Odds on Open podcast. Uh, it was a pleasure having a chat a few months back, and I'm really thrilled about the opportunity today to give a lecture that I have adapted from one that I've been giving to the Princeton University financial engineering department for the last handful of years, and it's titled Commodities Trading from First Principles.

议程

Okay. So a little bit about the agenda: - I'm going to talk about my background a little bit. - We're going to dip into what first principles actually mean for commodities markets broadly and for energy markets. - We're going to take a quick dive into the US natural gas market that I fondly refer to as Gas Vegas given its volatility. - We're going to talk a little bit about price signals, some trading, and some trades that I've put on. - And then we're going to finish up with some trends and observations of markets.

个人背景

I was an undergrad at Princeton University. I graduated in 2003 in the operations research and financial engineering department. While I was in undergrad, I had an internship at the Chicago Board of Trade. It was an awesome opportunity. But for those that can't see me in person, I'm not a huge guy. And back in 2001, the pit was filled with people that were over 6 feet tall and over 200 lb. And I was wrestling 133 pounds. So, I wasn't quite big enough to make it into the pits.

But I found an opportunity to get an internship with Goldman Sachs in their commodities department. I ended up getting a full-time offer. Worked there for a number of years. Loved loved nearly every minute of it — except the days I was losing money. But it was really really a wonderful experience.

I moved on to DRW in 2015 to trade commodities there, and I worked there for about three years. Again, wonderful experience. But I gave up professional trading in 2018. I still do a little bit in my PA. And I moved over to the exchange side of the business, and I started the Abbex Exchange and Clearing House in Singapore, and most recently Green Tiger Markets.

在高盛的交易范围

When I was at Goldman, I traded nearly everything except for what we refer to as breakfast — so no bacon, no coffee, no cocoa, no sugar. But I traded natural gas. That was the primary market that I was responsible for. And prior to Dodd-Frank, we were able to kind of punt around in some of the other markets. I traded a decent amount of crude oil, some coal. I love trading metals, platinum in particular, and then also love trading FX.

All these markets had their own characteristics, their own kind of liquidity constraints or volatility constraints, that I believe made me a better natural gas trader by taking positions in some of these adjacent commodities markets.

2000年代的 Nat Gas 市场

And so when I was a natgas trader at Goldman, and in particular in kind of the 2000s, the level of activity and volatility was extremely high, and we had some major major events that hit the market:

  • Hurricane Katrina and Rita in the same year, that took out a huge amount of Gulf of Mexico offshore production.
  • The blow up of Amaranth. Before the financial crisis — I think it's like 2007 — I think it was the largest financial loss of any institution from a trading perspective.
  • And then also we had John Arnold who — you can fact check me on this — we had always heard that he was the youngest self-made billionaire. He was a natural gas trader, really super high, and a great market participant for sure. But the returns that his hedge fund had were astronomical from the early 2000s until they shut things down in the middle 2010s.

Really really exciting time to be in the US nat gas markets.

第一性原理

Okay, so let's dive right into first principles.

There's one equation that you need to be thinking about as a commodities trader, and it's really really simple:

Supply − Demand = Change in Inventory

And so it sounds so simple, but really it's the foundation that commodities trading is built on. Yeah, there's technical factors that can cause the price to do something, and flows that are in the market that will cause it to do something else. But on a long enough time horizon, the supply demand balance is going to impact prices more than anything else. And that supply demand imbalance shows up in a change in inventory.

And so when we see supply greater than demand, inventory builds and in general prices fall. They might not fall right away, but they do fall eventually. If demand is greater than supply, inventory draws, prices rise.

Think about what's going on right now in the crude oil markets. We're seeing global inventories go down. And so the market is losing that cushion that it has against prices. And we're seeing some pretty big price moves in the crude market today. And that's demand is greater than supply, inventory is going down, prices are rising.

边界情况：仓储爆满或耗尽

And so when you get to these edge cases where storage is either full or empty, the only thing that you can do is move the price, because there is no inventory to either draw from or no place to put the excess. So the price does all of the balancing.

And when I think about markets, I think back to 2020 when the crude market went to minus $40. At that time it seemed, "wow, this is crazy. Crude oil shouldn't be minus $40." But there was basically nowhere to put it. And so minus $40 was the price that the market found to clear the price of crude oil that day. And it made perfect sense to me — like if you held those futures contracts to maturity and you took delivery, there was essentially no place for you to put it, or there was some risk that you would have a hard time placing it.

So storage — when it's full or empty, you don't have that cushion that the inventory gives you, and so the price has to do all of the balancing.

赞助商：Onyx

Most oil ETFs don't actually track the price of oil. They hold futures contracts, and many of them track oil for delivery up to 4 months from now. So when you buy an oil ETF, you're not betting on today's oil prices. You're betting on where the market thinks oil will be next season. That's not the kind of trade you meant to make.

Which brings me to today's sponsor, Onyx. They're the world's biggest market maker in oil derivatives, and they built the solution to this problem. The Onyx spot return crude oil etc., it tracks dated Brent — the price 78% of the world's oil deals are based on — and it reflects barrels shipping in the next 2 to 3 weeks. That exposure used to be reserved for oil majors and trading houses. Now you can buy it on Interactive Brokers. The ticker is OIL.

能源的两个核心主题

And so if we dive in a little deeper on energy specifically, there's a couple of maybe key themes that I would think about when I was a commodities trader, or when I was trading US nat gas and energy broadly.

主题一：能源是一切成本的根本

The first is energy is the fundamental cost of everything. So you think about $6.50 diesel prices today. Okay, well, that makes it more expensive to get your Amazon deliveries. It makes it more expensive to harvest corn. I mean, we're almost at the harvest or maybe it's even starting in some parts of the country today. And so that drives the cost up, and the farmer is going to need to get a higher price for his wheat because his cost of production has gone up.

And energy really flows through the entire supply chain probably more definitively than really any other factor. So energy is the fundamental cost of everything. That's just a general kind of statement about energy.

主题二：燃烧还是储存

And then when you think about like US nat gas trading, oil trading, there's an idea that energy comes out of the ground at a fairly consistent rate and you can either burn it or store it.

There's a couple of loaded words in there — which notably "fairly consistent rate". In the crude market, for example, we're seeing this massive disruption in supply coming out of the Persian Gulf. When you think to some of the times in the US nat gas market where it got incredibly cold and you saw some serious freeze offs in different regions around the country, that basically froze the gas in the wells. In those cases it's not a fairly consistent rate. But most of the time you've got a pretty good idea — like a really good guess for how much is coming out tomorrow is what came out today. And this idea of "burn it or store it" ties back in with the inventories.

市场作为价格信号

So markets matter, and markets are the way that price gets manifested in the real world. And so the signal that markets are sending when prices are high, it's sending a signal of scarcity — "hey, we're about out of inventories" or "our supply demand balance is really really tight". And that element of price discovery happens generally in commodities markets in the futures markets.

And so thinking about those key markets and the things that are sending price signals to the world: - Obviously we have oil. It's a huge market. Trades 5 billion barrels a day, trades 50 times the daily production. - You have the nat gas market globally. Breaking it down by regions, you have North America — which is the market that I focused on most. There's obviously Euro gas and power, and then you've got global LNG. (Now I would argue LNG is different than nat gas, but they all kind of fall under the same umbrella.) - And then obviously we have coal, and electricity markets.

不同能源的储存特性

So thinking about the idea of burn versus store:

  • Oil: Generally when oil's coming out of the ground, you're burning almost exactly the same amount every day. So you're producing about the same amount every day and you're consuming about the same amount every day. And you have these slight differences where the market's either tight or it's loose. And obviously today it's very very tight. And so inventories are going down. But in general, oil, we're consuming it at the same rate that we're producing it.

  • Natural gas: A little bit different. The entire summer in the US, we're injecting gas into storage caverns around the country to be used during the winter when it gets really cold. In the Northeast, for example, the gas is coming out of the ground at a fairly consistent rate, but we're not burning it as much during the summer. And so we're building inventories, but we know that the inventories need to be built because the system can't deliver enough flowing gas to the market during the winter.

  • Coal: A little bit different. Coal, you can dig that stuff out of the ground and stick it in a pile and wait. And because of that, it's a lot easier to store it. You essentially just need a cyclone fence — and even then, not really, because it's really hard to steal.

  • Power: At the other end of the spectrum. The power needs to be consumed at the instant that it's made.

From a graphical perspective, thinking about it from easiest to store to hardest to store: you have obviously coal (easiest to store, cyclone fence, maybe a couple of Rottweilers, and your coal is safe). Oil requires some tanks, because if you just pour it out, it will just spread all over the ground, and you don't want to see that happen. Natural gas though is a commodity that has to be stored under pressure. It's generally stored underground in caverns. There's a number of salt caverns in the US Gulf Coast that provide a lot of storage flexibility, and so gas gets injected in there one day and taken out the next day. In other parts of the country, you're injecting into depleted reservoirs and other aquifers, and the cycle availability is significantly different. But that nat gas needs to be stored under pressure and it needs to be transported via pipeline, whereas oil, not as much — stored in tanks, transported by pipeline or on a VLCC for example. It's just a very different way of moving the energy around. Power is very hard to store on a relative basis. Now the technologies are changing between lithium ion batteries at utility scale as well as some impounded hydro that's acting as batteries. But in general storing power is very very difficult relative to the other three forms of energy.

深入美国天然气市场

Okay. So let's get into the nat gas market. We've talked a lot about burning and storing, and the various commodities markets or energy markets.

为什么价格波动如此剧烈？

Digging into the US nat gas market, the question I get asked all the time is: why do prices move so much?

And it really comes down to the fact that natural gas is an extremely inelastic market in the short run. Now, in the longer run, yes, there's a lot of flexibility that can happen. But ultimately, if you turn your heat on during the winter and it's cold in Chicago, you expect your heat to come on, and you'll effectively pay any price to have your heat come on. And so because of that, when demand starts to get into the 90th, 95th percentile, you start to see some pretty wild price action because rationing demand with price is really really hard in the nat gas market.

天气驱动的波动

Gas prices also are very volatile because they are weather-driven. And if we think back to the weather in December of 2025, it was extremely warm for nearly the entire country. But that shifted in kind of early to mid January, from being essentially record warm to being record cold. And that swing in weather demand caused the prices to nearly double in a week. And so you don't see those types of swings in the supply demand balance in the oil market like you do in the US nat gas market and in the electricity market — it's happening pretty frequently. So on a spot basis, the price is extremely volatile. Gas specifically moves a lot because the weather can change a lot and weather is a huge part of the demand side.

仓储的限制

And then also storage. There's only a limited amount of storage. And so there's roughly 100 BCF a day that are coming out of the ground on any given day. It's a little over that now, but nice round numbers. The total storage capacity in the US is roughly 4.5 trillion cubic feet. And so you kind of do the math there and you say, "all right, it's about 45 days of storage." Now the storage caverns couldn't meet all of the demand. So you do need that flowing gas. But the storage is finite. And when you get into situations where you're having a hard time putting more gas into storage, you can see prices really evaporate. And that's back to that situation where price is the thing that is balancing the market. There's no place else to store it, so we're going to take price lower.

为什么美国价格如此之低？Henry Hub 的秘密

All right. So why are prices so low in the US?

And if you look back at prices kind of over the last 20 years or so — I realize this graph only goes to 2019, but it's the same story. In fact, it's much much worse for the rest of the world for the last 5 years or so. But the US — or the price of gas in the US — is essentially always lower than anywhere else in the world. And the question is why is that?

Yes, we've got great and super deep capital markets. We have a legal system that supports private property rights. We have a great pipeline system. And we've got pretty good geology. But any of these on their own doesn't really truly separate us from those other markets.

But the one thing that does separate the US nat gas market from global gas markets is the existence of the Henry Hub contract.

Henry Hub 的独特位置

And so when I say "the Henry Hub contract," what does that mean? That's the futures contract, which we'll get into the details in just a moment. But Henry Hub is uniquely positioned in that there's a number of pipelines that flow into and out of the Henry Hub. There's a decent amount of production that's in that region. There's also a decent amount of storage, and those various pipelines in general can be contracted out by third parties. So what that means is the Henry Hub is one of the most competitive gas hubs in the world. You have roughly a hundred companies that can make or take delivery of gas at the Henry Hub. And so it's essentially a knife fight in a phone booth at the Henry Hub on any given day in the physical cash market.

期货合约的标准化

And so for US nat gas, the futures contract has standardized all of the terms of trade. So it's Henry Hub, Louisiana. It's 10,000 MMBTUs per contract. Pipeline gas is the spec. Sure, there's some ethane that can be in there, but there's a fairly narrow range of spec that is pipeline grade gas. The delivery method of the futures contracts is physical via pipeline. Which is really really important. It doesn't settle based off of an index or a survey of where people say the prices are, but it actually physically delivers.

So if you're looking at "how much does it cost to store gas at Henry Hub?" — okay, well, I'm going to get paid X percentage to store from this, or it's going to cost me X percentage to store from month one to month two. But hey, the futures market is pricing something that's wider. You're like, okay, I should go long the front, I should store it, and then I should sell the second month and ARB all of that out. And it's all of that arbitrage that's going on by the market that basically keeps everything in line in the futures market. But it only works because it physically delivers. So if it financially settled, then there's no arbitrage opportunity. You're just praying that hey, you've called the index right.

基差市场

Okay. So Henry Hub — great futures contract, but it's not perfect for all players. And so this brings in the concept of basis.

We've seen many cases where the market is well supplied in Henry Hub, but it gets really cold in Chicago or New York or New England, and the prices there go ballistic. And if you were a consumer based in Chicago using Henry Hub futures to hedge your position, you have a massive basis from Louisiana all the way up to Chicago. And if it gets cold enough, all the pipes going from Louisiana to Chicago are going to be full. And so the price is going to have to balance the market.

And so what's ended up happening is the market has developed these various basis markets. They tend to trade spot — or all of them trade spot. I think it's like five or six hundred different points now. It was only like 200 when I was trading. So all of these points around the country can be traded, and some of them you can trade some forwards, but they generally trade as a spread to Henry Hub. So Henry Hub is the benchmark contract and everything else is trading as a spread to it. Now, most things are pretty correlated most of the time, but you do run into situations where, like, Southern California gas, it's doing its entire own thing, or New England gas is doing its own thing, but that's because it's constrained by the pipeline supply or the demand in the market.

Gas Vegas：极端波动

All right, so Gas Vegas. We've talked a little bit about the basics of US nat gas, the futures contract, basis, and how the market works from kind of a high level. But we're going to dive in now when natural gas gets extremely volatile, which it does at least a couple times a year. I like to refer to it as Gas Vegas.

So again, tying in burn versus store, changes of inventory: - In a bullish market, burn is greater than supply, and so storage draws down. - In a bearish market, you have supply greater than the amount that you're burning, and so storage builds.

And so that manifests itself in price. We can see here with this plot — the red line is the Henry Hub front-month futures contract back to the early 2000s. And you can see a spike in 2001, another spike in 2003, another one in 2004, another one in 2005, another one in 2007, another one in 2008, another one all throughout 2014, 2022. There's been a number of spikes in the market. But if you look at the inventories relative to their historical averages, you tend to see that the prices spike when inventories are going from fairly loose to fairly tight. And then the price reverts when the inventory goes from fairly tight to fairly loose.

需求冲击的典型案例

The demand shocks that the US nat gas market has experienced cause some of these price moves that are very very extreme, and they jump out from you on the chart.

  • 2000-2001 winter: Extremely cold winter. The price went to $10 for the first time. Prior to that point, the highest price Henry Hub had ever traded was like $4 or something like that. So it created an entirely new price regime during that winter.

  • 2003: Extremely cold right at the end of the contract. Storage was getting down to critically low levels, and you saw the price go from basically $6 to $10 in effectively a day. The market — it was right up before expiration. So the liquidity was a lot lower and everybody was squaring up their positions, and they were looking to see "hey do I need the gas for the month of March or can I wing it?" And the market effectively priced, "hey, you're going to need the gas." And so the March versus April spread blew out. It was a very trying time for many nat gas traders that I know. Luckily for me, I was still in college at that point in time, so I was just observing from the sidelines.

  • 2004-2005: Hurricane Ivan, Hurricane Katrina and Rita in 2005.

  • 2006-2007: When the price made its all-time high of around $16, there was an earthquake in Japan that knocked out a lot of the nuclear power plants, and Japan started importing a lot more LNG. And at the time, which might seem kind of strange today, the US was actually also an importer of LNG to make the market balance. And so the US and Japan were effectively competing for LNG cargos. And it took the price right up to $16 where the US was able to send that price signal to the market — tell the forward demand "hey, you need to tamp it down a little bit"; supply side "hey, bring on whatever you can; let's get a few cargos in; let's build a little bit of inventory." The market was roofing all the way through till it was right around New Year's 2007, I think. And then the weather broke, got extremely warm, and the price collapsed.

  • 2008: Big run-up in 2007-2008. Obviously, financial crisis happened in 2008. But at the same time, on Fourth of July 2008, we had Aubrey McClendon come out and say, "We found a Saudi Arabia of gas and it's in Louisiana," and the market never looked back after that moment. That changed everything. Thinking back over time, that was a moment where kind of everything changed.

价格信号：供给端的页岩革命

Okay, so we've talked a lot about markets being tight, markets being loose, this idea of price signals where high prices tell the market to build supply. Like, how does that manifest itself in the US nat gas market?

I like to look at this map of the various shale basins in the US. And if you look at this map, you say, "man, most of the US has shale basins that could be drilled." Now, why isn't every state producing like crazy? Well, some of them are easier to access than others. Some of them are deeper, some of them are richer, some of them are thicker seams.

水平钻井技术的转折

But this idea of the shale revolution really got into gear in the late 2000s as hydraulic fracturing and horizontal drilling started coming into the market. And so that change from vertical drilling to horizontal drilling really changed everything.

So if you were drilling for gas in the late 90s or early 2000s, you would get a rig, you'd drill straight down, you would maybe frack it, and effectively the gas that was around the wellhead — or sorry, around the well that you drilled — was all the gas that you could get. Now the technology changed such that the drilling rigs would start vertically but then they would turn horizontally, and they would be able to drill through thousands of feet of shale. Which is really what it took, because the amount of gas per volume of shale tends to be a lot lower than a conventional reservoir. And so if the volume of gas is a lot lower, you need to have a lot more exposure in basically the bore face or the producing part of the well. And so that horizontal drilling technology, the great computing power that was being applied to it, really set off that shale revolution.

And so it's still going on today. I would argue that the US gas market is constrained by pipelines, not by geology. And so the ability for drillers to go in, drill wells, and get that gas to market — the most challenging thing for some of them is finding pipe capacity to get that gas to market. And this trend from basically lower left to upper right in the various shale basins around the country, I would expect that that's going to continue for quite some time.

价格信号：需求端的增长

All right, the other side of the coin — low prices build consumption.

So all this nat gas that we've been producing — which by the way, much of it is actually a byproduct of just drilling for crude oil. Like when crude oil prices are high, natural gas is also often found in the same locations, or in the stream with the crude as it's coming out. So the shale basin productivity plus all of the associated gas means we've got way more gas today than we had 20 years ago. I mean it's roughly three times as much gas today as we had — at least two and a half times. So where does it all go?

需求结构

  • Industrial side: Yeah, there's industrial consumption. It doesn't change much from year to year. Though the onshoring of some manufacturing, we're expecting to see demand go up. Maybe building some of these steel mills, maybe they're going to be consuming a lot of energy. But on the industrial side, yeah, it's pretty static from one year to the next.

  • Residential and commercial consumption: It's nearly all heating and air conditioning demand. So during the summer, when you flip your AC on, it's pulling electricity. Natural gas is the kind of marginal supplier of electricity to the US power grid. So if it's hot in the summer, you're going to use more nat gas. If it's cold in the winter, you're going to use more nat gas and vice versa.

  • Power generation: We touched on that a little bit. Flip on your AC — power plant needs to produce more electricity, and in general, at the margin, it's going to be US nat gas.

  • LNG exports: I mentioned earlier when the price went to $16 in 2006-2007 that the US was an importer of LNG. Well, today we have so much gas that we're the world's largest exporter of LNG.

  • Data centers: The real wild card in my mind is the data centers. I've read a number of forecasts that have just some astronomical levels of demand. And I think there's some concern in the gas industry whether enough gas can be produced, but given the profitability of both data centers and if the gas price were higher, I feel like they're going to find a way to make it work.

从煤炭到天然气的转变

When looking at the sources of electricity from call it 15 years ago to more recently, the US was burning quite a lot of coal in 2010. And in fact roughly twice as much coal was used to generate electricity — or twice as much electricity was generated by coal as by US nat gas. That flipped.

And the reason it flipped is because of the shale revolution, which caused excess supply and forced the prices down. And it made gas competitive with coal, because historically coal was a really really cheap commodity. You just dig it out of the ground and you burn it and it's really really easy. Gas became even easier. And when you factor in some of the environmental characteristics to burning gas versus burning coal, gas started to win in — you know, there's been substantially zero coal plants built in the last decade. So at least in the US.

Aubrey McClendon 的被低估影响

So was this a case of "hey, the government said you can't burn coal anymore, and the market just picked gas"? Yes, that was a factor. But I would argue that this man on the left, Aubrey McClendon — his impact on the US is massively understated. He was a master at being able to raise capital and go out and drill as many wells as possible. And people viewed him as being reckless. Yeah, he was a mad driller. The guy loved drilling for gas. And that incremental production caused the price to go down, and it made gas-fired power plants very competitive with coal, and it was really easy for the market to switch.

交易的本质

Let's talk a little bit about trading. So what do traders do? Is it buy low and sell high? I feel like that's not really a very great description of what traders do. So I think it's something else.

And when I was at Goldman, we developed this framework — or at least I was taught this framework — where what is trading?

四步框架

1. Idea Generation: This is doing your research, coming up with a view on the market. "Hey, I'm bullish crude oil. I'm looking at what's going on in the Middle East. I think that's going to be disrupted for a long period of time, and in fact, I think the hostilities could get even worse and it's going to cause less crude to come out of there. So that's going to make crude tighter and makes me bullish crude oil." Okay, that's my idea generation. I'm bullish crude oil.

2. Expression: Now thinking about how do I express that bullish view on the market? Do I sell puts? Do I buy calls? Do I buy futures? Do I buy time spreads? Do I buy Exxon stock? Do I buy Marathon? Like what should I do? If I pick something like, "you know what, I'm going to buy Brent because I think Brent is going to be even tighter, but I don't want to buy spot month Brent, I want to buy three months out or so because the curve is pretty backwardated, but I think it's just going to roll up the curve." So I'm going to express it by buying three-month out Brent futures.

3. Execution: How do I get into this position? Do I just call up my broker and say, "you know what, I've got — I can buy a total of 100. I have enough money that I can cover the margin on 100 units. Okay, just go and buy those." Or do I do something different? And do I piece it into the market? Do I wait for it to dip? Do I do a little bit and if it starts working and I get some confirmation from the market, do more? So it's this is the tricky part of being a trader. It's all about timing.

4. Money Management: Once I've come up with my idea, I decided how I'm going to express it, I decided how I'm going to execute it — then the most critical factor is money management.

顺境中的管理，才是最难的

Most people think about money management being what do you do when things are not going well. Like yeah, you can set your stop limits. Hey, eventually you'll run out of money in your account and your clearing broker will liquidate you maybe against your wishes. But there are things that can happen — well, they're within your control if you take your risk down. So basically money management is what you do when it's not going well. Okay, hey, if crude comes back to $70, I need to get out. Okay, so I've got my downside scenario.

The question is: what do you do when it's going well?

If you bought Bitcoin at $300 in 2017 and sold it out at $900 two or three months later, you probably felt pretty smart, but then it proceeded to trade to $120,000. So what do you do when it's going well? And that's a question that — at least for me — that's the hardest question to answer. "Okay, well, I need to constantly be looking at the market. Do I still believe in the trade? Do I still believe in it at this price level? What's my risk/reward? How is this thing — who's left to buy it from me? If I'm long, who else needs to buy this thing?" And if I have a hard time answering those questions, I should immediately start reducing risk. I don't need to get out of everything. But if I'm less convicted when the price has moved up because the underlying supply demand balances are changing, I need to adjust my position.

案例：白银交易

Let's look at a market very near and dear to my heart — silver.

I have been watching silver for basically my entire adult trading career. I was born in 1981, so the first big move in silver happened before I was born.

Bunker Hunt 的故事

But I imagine most people don't know who that is on the left hand side. That's Bunker Hunt. At one point in time, he was the world's wealthiest man. He bought somewhere between 200 and 300 million ounces of silver physical along with futures in the late 70s in the kind of $2 to $4 range, and it ended up trading up to $50. And so he was one of the world's wealthiest men. It was outrageous.

Now it all came to an end very very quickly. The futures exchange, the COMEX — I think it was the COMEX — changed the rules and said "only liquidating trades," and the market proceeded to trade down something like $30 or $40 without really touching the sides. And so he got margin called on a lot of his positions, and yeah, it was not a very good situation. He ended up all right.

两个 50 美元高点

But the market traded up to $50 in the early 80s. It traded up to $50 again in I think it was around 2011. And if you recall after the financial crisis, the Fed was doing its zero interest rate policy. There was helicopter money basically coming in. You had quantitative easing. You had all these different things that basically meant there was more dollars out there chasing the same amount of stuff. And silver was one of the ways that the market manifested that and demonstrated it. And the price moved up quite dramatically, traded up to like $50 or so, before the market said "all right, we've had enough. The price is high enough. We're going to kill off demand. We're going to increase supply based on these prices." And the silver market entered into another bear market.

But because this high that was hit in 2011 was roughly the same high that had been hit 30 years earlier, the market had this psychological block to it, which said "well, the highest that silver can go is 50 bucks."

盘绕的弹簧

And so anybody who's been watching the silver market for the last 12 months or so knows that it can do something a lot different than 50 bucks. I was extremely bullish the silver market and had a decent-sized position on. I was looking at the market, looking at the supply demand balances, and saw that the market was tight — it was in deficit. So demand was greater than supply for like five years in a row. And if you factor in ETF silver that was being held, it was almost like eight years where the market was in structural deficit.

But the market wasn't moving up. You could have bought at 35 bucks in the middle of 2025. And so the market was kind of bouncing around a little bit. It had made a low, you know, post-pandemic or middle of the pandemic low at like 12 or 13 bucks, and it had bounced back, but it was still kind of trading sideways. But the market was in deficit, and it felt like if you watched the price action and you just sort of looked at the market, you could kind of see that the market was kind of coiling like a spring. It was because that structural deficit existed, and so you just had this steady bid to the market, but it didn't want to rally, and it wasn't demonstrating it in the price action.

白银的供需结构

Taking a step back and thinking about what's driving silver prices:

  • Supply side: Most silver is produced as a byproduct of mining for other metals. Only roughly a quarter of silver is from primary silver mines, meaning their main focus is mining for silver. And then to balance the market out, you get some recycling. So if you think about grandma's silver tea set — if the price gets high enough, all that stuff starts to get melted down again.

  • Demand side: A number of different sources of demand. You've got industrial demand — think like solar panels, electric vehicles, your iPhone, Tomahawk cruise missiles. There's a lot of silver used in all those because it's such a great conductor. There's a decent amount used for jewelry, but that is a relatively modest amount. And then there's a huge amount of investment demand as people want to get out of dollars and into some hard assets, and maybe they think "hey, I can't afford gold, so I'll just buy silver."

  • Gold-silver ratio: One other factor to look at in the silver market. Gold was about 100 or 110 times the price of silver in mid 2025. And if you look at that over time, that's a pretty high ratio. It can go — it's generally a lot lower than that.

And so thinking about the market, it was a coiling spring. The gold silver ratio moved to not all-time highs but definitely kind of like fifth percentile or so. And the market was really setting itself up for a move.

应用四步框架

So for silver, the idea generation side of it is: "hey, silver looks tight. The market's in deficit and it looks like it's going to be tight for a while." A lot of this incremental demand was coming from solar panels, and just looking at the installed capacity around the world and the demand from solar panels, it's going to be pretty high. So bullish silver.

How do you express that? Well, at the time the way that I expressed it was I started buying futures. But I believed that the market could reprice and go to an entirely different price regime, and the market was not pricing that. So you could buy $70 calls, $80 calls, $100 calls — and at the time they felt like they were a couple of cents, they were really really cheap. So I bought futures as the core position and then options which would kick in if the market actually did redefine itself.

Execution came to buying a little bit and basically scaling in as the market confirmed that it was looking to go. So I started buying in the low $30s. Yeah, there was a couple of drawdowns before it finally ended up taking off. But silver is liquid enough that at the time you could generally get some on and you wouldn't miss it too badly.

顺境中的失误

And so then it's the question of money management. We talked earlier — hey, what do you do when it's not going well? What do you do when it is going well?

One of the failures I had on the trade was I wasn't constantly re-evaluating "hey, should I still be bullish here at $120?" At the time I was thinking "man, this thing could trade like three, four, $500. It's going to the moon. This is going to be like Bitcoin again, and I've got a big position on." That thinking was kindly communicated to me to be wrong by the market, with the late January selloff from $120 to $65 in essentially one day.

趋势与观察

Let's try and tie some things up here with a few trends that we're seeing in markets. Some broad trends as well as some observations.

1. 你永远大不过市场

One of the key observations from my time being a trader at Goldman Sachs is: you are never bigger than the market. And so you can have a big position, but you should never put yourself in a position for catastrophic losses. And Amaranth is a great example of a firm that had massive positions on. They were way too big for the market, and when the market turned against them, they basically closed out the fund.

2. 鸭型曲线（Duck Curve）

A trend that we're seeing in energy that I think is worth keeping an eye on — particularly as more solar comes into the market, and potentially more storage from batteries and perhaps from hydro storage — is this idea of the duck curve, which is midday prices being extremely depressed as people are installing solar panels. And at a time when they used to consume a ton of electricity, the actual midday supply is a lot higher, and it causes the price to go down. So we see this in the California market for example. It's somewhat subdued in the Texas market, though we have a lot of solar there. But you look at some markets even like Philippines electricity — because they're installing so much solar there, you're starting to see prices depressed during the day but not as much as they are in places like California. So duck curve is definitely something to keep an eye on in power markets around the world.

3. LNG 出口的放量

Export of LNG by the US over the next handful of years is going to be a game changer. The question — I think probably a better question — is: where's it all going to go? Because the US and Canada are really ramping up exports of LNG, and the question on the demand side: okay, can the US gas market deliver enough gas to these terminals on a consistent basis because they're all contracted out? And once that gas gets turned into LNG and put on a vessel, is there actually a home for it?

I think the forward market right now is telling you that prices in kind of 2030, 2031 for LNG are going to be a lot lower than they are today. Now today they're tight because obviously we've got things going on in the Persian Gulf, and so supply is restricted. But we'll sort of see how this market is going to develop, because there is so much LNG export capacity coming to the US. It's going to have big impacts on the supply demand balance for US domestic gas and then for Euro gas and power as well as JKM.

4. 衍生品自动化，实物交易仍靠人

One other observation that I've had kind of over the last decade or so: when I was trading gas, there were definitely physical gas traders and derivatives traders. I was a derivatives trader. What we're seeing is a lot of that derivatives trading being automated, and it's been going on for a while. Yes, there still are some humans that are trading derivatives, but when it comes to banks having big trading desks where there's an option guy and a futures guy and all the different stuff that's tied in there — a lot of that's happening on a much more automated basis.

But one of the interesting takeaways is that the physical side of the business is actually probably more interesting today than it was 20 years ago, because there are so many more pipes, there's so much more gas production, there's so much optionality that's built into so many of these contracts. Being a physical gas trader, reading the contracts, understanding them, understanding where the optionality lies — is really a skill set that is in demand. It's going to be in demand for quite some time. Claude's pretty smart, but I think when it comes to moving physical molecules, those guys are going to have a job a little bit longer than the average bear.

5. 时间视野的分化

An evolution in trading firms has been a bifurcation of what I would call time horizon. And so you have very short-term trading, latency sensitive — Jump Trading, DRW, Citadel, the market makers of the world. Their whole business is built on speed. And then on the other side — which are very few of these players now, and Warren just recently stepping away from the business — you have Warren Buffett, and he would buy businesses or make investments in companies and hold them for decades, because he would get in at a good price into a business that he understood and he believed that over time that it would outperform. And you look at his returns for the last 60-odd years and they're pretty good.

结语：名声与房子

So if I can leave you with one closing thought — it was a really really good piece of advice that I received when I was in college and I was thinking about taking a job on Wall Street. It was from a mentor of mine who spent some time at Lehman Brothers and Solomon Brothers, and he gave me this really really great piece of advice. He said:

"If you can leave Wall Street with your name intact and your house paid for, you're ahead of 90% of the people who go there."

And at the time, he told me this a couple of times, and I was like "okay, yeah, yeah, yeah, okay. I got it." But after spending the better part of 20 years working on Wall Street, it's really begun to sink in. There's going to be a lot of opportunities to basically sully your name. There's going to be get-rich-quick schemes. There's going to be opportunities to maybe do something dishonest. But ultimately at the end of the day, your number one asset that you have is your name. And so your number two asset theoretically is your house. And so if you can have that house paid for, you go to Wall Street, you do well financially, you have your house paid for, and you don't have any other worries — you're ahead of 90% of the people that go there.

All right. Well, thanks everybody. It's been a pleasure. Ethan, thanks so much for having me again, and look forward to reading the comments section.

观看原视频 →
