## 一、库存即缓冲：被忽略的"价格暴力定理"
John 讲的那个"一行公式"——供给减去需求等于库存变化——表面看像废话，但真正的洞见藏在**边界条件**里：当库存耗尽或爆满时，价格必须独自承担全部再平衡的任务。这就是为什么 2020 年原油会跌到负 40 美元：不是油突然变成了坏东西，而是**缓冲系统失灵后，价格被迫承担起本应由仓储承担的职责**。
这个原理远远超出了商品交易。它其实是一切"缓冲-信号"系统的底层律法： - **急诊室没有床位时，分诊医生的决策会变得残酷**——因为再没有空间让错误被稀释； - **一个人情绪"库存"耗尽时，一件小事可以引爆剧烈反应**——因为心理冗余为零，波动直接传导到行为； - **AI 上下文窗口接近爆满时，模型开始丢弃或幻觉**——没有空间，Token 就只能通过"价格"（概率权重的畸变）来清算。
**库存是文明的减震器。** 当你观察一个系统突然变得"疯狂"时，先去看它的缓冲池，而不是去看它的驱动力。
## 二、Henry Hub 悖论：合约设计打败了地质禀赋
最反直觉的观察是：美国天然气比全世界都便宜，不是因为资本市场、不是因为

item.title: [Sequoia Capital] Bringing Continual Learning to Every Company: Trajectory’s Ronak Malde
item.dc:creator: Sequoia Capital
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最意外的观察：Trajectory 不是在卖"更好的模型"，而是在卖"告别垄断的权利"

表面上，这是一家做 continual learning 基础设施的公司。但如果你把 Ronak 说的话逐层剥开，会发现一个藏得很深的叙事：前沿大模型实验室正在重演 18 世纪东印度公司的角色——它们垄断了"智能的制造"，所有企业都是向一个神谕（oracle）进贡的藩属。Harvey 做了 30 年法律积累，却只能在别人家的模型上"写 prompt"；Rogo 懂金融研究的每一个微表情，却只能租用 GPT 的"通用大脑"。

Ronak 真正在卖的，是让每个垂直公司重新拿回自己命运的权利（"shape their own destiny"）。这不是技术产品，这是一次反垄断的生产资料再分配。他引用 Adam Smith 不是修辞——他真的认为 AI 正处在"前工业革命阶段"，而 continual learning 就是让"手工作坊"进化为"专业化社会"的那场革命。

二、跨领域连接：从 AAA 地图到 Google Maps，再到——金融衍生品定价史

Ronak 用 AAA → MapQuest → Google Maps 来类比 continual learning 的三个阶段，这个类比很美。但更深的一层联系他没说：这与金融学里从 Black-Scholes 静态定价模型到实时动态对冲（delta hedging）的演化，是完全同构的。

  • Black-Scholes（1973）= 预训练模型：给定假设，一次性算出价格；
  • 实时波动率曲面校准 = RLHF / 微调：定期用新数据修正；
  • 高频 delta hedging = continual learning：每一笔成交都反过来更新整个头寸。

而他提出的 "trajectory 作为经济价值单元"，本质上就是把"token 经济"升级为"交易经济"——这与芝加哥交易所从"报价"到"成交回路"的转变是同一个物理。谁控制了反馈回路的闭合速度，谁就控制了整个系统的有效信息密度。所以当他说 "unit of work is a trajectory" 的时候，他实际上在重新定义AI 时代的度量衡——从卡路里换成了做功。

三、藏在"好奇心"背后的哲学暗流：他其实在反对硅谷主流的 AGI 路线

这段最容易被忽略，但最锋利：Ronak 把当前研究明确分成两派——RSI（递归自我改进） vs Continual Learning——并毫不掩饰地站队后者。

这是一次伦理立场的技术化宣言。RSI 路线（Ilya、部分 OpenAI、部分 Anthropic 都在思考）本质上是"把模型关进黑盒让它自己卷自己"，是一种无人类参与的智能爆炸。而 continual learning 坚持"必须通过与人类交互来学习"——这意味着： - 模型的进化速度被人类的工作节奏锚定，无法失控逃逸； - 每次学习都携带一次人类意图的"签名"，对齐问题被结构性地嵌入到训练循环中，而非事后补丁。

这是一种非常罕见的技术上的保守主义浪漫：他认为让 AI 变慢一点、更黏人一点，恰恰是让它变得真正强大的前提。

更惊人的连接是：这与儿童发展心理学中 Vygotsky 的"最近发展区"（Zone of Proximal Development）理论几乎一模一样——学习只在"学习者当前能力"与"有经验者的引导"之间那条缝隙里发生。Ronak 等于在说：AGI 不是 Prometheus 式的盗火，而是 Vygotsky 式的师徒制。

四、一个隐藏的产品哲学 bug（或者说，更深的洞察）

他说"产品经理像园丁，设好 trellis，产品自己生长"——听起来很美。但这里有一个自我指涉的悖论他没有点破：

如果产品是自我进化的，那么"园丁的审美（taste）"本身就是最稀缺的资源。

当每个公司都能 one-click 训练自己的模型时，差异化不再来自算法、数据或算力，而来自"你知道什么是好"的能力——这恰好是 Ronak 反复说的 "what good looks like"。

这意味着：continual learning 普及之后，"品味"将成为新的护城河，而品味是极难规模化的、极度依赖创始人心智的、几乎无法外包的东西。换句话说，AI 工具化越彻底，创始人本人作为"审美源代码"的权重就越高。

这呼应了一个更古老的真相——文艺复兴时期美第奇家族不是最好的画家，但他们定义了什么是好画。未来的 AI 公司 CEO 会越来越像美第奇，越来越不像工程师。

📝 转录文本

开场：来自 Apple 的产品哲学

A lot of our philosophy in product actually comes from Apple. In like the early 2000s, you had a computer that had access to the internet and you had a phone that you could make phone calls. And I think no one really thought to put the two together until Apple said, "Okay, what if you actually put the internet on a handheld device and combine the two?"

And I think by doing this of basically putting training, eval, and deployment in one place, making that just dead simple for every single person to do. And then you can close the loop and basically now upload that model back to production, gather new traces. It suddenly is this magical paradigm that I think every single company is going to adopt very soon.

[music] [music]

什么是 Continual Learning？从 AAA 地图到 Google Maps

>> Reach, thank you for joining us. It's a pleasure to have you. We would love to dig into a bunch of what you're building, how you see the world of research, and where you think the future is going. Um, maybe to start, you guys spend a lot of time thinking about continual learning. Can you define it for us? I think you've also said this field is in a state of pseudo continual learning. What is real and how will we know when we get to the real thing?

>> That's a great question. So, uh, when I think about continual learning, I actually think the human brain is a really good model, uh, for where we should aspire to get to. Like in some sense we are true continual learners. We learn online. We are constantly updating, iterating.

And I think the world we're in right now with agents and AI uh is kind of like you said pseudo continual learning. When I was growing up, my family used to do a bunch of road trips, right? And I don't know how you guys did things, but we would go to AAA back in the day and they would give us a bunch of these maps. They would highlight everything, and then we'd go on our road trip. And if there's any point where we wanted to change our route, we'd have to either call Triple-A or like go to a physical location.

And I feel like that's the world we're in right now where we have these amazing, amazing agents, they're very intelligent, we have these mapping algorithms, but you can only consult offline a couple of places. And anytime you want to update your course, you have to just do an entire mass batch update.

What the first goal and what we're building at Trajectory is first the ability to just democratize that access, right? To even just training these models and customizing them for what people want. I think of that as kind of like MapQuest, where suddenly it's still offline, but we at least got the ability for everyone to not need to go to AAA, but get the ability to map these algorithms.

But the final stage of continual learning is something more like Google Maps where every single time you're driving, every route that you make, it is updating. It's learning in aggregate what the fastest route is and where the traffic is. That's the world I want to get to.

架构层面的变革正在发生

>> That's a really good analogy. So we had recently we had Rich Sutton and David Silver on the show and both of them kind of made the comment that continual learning isn't really possible with today's architectures. I'm curious in your point of view what's doable, what's not doable, what's the state of play? Do we need major architectural leaps to kind of bring this to fruition? Where are we today?

>> Yeah. So it's funny because when you think about a transformer and LLMs, I feel like a lot of people have seen maybe Karpathy's tiny GPT video or something where you basically have the stack of attention blocks and transformers that are built on top of each other. And a lot of LLM scaling has just been stacking these transformers on top of each other.

But when you look at any paper like DeepSeek v4.1 flash that just came out recently, their architecture is actually kind of lobotomized or changed a lot of that base architecture, where you have things like fast and slow memory within the weights. You have skip connections that are going between layer 2 and layer 50.

And so I think these architectural changes are actually already happening within the base models. And it will be a key component, I do agree, for continual learning. Where I want to sit is basically leverage all of that technology and research that's happening at the architectural level but then actually connect the dots to the real world.

Because at the end of the day, the real value of any AI progress, but certainly continual learning, is how are people actually using models in the real world. And I think companies have this idea of basically what good looks like in their mind and the hardest part of this entire loop is then translating that to actual improvements for the model. I think that's where that missing layer is.

从 Windsurf 到 Trajectory：Aha Moment

>> Yeah. So how do you connect the dots to the real world and how much of that is product or productizable and how much of that is just hand-holding and helping people through the process?

>> Yeah. So up until now it's been really hard to just go from this fact of data to intelligence. Up until now that's only been in the labs. And you need a massive research team.

So in the last couple years we started to have vertical companies going into this space as well and building a massive research team. I was previously at Windsurf where we embarked on this journey and trained a model. So did Cursor as well with Cursor Composer. But the problem was you needed hundreds of millions of dollars of R&D in compute. You needed a really massive research team to invest in, and then you also needed a lot of time. So it took us six to nine months to actually get to that point where we could train a frontier model. And that is with a kind of hand-holding sort of consulting model. That's still sort of the world that we live in.

I think any good product exists when you have every single company in the world trying to do the same thing over and over and over again. And if you can package that into a really beautiful interface that just says "here are the knobs and levers that you care about to translate that what good looks like," and then everything else is packaged away — I think that's a beautiful interface to do that.

>> What did you and your co-founders see when you were at Windsurf and when they were working on models as well to help you realize "hey this is repeatable, that there is a product to be built"? When did you have that aha moment and that realization?

>> Yeah. So part of it was, you know, we were training these models on production. Basically, saying what are all these edits, the retries that are happening in the product, and learning from that at Windsurf. Combined with that, my co-founders — Michael was at DeepMind as well, he was working on Gemini Robotics, and they're starting to see the same thing where you could actually deploy these robots in the real world, build continual learning infrastructure to basically allow these robots to update every single day. And then Arjun was at Apple working on the Vision Pro. The same thing was he was basically saying "how can we take artist feedback and use that for multimodal foundation models."

So in one way or another, all of us were basically figuring out this grand alignment problem of how do you actually take this feedback from the real world and improve the models. The problem is we were all at these big research labs, right? And so I started to realize okay, continual learning is going to be the next learning paradigm.

Is there a way that I can actually do this within the labs? And the thing I very quickly realized is at DeepMind, our entire focus was training one massive model and then distributing that one model to everyone in the world. And that's been a winning business model obviously across the board.

But if you want to basically take one model, customize that for a single person and then distribute that one model just for that customer — like for example what our platform does with Harvey — that is an immense amount of infrastructure for a massive lab to build just for one customer.

案例：Harvey 的"命运自主权"

>> Yeah. Talk about what you guys have done with Harvey maybe as an example.

>> So Harvey basically — they were up until now riding on top of the frontier closed-source models, right? And they've been able to build incredible interfaces and products on top of that that help tons of law firms in the world.

But what they realized is they have an immense amount of knowledge of data, of all of this nuance built up that they are actually able to see what the law firms actually care about and the built-up experience of just 30 years of working in this domain. And with using frontier models, they're unable to actually take that data and use that to their advantage.

And so what they realized is, hey, okay, they're able to construct a legal agent benchmark — and what they released — using all of the expert information that they have. And then if they get the power to basically use that data to train a model, then they get to shape their own destiny.

So with Trajectory, what they were able to do is train a model that is six times cheaper and it goes from around 4% accuracy for an open source model to around 18%. And this is — there's still so much room to grow obviously what they're able to do, but now suddenly get the power of a research lab. And on top of that, the nice part is these models end up being six times cheaper than the frontier, and so you're able to expend so many more tokens to achieve these tasks.

为什么叫 Trajectory？重新定义"工作单元"

>> So you picked the name Trajectory as it's related to this continual learn concept. How did you pick the name and tell us how it fits into what you guys are doing?

>> Yeah. So it's funny because the world right now is very focused on tokens. And I think a lot of people view tokens as a unit of work. But if you think about the way that we interact with other humans, I'm not counting the amount of words that you're actually talking about, right? And with co-workers, we a lot of the time are thinking about a task or a trajectory. And that's the unit of work that I really want to get to.

In RL, it basically is synonymous with a rollout, or what you would actually do in a training stack. And with continual learning, you have an RL training stack that's like a rollout engine and a trainer. A rollout engine is just like in a simulation basically doing a bunch of rollouts and doing these trajectories. In the real world for continual learning, your rollout engine becomes just the inference and the tokens in the real world. And now suddenly your trajectories are the tasks of economic value that are happening.

And so I want this basically paradigm to propagate where the unit of work that we think about is a trajectory. Beyond that, I think for also people that don't understand RL, it is also super nice that we are basically letting companies just own that path and really grow on their own. So I think it has this nice double entendre.

Continual Learning 的核心组件

>> And Kashi, I like this idea of a trajectory as like a unit of economically valuable work. You've also a couple times talked about "what does good look like," which kind of sounds like an eval or a benchmark. What are the core primitives for continual learning or what are the key ingredients that kind of go into this?

>> Yeah. So our goal at Trajectory is to actually limit these ingredients so that it is literally just, you know, what good looks like. However right now there are a lot of components that companies need, and then we as our product as well try to bridge that gap and make that as easy as possible.

So right now as a company you need a couple things.

第一：追踪 (Tracing)

One, you need to be able to trace all of your trajectories that are happening in production. And there's lots of AI native companies that have gone through this transformation where they're logging not just the main agent call, but also all the sub agents, what's happening in the product as well, any feedback that the user is giving. The ideal world is you get this kind of perfect timeline of all of those things so that you can track them. So that's the first step.

>> And just on that, what are people doing that in today? Like where do those traces live?

>> Yeah, in my view I think the entire ecosystem of continual learning needs to be a lot of players that basically build up all this infrastructure. So some companies are doing this in-house, but there's also a lot of great products out there like LangChain, like Braintrust, Raindrop, where you can basically plug into your infrastructure or your production agents and then basically trace all of these things. So what we're finding is a lot of AI native companies will use a lot of these products in order to get that first step out of the way.

>> Okay, so we got traces and then what?

第二：可回放性 (Replayability)

>> So, that's traces. The second part is then making these replayable. You need some sort of infrastructure to say, "hey okay, given a trace that I've seen in production, how can I actually then replay that for an eval to see what good looks like," or right now for training as well.

And so that's where companies also need to invest some sort of time. What we make really easy in our product as well is to bridge that gap. And so if you bring your traces and you say okay, here's just the concept of an environment that I might want — in more technical terms it's a Dockerfile or some sort of system requirements — then you can basically replay that entire trace.

第三：算法与奖励 (Algorithm & Reward)

So that's the second part. And then the third part is then the actual modification or the algorithm. And I think that's where it's really difficult to do this in-house as a company — is basically the entire training stack, the entire loss function, the reward function, all of these sort of components that need to be built up to translate these tasks into actual improvements for the model. And so that's the main part that we want to abstract away off the bat.

研究前沿：GRPO 与 Group Size One

>> To your point on abstracting away some of that, what has been abstracted thus far, what's next? You know, how does this product come together over time?

>> Right now it's mainly you bring traces and reward and some notion of an environment. The two parts here that require a bunch of manual work is the environment — actually constructing this thing that matches the real production. And a lot of the time it's actually impossible to create a perfect environment, right? And then the second part is reward. A lot of the times a legal workflow or an investment banking workflow doesn't have some perfect verifiable reward that you can train off of, right? And so these are the two areas that we're really pushing on the research side.

关于环境 (Environment)：

So for the environment, there's an algorithm called GRPO. That's the main kind of post-training algorithm that exists right now. What you need to do there is — imagine you have a player that's in a video game, and it's basically going around and hopping around a bunch of platforms, and then at the end of the day you get some reward. What's needed here in GRPO is basically comparing like the same task, the same level of the video game, and you need to play that out eight times or 16 times, and we call that a group.

Now the thing is with humans, a lot of the time we don't need to replay the exact same environment over and over again. We're just in the world experiencing and doing one rollout. And so the goal is: could we modify GRPO as an algorithm to get to a world where it is what we call "group size one" instead of needing a group of 16?

And so we've made a lot of strides here where now, if you can take 10,000 trajectories and they're all from different tasks, we can actually learn from just that one behavior or that one rollout. And so that's one algorithm that we actually released a blog post about — going into this group size one paradigm. And so that actually eliminates the need for an environment and all of this infrastructure that needs to be built out.

关于奖励 (Reward)：

The second part is for reward. And so this is another factor where let's say I have again 10,000 traces. The default is that I need to go and label every single one of those traces to say here's verifiable reward or here's what good looks like. And this is tractable. It's just a lot of work.

And so now our goal is: how can we actually reduce that amount of time needed to take this notion of what good looks like? So what we've realized is: let's say I have 10,000 traces. If I can smartly select 100 of them that are basically representative of all of these broader 10,000, and then have the customer or the user basically densely say "okay here's what good looks like, here's a rubric or verifiable criteria" for just those 100 traces — and then what we can do is basically train a meta-grader that learns from those behaviors of the 100 to the broader 10,000.

And with that you get a really clean interface that allows you to just propagate this reward across the board. So I think obviously it's not the perfect solution in that direction. The ideal goal actually is that you have some sort of observability interface where you're like "here is the five things my agent's good at, here's the five things it's bad at," and I just circle those five things and hit train. That's the world I want to get to and that's where we're pushing that research direction.

产品发布：One-Click Train

>> Very cool. So you have a product that you just released to do some of this. Tell us about it. What are you releasing in the product and who is it for?

>> Yeah. Up until now it's taken a massive research team a ton of time and a ton of compute in order to train these models. What we wanted to do is just make the easiest and most intuitive interface to train models and customize them for what you care about.

And so Trajectory, the platform that we released, is basically a very simple system where you can take your agent traces and "what good looks like." It's a one-click train interface that just takes a couple agent prompts, and then you can eval the model and then deploy it all in one place.

And I think the really magical part about this — a lot of our philosophy in product actually comes from Apple. When in like the early 2000s you had a computer that had access to the internet and you had a phone that you could make phone calls, and I think no one really thought to put the two together until Apple said "okay, what if you actually put the internet on a handheld device and combine the two?" And I think by doing this of basically putting training, eval, and deployment in one place, making that just dead simple for every single person to do, and then you can close the loop and basically now upload that model back to production, gather new traces — it suddenly is this magical paradigm that I think every single company is going to adopt very soon.

>> Very cool. Who is the product targeted at? Like who is the ideal customer for you guys today?

>> Yeah. So what we want to do is make this very simple for companies that have already their agent harness in order. They've spent a lot of time there, but that next step of basically modifying the most valuable part — which is the model — making that super super easy. So right now what the product is meant for is mainly AI native companies like Harvey and Rogo and some larger companies as well like Nvidia are already using the platform.

But the next step after this is: I want to also move beyond just the model. So another important piece is the harness as well. Because I think the model gets you efficiency — it gets you a model that has seen a task 100 times or 1000 times over and making that faster, cheaper, and more reliable. What a harness gets you also is new capabilities. It's just something that was not possible before.

And I think a lot of larger companies that are adopting AI, they also haven't done the work to optimize the harness for sub agents or for basically squeezing out that last mile even out of the frontier tokens. And so the eventual world is maybe you use a frontier model like Fable for 10% of tasks. And then for 90% of the time you can smartly route to a model that you've trained that is far more efficient and also gets you better margins.

案例：Rogo 的"智能密度"

>> Tell us some stories about some of the customers you've worked with so far. You gave us a little hint at Harvey, but maybe a couple more examples.

>> Yeah. So one really interesting one here is Rogo. And I think Rogo is taking a very interesting paradigm to agents that I think will become the future.

So right now the way people use agents are very much like synchronous, right? You prompt the agent, it goes and does its thing, and then it comes back. What Rogo is very interested in is not just this kind of verbose model that will go and basically spit out a bunch of garbage, right? What they want is just a very concise and clear finance agent that basically does the work that you care about. It can autonomously do things on the side, but then it comes back and is very efficient.

And so what the goal of Trajectory is, is to basically say okay, Rogo — what good looks like for them is they also want the idea of intelligence density. They want the idea that a model can do the same task but do that far more efficiently than the frontier models. They have the data to do that. And so with Trajectory, what they were able to do is train a model that is several times more efficient in terms of its tokens and also happens to be cheaper and faster, but then is also able to gain and climb on the things that they care about.

未来研究方向：好奇心与马尔可夫转移函数

>> Very cool. Okay, so we talked a little bit about group size one with GRPO. What's next? Like where is continual learning headed?

>> Yeah. So a lot of what we've been talking about right now is mainly just helping these companies translate over what good looks like for them into improvements for the model. I think to get to this true world where humans we are extremely efficient about learning from the real world, and we're able to have I think in-built curiosity as well about the world — I would say that's kind of one of the missing pieces to get us to agents actually learning kind of autonomously on their own via continual learning.

The models right now, they do a task but they don't actually accumulate any experience or learn anything about the real world. Whereas if you think about — let's say I'm throwing a football, right? I feel like as a human, maybe if I've never seen a football before, I actually have no idea what's going to happen. But I do that 100 times over and now I suddenly build this heuristic, right?

And the important part is I think with humans, like as kids, we are constantly exploring the world. We see a soccer ball, we see a football, and we kind of just try out things to build this mental model. And that makes us incredibly intelligent. Whereas with agents that doesn't exist right now.

And so we've done a lot of thinking of how do you actually quantify curiosity. And I think one interesting way to think about this is — so there's this idea in RL called a Markov decision process. And it's basically you can characterize the world as a bunch of state-action pairs. So a state is like "I'm holding the ball in my hand," and then an action is "I throw it," and then the following state is where does it all end up.

What LLMs right now are really good at is basically going straight from state zero to state one. They're next token predictors, right? But what's missing is that intermediate part of what is that transition function. When you actually go from S0 to S1, what is that transition function that happens? And LLMs don't really have a way of encoding that right now.

So I think the interesting thing here is with humans, we are very aware of when we don't know what a transition function is in the world. And we say "I'm basically going to try to figure out what this transition function is." And I think this is where curiosity comes in. And so if there's a way to basically quantify "here's all of the world that I don't know about right now and my goal as an agent is to figure out if I do this task what happens, I build this mental heuristic" — then I think we are starting to solve this curiosity problem and get to a world where you can autonomously learn and continually learn from the world.

对齐与 RSI 之辩

>> How do you make sure that an agent's curiosity is aligned with a user's objectives?

>> So I think that's actually one of the reasons why I'm very passionate about working on continual learning. So there's two kind of directions that it seems like research is going right now. There's RSI — recursive self-improvement — and there's continual learning. And both of these are very very tightly tied together, or very similar concepts. They're essentially just how does an agent actually learn from experience.

The thing is, RSI is all about taking a model, putting it in a black box, and basically making it the best AI researcher itself so that it can improve itself, right? But this is kind of a scary world, right? Because it exactly begs the question of "are these models and agents actually going to be aligned and have the best interests of humans in mind?"

Where I think continual learning takes a very different approach is it says "I want to learn from experience but learn from the experience of actually interacting with humans and then getting better at the tasks that they set out and that they want to do." And I think that's where the key difference is — is you need to allow these models and build the algorithm so that it keeps humans in the loop. I don't want to end up in a world where these agents are going rogue, and I think the way to do that is to keep on this alignment path.

团队构成：研究与产品的交叉点

>> You guys have done a bunch of unique things across product and research at Trajectory to bring these two halves of the whole together. Tell us more about what makes building at Trajectory unique and who are some of the people you bring together to make it happen.

>> Yeah. So the cool part that we are sitting in is the intersection of frontier research and product, where we have to modify the core RL algorithms in order to get to a place where you can actually learn from the world but also package that into a really beautiful and clean interface for people to train these models.

And so some of the research team that we've built had contributed to, for example, the co-founders to Gemini 3 and Gemini Robotics, other folks to GPT-4o at OpenAI, and building Muse infrastructure at MSL. But then on the product side as well, having people that have built scalable infrastructure at Stripe for payment SDKs. Also, we have the youngest design engineer at Netflix. These sort of people — and I think the intersection between them is where the magic starts to happen.

So the way we've actually structured the team: normally you have like a research stack that's the spaghetti codebase in one corner of the company, and then you have the product that's kind of well built out. What we've done is actually productionize the code base for training as well. So this means microservices, Kubernetes scaling, autoscaling of every single part of the trainer, the rollout engine.

And then on the design side as well, our design engineers are kicking off training runs all of the time and understanding deeply what the research experience is. I think this is a really interesting and cool place to be in.

A lot of this is also only possible because of frontier coding agents. Actually, most of the time now we are spending our time whiteboarding. We'll spend a lot of time just arguing about system design. And then the actual implementation is just a software factory of agents that will go and actually implement it.

产品人的未来：从工程师到园丁

>> So building a product here is not easy. What is the role of a product builder in a world of continual learning?

>> I think as a product builder you should be thinking about how you actually take these traces and experience in the real world and start to shape and improve the product autonomously.

So we're starting with the model right for Trajectory, and I think there's some interesting work to do there. Eventually that will be the model and the harness, and basically self-improving both of those. And I think once you have the harness — and products are kind of becoming more AI native, and so the harness is kind of becoming most of the product for a lot of these companies right — well, if you have the right to kind of self-improve the harness and then the product, then you have the right to kind of improve and self-improve the entire company.

And I think then products and product builders start to become almost like a gardener. Like you have your plant and it's going to grow autonomously on its own, and your goal as a product builder is to basically just set these trellises in the ground of "here's where I want to shape my product."

And I think this is going to be a very exciting world where you can just put a product out to a couple hundred users, it's going to grow on its own, and now we're going to have basically — you just imbue your taste into where the company grows. So I think that's going to be a very exciting world and companies should kind of start building towards that.

招聘与生态：为什么来 Trajectory

>> Yeah, for somebody listening who's thinking "boy, Trajectory sounds like a cool place to work" — what's the pitch? Why might somebody want to work at Trajectory?

>> So I think there's a couple things. The first thing is continual learning as a paradigm is the next learning paradigm. Any massive company that you can think of of the previous age — so let's take Google or Amazon or Facebook — they were all doing continual learning basically. If you think about recommender systems or ads, the idea is taking all of these preferences from the real world and then creating online systems that can learn and get smarter the more they're used.

And I think for agents that hasn't existed yet, and that's exactly the place that Trajectory I want to be in. We're starting with just V1 of the product, which is a very easy way to train models. But in aggregate, I want it to be a massive recommender system — every single agent should be attuned to what companies want and what every single user eventually wants. And I think that's going to be a fundamentally exciting world to get to.

There's a lot of work that needs to happen, and I also think Trajectory is not the only company in the ecosystem that needs to work really well to make this happen as well. Like two blocks down from us is Modal at our office that works on sandboxes and that powers a lot of the infrastructure that we have. And two blocks down from that is Thinking Machines also in SF. And I think there's like all these sort of companies that need to be built to basically power all the infrastructure to make continual learning work. But I think the product interface is where a lot of the exciting work can happen.

收官：弥合"智能"与"经验"的鸿沟

>> Yeah. One of the things you said when we were first getting to know you many many months ago was this idea that the world right now has plentiful intelligence thanks to the foundation model labs, and plentiful experience thanks to all the people who do hard work in lots of different domains every day. But there's this big gap between the two. And in some ways, continual learning is kind of the thing that bridges that gap. And it's kind of the thing that honors all of this earned experience that people have and makes it legible to the intelligence coming out of the foundation models.

And I thought that was like a very elegant and beautiful way to think about what it is you guys are doing. And then the question that leads to is: what is your most optimistic view of the future in terms of where continual learning can take us?

>> I love that question. A good example of this is Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations. Where we started out in the 1700s in this world where everyone was kind of doing the same thing, right? You would do this end-to-end workflow, you could call it, of an artisan.

And what he theorized basically is a world of abundance needs specialization. Where you want someone to basically not be context switching all of the time and work on the thing that they've built up experience about.

And it seems like in AI right now we're in this pre-industrial revolution society. Or even a hunter-gatherer sort of society where everyone is just doing the same work over and over again. We're consulting one oracle of technology.

I think what needs to happen is basically get to a world where it's no longer just one manufacturer of a car, one manufacturer of every single unit. But we get to a world of specialization where everyone can basically customize every single part of the harness, the model — and that's where we get to a world of abundance.

And there's a reason why only 1% of enterprises have actually been adopted by AI. There's so many workflows out there that are super manual and could be automated and actually increase intelligence based on all of these agents that could be in production. And so my goal is to basically take that 1% and turn that into 99%, so that we are actually learning from all of this built-up experience that lives in the world right now.

>> Love it. Thanks for being here.

>> Yeah, thanks so much for having me.

[music] [music]
