item.description:
## 一、最意外的观察：Trajectory 不是在卖"更好的模型"，而是在卖"告别垄断的权利"
表面上，这是一家做 continual learning 基础设施的公司。但如果你把 Ronak 说的话逐层剥开，会发现一个藏得很深的叙事：**前沿大模型实验室正在重演 18 世纪东印度公司的角色**——它们垄断了"智能的制造"，所有企业都是向一个神谕（oracle）进贡的藩属。Harvey 做了 30 年法律积累，却只能在别人家的模型上"写 prompt"；Rogo 懂金融研究的每一个微表情，却只能租用 GPT 的"通用大脑"。
Ronak 真正在卖的，是**让每个垂直公司重新拿回自己命运的权利（"shape their own destiny"）**。这不是技术产品，这是一次反垄断的生产资料再分配。他引用 Adam Smith 不是修辞——他真的认为 AI 正处在"前工业革命阶段"，而 continual learning 就是让"手工作坊"进化为"专业化社会"的那场革命。
## 二、跨领域连接：从 AAA 地图到 Google Maps，再到——金融衍生品定价史
Ronak

item.title: [Mercatus Center] Merve Demirel on the Costs of Migrating for Higher Education in India
item.dc:creator: Mercatus Center
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的发现：导师干预反而"锁死"了远距离迁移的大门

这项研究里最出人意料的一击，并非 129% 的迁移溢价本身，而是导师干预在远距离上"零效果"的沉默。按照经济学家的默认剧本，信息不对称一旦被打破，更真实的迁移者叙述应该降低认知摩擦、推高迁移率。但 Demiral 的数据讲了一个相反的故事：学生打完电话后，对 Pune/Mumbai 的评估几乎没有向上移动一毫，反而像是被"确认"了——"是的，我原先的担忧是对的"。

这意味着这些 12 年级学生根本不是无知者，而是惊人地精准的成本评估者。传统政策工具（信息海报、宣讲会、虚拟校园游）默认受众是"低信息理性人"，但这些学生更像是"高信息高摩擦人"——他们算过账，答案是"不去"。这个结果其实在学术圈内也有一个熟悉的影子：博士项目中，让在读博士去给本科生做"真实生涯分享"，往往反而劝退申请者，而不是吸引更多人。真相本身是一个劝退力量。

二、跨领域连接：性别歧视如何通过工资预期"间接放大"迁移摩擦

论文里埋着一个非常漂亮、几乎被自己弱化处理的发现：女性之所以表现出男性三倍的迁移惩罚，并不是因为她们对"离家"更反感（destination utility 两性接近）。差异来自分母——1% 工资增长对女性而言代表的绝对金额更少，因为她们从一开始就预期赚得更少。

把这个机制抽象出来，你会发现它是劳动经济学里一种罕见的"链式歧视"模型：性别工资差 → 单位百分比工资购买力下降 → 任何非经济成本在相对价值上被放大 → 女性在任何涉及"用钱买自由"的决策上都看起来"更保守"。这不是偏好差异，而是预期收入差异被除法重新编码成了偏好差异。

这个结构在其他领域也会出现："女性更风险厌恶"的行为金融学结论、"女性不愿创业"的创投观察、"女性拒绝加班机会"的 HR 数据——如果都用同样的分母重新审视，可能都在重复这个幽灵机制。换句话说，很多被归因为"女性心理"的现象，其实是"女性预期收入"的数学投影。

三、系统性真相：这个研究其实在悄悄推翻一个发展经济学的基本假设

发展经济学三十年来的隐含共识是"空间不平等 + 低迁移率 = 存在可被政策消除的摩擦"。Lucas、Harris-Todaro、乃至最新的 Bryan-Chowdhury-Mobarak 的孟加拉季节性迁移实验，都暗示"如果我们能把成本降下来，人就会流动起来，福利就上升"。

Demiral 的数据悄悄地质疑了这个链条的最后一步。当她把迁移惩罚细分，发现其中很大一块是安全、孤独、与父母分离、社交断裂——这些不是"错误信念"，不是"可消除摩擦"，而是真实的非货币福利损失。这意味着当一个农村女孩选择不去 Mumbai 读工程，她可能并没有在最大化问题上犯错，而是在做一个我们外部观察者看不到完整参数的最优化。

于是研究隐含了一个尖锐的政策转向：问题不该是"如何让更多女孩迁移"，而是"如何让迁移本身变得不那么昂贵"。前者是推人，后者是改造城市——改造的是 Mumbai 的夜间治安、宿舍制度、单身女性租房市场、女性友好的通勤网络。这其实把发展政策的焦点从人（人力资本干预、信息干预、现金激励）转向了空间（城市作为一个必须被重建的产品）。

有趣的跨领域回声：这和当代城市规划里"15 分钟城市"的女性视角重构（Caroline Criado Perez、Leslie Kern 的工作）是同一个母题——城市默认的使用者是男性，而女性为了安全地使用同一个城市，必须支付一笔隐性税。Demiral 的论文其实是把这笔隐性税在印度高等教育市场上第一次定价了：它值 129% 的工资增长，对女性而言是男性的三倍。

📝 转录文本

开场与嘉宾介绍

Welcome to Ideas of India, a podcast where we examine academic ideas that can propel India forward. My name is Shruti Rajagopalan and this is the 2026 job market series where I speak with young scholars entering the academic job market about their latest research on India.

I spoke with Merve Demiral who is at the Institute for International Economic Studies at Stockholm University. We discussed her job market paper titled "Migration Costs and Higher Education: Experimental Evidence from India." We talked about the education opportunities available to senior secondary students in Maharashtra, why some of these students prefer to study close to home despite recognizing the higher returns available from colleges in cities like Mumbai and Pune, measuring the non-financial costs of migration, and why those costs are especially high for women, and much more.

For a full transcript of this conversation, including helpful links of all the references mentioned, click the link in the show notes or visit mercators.org slash podcast.

Hi, Merve. Welcome to the show. It's such a pleasure to have you here.

Thank you. It's such a privilege to be here. I'm very excited.

论文核心问题的概述

I'm excited too. Your paper, I really enjoyed reading it because this is not an area I've thought about much. In this paper, you ask why students choose to remain close to home for college, even when they believe that studying elsewhere will produce sort of better labor market returns. And what you look at specifically in this context is whether access to a peer or a mentor, in this instance, a migrant mentor, will help them overcome the sort of like non-financial costs and frictions of moving.

This was fascinating to me because I'm an immigrant myself and I have moved very far from home for educational reasons. So it was fascinating for me to actually try and understand what kinds of frictions exist. And some of these frictions are really at like the district level, right? We're not even talking about moving 7,000 miles or something, you know, kind of move that you and I made maybe.

So, you know, in this particular study, you look at about just over 1,600 final year secondary school students across 52 schools in various districts in Maharashtra. And you're looking at them at that precise moment in their lives when they're making this decision, you know, about what to do next after secondary school, right? So this is about are they going to college? Where are they going to college? What kind of, you know, field they're going to look at? And also what their expectations are in terms of their life and how it's going to play out, right? So what are their expectations when it comes to earnings, when it comes to employment and things like that?

惊人的发现：巨大的"居家偏好"

And you find what I would think of as an extraordinarily large preference to remain at home, right? I really was not expecting this, preference to remain at home, but looking at the more aggregate data in India, I guess it adds up pretty well. The average student would need an increase equal to 129% of expected postgraduate earnings to accept studying away from home. So that's a very large premium or the other way of saying it is there seems to be a lot of stickiness to remain at home, or there seems to be some friction between the two to be able to bridge that particular gap.

And this penalty also increases with distance. So distance does play a factor. It's not just about stickiness to being home. It increases from about 39% for the students' own district capital to 93% for Pune and 196% for Mumbai and 303% for Nagpur. These are enormous numbers, right? I really did not expect this going in.

随机实验的设计

And then after you study this, you run a randomized experiment in which half the students are offered mentoring by someone from the same gender who's a university student who has migrated to Pune or Mumbai, and this is a sort of like long distance over the telephone kind of mentoring. Then you look at what assignment to mentorship does. The especially interesting result in this area is that applications to nearby district capitals rise by about 4.9 percentage points, but moves which are further outside, like let's say to Pune or Mumbai generally, don't see this big uptick, thanks to mentorship.

So there is something very interesting going on in this particular marketplace, and this is the marketplace for education and eventually for post-education employment. It is also the marketplace for migration and migration-related choices. So it's a fascinating study that you've done, and I can't wait to dig into it. But largely, have I summarized your paper well? Because you're looking at this at a lot of depth, plus there's a randomized experiment. So am I getting this somewhat right? And feel free to correct me.

I think you're explaining the paper beautifully and very intuitively. So I think you've gotten it.

研究动机：空间机会差距与低迁移率的悖论

Yeah, great. So I guess, Merve, my first question would be then, what was the motivation for you to study this or look at this and in this particular way? Because I've not seen too many studies like this one.

So in this project, what I really, really wanted to study was this longstanding puzzle that we see in a lot of different contexts, namely the puzzle where there are large opportunity gaps across space but it is accompanied by low migration rates. So people seem to be not moving to where opportunities are to a large extent and it's really puzzled economists for a really long time.

So I studied this question and I studied in a specific migration setting, right, and that is the question of where to study college. And I think this is a really interesting and high stakes setting to study because essentially this is a one-time decision that a young adult is going to be making very early on in their lives with very limited information and they're weighing up a lot of really consequential costs and benefits together.

So on the one hand, if a student is able to migrate, they're going to be able to access many more colleges, many more opportunities, potentially better colleges and colleges that fit their personality or fit their ambitions better. And they might be able to set up their adult lives in, you know, cities or locations where the jobs are paying higher or the quality of life is higher and so on and so forth. So you have this big long-term large investment that the students are able to make.

But you also have these immediate costs that they have to go through with it to be able to access those opportunities. And those costs can be really daunting. It can be, you know, financial costs of moving from point A to B, or it can be the non-financial or non-pecuniary costs, as I call them in my paper, that can be really things like moving away from your family home or leaving your existing friends behind and starting to, you know, take charge of everything in your daily life by yourself. So these can be really daunting or overwhelming for some students. It can be also very exciting for some others who really want to move away from home. But it really depends on the student.

So I was really interested in studying this. And it's a finding that consistently comes up in the literature that demand for higher education falls with distance. So the further away educational opportunities are, especially for higher education, because that's typically when we start thinking about migrating away from home, the less likely are students to take up that offer. We see this across a number of different contexts. It's certainly true in India. I have also some other work with a set of co-authors that really shows that distance is a first order cost in higher education decisions in Indian students.

My paper is really trying to understand what is that cost and how should we think about it? Should we think about it as barriers or should we think about it as just misinformation or should we think about it as students' preferences that we should respect and how, yeah, how do we approach it? So that's how I started studying this topic.

典型 12 年级学生的决策环境

This is fascinating, and thank you for the context, but now we are looking at not the general college student but a very particular kind of college student. You're looking at a couple of, you know, districts in Maharashtra and you're looking at the college decision for that particular student in, you know, grade 12 or senior secondary. So for those of us who are unfamiliar with that setting, what does that college decision really look like for that, you know, sort of like representative higher secondary student there?

Right. So for a student that's in my sample, the decision to study what to study and where to study after class 12 is a really complicated decision. So they are really looking at a number of different options. They're weighing up whether they should go to college, should they do vocational training, what kind of exams they should sit for. They're really going through a very stressful period in their times. Class 12 is really stressful. It's end of high school exams but also a lot of these different centralized exams that they're sitting through.

They're doing it, at least my students are doing it, in a kind of a low information, low support system setting. The students in my sample, they're more likely to come from under-resourced schools, or at least compared to the average school in their district. So they report, you know, very low availability of resources that would help them think through college decisions. Most of them don't have any support system at school, so they're really navigating a complex choice by themselves.

But on the other hand, they have a large opportunity gradient available to them if they were to start looking at colleges outside of their immediate locality. Of course that changes for every single student. I like to illustrate the example of a student who's wanting to study engineering and is looking at, you know, just in their immediate environment versus their districts and in the whole state, and, you know, adjusting for competition. So how many other engineering students are there that can take up that spot? The available spots for them can go from 70 to 10,000 or something. So it's really a crazy number, just the access number of seats that they can access by looking further is really large.

And of course, those better quality educational institutions are more likely to be at places that are large cities. So places like Mumbai and Pune. And those are the places where opportunities are constructed. So, yeah, in the setting, they have potentially large returns from migrating for college. Overwhelmingly so, they're not very interested in doing it.

样本学生的所在地与可及选项

Yeah. And these are not students like in the outskirts of Mumbai or Pune, right? You're looking at students in Sangli and Ahilya Nagar, where it's not the back of the beyond. So they do have some, you know, college opportunities and education opportunities and some potential, you know, post-university work opportunities. But at the same time, these are not huge urban agglomerations where you will really get access to this phenomenal peer group or, you know, access to the innovation economy or access to the largest labor market in your state or anything like that.

That's exactly right. So actually, thank you for reminding me. It really depends on what you want to study. So if you're instead looking at, for example, vocational training, then these students are already living at places where they can access that type of education. So it's really not the choice between not studying at all or not having any access to any type of education, but it's just accessing better opportunities or the best possible opportunity that you can get to.

Yeah, some of the students in my sample, they're in towns, they're in district capital. Some of them are in more rural places. So there's a bit of heterogeneity of what's available to each and every one of them locally. But yeah, this is sort of roughly what they're weighing up.

核心摩擦：信息、预期还是偏好？

Yeah. And, you know, you alluded a little bit in your earlier answer on sort of what makes this decision and, you know, this issue of distance so salient, but I wanted to get into that a little bit more. So what is the central, I guess, challenge or friction, right? Do these students just don't have information? Do they not perceive the economic returns to studying elsewhere? Or, you know, they do have the information and they can understand the expected returns are going to increase, but as you pointed out, there's just a strong preference to remain at home for whatever reason. And so what exactly is going on, you know, below the surface of this particular choice?

Right. So for the students in my sample, they do actually understand the gradient at least to some extent, because when I collect data from them about their expectations of expected salaries if they were to study at different destinations, so studying at home versus studying at District Capital or Pune or Mumbai, they do expect to earn somewhere between 16% to 30% higher, just comparing what they expect home versus these destinations. And this is an expectation or this is an increase that for the majority still stands when I account for the higher living cost or the cost of studying at these different destinations or to some extent the risk of them not being able to get a job after.

So to me, it's definitely the case that the students expect some economic returns to materialize after this investment takes place, but it simply doesn't seem to be enough to make them want to pursue that. So that could still be because of a number of different things, right? They could still have other constraints that I'm not capturing super well, or it could be that they simply don't think they would get into these colleges as they are more selective and competitive places. But none of these, as far as I can tell with the data that I collect, none of these seem to be the final answer.

So I really find a gap between students' intentions and the economic returns, and that makes me conclude that there must be something else going on, some other costs that is making them behave this way or that is making them to decide to study at home. And that's the sort of the central object of interest that I pursue.

如何测量迁移的"非货币成本"：离散选择实验

Exactly. Yeah. So let's get into that. So one of the most interesting things about the paper is actually measuring, you know, what you're talking about. How does one measure a student's unwillingness to migrate, right? And what does it mean to say when, you know, you write in the paper that the average migration penalty is 129% of expected earnings. Like, how do you think about putting that together, measuring that, calculating that?

Right. So what I want to estimate — so I can sort of measure somehow the objective returns or the subjective expected monetary returns from the student or from household data and so on. What's really difficult is to understand what is in this move for the student. So what's the cost of separating from home, separating from friends and so on and so forth. And that's not typically something we can measure from data that's available. For that I have to speak to students and, you know, get an estimation of what it's worth for them.

So again, just to restate, my goal is trying to understand what is the disutility that's attached to moving away from home to another destination, holding all of the financial aspects of this move constant. That means I need to find a way of introducing experimental variation into what destinations cost and what they mean to students.

And that's why I'm going to introduce this discrete choice experiment, which is step one in my paper. And I'm going to present the students with a set of colleges. It's going to be a repeated choice experiment and for each college I'm going to experimentally vary the destination and the expected earnings that the students should think about after graduating from that college. And that's going to give me a data set where I can calculate this utility of moving from one destination to the other, and that's going to allow me to price it in terms of the utility that an additional percentage of earnings brings to the student. So it's really a way to put a price on the non-pecuniary utility differences that the student is expecting to get.

And to really sort of make it concrete what exactly this choice experiment is: you can think of a student who's filling my survey in a tablet and they're presented with two colleges. These colleges are hypothetical. Each of them has five attributes. So it's the field of college, the location of college, the average salaries after graduation, and what it would cost in terms of living expenses and tuition to attend these colleges.

So I asked the student, look, here are two colleges. Imagine that you've gotten the marks to gain admission in both of them. Which one do you prefer? And the student can choose college one, college two, or they can choose, "actually, I don't like either of these. I'm not going to study at any college at all."

And to make it realistic and feasible for the student, I'm going to use information that I've elicited from the student to fill in the characteristics of that college. So the colleges are always going to be fixed in the field of what the student wants to study. So let's say it's engineering, they're always going to see engineering colleges, and they're always going to see colleges that are feasible for them. So the cost of living and tuition is going to be fixed and within the budget constraint that the student has previously told me earlier in the survey.

So it's really an exercise where I'm trying to shut down different feasibility channels in terms of budget constraints, in terms of can I get into it, what's the risk associated with it, and all of these things. And I'm just trying to capture what is it about living away from home in non-financial terms, but priced in the utility of 1% earnings. Yeah, that's kind of it what I do.

And then the 129% estimate comes from basically dividing this utility of a destination that's not home by the utility of 1% increase in earnings. And that is what essentially tells me, you know, these students on average would be indifferent from studying at home versus studying somewhere else, but only if that somewhere else gives them 130% more in expected earnings after graduation. So it really doesn't have anything to do with what they believe or what they think they're going to get or something. It's just a way to price this utility.

对迁移惩罚的分解：主观信念验证

Yeah. So, you know, the way you're looking at this, I mean, I love the setup so much because it's really looking at the relevant trade-off, right? This is not some hypothetical counterfactual that may or may not exist in their life that they're just kind of playing game with. This is a very realistic, you know, choice between two options that may almost present themselves in a few months in their life.

But in this particular instance, how do you manage to calculate some of the costs involved in this disutility? So for instance, are they just worried about the fact that hey, maybe the costs of food are uncertain, or are the costs of food large, right? Is the quality of housing uncertain or is the quality of housing poor? Like, what is a good way to think about that? Because that's really hard to capture. You just know what they are choosing, but how do you kind of decompose that, I guess, or what is below this, you know, what is making up this very large migration penalty?

Right. So that's an excellent question because that is exactly the nature of this object that I'm estimating, right? Conceptually, it's a very large object. It contains everything that I might think about moving away from home. And those are going to be, by definition, multidimensional. It's going to be subjective. And it's going to be a combination of what I think my life is going to look like across a number of different outcomes and how much I care about those different outcomes and different places. So it's really a composite object that captures many different things. But by whole design conjectures that it captures the non-pecuniary costs associated with movement.

So I do a validation exercise. I go out to students and ask them about their beliefs, about very specific things that they expect to happen if they were living and studying at these different destinations. So that can be something like me asking you, Shruti, imagine if you were studying in Pune, how safe do you think you would feel in your daily life just moving around in the city from one to ten? And I ask you the same question for a number of different destinations and for a number of different outcomes that I think capture some of the non-pecuniary outcomes. So that can be emotional outcomes, social outcomes or just practical aspects of moving.

So I do this for, for example, how much do you think your parents will approve, what will those who stay behind at your hometown think of you, how lonely do you think you'll be, how many friends will you have, how much will you be able to keep in touch with your friends and family back home. And I also ask about just overall thinking about all the practical things associated with a move, how difficult do you think it's going to be to move to a different destination. And that one's a bit of a special item because it's right away asking you about a relational question. So it's defined for home as, you know, not difficult at all because home is not to move.

So I measure these subjective expectations, as I said, for a number of different things. And then when I first just look at what these beliefs or subjective expectations look like for a number of different destinations, I find that overall students expect all of these to decrease the further away they are from home. So a student simply thinks that life away from home studying at these different destinations will look worse on average compared to studying at home.

Then again, that tells me these things correlate with the migration penalty. And if it is the case that it captures some aspects of the migration penalty, then controlling for them in the choice model that I'm estimating the migration penalty should attenuate some of the disutility that students attach to migrating away from home. So I also do that validation exercise, and I find that once I control for those beliefs, the disutility coefficients that are attached to each of these destinations shrink by approximately half or 60%. It's a little bit dependent on the specification. And that simply tells me, you know, these beliefs that I'm measuring, they seem to be relevant for this object.

So it's a sanity check. It's a statistical decomposition that I then do. And I try to understand to what extent each of these beliefs account for the attenuation of the coefficient. And then I find that they approximately capture 15, 20, 30% of this attenuation.

So that's a long explanation to just say, I measure specific beliefs and then I validate them against this object that I estimate from the discrete choice experiment. Both of them tell me, you seem to be capturing some relevant objects for these students and they do explain an okay share of the migration penalty or the disutility that I'm measuring.

介入设计：Campus Trail 导师项目

Yeah, this is super helpful because, again, you know, as I mentioned, when I first started reading the paper, like 61%, you know, home for reference, these numbers are just so large. So it's very useful to be able to unpack it the way you've done, you know, sort of decompose what's going on at each of these levels.

I also want to talk to you about like the gender difference. But before we get into that, I want to get to the meat of your paper, which is this Campus Trail intervention that you designed and that you implemented. Right? So this is the randomized trial where you have this migrant peer that is attached to the student. So can you tell us exactly what this Campus Trail intervention was and what happens during this, you know, peer or mentor interaction? And, you know, maybe if you can take us inside how both sides perceive this conversation, like whether it's the student or what kinds of peers are more likely to be attached to them and so on, that would be super interesting.

Right. So the idea behind this intervention is that we're talking about very subjective assessments of living at different destinations and being a student in different places. This is not a space in which we can think of, in my opinion, objective information interventions and things like that. But most of the time when, you know, in real life, if we're moving somewhere, if we're considering moving somewhere, we try to think of a person that we know there, maybe we can have a conversation with, and we try to ring them up and say, hey, what is your experience like living in this destination? So this is where it really came from.

I designed this mentorship program, Campus Trail, as a mentorship program that helps students make more informed decisions. And of course, there are many, many different mentorship programs that are aiming to do exactly the same thing. So what is really different or maybe a bit more special about this program is that it's also targeting these non-pecuniary aspects of choosing a college. And that also includes moving away from home and managing everything that comes with moving away from home.

So what I do is I recruit students who are either current or recent college students in Mumbai and Pune, most of them have moved away from home to come and study at these colleges. And I sort of train them to be migrant mentors. I say "train" with almost code marks because I'm not the one doing any training. They're the ones who know about the experience of moving away from home and navigating these really complicated period of choosing a college. But we essentially go through the point of this program, the safeguarding rules, some general tips on mentoring, and we establish, yeah, basically the ground rules of what this mentorship is going to look like.

So these students come with a lot of knowledge and a lot of insights into what it is to be moving away from home, and they can support the students who are currently going through that choice themselves. So they can provide a lot of information on how to apply to colleges, how to find information about colleges, and they can do that irrespective of the destination. But they can also offer specific tips and tricks and information about budgeting or finding housing or navigating the city in a safe way or arranging travel and, you know, anything you can think of.

导师 / 同乡网络的类比

Yeah. And this really makes sense, right? Because those of us who've been to university, you kind of see this as a university student experience. Like, you know, so many times when you migrate from a particular location, you see student housing where everyone's from the same country or city. And that's just a matter of networks or everyone's from the same course, right? They're all studying botany or something. And that's how they found each other. And then, you know, that becomes like the apartment that is rented to botany students. Each time one someone graduates, the next one comes in. So you actually do see this even on the other side. And now this makes perfect sense on exactly how this pipeline moves both in terms of easing the frictions, but also for those who actually end up taking that leap and making that choice.

Yeah, we also often see this as something that schools or universities do after a student accepts their offer. So I think that is also because, you know, people do recognize that these things are important. But what I'm trying to understand is that having access to these things beforehand, can that influence the outcomes or what the students are aiming to do with their lives to begin with. So that is roughly the idea behind the intervention.

导师匹配机制与通话内容

What ends up happening specifically is that these mentors are available for phone conversations and each of them commits a certain number of hours for each mentee. I randomly offer to half of my sample phone conversations with these mentors, and I make sure that the mentors and mentees are always sharing a gender and academic stream. That's partly to make sure that, you know, the information exchange is relevant for the students, given that everything is going to be very personalized. I mean, we didn't get to talk about the gender differences yet, but spoiler alert, it's a very gendered decision. It's very large. Migrating away from home, it looks different if you're a man or a woman. So those are the things that I have in mind when I make sure that they share a gender and academic stream.

The conversations are very personalized. So it's really up — it's not scripted. It's up to the mentee to follow up with the mentor and ask them about different things that they're curious about. So it's also really coming from a place of these students can use the mentors as a source of information. The mentors are not there to sort of advertise in a way their own choices or their own universities or anything like that, which I think is the beauty of mentorship interventions really. So it's really tailored to what students think is important for them.

最意外的结果：导师未能推动远距离迁移

So, you know, this is the most surprising result for me in your study, other than like just the size of some of these results, which is that mentors in Pune and Mumbai don't end up inducing the students who they are attached to to move to Pune or Mumbai. Instead, the response is a little bit more concentrated in the nearby district capital, right? So what is going on with the Pune and Mumbai mentors or these cities or the opportunities in those cities?

I agree. I was also surprised. So I mean, I look at the end of the intervention, I look at applications, I look at whether the students are moving to different cities and I look at how the students are thinking about different cities. And throughout all of these outcomes, it's really shining through that students, a subset of students at least, are getting more excited about moving to district capital or applying there. But really nothing seems to be changing for them or how they see the faraway cities. So whether they think it's a good opportunity, whether they think they'll be happy there and so on, none of these things seem to move for the further away cities.

And I sort of make sense of it in two different ways. So the first one is to go back to the discrete choice experiment. So to the extent that the migration penalty object that I'm capturing, if we take that very seriously, as you also mentioned, for a lot of the students moving to the nearby district capital, which on average is about a two, three hour move for most of my sample. That is the first available move that costs them less in some sense. So the non-pecuniary penalty or the migration penalty associated with such a move is much smaller than moving outside of the district to some of these bigger cities.

Compared with such a large penalty, my intervention, which essentially is a very light touch intervention for majority of the students, it just becomes a short phone call with a mentor who's further away. It doesn't do much to change the real costs or the real barriers that's associated with them.

Now, I have to say I was surprised to see not even sort of, you know, "oh, it sounds great to study at Pune, but I don't think I'll do it because my grades aren't enough" or so. It's really that students, I think, are coming out of these conversations thinking, you know, I think it's great to stay at home or at least close by to home. And they're not even getting excited about these outside options, which then leads me to think, yes, these students have talked to a real student who has done that move, and they just sort of reinforce their beliefs about how difficult or uncomfortable or unsafe or, you know, any of these other undesirable things that such a move will consist of.

So that I think is an interesting finding that I have, that it seems to be that most of this disutility that I'm capturing is quite difficult to move, and it is potentially consisting of real non-pecuniary costs or barriers that the students are seeing accurately.

从 PhD 类比看导师的"相关性"问题

So, you know, the way I think about the Pune Mumbai result, and, you know, maybe we can center it around something a little bit more familiar to you and me, which is, you know, doing an economics PhD, right? I feel like at different points in time, if you ask someone who's like doing their qualifying exams, they'll be like, "oh, good God, don't do a PhD, it's just a lot of work," right? Or if they're in the middle of the job market, it's like, "oh, this is so hard, the job market's terrible, please don't do a PhD, get a private sector job, you'll be better." And then a few years after that passes, it's like, "oh, you must do an economics PhD, it was the greatest time of my life," basically they've forgotten, right?

In fact, most people who are mentored to go on to do an economics PhD is usually by their undergraduate econ professors who have enough distance from that time. So one way I think about what may be getting picked up with the Pune and Mumbai mentors is they are still in the thick of figuring out how difficult that choice is to navigate, right? So maybe if it's someone like many years older or someone who just moved there and is still super excited and in the honeymoon phase, it might be a different conversation.

But the other way I think about that same conversation is someone who manages to make that leap and move to Mumbai or Pune suddenly seems like a very different type of person. Right? So sometimes it may also be like when you're talking to these mentors, you're like, wow, I could never be that. I could never do that. And that becomes the barrier. You know, almost like there are lots of people who look at PhD students and say like, wow, that person is so smart. I could never be that. Whereas all that person has done is taken like two, three years of classes and seminars. Right? What do you think is going on, you know, within this subset? I'm not asking for exact conversations, but what is your hunch on what's going on?

Right. So I think what you say about the relatability and sort of this distance that students have to mentors. So this shows up in my take up measure, actually. So out of all the students who are offered to have a conversation with these peers, almost all of them do have one conversation. But roughly half, and roughly only half, go on to have a conversation that lasts for more than 15 minutes. So I think this is where that relatability or how is this information relevant to me, "you're just putting me on the phone with some really highly educated, really big shot student from Pune," I think some of it is potentially driving some of the students are just not taking up because of that. They think it's a daunting thing to be on the phone with this person.

But among the students that do take up the intervention and have that conversation, I actually see overwhelmingly positive reflections of what they thought of the mentor. So they thought that the mentor gave them good advice, that it was relatable and that they trust the mentor and so on. And it's not that they just talk about the academic opportunities and so on. They do talk about safety or making friends or cost of living. So all these other dimensions, it does come up in the conversations.

What could be happening possibly is that the students, depending on what it is that they have their mindset on, they take up different topics or they ask about different destinations. And because the mentors are, you know, specifically instructed to help the students achieve the goals that they want, it could be that the information that they're giving to students who are wanting to go to district capital is simply about how to find colleges there or how to apply for scholarships there to make the cost of living more manageable or things like that. Whereas the topic of how to move to Pune is less likely to come up. So that's one conjecture that I have. I'm still working on trying to understand it more deeply.

It is possible that some of the students could have benefited from this intervention if it was a bit more structured, but it's also true that some of the students benefited it precisely because it was not structured and it was just tailored to their wants and needs.

性别差异：三倍的迁移惩罚

And now I really want to come to the gendered part, right? Because there are two different things going on with male and female students. One is just the treatment effects, and there seems to be a difference between male and female students on how they look at the intervention and their response to this kind of, you know, mentorship network or mentorship and intervention. And the second is of course the difference in the size of the effects, right? So maybe now we could get into that.

As I hinted earlier, it is a very gendered decision whether or not to move away from home. So just when we're already looking at the willingness to pay estimates — so what I need to pay a female student to make them equally happy to study away from home and comparing that with a male student, I find that that willingness to pay estimate is approximately three times as large as the male students. And my sample is majority female students, approximately 60-65% of them are female. So that is also somehow one of the driving factors behind those extremely large willingness to pay estimates that we see.

So what does that mean comparing men and women? We need to remember that the willingness to pay estimate that I'm calculating is essentially this utility attached to a destination divided by utility attached to a 1% increase in earnings. And if I look at these two objects for men and women, I actually find that this utility attached to the destinations aren't very different for men and women. What is really different is how much is a 1% increase in expected salary is worth for men and women. It's worth much less for women. And that is one of the reasons behind that is because women are just expecting to earn much, much lower salaries compared to men. So even if the additional value of 10 or 1000 rupees is the same for men and women, that represents a much higher increase for women. So that is really behind this large differences of willingness to pay.

So, yeah, I would essentially need to compensate men and women the same amount, but that same amount would represent a much higher increase for women. So that's on that one side. But at the same time, I also find that the women's subjective expectations about what life away from home is going to look like, well, they expect it to look much worse than men. And actually, the expectations that I'm capturing do a better job of explaining women's migration penalty than men. So I think that is also helpful in trying to make sense of what my results look like at the end of the intervention.

为何干预对女生无效

As you hinted already, I find that men are responding in applications away from home and moves away from home, and women really don't seem to be responding that much on those margins. And I sort of tie back to going back to the baseline discrete choice experiment. I find that women are just much less likely to be at the margin, so the intervention is trying to close a much larger gap. So whatever the intervention is going to do, whether it's correcting misperceptions or decreasing real costs, it has to do a massive shift. And simply that's not what the migrant mentors, I think, are able to achieve.

And it may not be a mentorship problem at all, as you pointed out, right? They're not at that point where mentorship is the thing that changes the decision on the margin. It could be, you know, family, parents, so many other things going on. Is the expectation that the girl is going to get married very early, at which point she'll be forced to drop out of university, as opposed to be able to continue things if she's married within the same district? So there are so many specific things going on that it seems very intuitive and contextually obvious to me when you point this out, like the moment you point it out, "oh yeah, that makes sense."

Right. Again, it's when I look at the specific beliefs that I even see a worsening that's attached to destinations away from home. So I think some of these things are coming through, like the girls are really not seeing studying away from home as a beneficial opportunity in any margin that I'm looking at.

So I think a lot of people have in the back of their minds that even if girls are excited about moving away from home, they're going to hit so many other constraints on the way, which absolutely is true in this setting. And I mean, maybe not necessarily for my sample, because they're essentially a selected bunch of students who are responding to this invitation to join the program. I essentially go to their schools and tell them, hey, I have this mentorship program. If you're interested in studying further, you can join it. So it is not necessarily going to be the representative class 12 student.

What I'm finding is that even before we get to all of those parental constraints or other marriage constraints and so on, the students simply start thinking that, well, I don't think this is a great decision for me. I actually start thinking that staying home is going to give me a more comfortable and more preferable environment to study in. So I think that's important to note that even though the parental constraints might be there at the end of the day, I don't have any evidence that that's where the students are getting stuck on. It seems that the students themselves don't really see it as a good opportunity.

父母偏好与学生偏好的对齐

Yeah. So, you know, on the parents thing, so you're not finding this difference between like parents preference when it comes to explaining the difference between the two genders, right? Male versus, you know, female choices in this instance. But your parents survey does suggest that parents are substantially more reluctant than their children to have their kids migrate. Right? So is the intervention in some sense almost for the wrong person in the sense that these students are still relatively young, their parents' influence or, you know, how they think about it or the parent preferences are still going to loom very large. If they were older, it might matter a little bit less. If they were younger, the student preference hardly matters at all. It's all the parents' preference. But at this kind of interesting age that you're looking at, maybe what you're picking up on is that the parents' opinions really matter a lot and their reluctance must come in some way.

Right. So I think that's exactly right. Of course, I'm looking at 17, 18-year-olds, what parents think are a big, important part of the decision. I do find, especially within my male students, I do find some evidence of the treatment effects that I estimate being contained in the group of students who at baseline have told me "I'm going to be the one deciding where to study and whether I study, not my parents, or not even together, I'm going to be the only one who's deciding." So I think that is a bit in line with what you're saying is that it is possible that other students were also more excited about going away to study at these destinations but they got stuck on what parents are thinking about. So for men, I think that's possible.

For women, I really don't find any evidence of that either. So for women, it could of course be the case that women heard something from their mentors but then the parents were telling them the exact opposite and then they choose to believe what the parents are saying and not necessarily a mentor who they don't know well and so on. So that is not something that I can speak to. But I really don't have any evidence of students' wishes and parents' wishes for my girls going in opposite directions. It really seems to be that everyone is aligned that it's just not a good outcome for the girls to move away.

Which I think is not — I don't think that means that that's where we should leave the conversation. I think we should try and think a lot more about what that means for these girls, that they are perceiving really, really large non-pecuniary cost of migration and it doesn't seem to improve with contact with mentors who can tell them about what life is like. So what do they consist of and what can policy do to change those real costs? And I think there's just a lot more to work on there.

福利与政策含义：更多迁移一定更好吗？

Oh, yeah. I find it exciting to think more about that. Thank you for explaining the paper so well.

But before I let you go, I do want to ask you about what your paper and your findings mean for both welfare and policy in this setting, right? So what is a good way to think about it? And second, when I finished reading your paper, my first instinct was, is more migration necessarily better? I mean, I'm obviously a migrant and I'm a huge votary of it and I've moved countries many times, cities many times. But it's not that obvious to me that more migration is necessarily better for most people other than me. Right? And I think I'm also an educational migrant and I moved away from university for my masters, for my PhD.

So it does seem to be the case that it's a certain type of person who either doesn't necessarily value these non-pecuniary losses very highly, so they just seem to value the economic returns very highly and they decide to do it. And in that case, migration becomes a very positive change in someone's life. But for most people, it really seems to be that that's not necessarily the case.

And I think as economists, we care a lot about accessing economic opportunities and we make sense of, you know, these spatial immobility by saying, oh, there must be a lot of costs of migration and these must be non-pecuniary in nature. And I think that's right. And I think that should really guide our thinking of when we design policy interventions, that we should target those things together.

So we think a lot about correcting misperceptions or getting people to opportunity. I think what my paper is saying is that, well, if we just do those things and not address any of the real costs of non-pecuniary, real non-pecuniary cost, first of all, we might be doing something that's not going to be super effective. And I think second of all, we might be doing something that's not necessarily welfare enhancing if it comes at the cost of, you know, large non-pecuniary decreases.

Instead, I think we can think about a lot of different interventions that target both of those things separately. So both getting people, you know, practical or financial support to help them go after the opportunities while at the same time targeting these non-pecuniary costs. So safety is something that comes up a lot throughout my paper. It's a very salient worry for girls. You know, one can think of it's just a fear of the unknown. It's just something that they would get used to. But I think what my paper says is that it's a real, real cost that the students are receiving accurately and they're pricing that into their information. So what we should be thinking about is how do we make girls migrate safely and not just how do we make girls migrate?

结语：被定价的"安全税"

Oh, absolutely. And the women's safety is, you know, at some point, we're all pricing this in. I mean, you've done fieldwork in India. I grew up in India. And sometimes it's literal dollars and cents, right? The difference between taking a metro or a bus late at night versus getting into an Uber, which is much more expensive, finding a better apartment or a shared apartment in a better neighborhood. So a lot of the safety is priced in and is much more expensive for women to be safe in these conditions than for men to be safe. So everything you said makes perfect intuitive sense.

Again, thank you so much for the paper. I had a great time reading it. I learned a lot. I'm really excited about all of your findings.

Thank you so much for having me. It was a pleasure to discuss my paper with you.

节目结束语

Ideas of India is produced by the Mercatus Center at George Mason University. If you enjoy this podcast, please subscribe on Apple Podcasts, Spotify or your favorite podcast app. Help us grow by giving us a rating and leaving a review. Follow us on Twitter at S. Rajagopalan and at Ideas of India. Also check out our initiative commemorating 30 years of India's market reforms at the 1991project.com.
