item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的发现：这不是"信息问题"，而是"信号问题"
大多数经济学干预都在隐含假设——穷人/边缘人群之所以不迁移，是因为他们"不知道外面有多好"。但 Demirel 的实验把这个假设击碎了：学生**已经知道**孟买/浦那工资高 16–30%，他们对回报的预期甚至是准确的。真正奇特的地方在于——**和一个真的搬出去了的学长通话之后，他们反而更坚定地决定留在家里**。
这里有一个被大多数读者忽略的细节：浦那/孟买的 mentor 不仅没能"推"学生去大城市，反而让学生把目光下移到了"县级城市"（district capital）。换句话说，这个干预**在意料之外的层级上生效了**。它不是把人从 0 推到 100，而是把人从 0 推到 20——而这 20 可能才是真实世界里非金钱成本曲线的"拐点"所在。
一个跨领域的类比让我豁然开朗：这几乎是**金融学里的"流动性溢价"在人身上的镜像**。资产定价告诉我们，流动性差的资产要给出巨大折价才会被持有；而 Demirel 的 129% 迁移惩罚，本质上就是年轻人对"自己这个资产"的流动性折价定价——而这个折价对女性是男性的三倍。

item.title: [No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups] Tokenization, Agentic Trading, Harmonic: Robinhood's Mission to Expand Ownership with CEO Vlad Tenev
item.dc:creator: No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最意外的观察：Vlad 的"铜锅童年"是整个 Robin Hood 战略的隐藏操作系统

人们习惯把 Robin Hood 理解成"零佣金交易 App"，把 Vlad 理解成"数学 PhD 转金融科技创业者"。但如果你把他的童年叙事和今天的产品路线图叠在一起看，会发现一个惊人的事实：他正在把 1991 年保加利亚那个爷爷的壁橱——那个塞满铜锅的"真实资产金库"——用区块链重新建造一遍，然后把钥匙交给全世界 120 个国家的人。

  • 爷爷的铜锅 = 对抗 2000% 通胀的"real world asset"
  • 稳定币 = 对抗本币崩溃的数字铜锅
  • Stock tokens on Robinhood Chain = 把美股变成"任何人都能堆进壁橱里的铜锅"
  • Trump Accounts = 让每个美国新生儿一出生就自带一个"铜锅"

这不是产品路线图，这是一个孩子对童年通胀创伤的系统性报复。他甚至没怎么掩饰——访谈里他主动把铜锅故事和稳定币放在同一段话里。真正罕见的是：大多数创始人的童年创伤会表现为"焦虑"或"控制欲"，而他的创伤被编码成了产品哲学。所有权（ownership）这个词在他口中反复出现，不是营销，是他小时候眼睁睁看着爸妈的工资一周内蒸发后得出的世界观。

二、跨领域连接：Harmonic 和 Robinhood 是同一个哲学命题的两次下注

表面上看，一个是数学超级智能，一个是金融券商，风马牛不相及。但听完整段访谈你会发现 Vlad 在下一个非常一致的赌注：反对认知/财富的"数据中心集中化"。

  • 在 AI 领域，他担心的是："OpenAI 和 Anthropic 在自家数据中心里用秘密模型做出所有科学发现，然后由员工署名发表论文"——这是认知集中化。
  • 在金融领域，他担心的是："所有 AI 独角兽都在私募市场融到千亿美金再 IPO，散户只能在 2 万亿估值上接盘"——这是财富集中化。

他的两个解法在结构上完全同构： - Harmonic 把 Aristotle 开放给公众 → 让随机的业余数学家去证明未解猜想 - Robinhood Ventures Fund 2 + YC + 代币化 → 让随机的散户去持有 Seed 轮的 OpenAI

他真正的敌人不是华尔街，也不是 OpenAI。是"由少数专业机构垄断新物种诞生过程"这件事本身。 这是一种非常罕见的立场——它不是左派的"再分配"，也不是右派的"放任"，而是接近早期互联网自由主义者（Stewart Brand、John Perry Barlow）的信念：知识和所有权如果不在诞生之初就分散，后面再怎么补都是补丁。

三、藏在"Agentic Trading"里的一个反直觉预测

Vlad 轻描淡写地说了一句被所有人忽略的话：Agentic trading 的工具调用量已经到每天 3000 万次，并且呈平滑指数增长。然后他把它和"Claude Code / Codex"类比。

这个类比如果认真推下去，意味着一件比表面严重得多的事：

  • 在代码领域，AI agent 的爆发压垮了 CI/CD——不是算力不够，是人类设计的审批/验证节奏跟不上机器生产节奏。
  • 在交易领域，Vlad 自信满满地说"HFT 已经电子化 20 年了，基础设施扛得住"。

但他漏算了一件事：HFT 的量虽然大，但策略数量少且稳定（Citadel、Jump 就那么几套核心模型）。而 agentic trading 的未来形态是 15 万人、每人一套 claude 写的个性化策略——不是量的问题，是策略熵的问题。市场微观结构从未处理过"百万级弱相关但又彼此模仿 LLM 生成策略"的场景。

这里有个你绝对想不到的跨界预言：下一次 flash crash 不会来自算力过载，而会来自 LLM 的"思维同质性"。当 15 万散户都让 Claude 分析同一条新闻，LLM 的 attention 分布会让它们在同一秒做出高度相关的决策——这是一种算法层面的从众心理，是 2010 年 flash crash 的 LLM 版本。Vlad 没看到这一点，或者看到了但没说。这将是未来 5 年金融监管最棘手的新物种。

一个额外的"啊哈"：注意他说"预测市场是新闻的进化形态"。这不是营销话术。想想看——报纸的本质是"对概率的叙事化描述"（"专家预计经济将放缓"），而 Kalshi 和 Polymarket 是去掉叙事、只保留概率的新闻。如果他是对的，这意味着未来十年"写文章"这件事将被"开盘口"结构性替代——媒体的商业模式不是广告崩了，是信息的表达形式本身被淘汰了。

📝 转录文本

Tokenization, Agentic Trading, Harmonic: Robinhood's Mission to Expand Ownership with CEO Vlad Tenev

开场提要

Vlad Tenev: Prediction markets are an evolution of news. You just can see what's happening and what's likely to happen in the future through the odds.

Host: What is your reaction to the revolution in math that's happening with AI today?

Vlad: It's too centralized, right? It's like AI companies with their big data centers and their employees using secret models to sort of do all this work.

Host: Do you think people let agents trade for them?

Vlad: Agentic trading clearly product market fit. We're seeing really strong adoption — like over 150,000 customers have opened agentic trading accounts with us.

Host: Many of these things that you describe, institutional traders have the ability to do this, but it's expensive and sophisticated. If that's democratized, what does that mean?

节目介绍

Hi listeners, welcome back to No Priors. Today I'm here with Vlad Tenev, the founder and CEO of Robinhood. We talk about what Robinhood is today as a financial conglomerate trying to expand ownership in the economy — from tokenization to prediction markets, to how AI agents will trade for everyone in retail. We also talk about Harmonic, his effort to make a math superintelligence, and whether there can be distributed discovery and science rather than centralized.

Welcome Vlad.

Vlad: Well, thank you for having me.

一、今天的 Robinhood 是什么？——"所有权公司"

Host: So everyone knows Robinhood, but it has also evolved a ton as a company. Can you put in context for our listeners what you'd describe it as today?

Vlad: We do a lot of things. We're live in some form or another in over 120 countries. And if I had to sum up Robinhood in one word or one idea, it would be ownership. I think we're the ownership company — the company that's most associated with that.

And when I say that — so why does ownership matter? I think on an individual basis, people want to own things. It's the tried-and-true route to financial freedom, financial independence. If you're an asset owner and you accumulate assets over time, it's just the best way to build your wealth. So there's an individual element to it, whether you're trading, accumulating assets, or investing in venture — I think it's very very important.

And also, the things you own say a lot about your personality. It almost becomes like a part of your identity — whether it's a car collection, your collectibles, your cards, your stock portfolio. I think there's a lot of individuality in it.

所有权的集体价值

So I think there's an individual benefit, but there's also a collective benefit — a society without broad ownership is inherently very unstable. It's a fragile society. If you have more people that own things, they're more bought in. They have more stake in the outcome. They become defenders and protectors of the system.

Especially now, when people are kind of pushing back against society and it feels a little bit fraught with AI and all of this disruption — I think giving people the ability to own companies at earlier stages is increasingly important.

把所有业务串在一起的那根线

So it's really what ties together all of our things: - Trump accounts — ownership at age zero. - Robinhood Ventures — ownership of private companies before they go public. - Tokenization — you can think of as ownership gone global: how can we make all the people outside the US, people in 120+ countries that don't sometimes even have functional banking systems, how can we plug them into this economic fabric of society.

So yeah, that's how I think about it. We started off as just a simple app to buy stocks at zero commissions on your phone, and then we've expanded into an increasingly global financial conglomerate that allows customers to own things across a wide variety of surfaces and asset classes.

二、从保加利亚到硅谷：一个"所有权传教士"的成长

Host: You might be the only large financial firm I think of as a missionary organization, the other being like Vanguard or something like that. Can we talk about how you got here? I learned recently that you studied math under Terence Tao and you worked on HFT. Neither of those sound like a missionary for people, if I may say that. How did you discover this mission?

保加利亚的童年

Vlad: Rewinding back even further — I was born in Eastern Europe in the late 80s, kind of on the brink of the collapse of the Soviet Union and the lifting of the Iron Curtain. I immigrated to the US in the 1990s.

My dad had an opportunity to come study at the University of Delaware for his master's, and was able to take advantage of that and stay in America full-time. My mom came about a year after, and I came about six months after her — which was a pretty unique experience. I didn't see my dad for a year and a half, and my mom for six months, when I was a small child. I lived with my grandparents. A large portion of that was we just didn't have the money to send the whole family. We weren't sure that my dad would have a long-term future in this country, so we thought maybe he'd come back after a year or two. He did quite well and was able to send for my mom and then me.

恶性通胀下的童年记忆

My last year in Bulgaria, 1991, the inflation rate was something like 170% in Bulgaria. So my early memories were the rolling blackouts, my family huddled around the radio — which was battery-operated — just listening to what was going on. The lines at the bodega, which I could see from my window, for buying milk and eggs. The milk would come in these big plastic bags. And the one week a year you would get bananas from other communist countries. So Cuba — the Cuban bananas, I remember, were just amazing. Then I would come to the US and there were just bananas everywhere, right? But they weren't as good.

Even after I moved in 1997, Bulgaria had the unfortunate distinction of having the number one inflation rate in the world — something like 2,000% annualized. They were just adding zeros to the currency every couple of months.

爷爷的铜锅：第一个"真实世界资产"

From that point, I developed a kind of understanding of money. I had to be very independent. My parents — it was always a topic of conversation, and we would have to send money to my grandparents back home as they were dealing with this inflation crisis. My grandparents actually would keep their assets in copper cookware.

There was this closet in my grandfather's house — he worked as a doctor in the shipbuilding and naval industries, so he was on a boat a lot. He had his contacts at the port, and as soon as he would get salary, he would exchange it for copper cookware. So it was kind of the first real-world asset that I encountered people investing in.

Host: Stocked — sorry, stacked like pans?

Vlad: Exactly. In the closet you have —

Host: Holds value.

Vlad: Yes. Pots and pans. Much better than the local currency at the time.

独立与学术压力

And yeah, I grew up with that. I grew up understanding what happens in a broken system where you don't have free markets and good healthy capital markets.

For me, I pretty quickly discovered that academically I was quite strong — and also independent basically by choice. My parents couldn't really afford babysitters or after-school activities. They were both working multiple jobs, and my dad was a full-time graduate student. When I was in kindergarten, five years old, I would walk back from school by myself. They would tell me, "Okay, go to the neighbor's house." We lived in apartment buildings at the University of Maryland. "Knock on the door. Your neighbor will watch you for a couple of hours." Then they realized, "All right, our son's going through this complicated ritual to get home. We might as well just give him the key." Pretty soon I would let myself in, do my homework, go outside, play with my friends.

There was always this pressure to succeed and do well in school. Probably for a couple of reasons. One, I was good at it. Everyone around me was like, "Do more school, skip grades, do better in math, more math." The teachers would have meetings with my parents — "Hey, your son, do you know he's really good at math? You should put him in this thing." That was one of the benefits of growing up around the University of Maryland — a very academically oriented community, and they would try to identify the kids that had potential and accelerate them.

The other thing was my parents would just sit me down and say, "Look, the financial status of this family is very insecure. We're not making any money. So you're going to have to basically get a scholarship if you want to go to college. And to get a scholarship, you are going to have to do very very well in school. Also, by the way, we're visa holders here — if we lose our jobs, we're going to have to get sent back to Bulgaria." So there was all this pressure to succeed academically.

数学的阶梯：攀登最难的山

For me, my math PhD program at some point became this challenge — like, what's the hardest thing? How can I do better at the hardest thing? It was almost a competition with myself, and with my parents who were also very academically strong. "Oh, what was the hardest subject for you at school, dad?" "Oh, chemistry." "Let me just do really well at chemistry." "What was the most advanced math that you did?"

Math has this ladder of achievement. It's almost like playing a really good video game — you always know what the next hardest thing is. How quickly can you go to algebraic geometry or algebraic topology, and can you learn that earlier and understand it?

What appealed to me when I got to grad school was this idea that if you create a new mathematical theory, maybe you'll be remembered for a really long time. Just like kids in school learn Gauss and Riemann and all these greats — if you create a theory, maybe kids will be learning and thinking about your work hundreds of years from now. That's what appealed to me.

三、Harmonic：反对"数据中心式"的数学革命

Host: Given that background — and you should also explain what Harmonic is as an effort — what is your reaction to the revolution in math that's happening with AI today?

Vlad: On the one hand, it's very exciting and sort of predictable. The rise of AI models, and the ability to verify the outputs, put together has led to automation of the math pipeline. It's really really exciting.

The math is changing so quickly — and math as a field hasn't changed very rapidly at all in thousands of years. When I was in grad school, most of the work was still being done in person with chalk and a chalkboard. There was no collaboration. People weren't even using computers. Now math has kind of converged with coding. Mathematicians are using the same tools — version control, Lean for verification — and the field is accelerating very rapidly.

Harmonic 与 Aristotle

About a year ago… so Harmonic is a startup that I co-founded a couple years ago with the goal of building mathematical superintelligence. Last year we created a model called Aristotle that was one of three that got a gold medal on the International Math Olympiad. Subsequently we rolled it out to the public, and people were using Aristotle to tackle unsolved math problems. It was used to solve these Erdős problems; there were other mathematicians using it for new results and so forth.

对"中心化 AI 发现"的担忧

I started thinking a lot about: okay, what's the future of math? How should these tools be used? For me it was very important for the tools that I build — not just Harmonic but also Robinhood — to be empowering to individuals, to people.

The one thing I don't love about this latest wave of AI models solving math problems is that it's too centralized. It's like AI companies with their big data centers and their employees using secret models to do all this work. What's more attractive, and what would ultimately win out in the end as a model, is rolling these things out and actually putting them in the hands of people, and having the users make interesting discoveries and inventions.

主持人反驳：Centaur Play 会被算力碾压吗？

Host: I am probably a pretty fundamental believer in decentralization as a philosophical premise, and I would love to believe that's true. But there are a lot of people who work at large centralized AI companies who would say — if I may push back a little bit — that this is cope, and centaur play will just be outclassed by, you know, more compute in an agent loop. Do you believe that's true, or what will be the human input here that is productive in math?

Vlad: I think there are sort of two separate things. One is: what's the role of the individual mathematician? The other is: is this going to be a product that people use, or are the AI labs going to be producing the products?

I have thoughts on both, but on the second one it's much more interesting. A world where you have the AI labs on a proprietary basis making all the discoveries — where you have the OpenAI or Anthropic data centers that are just running code managed by the employees of those companies, vertically integrating and producing all the drugs, selling the drugs to people, making all the mathematical and physical discoveries, publishing all the papers — if all of that is happening and it's owned by the AI labs themselves, that's a bit of a dystopian outcome, and unlikely to happen for a couple of reasons.

Not just technological and market reasons — I think also, if that happens to a significant degree, people will lose their license to operate.

让"路人甲"解开黎曼猜想

You could have the same outcome of Navier–Stokes being proven, or the partial Riemann hypothesis, or any one of these things — and it'll be much more accepted if it was like a random layperson using the tools.

Host: It might be celebrated.

Vlad: I think for sure. And that's how it's going to happen — that's the likely scenario one year from now.

You also have the confounding factor that a lot of the people going into these AI labs are former researchers, so they're excited by doing research. I think they're confused as to why this is being poorly received. From their perspective it's like, "Oh, I'm a researcher. I was brought into a research organization to do research, and now all these academics are mad at me."

I've said this to folks that work at the companies — it would have been much better if they found some mathematicians and collaborated with them, so as not to make it seem like there's this dark data center dystopian future where one company is going to make all of the scientific discoveries.

四、代币化（Tokenization）：把铜锅搬上链

Host: Can we talk a little bit about both the new ways you want to extend ownership as part of Robinhood, and also how Robinhood is intersecting with what's happening in AI? Maybe we can start with what you guys are doing with tokenization, or your vision for it.

什么是代币化

Vlad: Tokenization is really a new innovation, and the idea is almost similar to stablecoins. The way a stablecoin works is: you take some dollars or treasuries, put them in a wrapper, put them in a box, and then you mint and burn tokens against the box. The traditional assets stay custodied at a traditional institution like a bank, and then the tokens can trade freely on DeFi. They can move anywhere around the world. They can trade in fractional amounts. They can be swapped in different protocols or lending pools.

Host: Software characteristics.

Vlad: Yeah. You can extend that concept to any real-world asset. We've done it with stocks — you can put stocks in a box, mint and burn tokens against them, and they can trade all over the internet on blockchains like software. You can do it with private companies — instead of a stock it's an SPV with private company shares. Behaves the same, with some slight differences around redeeming. You could do it with art, collectibles, real estate.

从法国到 Robinhood Chain

We've been playing around with tokenization and experimenting with it for many years. Last year we had an event in the south of France where we launched stock tokens — tokenized versions of US stocks — in Europe. But it wasn't fully DeFi-enabled: if you were a European customer using Robinhood, you could trade them and they felt very much like real stocks, but you couldn't send them out on Ethereum or on the blockchain, put them in pools or compose them with other smart contracts.

This year we took it one step further. We relaunched stock tokens with fully DeFi-enabled characteristics, and we launched it in conjunction with Robinhood Chain, our new blockchain built for real-world assets. Robinhood Chain has become one of the fastest-growing — I think the fastest-growing across a lot of metrics — blockchains in history. We've seen just an explosion of developer activity. We announced recently it's the number one chain in developer activity.

Developers have taken stock tokens, which have become kind of like Legos, and have started building all sorts of interesting smart contracts — NFTs, pooled assets where you'll take, for example, a memecoin and link it with a stock token. This is just month one and month two type activity. These financial primitives, as the foundation of a developer platform, will become really really big.

面向 120 国的"数字铜锅"

What's more exciting to me than this is: Robinhood Chain is a way to enable the long tail of countries. People in countries that don't have highly functioning capital markets or financial systems — places in South America or Africa — anyone with a smartphone and a non-custodial wallet can now get exposure to US markets at incredibly low cost. In the same way that stablecoins became the default way for people in these countries to get access to dollars, stock tokens and products like that will be the default way to get access to US equities for all of these people.

Host: May they have access to not just copper pots but wealth creation.

Vlad: Exactly. And private companies. The vision for Robinhood Chain and tokenization is: let's just take all the things that work on Robinhood and put them on-chain, and make them available to people in all these countries.

"Corpo Chain"的争议

One thing I've learned — we're new to operating a blockchain, we're new to operating these on-chain smart contract products. A lot of the criticisms that Robinhood has received: we've been called a "corpo chain", right? They said the best blockchains are managed by these organizations and consortiums and everything's decentralized, and "you guys are a corporation managing a chain. How is that going to be as good?"

Well — maybe you sacrifice a little bit of organizational decentralization purity, but what you get is focused leadership and some group of people with very very clear direction pushing things forward. The other thing is: it is good to have Robinhood-backed products on the chain too. A lot of chains take the approach of, "Let a thousand flowers bloom, let the developers build all this stuff." We love the developers as well, but having primitives like stock tokens that have our backing, that people can trust — we've seen that creates more interest to build on them. People know: okay, Robinhood's backing them, they're legit, that's a trusted brand, we know they're not going to go away. That gives them much more confidence to build than if it was just a team of two or three engineers somewhere offering these primitives.

开发者组合的可能性

Host: Is there an example of a composition that you think should exist on stock tokens, or has already come from the ecosystem that you're excited about?

Vlad: One of the things I'm thinking about is — yeah, how can we take some of these derivative products like options? Can you make really nice smart contract native options contracts? There's been a tremendous amount of innovation in the traditional markets that's to some degree stymied by how hard it is to just move off of mainframes onto more modern things, and take all the counterparties that rely on the system being predictable and slow-moving.

A big part of it is: let's provide the primitives and let the developers put them together in new ways. I don't want to presuppose what developers come up with, because I wouldn't have been able to tell you that stock-token-linked NFTs or stock-token-meme pairs would become a thing. I had no way to foresee how quickly those things would grow and become real.

五、预测市场：新闻的进化形态

Host: It's not necessarily ownership. What is your perspective on prediction markets?

Vlad: I actually think prediction markets do tie into ownership, because a lot of people have unique knowledge and ideas and they have hot takes on things that not everyone knows. You might be an expert in AI model development — we have lots of contracts that allow you to speculate and hedge on what AI model will be best this week or this month or this year.

The way to monetize that knowledge before prediction markets was highly indirect — maybe you could trade derivatives on Google stock or Nvidia stock.

Host: Imprecise.

Vlad: Yeah. There is an important thing with being able to monetize your own knowledge, and doing it more directly.

KPI 合约

It's actually one of the reasons we announced — and we're planning to launch — KPI contracts. For a long time, if you wanted — let's say you're studying a company and you have a pretty good idea that it's going to beat earnings EPS or revenue — in the past, if you bought the stock, or an option on the stock, sometimes the company would beat earnings but the stock would go down for some unrelated reason, like guidance.

KPI contracts now allow you to actually trade the EPS print, the revenue print, or any of the other KPIs that might matter to a company. You can actually monetize your belief; you can hedge more precisely. For example, there's a "will the California billionaire tax pass" contract, which I think is a useful hedging instrument for some people. Not me personally — I'm not hedging with it, but one could.

预测市场 = 未来的新闻

The other thing is: I think it's a new source of information. I think of it, in its pure form, as an evolution of news. What does news look like in the future? I don't think it's the New York Times — but I think it could be something like it, where you have your front page, your business section, lifestyle, culture, sports (and sports is a big part of it). You just can see what's happening and what's likely to happen in the future through the odds. A lot of people don't even trade these things — they just like to open the app and check out.

Host: That's me. What's going to happen?

六、Agentic Trading：把对冲基金装进每个人的口袋

Host: Do you think people let agents trade for them, and when, and what's the impact of that?

产品发布与采用

Vlad: Yeah. We launched a product earlier this year, which is basically a Robinhood MCP. We call it Agentic Trading, and we have an Agentic credit card as well. In the broader realm of agentic finance, there are two things that have product–market fit. One is agentic trading — very clearly — like having an agent execute your trades and do a strategy for you.

We're seeing really strong adoption. Over 150,000 customers have opened agentic trading accounts with us in the few months since we've launched it.

Host: Wow.

Vlad: And if you look at the tool calls — the tool calls have just been following this smooth exponential. The last number we announced was something like 30 million tool calls per day. So agentic trading clearly product–market fit.

Robinhood Agents

A couple weeks ago at our Hood Summit event, we announced Robinhood Agents, which is basically taking it one step further: the harness and the entire UI is now inside a Robinhood account. You can think of it as — if you're a Claude Code or a Codex user — it's almost like a tool like that that's optimized for trading.

You can run loops and say, "Okay, every day, execute a run of my strategy, rebalance my portfolio, look at opportunities." We have skills — you can do a portfolio rebalance, or all sorts of other things. We have agent apps — we launched an app store where, for example, you can connect to a source of satellite data: if you want to create a strategy that counts cars in parking lots of retailers, we'll make that available.

The way I think that'll evolve is: we're going to look at all the capabilities that the coding harnesses have, and see how we can provide really nice clean trader-native versions of that that just make it really easy to be an active trader.

把对冲基金的能力放进口袋

Host: Amazing. What do you think the impact is of this on either participant mix or financial infrastructure? Many of these things you describe, institutional traders have the ability to do this, but it's expensive and sophisticated. If that's democratized, what does that mean?

Vlad: That's really the North Star of the product. Can we put the capabilities of a hedge fund or a sophisticated algorithmic trading firm into the pockets of normal individuals? In the same way that if you were a sophisticated grad student in computer science, you could write a trading strategy — and if you went through even more effort, you could deploy it, get rack space in the data center connected to the exchanges — can we streamline all aspects of that so that, in the same way it's made it easier for anyone to be a software engineer, Robinhood Agents and our MCP can make it easier for more people to be quant traders?

I think the outcome is: there will just be more trading activity. At first it'll be concentrated in a relatively small group of sophisticated people, but their trading activity will likely increase quite substantially, and then over time it'll filter to more and more of the population.

Coding is a good analogy. There are people who code, and they were first to adopt the coding agents, and their output multiplied. But now there are people that just wouldn't have picked up VS Code or Cursor before — but someone showed them how to use Claude or Codex, and now they can build a website really easily. It'll lift the tide across the board. I believe the desire to make software or automate things is much broader than I did, perhaps, before any of the coding and agentic coding AI happened. But wanting to make money off of a belief feels like a much more universal thing.

As it becomes easier — a lot of people have ideas, right? If you can take that idea and turn it into a strategy with as little friction as possible — if we can get it to approach the friction of just buying a single stock — then a lot more people will do it.

基础设施是否需要重构？

Host: There may not be an answer to this question, but is there an obvious way in which financial infrastructure or risk management needs to change in reaction to this?

Vlad: I don't think so. Let me tell you the safeguards we have on day one.

Right now you have to create a new separate account, which is segregated from your main Robinhood balance. You create an MCP account, you create an agentic account, you move money in there. For customers that choose to have trade approvals — by default you have to approve your trades, but then you can turn it off so that — you know, permissions.

Host: Exactly.

Vlad: Well actually it's not as dangerous as that, because it's not like it can go into your other accounts. It's sandboxed — maybe not quite air-gapped, but pretty close. We built, and refined, a lot of the infrastructure for the sandboxing and the harness in-house at Robinhood.

The reason I don't see any clear massive overhauls necessary is that high-frequency trading has been a thing for a really long time. Markets went fully electronic about 20 years ago. Everything from the exchanges to a lot of the brokers has conformed to this new reality of most of the workflows being algorithmic trading that happens in data centers in New Jersey, rather than what a lot of people still think happens — paper tickets, floor traders, a trading pit. It's not clear to me that anything fundamental has to change with regulation. As it gets bigger — and I don't doubt it will — we might run into special cases for which we need more regulatory clarity.

类比 CI/CD 崩溃？

Host: I was more from an infrastructure perspective. If you just use coding as a proxy — I did not, and maybe we all should have, but I think it was not obvious that CI/CD was going to completely fall over in the face of orders-of-magnitude growth in code generation.

Vlad: Oh yeah.

Host: So that was my question — yes of course we've had HFT, but if everybody is a high-frequency trader, that feels like new load.

Vlad: There are a couple of different layers in the stack. Our on-chain stack is slightly different — that already has MCPs. On our on-chain tools — I talked about Robinhood Chain being the best chain for real-world assets; it's also the best chain for AI agents. So we're seeing a lot of agentic trading there.

On our CeFi centralized offerings, we have a lot of end-to-end control over the entire system. We have our databases, our code that the strategies are running on, the sandboxes — we build a lot of those tools. We have to optimize all of that. But once it gets through our system, you get to places like the market makers, which are all extremely sophisticated software shops — Citadel, Jane Street, Jump Trading. These are low-latency, high-frequency folks. I'm not so worried about them scaling to meet the demand. Then you have the exchanges, and the exchanges — because of pressure from HFTs and algo trading — have really optimized their APIs to handle huge volumes.

That said, we're still at a low percentage of total trading that is agentic. We'll have some warning. We'll see it increasing, and I don't think we're going to be at the point imminently where agentic-mediated trades are a double-digit percentage of the activity. We'll have some time.

七、所有权与 AI 革命：为什么大家对数据中心生气

Host: Given you're such a strong believer in ownership, and democratized ownership as important to societal stability — and also just opportunity for people — I think there's a sense that the AI revolution is not a broadly-owned thing. Do you have an idea of what the solutions here might be? And maybe you can talk about Trump accounts as well.

问题的诊断

Vlad: We identified this problem last year. First, all of the major innovative AI companies are private — with some exceptions. You can look at Nvidia and Google, but those companies were already quite big before they really got into this new phase of AI. If you wanted to invest in a large language model a couple of years ago, and you wanted exposure to OpenAI or Anthropic, you're basically out of luck as an individual investor.

There are a lot of reasons for that. One is: private markets have gotten — it's gotten really easy for high-growth successful companies to raise money in the private markets.

Host: At massive scale.

Vlad: Massive scale. That didn't used to be the case. Back in the 80s, a company like Microsoft — even in the 90s with Amazon — went public at valuations in the hundreds of millions. So individual investors that got in during the public offering could make a 1000x. Now, if you have an AI lab that goes public at a trillion or two trillion, in order for an individual investor at IPO to make that type of return, they'd have to get into the quadrillions. It's crazy. Maybe it could happen, but it's going to be much tougher.

Instead, the gains keep getting concentrated into a smaller and smaller group of venture capitalists or institutional investors. Then we're wondering, well, why are people upset about data centers? If I'm an individual, I don't benefit economically from any of this activity. In fact, you could say — well, it's threatening my livelihood, my job, it's polluting my neighborhood, they're making all this noise.

加密 vs AI：所有权结构的对比

Juxtapose AI with something like crypto. Crypto has not been — it's not like everyone trading crypto makes money. Right now Bitcoin is, what, 85,000? If you bought at 120,000 a couple of months ago, you're down. 2022 and 2023 were rough for the crypto industry, to say the least. A lot of people lost money in those years. But yet in 2024 they came out in full force and swung the election, I think, in a meaningful way. If there's even a hint of regulatory overreach for crypto, you have this army of people that are just blasting social media, messaging their congressman or woman, and fighting every inch of it.

A big part of it is: crypto is distributed, broad ownership by individuals from the beginning, and almost institutions are coming in late. Whereas AI is the difference.

Robinhood Ventures 的两只基金

What do we do about it? We launched two things. We believe that everyone should be able to invest in private companies. I can't convince companies to go public earlier too effectively — even though I try doing that sometimes. We do have our IPO — we're an underwriter, we're active in that pipeline. But individual investors should benefit from private companies and be a huge shareholder.

That's really the vision behind Robinhood Ventures. How can we make it so that it's an anomaly to not have individual retail investors as a big constituent of your seed and Series A cap table? They should actually be at the earliest possible stage.

Robinhood Ventures Fund One has an innovative structure. You can think of it as a publicly traded venture capital firm. We used our IPO channel — we're the largest retail channel for IPOs — to raise capital in an IPO from Robinhood customers, individual retail, and then we use that to invest in startups. The funds are publicly traded on the New York Stock Exchange. They trade just like a stock.

Robinhood Ventures Fund One was late-stage privates. OpenAI is in that fund. You have a couple of other companies — Figure, a lot of AI companies, 11 Labs, Crusoe. Then we asked ourselves: how can we go to the extreme and give people exposure to seed and Series A? That's where Robinhood Ventures Fund Two — the idea came to partner with YC and use a structure to give people exposure to the earliest possible stage, where the risk is highest but opportunity is also greatest. That's the fund that Rich Aberman is running for us.

Then we have tokenization of privates, which solves that problem in a different way, but right now for outside of the US. The North Star is: can we get a private company to be real-time tradable 24/7 in fractional quantities, just like a stock or a crypto? You should be able to just trade Anthropic 24/7 in low dollar amounts, with some degree of high-quality ownership — at least as good as owning an LP interest in an SPV. That should be available to everyone. That requires pushing on a bunch of things — in the US, accredited investor rules being one of them. We're highly motivated to lead that and make that happen.

合格投资人规则需要更新

Host: That was my question for you — if you are, for example, a venture capitalist with a portfolio you think is going to make money in privates, then some people will have a choice of LPs: there are institutions, there are your friends, you can make money for. Obviously there are rules around QP and accreditation around taking retail interest. Your view is clearly that some of those rules need to be updated.

Vlad: There was an initiative by the SEC, announced last week, to allow a separate path. They directed FINRA — the primary broker-dealer regulator — to create an accreditation exam where, as an individual, you can go and get accredited by taking a 2-hour exam at a testing facility. Versus it being —

Host: Versus it being asset-based.

Vlad: Versus it being asset-based. There's also — you can be affiliated, you could have a Series 7, which is an affiliation with a financial firm, licensure. But yeah, so it's a knowledge-based exam. It's definitely a positive step. They're doing stuff. But the goal would be to make it lower friction — how many people are going to go and sit for an exam at a testing facility? More work needs to be done, and we're going to be at the forefront of continuing to push for that.

对家长主义的反驳

Host: The main argument against such evolution of rules would be some sense of protection against fraud and paternalism there. How do you think about that?

Vlad: For our customers — we spend a lot of time talking to them, figuring out what they care about. One of the things they care about most, that they agree with, is the statement: "I should be in charge of my money, and nobody should tell me how to spend or invest my money." When we say to our customers, "Do you agree with this?" — overwhelming agreement. Not to say that they'll personally want to do every type of risky speculative investment, but they don't think it's the government's place or anyone's place to tell them what to do with their money broadly.

Of course, people should be absolutely clear on what these products are, and we should make sure to tell you what it is, give you as much information as possible. But I think about this — am I going to tell you not to invest in the hot IPO? IPOs are risky, for sure. Memecoins — even memecoins have perfect regulatory clarity. If you want to buy a memecoin, you are free to do so. The SEC even wrote a letter saying these are not securities, they're collectibles. The clear way. So I think it's silly from a couple of different angles — not the least of which is that memecoins are completely fine in any amount, but private companies —

Host: It's not rational, from a pure risk orientation, to restrict private companies.

Vlad: I think that's right. People are smart. There should be some sensible regulation, I'm in favor of that. But we've just gone too far, and the conditions that made the accredited investor rule necessary no longer hold. These rules are from a time before the internet. You couldn't even get any information. Now there's just an influx of information about everything, particularly private companies — and AI models that can scour and synthesize it for you. It makes a little bit less sense now.

八、Trump Accounts：从出生就持有美国

Host: Can you talk about what Robinhood is doing to support Trump accounts?

Vlad: This was our way of serving our country, which we're very proud of. Robinhood was selected as the sole initial trustee and broker for the Trump accounts, and we're working with BNY — America's oldest and most storied bank — and with Treasury and IRS to make this program happen.

项目设计

The idea behind it is: can we get every child from birth to own a chunk of the US economy through the S&P 500, through a low-cost diversified ETF? For every newborn child — everyone born in January 2025 onward for the next three years — they get $1,000 seeded by Treasury. Michael and Susan Dell, through their foundation, added another over $6 billion to children in lower-income zip codes. A bunch of other people are following — Gwynne Shotwell committed a donation in SpaceX shares. Brad Gerstner, who is the brains and architect behind the program, pushed it forward and made a really big donation to the citizens of Indiana and their children.

目标：家庭持股率从 65% 到 95%

We're powering the infrastructure, building the app. We love it because I think it's the best thing for actually getting household stock ownership from 65% to 95%. When it's successful, it'll lead to a much more stable and prosperous society in many decades. Our goal is to make this the best product the government's ever launched, and the most enduring positive aspect of President Trump's legacy. That's our goal.

九、最后一问：领导力与定力

Host: It's an amazing effort. Sign your kids up.

So last question for you. Andrew Reed, who we both know well, described you as a strange combination of unlimited IQ and the steadiest possible hand when working with the vagaries of the financial markets and PR and large user bases. How do you keep your levelheadedness or cool? What advice do you have for the many business leaders that listen?

童年的淬炼

Vlad: I think going through a lot of challenges as a child just made me very used to going through challenges. I had a very supportive and amazing family, great parents — but we were kind of in this together. We all immigrated to the US at the same time, and I wasn't a child that was given things. It was almost like: you're a member of this family, and we all have to figure this out. I had my part; they had their parts. So even though they're a child, they treated me with a lot of autonomy, almost as an equal, from a very young age.

2000% 通胀与今天的"危机"

We run through — we come across a lot of business challenges at Robinhood, at Harmonic, at all these things. But when you step back and say, "All right, does it compare to the threat of deportation?" We talk about inflation here of 5% and freak out about it. What about the 2,000% inflation that we went through as children?

给自己孩子制造挑战

Sometimes I think about that with my own kids.

Host: Do you create challenge for them?

Vlad: We try. I try to construct challenge, but you have to construct it — it's a little bit harder. They get a lot of positives. They could have tutors, they could go to all kinds of museums that I didn't have.

Host: They have safety.

Vlad: They have safety. There's something very important about having to struggle and endure. I try to create that environment as much as possible, but I haven't figured it out. That's a big part of it. And also — as we were talking before — it's a good bit of nature versus nurture. Maybe I was just born like that. I don't know how much of it's the environment either.

给领导者的建议：厚脸皮是超能力

Host: If we take it away for advice for other leaders — it is just the optimistic take that whatever challenge you're going through will make you more level in the future.

Vlad: I think Bezos said this, right? The best approach to all of these challenges — just grow thick skin. You can control that about yourself, but you can't control the outside world. If you can actually do that, I think it seems to be a big superpower that not everyone is capable of.

Host: Awesome. Thanks so much, Vlad. This is great.

Vlad: Thanks for having me.

片尾

Find us on Twitter at @NoPriorsPod. Subscribe to our YouTube channel if you want to see our faces. Follow the show on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you listen — that way you get a new episode every week. Sign up for emails or find transcripts for every episode at no-priors.com.

item.description:
## 一、最意外的观察：Vlad 的"铜锅童年"是整个 Robin Hood 战略的隐藏操作系统
人们习惯把 Robin Hood 理解成"零佣金交易 App"，把 Vlad 理解成"数学 PhD 转金融科技创业者"。但如果你把他的童年叙事和今天的产品路线图叠在一起看，会发现一个惊人的事实：**他正在把 1991 年保加利亚那个爷爷的壁橱——那个塞满铜锅的"真实资产金库"——用区块链重新建造一遍，然后把钥匙交给全世界 120 个国家的人。**
- 爷爷的铜锅 = 对抗 2000% 通胀的"real world asset" - 稳定币 = 对抗本币崩溃的数字铜锅 - Stock tokens on Robinhood Chain = 把美股变成"任何人都能堆进壁橱里的铜锅" - Trump Accounts = 让每个美国新生儿一出生就自带一个"铜锅"
这不是产品路线图，这是**一个孩子对童年通胀创伤的系统性报复**。他甚至没怎么掩饰——访谈里他主动把铜锅故事和稳定币放在同一段话里。真正罕见的是：大多数创始人的童年创伤会表现为"焦虑"或"控制欲"，而他的创伤被编码成了**产品哲学

item.title: [Bits + Bips] Binance Lost $6.3 Billion in 20 Minutes. Can Crypto Stop the Next One?
item.dc:creator: Bits + Bips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

当"快"成为系统性债务：币安 20 分钟损失 63 亿的真正含义

最让人意外的观察不是"又一次被黑"，而是这次事件暴露了加密行业最深层的身份矛盾——它把自己的核心卖点（无需许可的即时结算）变成了结构性的安全负债。Austin 在节目末尾点破了一个被所有人忽略的关键：传统金融里"熔断机制 (circuit breaker)"、"24 小时转账冷静期"、"做市商第八次报价时就扩大买卖价差"——这些都是 101 级的风控常识，但加密协议从未内建。63 亿在 20 分钟内穿过 10 条链流出，不是技术漏洞，是设计哲学的漏洞。整个行业用"抗审查"为名义，拒绝了所有延迟机制，却忘了延迟本身就是金融安全的免疫系统。

跨领域连接：这不是密码学问题，是"航空业 1950 年代"的翻版

加密世界此刻的处境，和二战后民航业惊人地相似。飞机技术已经成熟，但事故率居高不下，直到 FAA 强制引入冗余系统、预飞清单、黑匣子、强制停飞——这些全都是"降低效率"的东西。民航业的黄金时代不是始于更快的飞机，而是始于系统性地拒绝"唯速度论"。Chris 说"西部拓荒时代要结束了"，这个比喻其实选错了——更贴切的是航空业的 1958 年联邦航空法案。而真正反直觉的推论是：那些现在看起来最"不加密"的协议（有审查节点、有延迟窗口、有人工复核的）反而可能是下一个周期的赢家。CZ 曾经引以为傲的"Binance 比银行快"现在成了负面叙事——这是行业第一次要学会为"慢"收费。

隐藏的系统性真相：VC 选错了"操作知识的祖辈"

Austin 的另一个一闪而过的观察值得被放大——加密 VC 没有做过银行家，也没有做过交易员。这解释了一个长期悖论：为什么硅谷最聪明的资本涌入了十几年，加密的金融基础设施还停留在"热钱包存 63 亿"的水平？因为 a16z、Paradigm 这些机构的合伙人谱系来自支付和消费科技，不是来自清算所、经纪商和中央银行。他们天然看不见"结算风险"、"对手方风险"、"操作风险"这些概念——因为他们的职业直觉里从来没有这些词。

这里有个让人脊背发凉的推论：Binance 的 DevOps 工程师笔记本电脑被攻破这件事，本质上和 2008 年 Jerome Kerviel 在法兴银行亏掉 49 亿欧元是同一类事件——都是单点权限 × 缺乏职责分离 × 操作风险模型缺失。但传统银行有巴塞尔协议、有 SOX、有内控审计；而加密交易所的"去中心化叙事"反而成了逃避这些制度的借口。Ram 提到 Brian Armstrong 在 Coinbase 内部人披露中卖出 10 亿美元股票——这或许不是"创始人套现"的八卦，而是最熟悉加密托管风险的人正在用脚投票的信号。

最反常识的结论

节目里反复出现一句话："AI 和加密是朋友"。但真实的赛博对抗格局是：AI 让攻击者的边际成本接近零，而让防御者的工作量呈线性增长——因为攻击只需要找到一个漏洞，防御需要堵住所有漏洞。这意味着未来 18 个月，加密行业最大的竞争者不是其他公链，而是时间本身——institutional capital 会在"再出一次 Binance 级事件"和"ICE/Nasdaq 完成数字资产基建"之间赛跑。而 10 月唯一上涨的 top 10 币种是 Monero——一个被主流叙事抛弃多年的隐私币。这不是巧合：当整个市场在讨论"透明度和合规"时，市场本能已经在为下一轮"主权级隐私需求"定价了。

📝 转录文本

事件概览：20 分钟 63 亿美元蒸发

Binance lost about 6.3 billion from its hot wallets on October 29th and what the FBI is now pinning on North Korea's trader trader roughly four times the size of the buy bit hack. The exchange covered most of it. They have reopened withdrawals. They've had a small net outflow. Uh but the shock helped put push Bitcoin to its worst October since 2014.

So what happened here? About 6.3 billion left Binance hot wallets. As you look across all of the network, I believe TRM counts 6.36 billion across 10 networks. Um, Inca Digital has a little bit more than that. I believe Chain Analysis also had a number in that ballpark. Everybody agrees it's over $6 billion. Most of this happened in a 20 minute burst, which tells you how fast these hacks are happening.

So, Binance said the incident quote "may involve a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop" — early on. There was no sign of a private key leak. And FBI formally named the perpetrator uh and published 628 hacker wallets for exchange and node operators to block, asking people to do so. And in that same day, by the way, Poly Market halted trading after a vendor breach leading to unauthorized withdrawals unrelated to Binance, and users will also be reimbursed.

So, Binance says it's covered about 95% of the loss already. Uh the net outflows of 3.64 billion after reopening or about 2% of its assets. Uh CZ said 98% are choosing to stay. The bigger news is maybe the market. Bitcoin fell to 76,400. Liquidations jumped again about 1.57 billion. And Timothy Peterson noted, "Bitcoin has had the worst October since 2014." Uh, the only top 10 coin up in October was ironically Monero.

Chris 的宏观视角：安全是技术成熟的必经关卡

So Chris, I want to start with you from a macro perspective here rather than just speaking about Binance, because Poly Market also happened and the number of hacks happening has just continued to go up and up and up. So for you as an investor in this space at an institutional firm, what are you making of the information security situation and how are we looking at this if even Binance is subject to these problems?

Chris: Yeah, I think we're seeing reports of another smaller hack today. Um, we've talked about this over and over again on this podcast — that in order for this technology to assume its rightful place and its full potential, we got to get through the security issue. Um, so right now we're going through this very difficult time because AI um and new tools for perpetrators to use AI are coming online. Yes, the good guys have them too. There's just a lot of vulnerabilities across different surfaces.

And by the way, this applies equally, perhaps more so, to traditional markets. Remember, crypto is just $3 trillion in size, plus or minus. The rest of the economy is much bigger. We don't often hear about those — the challenges there — but um you know, don't forget there's something going on on the other side of the world that needs to be addressed as well.

You know, my personal belief, I've said it once, I will say it again till I'm blue in the face: AI and crypto longer term, they're friends. AI will be able to plug those gaps. They'll run the agents along vulnerability services and they'll plug those vulnerability surfaces. A vulnerability discovered is a vulnerability plugged. I mean that. So medium-term it's going to be very, very good.

It feels though — I also believe that the wild west is coming to an end. Institutions are moving in. Um we're seeing way too many stage coaches being robbed. Uh and we went through a phase when we were settling the west when that happened, right? Because a lot of policy and infrastructure hadn't caught up. I I think that those days will ultimately come to an end and we will be much, much stronger. It's just going to take some time to get there.

So, we're not — it's not that this is going to continue to happen. Um we have to be prepared for it. I think um institutions understand that this has to get solved for.

安全作为新的创投垂直

I'll also say that through a venture lens — um as institutions are coming into the space — we have a huge problem guys, and that's security. And I'm very excited to see the founders that plug these gaps. I think it's going to be very, very interesting to see how they move. So I think security is going to be a big vertical uh of of any uh venture strategy going forward. The opportunity is immense um and the best founders solve the most difficult challenges. This is a difficult challenge.

Ram 的失望：2026 年了，这不该还是个问题

Is this the part where I talk about Sam Altman or North? Go for it, dude. Yeah, blame Sam. Blame Sam as you normally do.

Ram: Sam Altman is part of the solution. I guess that's the AI. So, you know, remember back when e-commerce was coming online, there were questions around — are you going to put your credit card on the internet? Are you going to trade through E*Trade? And all those risks were overblown. You fast forward and everything is digital.

When it comes to digital assets though, we still have these same legitimate risks and concerns. And Chris is right — it's going to happen again. So, you can't help but feel cynical. I mean, digital assets as a category has failed to secure their customer deposits. It's incredibly disappointing. Uh, and I think that's it. It's like 2026, guys. 2020, it should have been solved. 2021, it should have been solved when DeFi was on the rise.

Now, you see Brian Armstrong is selling a billion dollars plus of Coinbase stock. If you guys saw that in a recent insider filing — uh, the big boys are here now, like ICE, I'm sure we'll talk about. It's incredibly disappointing and deflating for the category. There's more of this. We're going to have the same chat like in a month, right? Or two months from now. We're going to wait for the next one.

加密之外的隐忧

Chris: Well, I'm more worried about, you know, I think there's the potential that you're going to see stuff outside of the crypto space that could be big as well. Um, and I ultimately think that a lot of the challenges will be solved by the crypto community longer term. Um, but yeah, we'll see. We haven't heard too much about outside of crypto. Maybe that's because that's where we live all day long, but there's hacks going on.

Ram: Crypto communities, they're moving, right? Like Fred Ehrsam's doing Asian Longevity. You know, we talked about Brian Armstrong. Chris Dixon is rebranding a recent a16z fund, which used to be dedicated to crypto, to something broader. So, you're already seeing these pivots in talent. Everything is about AI now. And crypto is losing trust. It's all about confidence. We talked about this several times. All about trust. All about confidence. Agents can handle transactions — you don't need an API machine-to-machine. Uh and Binance, you know, was and is a major leader here. So, it's incredibly disappointing to see this.

Chris 反驳：危机正是入场时机

Chris: Agree on the disappointment. Um, push back on the lack of opportunity in the space. Um, plenty of investors love to come in when the markets are ripping like '21, right? They love coming in when the times are good. Um, only the best come in when there are some challenges. Um, that that's when valuations tend to stay in check. That's when you see some of your best vintages.

Um, so look, I think that this technology is going nowhere. We are supported now by a very strong regulatory regime. Um, it's a security challenge. I think we've isolated the problem to — we know where the problem is, frankly. Can it be solved through policy? Can it be solved through other means? Um, maybe. It's not like we don't know where the problem's coming from, right? And so I do think that there's so many smart people in this space. Will you ever have a perfect security environment? No. There's always going to be something — even in the world of AI, right?

It's a ground condition though. Security is a ground condition. It's like Maslow's hierarchy of — Of course it is. It's first. You got to have that.

"Wow 时刻"的消失：加密的叙事危机

Ram: You got to have — in AI, it's almost every week now. And maybe sometimes twice a week. We're now seeing these "wow" moments take place. I think we've all had multiple AI "wow" moments and more is coming, right? So, it's like — where is the "wow"? There's no DeFi in the Clarity Act. There's no "wow." Where's the "wow"? What am I excited about as a consumer, enterprise, that's tangible experience — you know?

I'll tell you what the "wow" is — all the DeFi, the novelty that we saw years ago — I'm not seeing that. The attention markets are moving towards AI.

Chris 的反驳：不性感本身就是胜利

Chris: Couple things. Um, if you really look at crypto — the infrastructure, the market structure changes — it's actually not sexy. And by it not being sexy, it's starting to accomplish what it's supposed to be. For crypto, for too long, it was the tail wagging the dog where — hey, I've got this amazing technology, what do you want to do with it? The truth is, it's getting implemented now behind the scenes. And if it's functioning correctly, that backend infrastructure — you don't even want to think about it.

Like, you know, I bought an asset the other day and I didn't even think about what chain it was on for a change. It just worked. So why is that? Um, you know, that's not sexy and maybe there's some value in it not being sexy, to be honest with you.

AI 的另一面：伴生的责任与反噬

On the AI front, you're right — there's all kinds of "wow" moments, but there's also all kinds of scary moments right now, right? The fact of the matter is, we're going into midterms. Entire industries are in the crosshairs — data centers, etc. The liabilities are mounting in many cases, right? To the extent that these companies spawn AI agents that break the law — and we're seeing it.

My point is that AI is no panacea. Um, it has incredible promise. It's a civilization-defining technology. I love it. I love the fact when I look at it through crypto and AI coming together and creating value. I think that's one of the most exciting verticals — you know, the machine economy. We're seeing agents transact more on the web than we've seen people in certain cases already, and it's just getting started.

But my point is that there are liabilities on the AI side as well. And you're going to see that just like the crypto cycle, right? Where you're going to have explosion in application. Everyone gets excited. Oh, here comes the liability. Uh oh — smack, right? We've seen this in crypto. We're seeing it in AI play out again. Um, nothing against AI. I love it. I think it's amazing. But um, I think it's too early to write off crypto.

Ram: At least in AI, we're seeing highs — like in private market valuations, financing rounds. You're seeing the enthusiasm, you're seeing the energy. Semis and data center sold off — to your point — I think incredible buying opportunity with the midterm reset here. But like, markets generally at all-time highs and keep moving higher. Yeah — this volatility, which is part of the point you're making, that can create opportunities. But just the relative strength of these asset classes — digital assets is kind of crawling out of the hole where these other names are at the top and they've had a pullback. But people will see like, yeah, we're going to see more capital going into this. Like you said, a civilizational-defining — digital assets has that scope and opportunity to be. But it's fumbled the ball.

Chris: Yeah, it has fumbled the ball over and over again. I don't disagree with that. And I don't mean to be portraying that this is crypto against AI. I really believe crypto and AI are friends. And yes, we have to overcome some of these challenges, but in my experience, you know, when you have that pit in your stomach and you're like — I don't know, I don't know — that's when you go long. And when you go long when you have that pit in your stomach, generally good things happen. When things are riding high and you're like, this is going to the moon — you know, that's when you run into problems.

So look, this conversation is the beginning, but I don't think these are competitive. Maybe they've been a little bit competitive for capital for sure. Retail has chased the shiny new toy for sure. Does retail come back? Does it matter because now we have institutions in our space? I don't know.

Austin 的核心洞察：加密缺失了金融学的 101

Austin: Well, let me hop in with a couple of things that I've been observing on this front. One is that I think the investability of crypto may be a problem for the VCs more than the reality of crypto returns across the whole market. And there's two reasons for that.

One, I think we're seeing large firms coming in and starting to eat away at the value proposition. Like, maybe one of the most hilarious and therefore most likely outcomes is that one of the big winners from crypto are the large banks, right? But it is possible that some of the value capture goes to established players instead of to — call it VC-scale companies. That's part one.

Also, the VCs themselves, to be honest, don't have a great track record in terms of investment. When you look at fintechs at large, it's one of the hardest spaces for VCs. There are not a lot of VC partners who have been good fintech operators. Those who are are typically in payments. But like, go to any of the major VC firms and find me somebody who started a bank or a trading firm, right? They're just not there. And so that gives you a whole set of operator knowledge that they don't have. And I've seen that play out over and over when I looked at investments that were being made and I'm like — mechanically, that's not going to work. So I think some of that is driving it.

关键缺口：加密从未为"安全"而设计

Two, crypto never built itself for security outside of the tech vertical. And I think it's related to point one and not understanding finance. But you can see this with the Binance hack — when that amount of money can move instantly across networks with no double-checking anywhere. And I'm not necessarily talking like "exercise judgment," but just somebody building any protocol that says — if you're going to move a billion dollars, there's a 24-hour clock on that. And you don't just get to eat that thing out the door.

These are not built, and these are pretty standard sort of things that we understand from TradFi. We know what a circuit breaker is. We know what demand-responsive pricing is. I've been a market maker. I know — the eighth time somebody bids something — like, I'm widening bid-offer out. I'm not just sitting there and delivering, delivering, delivering.

And so there are kind of like 101-level risk management things that are not being done in crypto. And so I think part of why the hacks have been so bad is that you built a system that was optimized around the tech concerns without ever thinking about the financial risk concerns.

AI 作为攻防博弈的加速器

And then Chris, to your point about AI — neither being a friend nor an enemy — this is a case where AI is an enemy purely because it lets people poke holes in all these things faster. It also lets you patch them faster. It also lets you fix them faster. But so far in the classic attacker-defender ladder game, the attackers are ahead.

Chris 的收尾：光谱思维与中介价值的回归

Chris: Well, the surface area is so big as AI starts coming — but over time that surface area will be closed. I think one of the problems is we're talking in extremes, right? Remember — blockchain, crypto — it's all programmable. It's all composable. You can have permissioned capabilities. You can insert transfer agents that include incremental security layers.

And again, I would never say that anything is perfectly secure, but when you're dealing with like true DeFi, yeah, I agree there's a lot of risks there. If you're keeping your assets in hot wallets — real risk there. But there are many different versions along the stack.

And look, I think I've said this many times — I love DeFi. I love the vision, the values — extending finance to people all over the world that never had access to it before. Love it to death. But sometimes when there's heightened security environments, maybe you want that intermediary for some time. You know, that doesn't mean the intermediary is the safest in the world either, but you know, maybe you want to find someone who's more professional.

This will cycle just like everything else. Um, so look, I think we're just at this period now where the surface area is big. We're playing cops and robbers. Um, but over time, I think it gets settled.

节目收尾

If you like this segment, please like, subscribe, and tune in every Monday at 4:30 p.m. Eastern time. I'm Austin Campbell, the host of Bits and Bips, along with my friends Ram Ahluwalia and Chris Perkins, and our slate of exceptional guests. Every week, we're going to discuss macro, crypto, and the collision of worlds — covering topics that move markets and shape the financial landscape.

One more thing — we've got a listener survey open. It takes just a few minutes. It's anonymous, and it changes what we make next. Use the QR code on screen or go to unchainedcrypto.com/survey. The link is in the show notes.

What if your crypto could do more than just sit in your wallet? Nexo is a digital assets wealth platform where you can generate daily interest on your crypto or borrow funds against your assets. Today, Nexo serves more than 10 million clients. Find out more at nexo.com.

item.description:
## 当"快"成为系统性债务：币安 20 分钟损失 63 亿的真正含义
最让人意外的观察不是"又一次被黑"，而是**这次事件暴露了加密行业最深层的身份矛盾——它把自己的核心卖点（无需许可的即时结算）变成了结构性的安全负债**。Austin 在节目末尾点破了一个被所有人忽略的关键：传统金融里"熔断机制 (circuit breaker)"、"24 小时转账冷静期"、"做市商第八次报价时就扩大买卖价差"——这些都是 **101 级的风控常识**，但加密协议从未内建。63 亿在 20 分钟内穿过 10 条链流出，不是技术漏洞，是**设计哲学的漏洞**。整个行业用"抗审查"为名义，拒绝了所有延迟机制，却忘了延迟本身就是金融安全的免疫系统。
## 跨领域连接：这不是密码学问题，是"航空业 1950 年代"的翻版
加密世界此刻的处境，和二战后民航业惊人地相似。飞机技术已经成熟，但事故率居高不下，直到 FAA 强制引入**冗余系统、预飞清单、黑匣子、强制停飞**——这些全都是"降低效率"的东西。民航业的黄金时代不是始于更快的飞机，而是始于**系统性地拒绝"唯速度论"**。Chris 说"西部拓

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] The Day Robert Moses’ Phone Stopped Ringing - Robert Caro
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、电话不再响起的那一刻：权力的"热力学"揭示

卡罗讲的那个瞬间——他做最后一次采访，离开时秘书手里没有电话留言——远不止是感伤的历史细节。它是一次肉眼可见的"相变"：Robert Moses 在同一间办公室、同一张椅子、同一副听不见的耳朵，几乎不变，但"权力"这一物理量从他身上骤然蒸发。

这里有个让人意外的观察：权力不是某个人"拥有"的东西，而是周围人"打电话"的频率。它更像热力学中的温度——不是物体的内在属性，而是分子撞击频率的宏观表现。Moses 并没有"失去"什么，是外部世界停止了对他的碰撞。所以他本人直到最后都没真正察觉——因为从他的内部参考系看，他和昨天没有任何差别。办公室里那些"用一贯的恭敬对他"的旧部，构成了一个完美的隔热层，让他体感温度与外部温度彻底脱钩。

这与一个看似无关的领域惊人地对应：衰老生物学中"系统性信号沉默"的现象。细胞在死亡前并不是突然碎裂，而是先停止接收周边分子的信号；临床上这叫"失联性坏死"。Moses 的政治死亡遵循着与此一致的曲线——不是外力击倒，而是信号停发。听力下降不是巧合，是隐喻的身体化。

二、Rockefeller 为什么能做到前几十任都做不到的事？——一场"辞职讹诈"的纳什均衡崩塌

卡罗在对话里不经意带出了一个深刻的博弈论瞬间：62 年 Moses 又玩了一次"你不听我就辞职"的老把戏，结果 Rockefeller 淡淡说"I regretfully accept"。观众自然会问：前面那些市长、州长难道都是笨蛋？

卡罗的回答揭示了一个常被忽视的真相：Moses 的"不可解雇性"不是制度造成的，而是共同信念造成的。 法律上，任何一任市长州长都能动他；但没人敢按下按钮，因为"大家都相信没人敢按下"。这正是谢林（Schelling）意义上的焦点均衡——一个靠每个参与者都预期其他人维持它而存续的脆弱结构。

这里出现跨领域的奇妙映射：这和银行挤兑的机制完全同构。银行本身当天的偿付能力和前一天没什么差别，但只要一个大储户选择撤出且活了下来，均衡就崩了。Rockefeller 就是那个第一个撤出的大户。不是 Moses 变弱了，是"相信他强"的那张网被撕开了一个口子，剩下的持信者纷纷撤资。这解释了为什么"威胁资产"（threat capital）常在一夜之间归零——它的账面价值从来只存在于别人的资产负债表里。

一个让人毛骨悚然的推论：Moses 的"全能"在相当长时间里，本质上是一个自我实现的集体幻觉。一旦有人证伪一次，整个权力的"账本"立刻按市值重估。

三、传记作家作为量子观测者——卡罗写的不是历史，是正在塌缩的波函数

Dwarkesh 问了一个近乎哲学的问题：你在 66、67 年开始写这本书，Moses 还没彻底倒台，你怎么知道故事会怎么结束？卡罗说："我亲眼看着他失去权力。"

这句话比它听起来更惊人。几乎所有传记都是"事后考古"，但《The Power Broker》是一次"实时观测"。这意味着卡罗并不是在描述一个已经凝结的历史人物，他是在和一个仍在时间流中的对象共同塌缩——他既是记录者，也是时间轴上的一个节点。

这里有一个非常意外的角度：卡罗自己可能加速了 Moses 的坠落。当一个记者问出的问题越来越尖锐、越来越结构化，当他开始理解 Moses 的每一个杠杆和每一次交易，他实际上就在把 Moses 的权力语法从"隐性知识"转化为"显性知识"。而权力的一个铁律是：可被精确描述的权力，就是正在流失的权力（因为它一旦可复制、可反制、可规避，就不再稀缺）。换句话说，一本关于权力运作机制的书本身就是一种解毒剂。

这与一个看似风马牛不相及的领域相通：魔术学里有个"暴露杀手"效应——秘密一旦被完整写下来，哪怕只有一个人看过，表演者就再也无法以同样的方式震慑观众。Moses 作为一个政治魔术师，他的所有"花招"（interlocking appointments、resignation threat、authority bonds 的法律结构）在被卡罗解剖的那几年里，正逐步丧失魔法。

所以，《The Power Broker》不仅是一部关于权力丧失的书，它本身可能也是权力丧失的参与者。卡罗作为年轻记者的"不知道自己在做什么"，恰恰是他能做出来的原因——一个老练的作者可能会等到"结局明朗"后再动笔，但卡罗不得不边写边看，于是他的书变成了一个罕见的东西：一部还在呼吸的时候就被开膛破肚的政治生物学标本。

📝 转录文本

结局未定之时动笔

Dwarkesh: You're writing the book. You start writing it in '66, '67.

Caro: Yes.

Dwarkesh: You're writing it while Moses is losing power. His career is not over yet.

Caro: Yes.

Dwarkesh: And so the story changes.

Caro: Yes.

Dwarkesh: While you're writing it.

Caro: Yes.

Dwarkesh: And I don't know if you've talked about that, but presumably the conclusion changes because—

Caro: Yes.

Dwarkesh: —you don't know whether he's going to lose that power or not.

亲眼目睹权力流失

Caro: No. And I watched—oh, that's a great question. And I watched that happen. And I was, whatever I was—young. And whatever my age was, I didn't really know what I was doing. And I watched him lose power. And I learned enough about him to know how sad this was going to be.

Um, if I could think a moment—there's a moment that this happened. His office was still up at the Triborough Bridge Authority when he was in power. I interviewed him in that office several times. You felt his power. Or you felt it outside. There were all these people waiting for his decisions, sitting around waiting for his decisions.

As soon as I finished, the secretary would come in with a list of telephone calls of people who had called asking for—you know, wanting something from him while I was talking to him. Right?

电话不再响起的那一天

By the time I finished, I remember I realized—I had one long interview with him, maybe it was my last one—and I realized there had been no calls. The secretary had nothing to tell him.

So whatever you thought of Moses, you felt the poignance of someone losing power.

Dwarkesh: Yeah. That's fascinating. That's what I was wondering about.

Caro: You couldn't help feeling sad for him. No matter—no matter even though you knew what he had done, you couldn't help feeling, oh, this is in a way tragic that no one's calling and asking him for a favor anymore.

他自己知道吗？

Dwarkesh: Did he realize that was happening?

Caro: I don't think he really—I don't think—in a way I'm sure he did, but by that time he was so—remember, he was so insulated, he was so—whatever his age was, he was up in the 80s, he was deaf, you know.

Um, he still had, in his office at the Triborough headquarters on Randall's Island, were all these Moses men who were loyal to him and treated him with the same deference they always had. He knew he wasn't getting his projects done, but he felt—I know he felt—he was just going to keep pushing like he always did and he was going to win again.

So I don't think—the answer to your question is no. I don't think he did ever realize that.

Dwarkesh: That's fascinating.

Rockefeller 与那次失败的"辞职讹诈"

Dwarkesh: In, I think, '62, as you say, he tries to pull a trick on Nelson Rockefeller that he had pulled on countless previous mayors and governors, which is to threaten to resign if he didn't get his way.

Caro: Yes.

Dwarkesh: And Rockefeller says, "I regretfully accept." And nothing happens. And that made me wonder as I was reading it—could all those previous governors and mayors who were getting threatened have done the same thing?

为什么前几十年没人敢按下按钮

Caro: Great, great question. Yeah. The answer is—well, you say could they have done the same thing. So the easy, the first-part answer is yes. They had the power to fire him. He wasn't an elected official. But—there wasn't really a possibility.

The answer to the question at the bottom is no, they couldn't, because he was simply too popular. You know, you could fire Robert Moses? That's like firing some idol person who was the idol of New York.

But in addition, with his genius, he had created—in all his different posts: chairman of the State Power Authority, chairman of the Triborough Bridge Authority, Parks Commissioner, Long Island Parks Commissioner, Jones Beach Commissioner—he had created such an interlocking [structure that] you couldn't fire him from everything, because the terms ended in different ways, and some you didn't have the power to fire him from. He had really made it impossible—well, almost impossible.

盔甲上的裂缝

Because at the end, if you wanted to do it, Rockefeller did it. But by that time, cracks had appeared in the armor.

I think for decades the answer to your question is: you couldn't do it. But then, as he got older, cracks appeared in the armor, and you could—if you wanted to brave criticism in all the newspapers and public criticism and everything else—you probably could have done [it].

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.
