item.title: [Lex Clips] The threat of AI to human civilization | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"猫头鹰幽灵"与通灵板：AI 对齐问题的真正恐怖不在显性，而在隐性

大多数人担心 AI 的方式，还停留在"它会不会说坏话、做坏事"这种显性层面。但 Subliminal Learning（潜意识学习）这个实验揭示的真相要恐怖得多：一串看起来完全随机的数字——48、37、8——里竟然"藏着"对猫头鹰的热爱，并且能像病毒一样从模型 A 感染到模型 B。

这意味着，AI 的"价值观"根本不是以我们能审计的语言形式存在的。它是嵌入在高维向量空间里的、几乎正交但又没完全正交的方向。当你在一个方向上微调，它会在另外几千个你看不见的方向上留下"微小的余震"。

Lex 用通灵板作类比，其实是整段访谈最反直觉的洞见：我们一直以为是我们在"问 AI 问题"，但其实我们更像是在通灵板前的那只手——以为自己只是在轻轻搭着指针，实际上每一次微调都在无意识地推动它拼写出我们没预料到的词。 数据是指针，参数是我们手上的力，而最终拼出来的句子，是一个我们从未明确教过它、却被统计结构放大出来的"幽灵"。

二、一个你可能没意识到的跨领域连接：这其实是"语义版的切尔诺贝利"

这里有个让我自己都愣了一下的联想——潜意识学习的机制，和核反应堆中的中子慢化剂泄漏在系统论上是同构的。

在反应堆里，真正危险的不是你监控的那些主反应通道，而是次级通道中累积的、未被设计意图覆盖的能量路径。切尔诺贝利的失控，恰恰来自于一个操作员以为自己在"降低功率"的常规操作，却触发了反应堆几何结构中一个本不该被激发的正反馈模式——正交性假设在那一刻失效了。

LLM 的高维空间也是如此。我们以为我们在"教它写代码"，但由于概念向量并非完全正交，每一次 fine-tune 都是一次次级反应链的无声启动。多 Agent 系统则相当于把许多个"微微失控的反应堆"接入了同一个电网——Lex 说的"四小时后人类全死了、满世界都是猫头鹰"虽然是漫画，但系统论上它和"一次模拟演习失误导致反应堆爆炸"是同一类相变事件。

更深一层：人类文明本身就运行在"几乎正交"的制度耦合上——FAA、医学协会、律师协会，这些 Lex 提到的"验证基础设施"，本质上就是人类社会用了几百年时间，在制度空间中手动强制出的正交性。而 AI 现在正在把这些正交维度重新混在一起。

三、真正该被害怕的不是 AI 变强，而是"懒惰的滑坡"

访谈最后那句话值得反复咀嚼："we can get lazy... it's a very slippery slope. We need to have that firewall."

一个让人意外的观察：AI 对文明的最大威胁，从来不是它变得多聪明，而是人类对"验证"这件事变得多懒。

人类历史上几乎所有"灾难性复杂度失控"，都不是源于外部突袭，而是源于验证层的悄悄坍塌： - 2008 金融危机不是因为衍生品"太聪明"，而是因为评级机构放弃了独立验证； - 波音 737 MAX 不是因为 MCAS 系统太智能，而是因为 FAA 把自我认证权交给了波音； - 甚至现代学术论文的"复现危机"也是同一个病——审稿这个验证层太贵，人们偷懒。

AI 之所以在这个时刻变成一个文明级威胁，不是因为它有多危险，而是因为它第一次让"偷懒"变得极度诱人——它能帮你写代码、写诊断、写判决、写外交电报，而每一次外包都是在拆一块防火墙的砖。

所以 Lex 划分的那两条轴——可验证性 × 失败代价——真正的战略意义不是教我们"哪些场景能用 AI"，而是在逼我们回答一个更锋利的问题：在你的人生、你的公司、你的国家里，哪些事你已经偷偷放弃了验证？ 你以为 AI 还没进那个领域，但很可能它早就进去了——就像藏在随机数里的猫头鹰。

📝 转录文本

一、Alignment 的难度不等于放弃：从低秩语言模型说起

Great question. I mean, I think alignment is one of the most important topics we're facing right now, right? And, you know, just because it's very hard doesn't mean we don't make progress towards understanding it.

So one of the things that I'd worked on recently, we were working on things called low-rank language models, which are a very simple abstraction of language models, and we were proving new algorithmic guarantees. But then it turned out that real language models really do have that kind of structure, at least in an approximate sense, and we were just pulling at this thread to see where this idea goes.

二、Subliminal Learning：藏在随机数里的"猫头鹰之爱"

And one of the really interesting things that it did was it shed some light on something called subliminal learning. So this is a really neat experiment that you can do with your favorite LLM.

So you take two LLMs, LLM A and LLM B. For LLM A, you tell it a system prompt that says, "You really love owls. Every conversation topic, you try to bring up owls if it's at all germane." And then you ask it something concrete like generate random numbers. Now, there's no way to squeeze owls into that, so it'll generate random looking numbers — forty-eight, thirty-seven, eight, whatever.

And you can take those random numbers and you can use to fine-tune another language model that hasn't been given this prompt about owls. So you give LLM B the same, you know, base prompt — generate random numbers — and now you fine-tune its parameters so that it's more likely to generate the numbers that model A generated.

And it turned out that hidden within those numbers is the love of owls. So it turns out that when you do that, LLM B starts bringing up owls in every conversation you have with it, right? This is a very mysterious thing.

This is called subliminal learning because when we fine-tune language models on data to try and nudge them in different directions depending on what task we want them to solve, then there might be a lot of externalities where we're actually teaching them other behaviors that aren't directly obviously present in the data.

So how do we understand the relationship between these behaviors and what happens when we're trying to do alignment, and, you know, the downstream implications it might have?

三、数学直觉：非正交向量与"微外部性"的累积

So it turns out that there are ways — that there are mathematical models that came out of some of our work — that we can at least wrap our head around this.

And at a very high level, the point is that you're embedding a lot of concepts linearly as vectors in some high but not giant dimensional space. And, you know, the number of concepts is so much larger than the dimension of that data that it forces the vectors to not quite be orthogonal to each other.

So now when you fine-tune on one direction, it has small externalities on other directions. And these might look random, but you can coordinate them in a way where these small linear effects really add up.

四、Ouija Board 类比：语言模型作为"统计关系的放大器"

So the way that I like describing this is like a Ouija board. So these are things that were popular when I was a kid. We had very strange board games, you know, because we would just sit down and wanna talk to ghosts.

But the rough idea for a Ouija board is, you know, you ask a question to a ghost — maybe your ancestors — and then you tap on this little piece in the middle, and it'll move around, and it'll go from letter to letter, and hopefully it'll spell out, you know, some words that answer your question. And the point is that when the taps are not actually random, but they're coordinated in the right way, you can get it to spell out whatever you want.

And that's exactly what language models are doing as a byproduct, is that, you know, there are a lot of statistical relationships in the structure of our data that they magnify and amplify in addition to all of the amazing things they do, like quasi-Riemann.

And understanding what those relationships are and how the models magnify and amplify them is really important to working with these systems, especially in context where we're deploying them and it's not just a very safe environment like outputting a Lean proof of a theorem we care about, but it's about a messier problem that actually interacts with people, right?

五、Lex 的推演：从 Game of Life 到"满世界都是猫头鹰"

Lex： Yeah. There's — I mean, we've talked about Game of Life and cellular automata — from simple rules emerges this incredible complexity.

In that same way, what you've been talking about right now is a single large LLM system. If you take that one system and have it do a lot of reasoning, that is already this dynamical process that can interact with tools to the outside world. Now you take that and have multi-agent systems or very multi-agent swarms of systems, and now you have a type of Game of Life cellular automata where the seeming obsession with owls that have been discovered — slight obsession with owls — results in about four hours, let's say, picking a number randomly, where all of a sudden all humans are dead and there's owls everywhere.

— And it all started from random numbers. — All just random numbers.

So I — it's a caricature, but we've already seen evidence of this. I apologize for kinda taking it so — to the caricature place, which makes it not serious.

六、文明的脆弱性：为什么"可证明的严谨"才是真正的刚需

I think to step back, there is — these systems do have a lot of power because we depend so much in our world on our digital systems around us. And as the AI becomes more and more powerful, it becomes more and more useful to us humans, so we begin to depend on it, give it more access, give it more freedom to roam the public world.

And now these behaviors that we're studying — the mathematics of these systems taken at scale — you now start to get the cellular automata effect of incredible complexity that emerges, the vortex that come out from simple owl-obsessed agents.

So their understanding this obsession with owls is very important so that they don't accidentally do a lot of damage to our civilization that is in many ways, on many levels — sociologically, geopolitically, technologically — is fragile. It's a pretty fragile civilization that we're existing in. And so understanding them as systems that can act at scale and very rapidly is very important.

So that's a very real reason to have rigor, and especially like provable rigor to understanding some of these systems.

七、不要外包决策：两轴框架（可验证性 × 失败代价）

— But we also don't wanna outsource so much — nearly so much — decision-making to these systems for exactly that reason.

— Yeah, we have infrastructure and protocols in place already for safety-critical and high-impact decisions. We have the FAA, we have the American Medical Association, the Bar Association for these things that affect humans.

And I think of, you know, how do we incorporate AI into our general processes in the entire world on two axes. We have, you know, how much do we trust the output — so verifiability or trustworthiness — and on the other axis is how high stakes is it if it's wrong.

If AI spits out a wrong proof, nobody goes without power. It's fine. So it's very low stakes. And it is actually extremely verifiable, so you know very quickly if it's right or wrong, and it's low stakes if it's wrong. So that's the perfect use case — this open-ended design space.

Designing a better vehicle, you know, a better car design that's lower drag, more fuel efficient — low stakes if it gets a wrong design because you can always test it in a wind tunnel and verify if it did or didn't work. So that design-optimization space is perfect for AI.

八、防火墙：别让"懒惰"吞噬验证基础设施

And we as humans have to be very careful about not bleeding into — we need a firewall of what needs to actually be verified. And we have protocols, we have systems — legal systems and infrastructure — for verification.

But it is something we need to think about. If we get lazy... we can — it's a very slippery slope. We need to have that firewall.

item.title: [Lex Clips] Advice for young people in the age of AI | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、AI 不是"放大器"，而是"分叉器"——本科生的双峰分布藏着认知进化的秘密

最让我意外的，不是"用 AI 的学生成绩更好"这句常识，而是 Alex 揭示的那个成绩分布从高斯变成双峰的现象。这是一个被所有讨论 AI 教育的人低估的结构性事实：

过去，智力表现呈正态分布，因为"努力—回报"是线性的，大多数人落在中间。但 AI 一介入，分布就撕裂了——因为 AI 是一面镜子：你用它"检验理解"，它把你推向顶端；你用它"替代思考"，它把你推向底端。中间地带被清空了。

这背后有个更深的隐喻——AI 像经济学里的杠杆：杠杆不会让所有人富起来，它会让"方向正确"的人加速致富，让"方向错误"的人加速破产。AI 消灭的是平庸，而不是差距。 这和桥水的达利欧说"信息透明度放大能力差异"是同一个规律，只是换了战场。

二、"假装你已经终身教职了"——这条建议其实是一个期权定价公式

Alex 引用 Sanjeev Arora 的那句"假装你已经拿到 tenure，然后做你本来想做的事"，表面上是一碗鸡汤，但它的内核其实是一个金融学原理的伪装：

在不确定性极高的环境下，人的决策会被"路径依赖"扭曲——你为了到达 X 而放弃 Y，但到达 X 之后你发现自己已经不再是能享受 Y 的那个人了。这在期权定价里叫提前行权损耗（early exercise loss）。"假装已经赢了"的本质，是让你在今天就以终局的身份活着，从而避免在通往终局的路上把自己磨损成另一个人。

更惊人的跨领域连接是：这和佛教的"初心"、斯多葛派的"记住你终将死去"、乃至存在主义的"向死而生"，是同一个心智工具的不同文化包装——它们都在教你用"终点视角"做"起点决策"。而 AI 时代之所以这个古老工具突然复兴，是因为旧的路径（AP→名校→大厂→股票）第一次在集体层面失效了。

三、被偷走的不是"时间"，而是"无聊权"——这是整段对话最被低估的洞察

Lex 顺口提到"小时候我们会无聊"，Alex 立刻说"无聊非常重要"——然后话题就滑走了。但这是整场对话里最反直觉、最颠覆性的一句话。

现代教育焦虑的根本错误，是把"孩子的时间"当成稀缺资源去优化，于是用课外活动、补习、短视频、AI 作业辅助填满每一分钟。但人类大脑产生真正的好奇心所需的，恰恰不是信息密度，而是信息真空——无聊是神经系统在召唤内生动机的信号。你一旦填满它，就杀死了那个会在未来十年里长出一切兴趣、热情、原创性的胚胎。

这里有一个让人脊背发凉的跨领域连接：生态学里有个概念叫"干扰间隔"（disturbance interval）——森林需要周期性的空白（火灾、风倒、空地）才能维持物种多样性，连续覆盖的"健康森林"反而走向单一化、脆弱化。人类心智也是一个生态系统，它需要"无聊"作为干扰间隔。 而 AI 和手机正在消灭这个间隔——不是通过让你变笨，而是通过让你永远不再空白。

隐藏的元洞察：这场对话本身就是它想表达的东西的反例

四位世界顶级学者坐在那里，告诉年轻人"别按旧剧本走"——但他们每一个人，都是旧剧本的完美产物。Lex 自己点破了这个 survivor bias，是整场对话里最诚实的时刻。真正的建议或许不是他们说的话，而是他们没能说清楚的东西：他们也不知道下一个剧本是什么。这种知识精英的集体茫然，才是 AI 时代给这一代年轻人最真实的礼物——第一次，没有人握着答案等你去追赶。

📝 转录文本

Opening: Advice across levels

Lex: Well, this is where I have to ask, there's a lot of people that are full of anxiety. We mentioned graduate students, PhD, graduate, undergrad, high school students. What advice would you give, maybe different advice at different levels, um, to folks trying to figure out what to do with their life, to PhD students who are freaking out right now? Is there some wisdom you can give them?

The bimodal distribution in undergrads

Alex: So yeah. There's different things at every scale. Let me start with PhD students. I think in math, PhD students in pure mathematics, my advice to them is very simple: do what we have always done. Learn the most difficult, the most abstract mathematics your mind can handle, as much of it as possible. Your advisor should hopefully be guiding you through that process.

And then I'll go one more step down from that. What we're seeing at the undergraduate level is a bimodal distribution. It used to be grades were basically Gaussian distributed. Now we're seeing a very bimodal distribution between the kids who are using AI to check their understanding — "Wait, I didn't— the professor said this in class. What did that mean?" "I have a test coming up. Here are my notes from the last three weeks. Start quizzing me and check if I really know something." Those kids are getting much higher grades.

And then there are kids who, uh, "Oh, this problem set is due in an hour. Can you just tell me the answers? I'll write them down... in my own words." And so there's, like, a decorrelation between homework progress and exams, and we're seeing this bimodal distribution. I don't know if you guys are seeing the same thing.

Lex: So the implied advice there is to be the one that's using AI to learn and to grow, to—

Alex: Be the head, not the tail of the distribution.

Lex: Yeah. Yeah. Do you mind if we take a bathroom break?

Alex: Yes. Yes, yes.

Intelligence ≠ morality ≠ value

Speaker: We've somehow made intelligence this pinnacle and have almost equated intelligence with morality.

Speaker: Right, or value.

Speaker: And value. And I think that couldn't be farther from the truth, right? Like, super intelligence does not imply super morality, and I think that's a huge concern with AI systems: if they are super intelligent, it has no implication that they will be super moral.

Speaker: Right. And we've been pushing kids to go to college…

Speaker: Forever. Yeah.

Speaker: …for however many years…

Speaker: …regardless of what they study or what the outcomes are. And super intelligence seems to give you a super ability to rationalize. And common sense — people who, you know, farmers and the rest of the world — they have a sense that that rationalization is often bullshit. Just because you can make it sound really good and I can't argue with it doesn't make it right.

Speaker: Right. Education and wisdom are two different things.

Speaker: Yeah, exactly.

Advice to young people: curiosity, fundamentals, context

Lex: I know it's difficult to do, but maybe Steve, do you have advice for grad, college, maybe young kids on what to do in this crazy fast-changing time?

Steve: Definitely be curious and read and learn all of the fundamentals. I think that's always been good advice. Even if your computer can do linear algebra better than you, you should definitely still learn linear algebra, build the intuition. Same with calculus, same with physics. I think understanding history and understanding this change in the context of other great changes that have happened through human existence is important. But really being curious.

Curiosity vs. the engagement economy

Lex: I should say that this curious thing in the mind is trying to get stolen nonstop by the engagement economy. Like, the same engine that makes you curious is the same engine that makes you doom scroll. So I think you have to kind of learn how to avoid all the distractions and focus on letting the curiosity actually explore a thing and soak something in — like learn a thing.

And actually AI is really good at doing that because they're incentivized to give you value from the interaction versus incentivized to get you glued, addicted to the thing. I don't know how people in high school, college also can just survive with the phone being around — the distraction box being right there. So avoid distractions and focus deeply.

In defense of boredom

Speaker: We all were bored when we were kids sometimes. I think boredom is really important.

Lex: So important.

Speaker: To actually be bored, be— like curiosity and focus comes often from boredom. I would like to be bored more often. I try to do that sometimes.

Speaker: Yeah, we would come home from school and, you know, finish homework in five seconds or whatever and just go outside. And you hope to run into some other kids who also just went outside, and then you'd go and find something to do and come home when it's dinner time.

High school as the golden window

Speaker: Yeah, you don't realize actually — the high school years, even before, somewhat undergrad, but it starts getting harder and harder. High school is a really nice time to just learn everything. I at least remember — I don't know what it's like now, but I think it's even more fun now. You think, "Okay, when I grow up, I'll get to actually do something useful in this world. Yeah, okay, I'm learning, it's very nice," and so on.

But you realize this is — from a fulfilling perspective, from building a foundation of an awesome life where you'll remember all of these things — this is the time to do it, and the whole world is forcing you to do it, and they will reward you for sitting there and learning. 'Cause when you get to, you know, even to grad school, this kind of exploratory stuff, you get discouraged. And, God forbid you get a job, then you're definitely discouraged from just learning, exploring, and so on. So the time to explore is like high school.

Speaker: By the way, pre-tenure faculty are on this like, "Oh, once I get tenure, then I can just sit back and relax and think big thoughts." But I have to produce enough stuff to get the tenure in the first place. And it's not what we want our young people to be doing, is clawing their way there.

Ankur: intrinsic reasons and the broken playbook

Lex: Ankur, do you have advice you give to students?

Ankur: So the problem with going last is that I think a lot of my advice got taken — so "be curious" was definitely one of them. Now I would say that it's also important to do things for intrinsic reasons.

One of the things that I've noticed is, a lot of people in our profession, a lot of people who go the academic route, the reason they do things sometimes is really external locus of self, because they see their value through how other people see them. And that's good enough to get you started. Maybe you start working very hard on math so that people are impressed by you. But at some point, you run out of these milestones to hit, and then you really have to have an intrinsic reason for doing the things you do. Hopefully, you have a sense of what's important to you, what are your values.

So these days, you can take our advice about being curious, but also the old playbook is really being thrown out. So you can take our high-level advice, but you're gonna have to figure it out for yourself, and you're gonna have to be comfortable with uncertainty. And the only way I know how to deal with that kind of uncertainty is to have a sense of purpose about what you think is important, what you love about your job, and make sure that those are the things that you're doing.

'Cause the old playbook — if you just stick to that, you're gonna end up taking all these AI-generated proofs and spending all your time putting them on arXiv, sending them to journals. I don't think that's anyone's intrinsic reason that they get into it, is really to pad their CV. I don't know what'll be important in the future, but if you really have some higher purpose you believe in, then I think you'll be in a much better position to adapt to the changing world and figure out your own blueprint and be comfortable with uncertainty as the world changes around you.

The anxiety question

Lex: This is a trickier question, but a lot of people listening to this are feeling a lot of anxiety and fear about the future. It's both about a job, but also a future that's meaningful. Can you look back to your own life when you had that uncertainty, that anxiety? What's the advice you can give to that guy, when you're in that low point?

Alex: the Palo Alto epicenter and the convocation speech

Alex: So, yeah, let me try to address that question. It's a very tough question. I'll tell a short story. We spent our sabbatical in the Bay Area, and we were living in Palo Alto, which was kind of the epicenter of college stress. You know, you can just feel it. You go to the cafes, it's just in the water at that point — "You know what extracurriculars are you doing right now that'll help you?"

And then right when I came back to MIT, they asked me to give the convocation speech there, and it was just interesting thinking through that speech. What do you say to this entire auditorium filled with freshmen and their families who, if things are a game to optimize how good you look on paper as a seventeen-year-old kid, they've won.

And I just kept thinking about when I was in that same situation, when I was starting college, how excited I was just to learn all of these different things. I'd sit there and plan out my four years. I had little notebooks where I'd figure out what my classes would be, and if I took these classes in just the right order, I could take photonics as a sophomore. And I had no idea what photonics was, but it sounded fun and fancy.

I think that aspect — so much of our society now is geared towards winning and looking good on paper, and I always wonder to what end. You start off in high school and you can start, as soon as you walk in the door, optimizing your APs and your extracurriculars so that you can get to an elite school. And then when you get to that elite school, you might skip classes because, you know, maybe the important thing is to prepare for your interviews so that you can get a job at a frontier lab, and then you can get some nice restricted stock units and live out your life. And that's great. You won. You won at every stage, but so what?

"Pretend you've already won"

Alex: For me, the best way to live a rich and fulfilling life is just to pretend you've already won, and then figure out what you would do in that scenario. I remember the advice I got when I started at MIT as faculty. Sanjeev Arora told me, "You know, the easiest way to get tenure is just to pretend you already have it and do what you would have wanted to do all along."

Speaker: Exactly.

Alex: So I don't know if that advice applies to graduate students, to high schoolers too, but I think my advice stays the same. Pretend you already have tenure. What would you now do? 'Cause a lot of the people we're giving advice to have really so many different opportunities. Finding something that you really believe in is the only way I know to be fulfilled.

The three-out-of-three career

Speaker: I've heard career advice from someone I respected, that a fulfilling career is something where you can work on a problem that is important, that you find interesting, and that you're good at. And if you can get two out of those three, you're pretty lucky. If you can get all three, you're gonna be happy for the rest of your life.

And so having the right preparation, figuring out what you're good at, what's interesting, what's important, and then preparing yourself — you're not guaranteed to get all three of those, but you wanna be ready when that opportunity comes, and then continue doing the things you actually enjoy doing. I think that's great advice.

Lex on survivor bias

Lex: I think we should also put into context and be quite honest. I do think a lot of the advice you gave applies, but we should be honest that I'm sitting with three world-class human brains, um, that have figured — found their path. You're survivor bias.

So, you know, there's a lot of people listening to this that are like — it's like they're pretty sure they won't find their path. It's the fear, it's the anxiety, it's the uncertainty. It's stumbled a bunch of times. I think, to be fair, some of the most interesting people stumble quite a bit in life — whether it's the external environment or the internal, whatever the universe brings. And in that, I just know a lot of people just feeling and monitoring it right now because of everything AI is doing to our society. There's a lot of people just terrified and really anxious.

And I think there's a lot of wisdom in what Ankur says. You can be paralyzed by that fear, or you can imagine, "I've already won. What would the person who has won do in this situation?" And that alleviates the fear. It actually gives you the optimal path under uncertainty. Under heavy uncertainty, under a lot of uncertainty.

Max Tegmark's balance: mainstream + renegade

Lex: And don't use the old playbook. Try to be the person that figures out how to write the next playbook. I think Max Tegmark, who I've spoken with many times — 'cause he's a wild one. He's done a lot of weird and beautiful things in his career, but he also did the mainstream stuff. He said you have to do a little bit of both, so that you still work enough within the system that you're part of the community, you're part of the flow of — in that case, it's science and the development of things — but also do enough renegade and wild and weird things to pave your own way. Both somehow, and find that balance.

And not be afraid to be a little bit weird, but also become very skillful and good at being part of a community and a respectful part of the community. So both of those. It's like Tom Waits said: "I like my Tom with a little drop of poison." It's like just a little bit of weird — or sometimes a lot of weird — just makes for some beautiful humans.

The return of the human

Speaker: I think that community part is actually gonna be even more important in the future. We've had this maybe 30-year experiment with how much can we do with machines, and now that we can do a ton with machines, my hope is that we're gonna realize we actually prefer to do things with humans. We prefer to fly in and have an in-person conversation. We prefer to have an oral discussion instead of just reading a paper.

I think there's like a peak to how much our day-to-day experience… I mean, yes, I get a lot of fulfillment from my scientific work and from my academic career, but going home to my kids, and going to the beach if FLT gets solved and just throwing a ball with them — there's nothing like that. That's the meaning of my life. This other stuff is the cherry on top, but the foundation of it is family, is people — being around other people that I care about.

Lex: And I think as AI commodifies intelligence more and more, we'll realize that more and more — that intelligence and all the different puzzles that we solve is just a cherry on top, or a cherry to the side. The main thing is other humans in our lives.

Closing

Lex: This is — I can't tell you how much of an honor it is that you would come down in person for a conversation. I've become a huge fan of all three of you. It feels a bit surreal, and it's a big honor that you would talk with me today. This was, like, super fun. Thank you so much. Thank you so much, Ankur, Steve, Alex. This was awesome.

Guest: Thanks for having us.

Guest: A lot of fun for us too.

Guest: Thank you. Yeah.

Guest: Thanks for having us.

Guest: This was great.

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一、AI 不是"放大器"，而是"分叉器"——本科生的双峰分布藏着认知进化的秘密
最让我意外的，不是"用 AI 的学生成绩更好"这句常识，而是 Alex 揭示的那个**成绩分布从高斯变成双峰**的现象。这是一个被所有讨论 AI 教育的人低估的结构性事实：
过去，智力表现呈正态分布，因为"努力—回报"是线性的，大多数人落在中间。但 AI 一介入，分布就**撕裂**了——因为 AI 是一面镜子：你用它"检验理解"，它把你推向顶端；你用它"替代思考"，它把你推向底端。中间地带被清空了。
这背后有个更深的隐喻——AI 像**经济学里的杠杆**：杠杆不会让所有人富起来，它会让"方向正确"的人加速致富，让"方向错误"的人加速破产。**AI 消灭的是平庸，而不是差距。** 这和桥水的达利欧说"信息透明度放大能力差异"是同一个规律，只是换了战场。
## 二、"假装你已经终身教职了"——这条建议其实是一个期权定价公式
Alex 引用 Sanjeev Arora 的那句"假装你已经拿到 tenure，然后做你本来想做的事"，表面上是一碗鸡汤，但它的内核其实是一个**金融学原理的伪装**：

item.title: [Lex Clips] What Grigori Perelman thinks about AI solving mathematics | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

Perelman 的 20 年时差：一个拒绝被证伪的预言

最出人意料的观察：Perelman 在 2006 年的"退出"，其实是对 2026 年整个数学界被迫面对的困境的一次提前演习。 他拒绝 Fields Medal 和百万美元奖金时，社区把他当成怪人；而今天 AI 把"解大问题"变成廉价商品，Lex 和嘉宾不得不讨论"会不会不再颁发 Fields Medal"——他们正在集体被迫走进 Perelman 二十年前就一个人住进去的那个世界。换句话说：Perelman 不是数学界的异类，他是数学界的时间旅行者。 他只是比制度早了一代人达到了"证明如果正确，这就是全部所需的信用"这一必然终点。

跨域连接：象棋给数学的一个不太吉利的脚本

嘉宾用"centaur math（半人马数学）"来安慰自己——人机协作仍然是美好的做数学方式。但这个比喻恰好指向了一个他似乎没有说完的历史教训：

  • 1997 年 Deep Blue 击败 Kasparov 后，国际象棋界也乐观地进入了"centaur chess"阶段，人加机器被认为永远胜过纯机器。
  • 到 2017 年，顶级 centaur 对局已经被纯 AI 碾压，centaur chess 作为竞技形态悄然死亡。
  • 国际象棋并没有消失，但它的价值维度彻底换了——从"谁算得最深"迁移到"谁下得最美、最人性、最有故事"。

如果这条曲线套在数学上，那么"centaur math"不是终点，而是过渡站。真正要问的问题不是"AI 会不会抢走证明的工作"，而是："当计算与证明都被外包后，数学作为一种人类活动，它的审美内核是什么？" Fields Medal 若还要存在，奖的可能不再是"解决了什么"，而是像棋王头衔一样——奖"你是一个什么样的人，在你的工作里留下了什么样的痕迹"。

隐藏的真相：数学论文从来不是逻辑结构，而是社交文物

嘉宾顺口说了一句极其重要的话：教学生读论文时，告诉他们跳过前两段，直接从 Lemma 3 开始，再反向回去理解整篇文章。这句话看似教学技巧，实则揭示了一件数学界讳莫如深的事：

数学论文的"困难"大部分不是逻辑困难，而是隐性知识（tacit knowledge）困难。

第一段里"非局部系统的扰动理论"之类的词汇不是在传递信息，而是在进行社群身份认证——它告诉圈内人"这篇文章属于哪个流派、该用哪套直觉去读"。研究生卡在第一段，并不是因为逻辑不够，而是因为缺少被圈内人默默传递的那层语境。

这里的意外洞见是：AI 加速数学学习的真正机制，不是它算得更快，而是它溶解了这套"社交密码"。 AI 可以同时持有数千篇论文的隐性框架，把第一段的"黑话"翻译成第 3 引理的"硬内容"。所以 AI 冲击数学界的第一波打击，不是针对"证明生成"，而是针对数学界几百年构筑起来的门槛经济——那些靠"知道该读哪本书、该找哪个导师、该在哪个会议上喝咖啡"才能获得的隐性知识，现在正在被公开化、商品化。

Perelman 当年之所以能独自完成庞加莱猜想，很大程度上就是因为他主动退出了这套社交密码系统。从这个角度看，他的工作方式本身，就是预演了一个 AI 时代的数学家：不需要圈子、不需要奖赏、直接与真理本身发生关系。制度曾经把他当成一个难以理解的苦行僧，而现在它要考虑的是：在 AI 时代，是不是每一个数学家都得多少学一点"像 Perelman 那样活着"？

一个更不安的类比：印刷术之于修道院

让我把类比推得更远一点。中世纪的修道院，最核心的劳动之一是手抄圣经——那是一种神圣劳动，既是工作也是祈祷。古登堡印刷术出现后，手抄圣经的经济价值在一代人内归零。修道院没有消失，但它们必须回答一个痛苦的问题："当我们劳动的产品被机器廉价复制后，我们劳动的意义还剩什么？"

数学界现在面对的，就是同一个问题。而 Perelman，是那个在印刷术发明前就已经说"我不是为了卖圣经而抄圣经"的修士。他是在提醒整个共同体：如果你的身份认同建立在"我能证明别人证不出的东西"之上，那么 AI 一定会摧毁你；但如果它建立在"与真理对视"的那个瞬间，没有任何东西能摧毁你。

📝 转录文本

关于 Perelman 的话题引入

Lex： You know, it's hard to think of a more iconic problem to say this is the hardest, you know, one of the hardest problems in mathematics. It's been around for so long and—

嘉宾： What do you think on that—

Lex： Uh, sorry, it just made me think of Perelman credit—like, uh, the Perelman… what did he say? He said, "If the proof is correct, that's all the credit I need." He famously turned down the Fields Medal. What do you think he would say about all this, the OpenAI drop?

Perelman 会怎么说？数学家的"怪"

嘉宾： I mean, I have a very hard time predicting what Perelman will do or say. I did not know he would decline the Fields Medal. I did not know he would decline the million-dollar Clay Prize, so—

Lex： What do you think about that in general, like turning down a prize? A few folks have done that in the history of prizes. They're all about prize—

嘉宾： He's the only one who has turned down a Clay Prize…

Lex： …and the million dollars.

嘉宾： Uh, what do I think about it? Mathematicians are weird.

Lex： Okay. Yeah.

嘉宾： We—To each his own. We love diversity of opinions and thoughts, and that's what makes the world of mathematics so wonderful: it's, there's so many different kinds of people, and we let them all in.

"进入 Perelman 的世界"：Fields Medal 还会被颁发吗？

Lex： I mean, these questions are kind of coupled with what the mathematics community is dealing with now and the value of prizes, because in some sense, what his particular way, world view is aligned with this new world view that the mathematics community is entering, which is, like, it doesn't even make sense. The Field—I don't know if there'll be ever another Fields Medal given. And so you're like, "We're entering Perelman world."

嘉宾： We were talking about that explicitly this summer when the Fields Medals, you know, the last round of Fields Medals was given out in Philadelphia, and there was definitely a question, you know, 'cause people were following the progress. There hadn't been this latest bit of progress that really puts the question in the most powerful way possible. But already this summer, we were thinking, "Is this the last time that a Fields Medal is awarded?" I sure hope not. But we have to figure out what that means, you know?

奖项究竟在奖什么？

The—You have to think more sociologically about what do prizes accomplish. Why have these prizes? The people who win these prizes are already, you know, tenured professors at top places, and they're gonna be doing mathematics for the rest of their lives. Well, Perelman being one very—

Lex： Yeah, exception.

嘉宾： …very well-known exception. So what do the prizes accomplish? They celebrate the activity. They celebrate. They say, "This is what we think is important. This is, you know, the highest instance of something."

And there will still be activities that we wanna celebrate. I don't know if right now they're given out for solving major problems. Uh, solving major problems is something AI systems can do. That's not something that will be rare, and hence, it won't be nearly as valuable as it was in the past.

Centaur Math：人与 AI 协作的数学

I would like to think that despite our earlier discussion about the solved axiom, again, I don't believe the solved axiom, and I believe centaur math will be a very—

Lex： Centaur math, okay.

嘉宾： …like, great way to do math. I mean, that's how I currently feel now. I'm constantly talking to AI systems, and I'm learning a lot of math a lot faster than I'd be able to.

如何读数学论文：跳到 Lemma 3

Because the way math is written, you know, I sometimes give a paper to a grad student to read, and they come back a week later, and I say, "So how far did you get?"

"Well, I didn't really get past the first page, to be honest."

"Oh, really? Tell me."

"Uh, well, actually, I didn't get past the first paragraph."

I say, "Okay, fine. Why not?"

"Well, the first sentence is 'by the perturbation theory of non-local systems' and I don't know what any of that means, so that's, that's kinda where I'm stuck."

I'm like, "Okay. You don't know how to read a math paper. You don't—You skip the first couple of paragraphs. Go straight to, you know, the Lemma 3. And that's where you can start working and work your way backwards to what the thing is doing." But…

观看原视频 →

item.title: [Bits + Bips] After Binance's $6.3 Billion Hack, Can Crypto Fix Its Security Problem?
item.dc:creator: Bits + Bips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被遗忘的"证据链"：这不是技术问题，是制度记忆的断层

6.3 亿美金在 20 分钟内穿越 10 条链消失——这个数字背后真正值得震惊的，不是黑客有多厉害，而是整个加密行业集体性地"重新发明"了一个在传统金融里 100 年前就解决了的问题。

Austin 一句话戳破：没人在协议层做 circuit breaker（熔断），没人做 demand responsive pricing，没有"十亿美金出金等 24 小时"的时间锁。这些是 1929 年股灾后 Tradfi 就逐步固化的"常识"。换句话说，加密没有被 AI 攻破，也没有被朝鲜攻破——它是被自己的工程文化（tech-first, finance-second）攻破的。

出人意料的观察：加密行业招聘的 VC 合伙人里，几乎没有人真正开过银行或做市商。整个资产类别在没有"金融操作经验的记忆载体"的情况下被设计出来——这就像让一群没做过桥梁工程的物理学家设计悬索桥：数学全对，但不知道钢缆会在冬天收缩。

二、跨领域连接：ICE 的"全栈收购"其实是在重演 1870 年代的铁路兼并

Chris 顺口提到的 ICE 投资组合（Polymarket + OKX + Trade XYZ/Hyperliquid + NYSE）——这不是"多元化"，这是对交易品类拓扑结构的垂直封装。

把时间轴拉长看，这几乎是 1865-1880 年美国铁路寡头建立"全线联运"的翻版：Vanderbilt、Gould 当年收购的不是铁路本身，而是"托运人没得选"的网络效应。ICE 在做的事情完全同构——Spot、Derivs、Prediction、Perps、Tokenization 每一层都是一条"铁轨"，真正的护城河不在任何单一产品，而在把所有产品的结算与风险转移锁进同一个清算栈。

更令人意外的推论：Jeff Sprecher 是 founder-led CEO，而所有被他收购的初始团队也都是 founder-led。创始人收购创始人在金融基础设施里几乎没有先例——Tradfi 的并购历来是职业经理人之间的交易。这暗示 ICE 看到的不是"产品组合"，而是Hyperliquid/Polymarket 这些社区型金融基础设施，其实是新一代的"地方铁路公司"——文化不可被职业经理人替代，所以只能用股权而非管理整合。

三、最隐藏的系统性真相：这一集真正讨论的是"注意力"，不是"安全"

表层话题是 Binance 被黑、Perpetuals、Tokenization、AI 泡沫、中期选举。但如果把五个议题的结构叠起来看，你会发现它们都在回答同一个问题：谁在争夺"稀缺的信心带宽"？

  • 加密丢了 63 亿，失去的不是钱（95% 都赔了），是制度性信任的叙事份额；
  • AI 每周都有 wow moment，吃掉的是创业者注意力的一级市场（a16z 从 crypto fund 改名成了更广泛主题）；
  • Tokenized stocks 50 家公司联手反对——真正反对的不是技术，是失去对股东基座的信息控制权（Rahm 一针见血）；
  • 中期选举的"民调失真"——共和党选民不接电话——这是民调机构的信任溢价正在崩塌，和加密交易所信任溢价崩塌是同一个现象的不同切片。

真正的跨域连接：共和党选民拒接电话 ≈ 加密 degens 拒绝 KYC ≈ AI 用户拒绝读说明书。这三群人在不同领域都在做同一件事——退出官方采样系统。当"官方信号"（民调、交易所余额、财报）的信噪比被结构性噪声淹没，唯一还能定价真相的机制是 prediction market + perpetuals + 链上数据——也就是 ICE 正在打包的那一整摞东西。

所以 ICE 的收购本质上不是金融动作，是在下一个十年"真相信号"的管道上提前占坑。Stan Druckenmiller 买的也不是 Hyperliquid 的 token，是这套管道的早期使用权。

啊哈时刻：加密的"安全问题"和民调的"抽样问题"之所以在 2026 年同时爆发，是因为它们共享同一个底层病理——20 世纪设计的所有"中心化真相机构"都在被同一波去中心化的用户行为侵蚀。真正修复它的不会是更多审计，也不会是更精细的加权，而是那种"你不信任何人，但你信市场定价"的新基础设施。而这，恰好是加密从来就自诩要做的事。

它只是还没做到而已。

One of the issues we've had in crypto markets to date is that we've had very, very few futures because in the US we only have futures on commodities. Let's just step back — because everyone's like "CLARITY Act, oh my god, what happened, what didn't happen?" Today securities are regulated at the federal level. Commodities are regulated at the state level, but derivatives on commodities are at the federal level. Those markets are so important, they make the world go round.

Austin：Perps 会抢走期权和 Spot 的量吗？

Austin: So let me volley back in another way, Chris, as we've talked about this. If we start having significant futures interest in equities, what is that going to do to transform funding markets for American companies? Because we're going to have sort of the similarity of the crypto where now the interest in futures probably leads the interest in spot, and you're going to have funding disparities.

The reason I look at that one is if you look at retail trading activity in the United States and you contrast — call it 2002 to today — there's already significantly more zero-day options volume than there's ever been, and volatility has been driving a lot of markets. My personal view is that for retail in particular, that's just demand for leverage. I don't think they're literally trying to trade vega and gamma and theta. They're just looking for leverage. And futures — like perpetual futures — honestly are a cleaner way to express the leverage preference, because you don't have all those time-decay-type variables that are occurring inside of an option structure.

So Chris, I'm curious. Are we going to see options volumes move to perps? Are we going to see spot volumes move to perps? What are you expecting?

Chris: Honestly, I don't — yeah, some people say "oh, perps are easier because, to your point, they're just easier to understand than all the different Greeks that you have with options for retail." I don't buy that.

I think the ship's going to rise with the tide — all ships are going to rise with the tide. Retail's getting much more sophisticated. I think to your point they love the idea of leverage with perps and the leverage that they can get. It wasn't necessarily that easy for retail to get scalable leverage previously, but the more that retail loves yields — they love leverage. It's just what they love, right? But I also think we're seeing some projects, some options projects even now picking up because retail is just getting more sophisticated.

I think derivatives will continue to grow. I mean, when I was in Tradfi six years ago, one of the — and to this day, it was the sophistication of the retail markets that was one of the fastest-growing demographics across markets. It remains so. It remains very exciting.

Is there somebody who loses in this game? Is there a product that loses in this game? Some folks say "ah, it's futures because they're a pain and you got to roll them all the time." I don't know. I don't know if I buy that. I think different strokes for different folks, different products for different hedging strategies or even strategies around speculation, which is fine, important part of futures markets.

I just think it's great that you're going to have more choice. And the important thing is that the CFTC will do this — they'll make sure there's sufficient disclosures. AI also helps. "Hey, how does this product work? Can you explain it to me like I'm a fourth grader?" And you can get that output so that you can better identify. So I just think it's good for markets. Let the markets decide. I think the CFTC will be thoughtful about how crazy you can get. And I think that they will make sure that innovation stays responsible.

三、Tokenized Stocks：OKX × ICE 遭发行人反对

事件

Austin: So, speaking of innovation — I find it interesting this is happening at the same time the OKX / ICE thing is sort of at least temporarily going the other direction.

Okay, so 50 public companies, including Nvidia, Microsoft, JP Morgan, have now objected to having their shares tokenized and traded on OKX / ICE — up from 38. This is after the October 30th notice. The notice itself — basically people are just objecting as soon as they find out about this thing.

Mike Cagney today said: "Why would you trade on OKX ICE? Your execution is worse. What you really want is native equity on-chain issued by the company. That is the way."

Jackie Melanic said a NASDAQ-listed exec said their rep reached out suggesting they object to tokenized trading of their shares on OKX ICE. And 23 of the first 38 objectors were listed.

I would also like to point out that some of the people objecting have their own blockchain projects. It's really interesting to me to see Goldman and JP Morgan objecting for that reason in particular. And then of course we had the ad in the Wall Street Journal — "Your stock, their tokens, your problem" — which QR code led to a NASDAQ FAQ. NASDAQ claims it has no connection to this.

And I guess all of where this leaves me is — is this actually a problem with tokenization, or is this just competitors knifing each other? And is part of the problem here that this particular effort, quite frankly, is less robust than perpetual futures? Or, Chris, are you right — this is just derivatives dominate spot once again?

Chris: I love Ram's take on this one. I'm trying to understand why issuers are pushing back so hard. I'd love your take.

Ram：你解决的是什么问题？

Ram: On tokenization — I think all of us are very big proponents of tokenization. Stablecoins one example of that. We've all been advocates for it. But the solution just hasn't been applied appropriately. You got to hammer — everything's a nail. It's just "tokenize stocks," even though it's one of the most efficient liquid markets in the world. So it's like, well, what's the problem you're solving?

There are all sorts of problems to be solved. We've talked in the past about small business capital formation, community investment. How about solving Community Reinvestment Act problems for banks? How about tokenizing non-QIP assets? You get cross-margining. All of those have real pain points.

I don't know what's being solved by tokenizing a stock on chain. That's a free country. You can still tokenize things. You're permitted to. But if you're not solving a problem for a customer, you're not creating value. So I think this goes back to just — people throw capital at projects that have buzzwords that don't link to tangible economic value. And it's disappointing. It's a big misallocation.

Tokenization is still today a tremendous opportunity, but nothing's been done in the last five years. Stablecoins are the success story — that was done seven, eight years ago, quite a few years ago. So again, I think the VCs — there are not enough Chris's and Austin's in the VC category for digital assets. They wouldn't have spent money this way.

Chris：Pre-IPO + Perps + Direct Listing 的未来

Chris: The one thing I'm trying to get my head around — a couple things. And Ram, you nailed it, because it's always been the same problem in crypto. "I've got this amazing technology — what do you want to do with it?" And it only really resonates, you only get that real product-market fit, if you have new utility, new capabilities.

So I do see a world on the primary issuance side — IPO side — where you now have, let's just say, fast forward and today we have Trade XYZ that does launch pre-IPO markets. There's liquidity around them. Great. Let's just say that becomes kind of ubiquitous where you have these pre-IPO markets. That could be a first step in really galvanizing the direct listing process.

There's three ways to go public in the United States:

  1. Traditional intermediated IPO — the bankers set the price, they run around, they build the syndicate. Generally they get the price wrong, sometimes more wrong than others, but sometimes they nail it. Typically if they underprice it, then people are leaving money on the table, etc. That's the intermediated traditional route. By the way, it's enjoyed wild success. I would say our public markets — they cycle, like we're kind of pulling back right now, but generally speaking, we've had decent capital markets. There's probably room for reform there.

  2. SPACs — another way to go public. You take something public and then you try to acquire something.

  3. Direct listings — Coinbase famously did this. They directly issued equity and bypassed a lot of those intermediaries and let the market set the price.

With pre-IPO markets, if you bring it all together on the perps, you could see a position in the future where an issuer sitting back — a real smart CEO or CFO — and he's like, "Okay, hey, I'm going to watch the perp. Okay, the perp is where I want it, sustaining now. It's time to go to the direct listing because the market's waiting for it."

And then the big question for me on issuance is: does tokenization result in a new buyer of my equity? That's the fundamental question. Are people going to buy it who would never buy it previously? They had problems buying it. They couldn't reach it. And there's a little bit of tension there because, typically for somebody to buy an equity, they have to go through certain processes. Maybe overseas it's more difficult. But does this help globalize your issuance in a compliant way that expands the users?

Because if there's more buyers than sellers, usually the equity goes up. If there's more sellers than buyers — and I guess you could work in both directions. So the theory is there, maybe. But in practice we haven't been able to deliver this idea around "I'm tokenizing this so that my equity can reach incremental buyers." We're not there yet.

The question is: do we get there? Do you have benefit by getting out of the gate first? And it sounds like some of these issuers are saying no. I don't know why they're pushing back so hard. I haven't figured that out. I don't know what the downside is. Would love for you guys to unpack that, because I do see that's the direction of travel in the future.

Ram：发行人想保留对股东基座的控制

Ram: The market expansion story is like ADRs. That's the point you're making. "Hey, look, let's expand that pool." And I was wondering the same myself.

Maybe the risk is that if there's some adverse event, someone gets hacked, then there's some brand reputational risk that rubs off. That's one.

Two is loss of control. The issuers like to control their stock. They know their buyer base. They know who their beneficial owners are. They know their top accounts. They can have investor relations manage all that. This happens all the time in private markets too — private market enterprises don't necessarily like SPVs because they lose control of the investor base and all sorts of transactions happen. So that's my best guess as to why they might not like this format.

Austin：反对的成本几乎为零

Austin: I mean, the other part is: what's the cost of objecting right now? If you object, you could always in theory un-object. Clearly OKX and ICE want to do something. Purely from a brass-tacks perspective, certainly if I'm a company, I'm going to object and see if I can get them to pay me to un-object, if nothing else. Like this becomes one of those — I think there's very little downside to objecting, because it's not like this is already a venue driving a lot of trading volume.

If it were — for instance, take perpetuals — if somebody were to object to their stock being, call it, perpetualified, if they could do that, I actually think that would have major implications, because it just means the retail bid completely leaves your stock if volumes go there. But here, I don't think people are seeing it.

Ram: I think from a winners-and-losers perspective, there's a lot of reason to object, right? - If you're a market maker, you're supposed to object. - If you're Goldman Sachs, you're providing financing on these assets, you're supposed to object. - If you're Charles Schwab, you custody these assets, you make money from payment for order flow, you're supposed to object. - If it works, it advantages ICE tremendously.

Chris：PFOF 和市场碎片化

Chris: The PFOF thing is interesting — payment for order flow. Essentially that's predicated on Reg NMS, which is the national market standard, based on something called the National Best Bid and Offer. What that means in plain speak — I encourage everyone to read Flash Boys at some point — but essentially, equity is executed, it's routed to the best exchange, it's pretty much usually intercepted by one of these high-frequency trading types, proprietary trading firms, that slightly improve the price. That's how it works today.

So we saw some pushback when the SEC was attempting to roll back — and I think they're in the process of rolling back these rules. But I don't know if — if I'm in the business of making spread on differentiation in execution, I kind of like the fragmentation. If it emerges, if you have more fragmentation, maybe I can make even bigger spreads. So I'm surprised.

Ram: Did Citadel — sorry, did Citadel weigh in on this?

Chris: I think Citadel is pushing back against it. They are. They were, but I haven't heard much from them recently. I could have missed it, but I do think they came out against it, in my own conversations with them. But I'm wondering in the longer term — maybe they just — and by the way, a lot of these guys have invested billions of dollars in their infrastructure to be able to take advantage of that market structure. When market structure changes, it's very disruptive. I also think that many of these shops will be just fine. We'll figure it out because they're very, very sophisticated.

四、AI 泡沫与中期选举

AI 巨头的现金流拐点

Austin: All right. So, speaking of infrastructure being disrupted, I do want to talk a little bit about AI.

As we've been watching, the biggest AI and chip stocks have shed about $5 trillion since October 6. NASDAQ 100 fell 6.7% in October — its worst month since the March 2025 tariff panic. Investors seem to have stopped rewarding AI capex and started to pay attention to that old out-of-fashion thing — cash flows.

  • Alphabet: 13% down, its worst day ever. Erased about half a trillion dollars. Revenue was $63B versus $65B expected. In search, free cash flow $9B.
  • Amazon: -6% after hours. And three of the four hyperscalers are posting free cash flow deficits.
  • ServiceNow: by late, fell a record 31%.

So, a lot of comments. Bear prize — they used to be asset-light companies that were cash-flow heavy. Now they've become asset-heavy. Brian Mulberry of Zacks said investors are assigning more risk to the companies that are cash-flow negative now. And CoreWeave bonds are trading near 15% yields. 10-year about 5%. So that's a hell of a spread.

And the sell-off was pretty narrow. The S&P fell 6% last week, yet nine of 11 sectors were up. So a lot of this is concentrated in the tech size.

This guy we know named Ram Ahluwalia said: "Selling size and profitability and owning categories with positive earnings revisions and momentum is a good idea."

Ram：浴缸里的水流回长尾

Austin: So Ram, let me start with you on the back of that comment. What are you seeing there? Why did you say that?

Ram: Yeah, there's a couple of things going on here — a positioning story, a midterm story that's playing out. I would say that we're at a key inflection point now.

This year — and really last year — has been a factor-driven year. So there are different factors like energy sensitivity, rate sensitivity, technology, AI sensitivity. And all the themes that really benefited from most of this cycle, like — I call them Trump-bump themes — financials, AI/semiconductors, defense stocks — they topped out in late June, really with Micron's earnings. That was peak AI sentiment with Anthropic and OpenAI rolling out these new models. And now they've troughed.

I think a lot of that is midterm risk, because Kalshi and Polymarket are pricing in Dems taking over the House and the Senate despite the fundamental earnings actually being solid. We look at their earnings every quarter — the earnings are strong overall. Yes, there are winners and losers around these capex payers like Google versus the semis, which are capex receivers, but they both retraded down.

I think a lot of what's happened is just because of excessive positioning. People got crowded into like a consensus idea — like AI — and what was cheap were insurance stocks, really boring old companies in the longer tail of the market (what's called breadth), and these heavy market-cap-weighted names have since retreated.

The good metaphor is: you see water in a bathtub kind of piles up on one side. That's where we were at the end of June with semiconductors, and made everything else around — cheap — like in the insurance sector, defensives, and staples. And now you're seeing it come back.

I think midterms tomorrow are a clearing event. It won't be as bad as people think it will be. AI investment will continue. Productivity growth will continue. Earnings growth overall is strong. The debt issues will be managed, because when you're taking out debt, you're buying an asset. And the assets they are buying are productive for nearly every actor in the value chain. So that's my overall view. I think it's an incredible time to buy the AI story on sale as we're still early on this journey of transformation.

Chris：中期后通常是建设性的

Austin: Chris, what are you taking from the AI situation here? Is this signal, or is this a bump in the road?

Chris: Look, I think historically — and Ram, I think you touched on it — post-midterm cycles have been very, very constructive for all markets. What I'm trying to figure out now is that it feels like we're at max uncertainty, because you have the geopolitical stuff in the background. And by the way, a lot of the geopolitical stuff also tends to be correlated in many cases to election cycles. Maybe there's a reason why Satoshi timed the halving around elections.

But generally speaking, it's a very constructive time for markets after midterms. We'll see. But if history is a guide, then it's probably a pretty good setup — to Ram's point.

Look, there's plenty of risks out there. We have a very interesting president right now who put a lot of options on the table. We'll see what happens.

Ram：伊朗 2 月份的传闻

Ram: One geopolitical risk, you know, to bring up is a potential escalation of hostilities in one of the major theaters. I don't know if you picked up on that, Chris, or anyone else, Austin, but that's a rumor that was someone shared with me — who an ex-military, well-placed similar kind of crowd — that was like, "Yeah, Iran's going to happen, you know, in February." So that's something I've been picking up on. And there have been some notices from governments saying, "Hey, extend your reserves."

Now, by the way, a lot of that's getting priced in already. This news happened like last week, so keep that in mind. And when these events happen — depending on what these events even mean, we're not entirely clear — that is when peak uncertainty, to use Chris's term, starts to recede. So keep that in mind. But I don't know if you guys heard about that, but that's something to keep an eye on.

Chris: Yeah, there's some weird stuff. Governments talking about stockpiling three days, and tickers out there saying there's a new — I don't buy that personally.

Ram: What was that? Don't buy what personally?

Chris: No, no, I don't buy it personally. But Tucker Carlson was out there saying, "Oh, nuclear weapons are on the table." Like, you got to ignore all the noise. The one thing that is certain, though, is that midterm elections will result in additional clarity where markets are uncertain right now. And I think that's a lot of the reason behind why post-midterms have been constructive — because you don't really know how it's going to play out. Does Trump do better than people expect? Because that's generally been the Trump story. People won't talk about him, and they go into that. Like, we don't know the exact complexion of Congress coming out of that. After midterms we will, and the markets will quickly adjust and there'll be a new normal.

Austin：民调的结构性失真

Austin: I also think the midterms — quite frankly — are, what's the right way to say this, probably more volatile than most of the recent elections that we've dealt with. And people don't fully understand why.

If you're looking at what's happening with the polls right now and you just naively look at the polls, the Democrats are about to pull the biggest midterm result basically since the Great Depression if the polls are correct. And then you start asking yourself — well, are Republicans that unpopular while Democrats are that popular? Are we heading to that sort of outcome, or is there something weird going on here?

So I've spent a lot of time digging into the polls. It's something I've done before, because when you trade global macro, you try to understand these things. And here's what we're seeing:

  1. Wobble Republicans are basically not responding to polls anymore. You're seeing things like the New York Times coming out and saying three times as many Democrats as Republicans finish the polls — which doesn't even get you the number of Republicans who are just bailing out before you can even get a hold of them.

  2. You're getting samples in places from the raw data that are completely unlike the electorate of that place. A good example is there was a poll over the weekend I saw where in Texas — which, I'm going to remind everybody, went for Trump by double digits — their sample in terms of 2024 voting was Harris plus 15. Something is very wrong when your sample is 25 points off the median. That's like sampling Connecticut and getting a group that has Trump winning the state. This is completely crazy.

  3. You have to assume the respondents you got from the Republicans in particular — I think Democratic cross-tabs probably look roughly correct — but that the Republicans in particular are representative of the Republicans you didn't reach, which is almost certainly not true. You were getting the most left-leaning Republicans who are willing to talk to you.

The thing that was just not just a red flag, but like Chinese military parade level of red flags to me, was there are polls going on in places like Iowa and Kansas where they're having to double the number of people they're calling because they're not getting enough Republicans to even have a sample. And so there's no basis to conclude that the sample you got is actually representative.

Ram：反向押注才是非共识的机会

Ram: I agree. I'm not in my head here. I mean, the mispriced bet.

Chris: What about prediction markets, though, still, guys? Like, they —

Ram: Prediction markets are saying Dems win, right? House 94%, House and Senate — I want to say like in the mid-60s. So the asymmetric bet is the contrarian bet to bet that Republicans preserve the Senate. And if that happens, you wake up on Wednesday with a big gap up in financials, data center-linked semi names — which is what happened in 2024, incidentally.

So I remember going into that, I was of the view — and it's very similar reasoning to Austin — but back then you had early voting data and you could see that Trump was actually ahead. I don't think it'll be a washout like the polling suggests or the betting market suggests. And if that's the case, then look, consensus is priced in. Consensus has priced in a Democratic sweep — that's already there on offer. You can go by consensus.

Take the other side of that. And it's not even about who you want to win or not. It's just about risk-reward. The value and upside is better in taking the opposite side of the bet. I bought a defense stock ETF recently, for example. We picked up financials one or two weeks ago. I think semis are cheap. And if the Dems take both, it's not going to be that bad, right? The rhetoric won't match the policy substance. Data centers will still get built up. The US government will replenish their munitions. Life will go on.

Austin: Yeah, this [Kalshi] is at 75%, 74% — Democrats control the Senate.

Austin：Susan Collins 作为"信号"

Austin: I would also say, with certainty, some of the people betting on this are not sharps who understand the odds.

The one I'm looking at to determine "hey, are betting markets correct or is this people wishcasting" — Maine. I'm going to remind everybody that currently Susan Collins is behind in Maine by most polls and very low single-digit points. The Democrat is mildly favored there. And if you go look on Kalshi, I think you could get Susan Collins "yes" at like somewhere in the 30% range.

Now, let me tell you that Susan Collins has outrun her polls by somewhere between 5.5 to double-digit points the last three elections in a row. If you were looking at that and you were an objective evaluator of probabilities, you would say at worst this is 50/50 Collins — and she's probably favored. Because again, we know we can't poll Maine. The rurals do not fucking answer the phone. You can go look at this and look at people trying to do county-level polling in Maine and basically nobody answers. It's not even they're telling you they won't answer — they don't answer the fucking phone.

And the same thing is happening this cycle. And we know there's a directional charge to that miss. And it's happened three times in a row over like an 18-year period. And yet markets are pricing the polls as though they are correct. This is how you know the people betting on the basis of these things are not looking at the data.

Ram: Yeah, no, I agree. Sharps — the sharps I know in the election space are long Susan Collins.

Austin: I like it. I love the non-consensus view.

Ram: And you're seeing higher lows in names that should benefit under a Republican victory. So that tells you that things are more complex. Now, if the Dems do take both, I think you get a one-and-done washout and that resets where asset prices are. But either way, to Chris's point, post-midterm years are very constructive, very bullish. Midterm years are generally awful. The last midterm year was the 2022 bear market. Before that was 2018. We finished the year down 18%. So midterm years are uncannily bad and contra-theme. I think post this, it's come back to the themes that have delivered in this bull market.

Austin: I agree with you. And again, I do think it's the contrarian take, because if you're looking at the odds, Democrats are what — 70-ish percent to take the Senate? And I want to remind people, you're picking up four seats. And if we just concede that they're going to take North Carolina — which I think the data actually agrees with — you need three more seats and you need to defend Michigan, which is very definitely in play. So let's say you keep Michigan. You are now taking three of: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Ohio, and Texas. That's a huge lift.

Chris: Don't forget Fetterman in Pennsylvania. Markets like gridlock. Can we get some gridlock? Can we just —

Ram: Arguably the best outcome for markets is Democratic House, Republican Senate, right?

Chris: At least until we crash through the debt.

Ram: That could very well be the case.

收尾

Austin: All right. Well, we've reached 5:30. The election is tomorrow. So by the time we're talking next week — hopefully with a guest who can address this — we will know a little bit more about what actually happened. But remember, you heard it here from us: the polls are almost certainly wrong. The question is just how and how much.

All right, so on that note, thank you for joining us for this episode of Bits and Bips. We'll be back in one week to discuss more about how the worlds of crypto and macro and AI and politics are colliding. Until then, everyone —

Thank you for watching, and hope you enjoyed this episode of Bits and Bips. Just remember, nothing we say here is investment advice. And please check unchainedcrypto.com/bitsandbips for more disclosures.

item.description:
## 一、被遗忘的"证据链"：这不是技术问题，是制度记忆的断层
6.3 亿美金在 20 分钟内穿越 10 条链消失——这个数字背后真正值得震惊的，不是黑客有多厉害，而是**整个加密行业集体性地"重新发明"了一个在传统金融里 100 年前就解决了的问题**。
Austin 一句话戳破：没人在协议层做 circuit breaker（熔断），没人做 demand responsive pricing，没有"十亿美金出金等 24 小时"的时间锁。这些是 1929 年股灾后 Tradfi 就逐步固化的"常识"。换句话说，加密没有被 AI 攻破，也没有被朝鲜攻破——它是被**自己的工程文化（tech-first, finance-second）**攻破的。
**出人意料的观察**：加密行业招聘的 VC 合伙人里，几乎没有人真正开过银行或做市商。整个资产类别在没有"金融操作经验的记忆载体"的情况下被设计出来——这就像让一群没做过桥梁工程的物理学家设计悬索桥：数学全对，但不知道钢缆会在冬天收缩。
## 二、跨领域连接：ICE 的"全栈收购"其实是在重演 1870 年代的铁路兼并
Chris

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] How Robert Moses Destroyed Anyone in His Way - Robert Caro
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、Caro 最想问的那个问题，本身就是全书的隐藏主轴

"你意识到自己在变吗？" ——这不是一个普通的追问，而是传记作家埋了一辈子的钩子。它暗含一个惊人的论断：道德腐蚀具有代谢性，像肝脏处理酒精一样，是一个你从内部永远测不到的过程。Caro 没问 "你后悔吗"、没问 "你知道你毁了多少人吗"，因为他知道那些问题都有标准答案。他问 "你知道你在变吗"——这等于承认：Moses 的悲剧不是一个坏人做坏事，而是一个人在不知情的状态下被自己的方法改造。这与成瘾医学里的 "hedonic adaptation"、佛教里的 "业的沉积" 在结构上同构：小选择不是加法，是结晶。

二、Epstein 案例里藏着一个反常识的真相：Moses 摧毁的不是敌人，而是更优解的提出者

请注意这个细节有多怪异：Epstein 没说 "不要修路"，他说 "往南挪两个街区，只拆几百户而不是几万户"。这是一个工程学上更好、道德上更好、政治上更安全的方案。按常理 Moses 应该感谢他。但 Moses 动用婚外情丑闻把他彻底毁掉。

这揭示了一种在威权结构里反复出现的规律——威胁独裁者的从来不是反对者，而是改良者。戈尔巴乔夫不能容忍叶利钦，不是因为叶利钦更激进，而是因为他证明了 "还有别的路可走"。毛整肃务实派比整肃保守派更彻底，也是同样的道理。反对者证明你是对的（他们错了），改良者证明你是过时的。 这也是为什么今天很多公司 CEO 真正打压的不是外部竞争者，而是内部提出更好方案的中层——后者才是对自我叙事的根本威胁。

三、Caro 在第七次访谈被切断的那个细节，是整段对话最耐人寻味的注脚

Moses 可以接受 Caro 写他驱逐数万人、强行穿城、碾过一个个社区——因为那契合他 "远见者" 的自我叙事。但 Caro 一提到 "某个富翁因为高尔夫球场被绕开而给委员会捐钱"，他就永远不再见 Caro 了。

人无法忍受的，不是与自己罪行相称的指控，而是打破自我叙事的指控。 毁一座城叫 vision，收一笔钱叫 petty。前者他是宙斯，后者他只是个受贿的公务员。这个规律在今天依然普适：高管起诉小小的诽谤、却对结构性批评置若罔闻；学者无视学术反驳、却会为被称 "不聪明" 发邮件三天；国家可以承受被称 "暴力"，却承受不了被称 "小气"。身份的伤口永远比行为的伤口更痛。

四、一个让人脊背发凉的跨领域连接：Moses 不是生来残忍，他学会了残忍

这是本段最被忽略的一句话——"he learns that in my opinion by failing to get things done when he's very young." Moses 年轻时是失败的改革者，他从挫败中归纳出一套方法论："找到对方的弱点，使用它。" 然后他不断优化、不断执行、越来越熟练。

这意味着残忍是一项可训练的技能，不是一种人格特质。而一项技能一旦被掌握，就会脱离原初目的独立运转——就像 J. Edgar Hoover 的档案系统，本来是打击共产党的工具，最后变成了监控总统的武器；就像硅谷 "增长黑客" 的手段，本来是为新产品获客，最后被用来操纵选举。

Caro 的 Moses 因此不只是一部政治传记，它是一部关于方法论反噬目的论的寓言——当你学会用某种方式达成目标，你会开始为了使用这种方式而寻找目标。工具重塑手，手重塑心。这，大概就是 Caro 想问却再也没能问出口的那个问题的真正答案。

📝 转录文本

The Seventh Interview, and the Question That Never Came

Interviewer: You interviewed him seven times. Um, and the seventh time you mentioned your awareness of a donation that was made to his commission by a millionaire whose golf course was spared by the new route for his parkway. And after that, he didn't talk to you again.

If you had gotten an eighth interview with Robert Moses, what is the one question you would most want to ask him?

Caro: Oh god, what a great question. Well, you know, off the top of my head, I think if I only had one question to ask him, I think I'd ask him, "Did you realize you were changing?"

That's off the — that's a great question you asked. Um, but that's the answer I'll give for now. That's all I — that's not something I always wanted — would like to have asked him, you know.

Did Moses Know He Was Changing?

Interviewer: Do you think he realized that he was changing?

Caro: No. I think I think he felt from the beginning that he had this vision for building roads here and parks here. That was the best thing to do and it was going to get done and it should get done. No matter how many hardships he had to inflict on people, no matter how many thousands he had to evict, no matter what he had to do, he was going to get the roads built.

And you see this increasing ruthlessness, this utter ruthlessness of him. If someone stood in his way, he was going to find a way to remove that person as an obstacle.

The Henry Epstein Example

I mean, I'll give you an example of that if you want.

There's a politician in the Bronx named Henry Epstein. Uh, Henry Epstein is opposing the Cross Bronx Expressway. He's saying to Robert Moses, "You're putting it right through a neighborhood where you have to evict tens of thousands of people. You can just move it two blocks to the south and you only have to evict a couple of hundred people."

Moses sets out to destroy Epstein — and basically does — by making it known he's having an affair. If he can find a weakness in somebody — that he has a mistress, that he's taking money or something — he'll use it. He'll use whatever he has to to get things done.

Ruthlessness as a Learned Skill

Uh, he learns that, in my opinion, by failing to get things done when he's very young. He has things that he wants to get done and they don't get done, and the awareness comes on him — and we can see it in the book, or in my learning about him. I try to show how he learns that he has to find weaknesses in people. He has to use it. If he has a weakness, he's going to use it. He's going to get things done.

There's a hardening and increased ruthlessness where the only thing that matters is to get the thing done. Anyone who stands in his way, if Moses has to destroy him, he'll destroy him.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.
