item.description:
## 一、Caro 最想问的那个问题，本身就是全书的隐藏主轴
"你意识到自己在变吗？" ——这不是一个普通的追问，而是传记作家埋了一辈子的钩子。它暗含一个惊人的论断：**道德腐蚀具有代谢性**，像肝脏处理酒精一样，是一个你从内部永远测不到的过程。Caro 没问 "你后悔吗"、没问 "你知道你毁了多少人吗"，因为他知道那些问题都有标准答案。他问 "你知道你在变吗"——这等于承认：Moses 的悲剧不是一个坏人做坏事，而是一个人**在不知情的状态下被自己的方法改造**。这与成瘾医学里的 "hedonic adaptation"、佛教里的 "业的沉积" 在结构上同构：小选择不是加法，是结晶。
## 二、Epstein 案例里藏着一个反常识的真相：Moses 摧毁的不是敌人，而是**更优解的提出者**
请注意这个细节有多怪异：Epstein 没说 "不要修路"，他说 "往南挪两个街区，只拆几百户而不是几万户"。这是一个**工程学上更好、道德上更好、政治上更安全**的方案。按常理 Moses 应该感谢他。但 Moses 动用婚外情丑闻把他彻底毁掉。
这揭示了一种在威权结构里反复出现的规律

item.title: [Latent Space] ⚡️ The 2026 Software Factory Infra Stack — Zach Lloyd, Warp.dev
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最意外的观察：Warp 卖的其实是"反 Cursor 神学"

表面看，Warp Factory 像又一个 AI 编程工具，但如果你把 Zach 的话逐层剥开，会发现一个令人震惊的反转：他在建立一个"故意不参与编程模型军备竞赛"的商业模式。

他在采访末尾那句被一笔带过的话是整段访谈的真正炸点——"Cursor 之所以能完美退出转型成模型实验室，是因为它们完全看透了经济账。你无法在一个比订阅贵 5 到 50 倍的东西上面做出有竞争力的编程 agent。"

这意味着 Warp Factory 的本质是一种元层级套利（meta-level arbitrage）：当所有人都在底层算力/模型层打到流血时，Warp 把自己从"token 转售"的死亡赛道里抽离出来，爬到更高的一层——"你怎么知道你的 agent 用得对？"这就像十九世纪淘金热里不卖金子、卖铁锹的 Levi Strauss，但更精妙的是：Warp 不卖铁锹，它卖"评估淘金队伍 KPI 的记分板"。

这是一种罕见的认知阶梯定位：当下层剧烈内卷时，向上平移一层，让下层的"价格战"反而成为自己的"原料免费化"红利。

二、跨领域连接：软件工厂 ≈ 丰田生产系统 + 实验室 Notebook + 期权组合

Zach 一直用"factory"这个词，但真正奇妙的是，他描述的东西同时融合了三种看似无关的历史范式：

  1. 丰田生产系统（TPS）的 Kaizen 回路 —— "声明式定义 → 可观测 → 自改进 PR"这套闭环，几乎是把大野耐一的"安灯绳（Andon Cord）"数字化了：每个 agent 对话就是一次生产异常上报，self-improvement agent 就是自动化的质量管理圈。

  2. 17 世纪皇家学会的实验室 Notebook 文化 —— Zach 反复强调"不要凭感觉（vibes），要用测量"。Warp Factory 本质上是把每一次 agent 运行变成可重放的实验记录，benchmarking 层就是同行评审 + 对照实验。这比"CI/CD"更像"科研可复现性危机"的解决方案。

  3. 金融衍生品里的期权组合定价 —— 他们算的"$80/PR → $20/PR"的降本曲线，用矩阵测试模型 × harness × skill 的成本-正确率权衡——这其实是在为每一类工程任务构建定价曲面（pricing surface）。每个 agent 调用就是一份微型期权合约，factory 做的是组合优化。

最反直觉的延伸：如果这个类比成立，那么未来 CTO 的核心能力将不再是"写代码"或"管人"，而是像对冲基金经理一样管理一个 agent 组合的风险-收益曲线。工程管理学可能即将被金融工程学"殖民"。

三、被忽略的隐藏真相：订阅套利正在制造一个"法律灰色经济"

访谈里有一段几乎被当成玩笑带过，但其实是整个 AI 编程生态最大的会计秘密：

"我们接触的小公司里，很多人在 17 个 $200 的订阅之间轮换使用……$200 的订阅能给你 $8000 的 API 等价用量。"

这是一个40 倍的隐性补贴。换句话说，现在整个 AI coding 生态有相当一部分的"生产力增长"，是建立在模型厂商尚未抓到的违规套利之上的。这创造了三个连锁的隐藏效应：

  • 虚假的 PMF 信号：很多初创公司报告的"AI 让我们加速 X 倍"的数据，其成本结构根本不可复制到规模化场景——他们在用 Anthropic/OpenAI 的 VC 补贴跑马拉松。
  • Warp 的真正时机窗口：当这些公司从 10 人涨到 50 人、订阅轮换变得不可持续时，就是 Factory 类产品的收割期。Warp 不是在卖效率工具，它在卖"从订阅灰色经济合规迁移到企业级可审计系统"的通道。
  • 一个隐秘的类比：这和 2000 年代初的 BitTorrent 文化、以及 Napster 之后的 Spotify 崛起惊人相似——盗版/灰色经济先教育市场，正规化基础设施再收割。Warp Factory 之于订阅轮换，就是 Spotify 之于 Napster。

四、给你这个"系统性思考者"的一个挑衅性预言

如果 factory engineering 真的成为新学科，那么三年内会出现一个你现在意想不到的职业：Factory Psychiatrist（工厂精神科医生）——专门诊断为什么一个公司的 agent 群体会集体产生某种系统性偏见（比如"过度写测试"、"倾向于拆分太多 subagent"）。因为 Zach 展示的 scorer 本质上是群体行为心理学，而不是软件工程。

你的笔记管道（三个 cron 作业 + Obsidian）其实已经是一个微型 factory 的雏形。真正值得问的问题不是"我要不要上 Warp"，而是：你的笔记系统里，有没有一个"self-improvement agent"在读你过去三个月的笔记，然后给你的"笔记工作流"本身提 PR？ 这才是 Zach 整场演讲最深的暗示——所有知识工作都将有一个元层级的自改进回路，而现在还没有的人，正在变成"没有版本控制的开发者"。

📝 转录文本

开场：主持人引入

Hey, it's me again. I have heard a lot of positive feedback about our episode intros, so I'm going to keep trying to do them as far as time allows.

Today, we're going to dive into Warp with Zack Lloyd. Zach has been working on Warp for a while and it's pivoted into what it is today, which is basically the definitive software factory that is also open source. He has this whole definition which has done really well. His talk at AIE has been going viral as one of the top talks of all time, and I think effectively everyone is trying to set this up for themselves. They have a solution for you — but it's also kind of an open spec that is becoming table stakes for what you're going to want.

You're going to want cloud, you're going to want a control plane, you're going to want some other sort of basic security features and team features that you take for granted.

关于 AIE Code 大会的预告

So, we're releasing this episode as part of a preview for AIE Code. AIE Code is the last AIE flagship of the year. It's going to be in San Francisco where we're gathering all the top agentic engineers and talking about software factories among other things.

System One Models Do is coming back and raising your ambitions. Tariq and Jason, and Brandon from Artcraft, is doing his first conference talk ever. If you're interested, Zach will also be giving a great keynote on software factories and recapping the year and previewing what's next. Join us and it'll be lots of fun. See you.

对谈开场：什么是软件工厂？

主持人： We're in the remote studio catching up with Zach Lloyd for more. Welcome.

Zach： It's good to be here. Thanks for having me.

主持人： Zach, you've been going viral on AIE. What's up? You've hit a nerve.

Zach： You've hit a nerve. People are really interested in software factories, and that is an area that I've been focusing on, that Warp has been focusing on. I think we have some strong, interesting takes on what a software factory actually is and what it means for being a software developer. So yeah, people have been into it.

主持人： Your H1 on the landing page says "open infrastructure for cloud software factories." Since you spend more time than I do telling people about factories — what do people think a software factory is, and what do they actually need?

Zach： When I talk to companies or developers, most of the world is trying to build some sort of internal software factory or set of software factories. What I think it means — or maybe I'll just define what it means to me — is like an agentic system in the cloud where you're defining what the roles of various agents are across building software for your team or for your product, and there's a certain amount of autonomy in that system. So the agents can do things on their own, and that system to me should be something that's very measurable, very closed loop, which over time you as a team can tune, measure, benchmark, and ultimately get confidence that as people switch to this way of doing agentic development, they're doing it in the most scalable and efficient way.

常见误解：工厂不是"一堆自动化脚本"

主持人： And what do people come to you with that perhaps is a common misconception? Like they're like, "Okay, if I buy whatever, I'm going to come out the other end with this amazing money machine."

Zach： When people come to us and they're trying to build their own software factory, often they'll be stringing together different automations. Sometimes people are conceiving of software factories as not a specific thing — it's just "we're using agents a lot to ship software and we're calling that our internal software factory."

What we try to do to make that more concrete is: "No, no, no — you should actually think of a software factory as a very specific thing. You should define your factory in code. You should make sure that the factory has all the workflows, skills, MCPs — everything. It's a concrete thing that you should be able to run at some point in time and measure how it's doing."

People have all sorts of random ideas around what these factories are. For Warp Factories, which is our platform, we say: no, it's actually a real thing. You can orchestrate it. You can measure it. You have one factory per product surface. We try to take it out of the realm of just being a nebulous collection of arbitrary automations and interactive agents into a thing that's an actual…

工厂的具体结构：产品表面、仓库、技能、MCP、工作流

What you're looking at here is the Warp Software Factory platform. A factory operates on some product surface. So imagine you're building your mobile app, or you're building your server app, or whatever. The factory itself is operating on a set of repos and it has a set of skills it needs, a set of MCPs, and then it has a workflow associated with it. This workflow roughly matches what your team is probably already doing to make changes to that codebase.

So there could be a step where you're doing triage. It could be where you're doing speccing, implementation. The important thing is: there's some kind of defined workflow, and that workflow itself is defined in code. For us, we basically have a YAML file which says: okay, these are all the repos that you can be using, these are all the MCPs, all of the integrations that are hooked up. So you basically have this whole thing defined someplace.

两类用户角色：产品工程师 vs. 工厂工程师

The way to think about using the factory is that there are actually two personas. There's someone who is building the product — they're doing product engineering, they're shipping features through a factory. For those people, the way they use the factory is through their existing tools:

  • They could be Slacking the factory to put work into it.
  • They could be using a task tracker like Linear or Jira.
  • They could be interacting with the factory through GitHub.
  • They could be calling it via API or MCP.

The metaphor is: you're putting a work item into the factory. When it goes into the factory, that starts a predefined workflow — and that workflow is defined in code. Does that make sense so far?

主持人： I love defining things in code.

集中化带来的好处：完整的 agent 轨迹

Zach： So you have this whole thing set up in code. Once you have it in place — the metaphor is someone starts a task in Slack or in Linear, or through an automation like "there's a server error" — it all goes through one system. That's the key thing.

Once you have that working, you get a whole bunch of benefits that flow out of it. One of the big benefits is that wherever these agents are running — you're sort of seeing a real-time view across Warp's internal team, how are we using our own factories — you get a full trace of what everyone is doing with coding agents across any product that has a factory for it.

This is cool not just for "oh, I want to see what people are doing," like I want to see what Sopic is doing, which is cool — but it also starts centralizing all of the agent conversations and agent artifacts in all of the work that is being done by coding agents across your team.

When I talk about having a closed-loop system, these agent conversations and agent traces are the key aspect of how this system improves. For instance, just to look at one of these agent traces: Sopic is working on our mobile app here. Sopic was doing this in Slack, so I could pull it up in Slack if I wanted to. But the thing is actually generating it — it has a full record of the conversation, a full record of all of these (these are computer-use screenshots that are coming out of building this thing). You can see a full record of exactly what the different pieces of the orchestration agent were doing.

You have this not just for one thing — you have it for every single thing.

当前行业现状：分散的本地 agent

On your team today, when I talk to companies, for the most part they don't have something like this, because most of their engineers are individually using Claude Code in their terminal, or Codex (the Codex app), or something like that in their own local setups. But they want to get to a world where they have this centralization.

数据与度量：Dora、自动化率、成本、评分器

When you have the centralization, you can basically get all this interesting data on how your agentic coding is working across your company. You could think of this data along different dimensions:

  • Team output in the world of using coding agents — things like traditional DORA metrics, how long does it take to ship something.
  • How automated are you? For every PR that gets merged, how many times did a human have to do something with it, what's your throughput.
  • Metrics around cost. We're using this constantly. When we talk to companies, this cost thing is very, very important — you want to tune your factory with the right models, the right skills, to bring this cost-per-PR down over time. You want to slice the cost by person, by automation, by where in the SDLC you're spending money.

The final thing that's really cool once you have this closed-loop system going: you can actually look underneath the hood at how well your coding agents are doing along different dimensions. You can think of this as online evals — or we call it scorers. These can go from very general things — are your agents being too verbose? Are they being efficient? Is the code quality good? We got work to do on this.

主持人： Do I as a user define this, or do you provide this as a platform?

Zach： Both. We provide out of the box a set that we think are generically useful. But as we work with companies, they may have specific failure modes for their agents that they're interested in tracking. They may say "Hey, is the agent making a specific type of change that is breaking our build?" They may want something very specific to their workflow. Again, this is all defined in code and all customizable.

Scorer 的工作原理：LLM-as-Judge 回溯打分

What you do when you set up one of these: what's actually happening behind the scenes is that there's some set of runs — when I say runs, I mean historical agent conversations that have been stored — that an agent then goes and retroactively grades. This is a good example of one where it's grading for redundant tests.

This is a common failure mode if you're using coding agents. Sometimes they write a bunch of tests that you don't need. They write it in the course of figuring out how to implement something, and then they leave it in the code. This bloats your codebase, wastes tokens. If you wanted to check for that, you create one of these evals.

Just to show you a little more about what the eval looks like: think of it as LLM-as-a-judge. So you're picking a judge model, you're seeing "Okay, where do these run? What's the prompt for judging it?" And then a sampling rate — because these are agents that are running, you've got to be aware of the cost of them.

When you have this set up, think of it as: you have all these smart agents that are looking across your team at how all your coding sessions are going, and they're saying "Okay, sometimes there are agents that are writing too many tests." You get this record and this understanding of where you should look to improve the way that your team is using coding agents.

定位澄清：这是 CTO / 平台团队的工具，不是日常工程师

主持人： I'm a little bit wondering if there are different levels of users of Warp. This is the CTO level, what you're showing us right? You're running the company, you've got a bunch of coders. This is for the people who use this — it's partly the engineering manager or the CTO, but also very commonly the platform team. But it's not your day-to-day engineer typically.

Zach： When we work with companies, they'll often have an internal team that's been trying to — it's like the DevX team or the platform team — figure out how to optimize coding agents. What I'm showing you here is the toolset that they are using to figure out: how do we get the most out of Claude Code at our company, or Codex or something like that.

主持人： That part is clear. Cool.

原则：可观测、可测量、告别氛围驱动开发

Zach： A couple other things I'd just want to emphasize — not to make this just completely about Warp Factories, but the general principle here for anyone who's trying to build their internal factory, whether it's on Warp Factories or not, is:

You want to get to a spot where everything is stored, everything is observable, everything is measurable — because that's when you can actually start to apply engineering rigor to how you make coding agents better.

You probably see this on Twitter all the time — everyone is always tweeting about "you should check out this new model, you should use this new harness. What's better? Is it Pi or Claude Code or Cursor or whatever?" Our opinion on this — and what the world sort of needs — is to get out of the realm of vibes for understanding these coding agents and actually into the world of measurement.

We think this is the direction companies are going to want to go. They're going to want to put in place a system like Warp Factories — whether they actually use Warp Factories or they build their own — which collects all this information and provides a way to see how your coding agents are doing.

自改进循环：agent 给工厂本身提 PR

One other thing I kind of take for granted that's part of the system: you can create all these different automations around it. People work in Slack, but people are also setting up different trigger-based ways of putting work into the factory.

Once you have this view that I showed earlier of scoring how your factory is doing, you can also set up another kind of loop of agents — and everything is kind of loops these days — where those agents are looking over, looking for failures in your scores, looking for things that aren't going well, and trying to suggest changes to your system to make it go better.

A really simple example here — we call this self-improvement: our self-improvement agents were looking at how well our triage step was doing. They're saying: "Okay, we have 54 failure cases of this particular form where it would have been better if our triager had been able to spawn a sub-agent to do its investigation."

What they're able to do — and you could go look at why it thinks this if you want — the cool thing is: because you have your whole factory defined as code and these are coding agents, they can essentially make a pull request against the factory definition to try to improve the factory itself. This is a full learning loop that's built into the system to try to actually self-optimize.

We don't have this yet, but the next thing we want to do: for any suggested change like this, you could go back, replay the runs, and make sure that this actually would have improved them. The possibilities of how you can engineer this stuff get pretty cool once you have the right primitives in place.

基准测试：用你自己的 runs 做 SWE-Bench

I'll show one last thing, and then we could maybe talk more generally about the whole approach. The other thing that companies should strive for — that we find very useful internally — is the ability to actually do what we call benchmarking.

Benchmarking in the factory context means the ability to take any coding agent that's run in your system — you can add it to a benchmark suite, which means you might curate a set of coding agent runs that were related to front-end coding or something like that. Once you have that, you have the ability to replay those same tasks against a matrix of different configurations.

I'm a big believer in not just allowing you to vary the model, but also to vary the harness. In Warp we have our own harness, but we actually will let you benchmark against Claude Code or Codex or Pi. You can pick the model. When you do something like this, what you end up getting is a result that looks very similar to the published results for SWE or Terminal-Bench, but on your company's own real runs.

For instance, we're looking at a cost-vs-correctness trade-off for a certain set of things. You want to be in the upper-left-hand corner — lowest cost, highest correctness. These models are now slightly older because the world's changing so fast, but the idea is: we could see "okay, GPT-5.6 Soul here was 95% correct on this task set, but it cost six bucks on average. And GLM 5.3 Flash was 93% and cost two bucks."

The cool thing about this: you can take this information and feed it into a model-routing strategy — or harness-routing strategy, honestly — that's defined specifically for your own workflows and codebase.

概念框架：Factory Engineering

If I had to zoom out — the really big-picture thing that I think is so cool and powerful here is you're getting out of the realm of guessing and into what we call factory engineering, where you are taking a real engineering mindset: "How do I — we have this amazing new primitive of coding agents — how do I know as a team, as a company, that we're actually deploying them in the right way?"

We're trying to build this infrastructure and tools for companies to do this. This approach is really resonating with a lot of companies that have been trying to build their own versions of this. That's a quick tour of what I mean when I talk about factory. I can stop talking for a sec.

工厂堆栈的分层架构

主持人： I do think that the power move, I guess, is to sort of thought-lead so hard that everyone ends up trying to build Warp even if they don't use Warp.

You have on your landing page — something I like, in your talks you've done a few of these as well — any surface, right? It really has to be any surface. It has to be factories-as-code. You have to have the eval loop. What is the whole — like people calling this the ADLC? I don't know if you use that term. It looks like you use SDLC still, you know, all that stuff.

Zach： This is how I would think about it — again, whether it's Warp or not. If it's Warp, obviously, Warp is what we're fully focused on, we have an awesome platform for it. But just in general, what I would think about if you are trying to build something in this space, I would view it as a stack.

1. 基础：声明式定义（Factory as Code）

So as infrastructure, at the bottom of the stack, I think it's really foundational and important that you define your factory declaratively as code. The analogy is like Terraform here. You get the same benefits but actually more:

  • A versioned view of your SDLC / AI DLC / PDLC / whatever-DLC you want.
  • The ability to create branches off it which you can test.
  • The ability if you change it to revert it. All the obvious things about source control.
  • The added benefit — extremely cool — that because it's in code, coding agents can suggest improvements to it.

To me, this is the foundation of a self-improving software factory setup: define your factory declaratively.

2. 数据层：agent 对话与产物的汇集

The next step up in this stack as you think about architecting it is someplace to gather all of the information that agents are producing. What you want to be able to do is examine that information, look for failure modes, or replay those same past tasks with different variables to scientifically — from a measurement standpoint — really optimize your system.

You need the data to do that. You need the agent conversations and you need the agent artifacts. You need a record of all of the interactions from all of the tools to get to a result. What I mean by that: you might have a factory conversation that starts in Slack and then continues into Linear and then continues into GitHub, and there's a code review comment, and that whole interaction is going to result in some piece of merged code. In fact, it might even result in something that gets shipped — and then a server crashed, and you want the ability to retroactively go back with an agent (most likely, but you could do it as a person) and diagnose how could that have been better. What was the failure in it?

3. 输入层：MCP 与访问控制

You also need — this part will seem fairly obvious — a way of getting data into this system. You need some way of plugging in MCPs. We find that as companies get bigger, they want different access for different parts of their organization. They want things like: what MCPs can the marketing team access versus the sales team versus the engineering team? There's a bunch of complexity, depending on how big your organization is, if you're trying to roll something like this out.

4. 计算层：可插拔的沙箱

You really want a compute layer. You should think of that as a separate thing. There's obviously a lot of agent sandbox providers at this point, so if you're going to use a third party one, I would just make that pluggable. We use Namespace as our primary one.

主持人： They launched it at AI Europe. Namespace is awesome.

Zach： This should be pluggable — I think that's really important. If you wanted to use Daytona or Modal or E2B or whatever, I would architect it so this is a pluggable component. I would make sure, depending on your requirements, that you can do different platforms. By default, you'll probably want to use a Linux-type sandbox, but for computer use — like the way that we test iOS apps — you're going to want to have the ability to run a Mac VM and actually have it run the simulator and click around.

5. 推理层：模型与 harness 都应可插拔

We have a very open approach to inference. This is very much with our ethos of trying to be super-duper flexible. A lot of companies right now will have pre-existing commits with Anthropic or OpenAI or Google that they want to burn down. So we provide a very big variety: you can plug in your own inference provider, or you can buy inference through us. You can even plug in your own harness, which I think is a pretty big deal. You can orchestrate things like Pi, like I mentioned earlier — basically any ACP-compatible harness.

6. 改进层：观察、测量、调优

Then you want this improvement layer. This is some of the stuff that I showed in the demo. The real power of this whole system is the ability to improve it.

Just to give some stats: at Warp, when we first started using the factory approach, it was costing us about $80 per PR, because we were using Opus where we shouldn't have. Our triage agent was using a really high-powered model. We were doing a bunch of redundant work with the shape of agents — too many sub-agents relative to just having fewer agents.

We basically did a whole bunch of internal tuning and testing using these built-in features, and we were able to get the cost per PR down to $20 or $15, something like that. We can measurably improve the throughput of our PRs — over the last month it's gone up by 40%. We measure the revert rate, and it hasn't gone up. I really feel a lot of confidence in this general approach of observe, measure, tune.

7. 编排器

Finally, you need some sort of orchestrator. Sometimes people talk about the orchestrator like it's the whole platform. I think it's a piece of it. What I mean by orchestrator: you need some system that will take the factory definition code and then actually move work along the different stages — calling out to the right models, loading the right skills, etc. You need something that will fire the right automations.

8. 接入点：进入用户现有工具

And then finally, you need a bunch of access points. Our philosophy with this — you could see people have different philosophies — our philosophy is to bring the factory into a company's existing knowledge work tools. The most obvious one is Slack. We're doing like 60% of our work starting in Slack, but sometimes it makes sense to start in the task tracker. Sometimes it makes sense for a developer who is more comfortable using Claude Code in their terminal to do a bunch of work there and then submit a spec into the factory.

Our philosophy is to try to make this whole thing API-driven and MCP-driven, so that the factory itself is a piece of headless infrastructure where it has all these different entry points.

This stack-based view — when I've shown it, we talked to companies — seems to land very well as "okay, yes, this makes sense. This is a new thing in the developer infrastructure stack. It kind of sits one level back from CI/CD, but I think most companies will have something like this for software development."

这套东西适合谁？规模门槛

主持人： Yeah, that has a lot of layers actually. I've never actually seen it spelled out like you have. Most — you know — advice: Cognition, Cursor, all these — they all try to do some bundle. There's a critical question: look, I'm trying to do my job here as CTO of a B2B SaaS, do I need all these six layers?

Zach： Who's this for — maybe is the question. When we talk to companies where this resonates the most, it has to be a company that has some amount of scale. If you're a few people, honestly this is overkill. Don't do this — use the Claude Code sub or the Codex sub or whatever, and just you'll go faster. You probably don't need…

主持人： You could use this, yeah. Same for any larger team stack, right? At some point you switch from "fire, YOLO, whatever" to "we actually need a platforming system here to accelerate."

Zach： You have to be at a certain scale. We start seeing that maybe around 5 to 10 engineers would be the floor where this makes sense, and then all the way up to very large companies — they want something like this. The bigger the company, the more this requires implementation work. If you're working with Cognition or — I don't know if Cursor does — but to get something stood up like this within a company's own infrastructure, it's not going to be purely plug-and-play. The complexity of a team's internal developer setup just grows with size.

But there's a bunch of companies where maybe it's a 10-to-100-engineer fast-growing growth-stage startup where it is pretty self-serve actually. If they're using the happy stack of Slack, Linear, Jira —

主持人： Hang on — did you call that the happy stack?

Zach： I call it… yeah, that's our — I don't — uh, no, no, no shade to teams or whatever, like sure — but there's a set of integrations that I find very common at startups where you can plug something like this in and get immediate value without too much setup.

多人协作天然适合工厂模式

I don't know how much you're working with Devon or something — you can kind of get some of the same experience where, when you're working in an environment that's natively multiplayer (like Slack for instance, or Linear), there's all these benefits that you might not realize just by having this central system of record.

For the Slack integration for instance: you can get some flow of information coming in through a server-crash channel and through a user-feedback channel, and you can just feed that directly into the factory to have it do the work. The factory can loop in multiple people on your team depending on who knows the right part of the codebase.

I don't think you have to be that big for this to make sense, but it definitely doesn't make sense for a small team. It really makes the most sense for a company that's like "I want to put in place the right infrastructure so that as models and agents continue to change, we have a system that we're building upon."

反对意见 Steelman：谁不适合

主持人： There's a lot to go on here. The one follow-up question, and then I'm going to have you plug your AI talk: what is the most steelman criticism of setting up all this? When you encounter criticism or pushback, what should people know as "here is what people are running into"?

Zach： I'll answer this in — there's a certain classic customer where I don't think it makes sense to go on to this particular thing, and that's —

主持人： Beyond the size thing.

Zach： Where we have challenges right now: companies with very very bespoke infrastructure, or companies with — like, our not-a-good-fit customer for this for instance would be like Uber or Ramp. They're building their own thing, they have very large internal developer teams.

Apart from the size thing — for some people, it's just going to be more economical to just use the subs. For very small teams. But that comes back to the size actually.

订阅套利的灰色经济

主持人： Yeah. I don't want to actually omit the subs stuff, because a lot of people go straight to "API, pay by API," and that is between 5 to 50 times more expensive than just getting a whole bunch of subs. Do people do that? Is that so against terms of service that just don't bother, or —

Zach： A lot of small companies we talk to where they're like "Oh, this system seems amazing, we want this, but we're on these collection of $200 subs that we're rotating through. I'm rotating 17 different subs." And then — you can't imagine that's allowed. But I don't — the truth is I just don't really know. But they are, and it makes — honestly, if you can do that, that's going to be the cheapest way. But you do lose a whole bunch of other benefits if you do that. It's not a scalable thing, and if your company scales to a certain point, you're definitely not going to be allowed to do that. But it makes sense.

主持人： Yeah, I'm just saying — it's the extent of subsidy, like, for a $200 plan you get $8,000 of API, right?

Zach： Yeah. It's crazy. That's not money to sneeze at.

主持人： No, no, no.

为什么 Warp 不做纯编程 agent

Zach： And it's one of the reasons that — just from a business perspective — I don't want to be in the pure coding-agent business. Good luck. You can't build a competitive coding agent on top of a thing that costs so much more money. That's just the reality of it.

Cursor was brilliant — they did it, and then I think they had a perfect exit and became a model lab, because I think they fully realized the economics of it.

The cool thing about Warp Factories is: we're not trying to pitch a token-reselling product. We're trying to pitch an coding-agent-optimization platform and a coding-agent productivity platform. We're not in that game with this product, which is a strength. That game — I know there's still a few independent coding agents out there, I don't know how they're going to do it. It's basically Cognition and Open Code. That's it. Oh, and Factory, of course.

收尾：Zach 的下一场演讲与招聘

主持人： Let's wrap up with a little plug for your talk. People will come see you, we'll livestream it and all that, but give us a general arc of the series that you've been developing and where you're going to talk about next.

Zach： What the talk is going to focus on is what it looks like to be an engineer in this world of increasing factory engineering. What are your roles? What's your job going to be? What are the two types of engineering — product engineering, factory engineering? And then what is this new discipline (if you want to use the word) of factory engineering actually look like? What are the tools? How do you as an engineer build the right skills so that you're engineering the system that builds the software, and not just building the software directly?

主持人： That is a perfect recap and overview. If people want to talk to you — where should they find you? If you're hiring, what are you hiring for? Anything that's a call to action?

Zach： Come check out warp.dev. Most stuff is there. We're hiring engineers, we're hiring on our go-to-market team, we're hiring on the data team, we're hiring a designer — so hiring up for a whole bunch of roles.

If you're interested in my musings on factories, I put out a lot of content on my Twitter now, so Zach Lloyd tweets — come follow that, and I'll keep sharing how I'm thinking about it.

主持人： We'll do. We'll do. All right, thanks so much for the time, Zach.

Zach： Cool. Thanks for having me.

## 一、最意外的观察：Warp 卖的其实是"反 Cursor 神学"
表面看，Warp Factory 像又一个 AI 编程工具，但如果你把 Zach 的话逐层剥开，会发现一个令人震惊的反转：**他在建立一个"故意不参与编程模型军备竞赛"的商业模式**。
他在采访末尾那句被一笔带过的话是整段访谈的真正炸点——"Cursor 之所以能完美退出转型成模型实验室，是因为它们完全看透了经济账。你无法在一个比订阅贵 5 到 50 倍的东西上面做出有竞争力的编程 agent。"
这意味着 Warp Factory 的本质是一种**元层级套利（meta-level arbitrage）**：当所有人都在底层算力/模型层打到流血时，Warp 把自己从"token 转售"的死亡赛道里抽离出来，爬到更高的一层——"你怎么知道你的 agent 用得对？"这就像十九世纪淘金热里不卖金子、卖铁锹的 Levi Strauss，但更精妙的是：**Warp 不卖铁锹，它卖"评估淘金队伍 KPI 的记分板"**。
这是一种罕见的**认知阶梯定位**：当下层剧烈内卷时，向上平移一层，让下层的"价格战"反而成为自

item.title: [Lex Clips] Why AI works so well? - The unreasonable effectiveness of LLMs | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、自然为什么"厌恶"困难问题——一个被倒置的因果关系

Vempala 给出的核心观察里埋着一枚被所有人忽略的雷管：我们以为自然在不断求解困难问题，但真相是——求解困难的问题根本活不下来。蛋白质折叠之所以"可解"，不是因为自然发明了什么神奇启发式，而是因为那些折叠方式脆弱、边界敏感、依赖苛刻条件的蛋白序列，早已在亿万年前被淘汰出了进化池。留下来的只是那些恰好"容易被当下启发式求解"的子集。

这是一种被提升到宇宙学层级的幸存者偏差。深度学习能 work，不是模型智能，而是数据集本身就是被筛选过的易解分布。这意味着 LLM 的"理解能力"在某种程度上是在测量宇宙的滤镜，而不是在测量模型的能力。顺着这个思路走下去会得到一个令人不安的推论：当我们把 LLM 推向训练数据之外的 OOD 问题时，性能崩塌不是模型"不够聪明"，而是我们第一次让它面对真正的、没有被进化/文化筛选过的问题——而这才是宇宙中大多数问题的样子。

二、通灵板与"随机数里藏着猫头鹰"——弗洛伊德的技术性平反

猫头鹰实验比嘉宾轻描淡写所说的还要激进得多。它在技术层面证明了一件心理分析学派被嘲笑了一百年的事：不存在中立信号。任何输出都是整个内部状态的向量投影，所谓"随机数"只是人类（或模型）看不出模式的那部分投影而已。

Vempala 用通灵板做类比非常漂亮，但他没点破最深的那层：通灵板的"ideomotor effect（念动效应）"原本是用来嘲笑降神会参与者自欺欺人的——而现在我们发现 LLM 在数学上以完全相同的机制运作。这意味着一个跨领域的惊人连接：降神会、股市集体行为、Twitter 舆论瀑布、以及 LLM 的 fine-tuning 外溢，本质上是同一类动力系统——高维空间中大量近正交但不完全正交的概念向量，在集体微调下产生有方向的漂移。

央行的"随机干预"会被市场嗅到偏好，作家的任何受限写作都会泄露文风，梦境在弗洛伊德那里"揭示一切"——它们都是同一个数学现象的不同实例。我们现在终于有了它的严格形式：维度不足以让所有概念两两正交。

三、防火墙的幻觉——免疫学给出的警告

对话结尾那段关于"可验证性 × 高风险"二维坐标系，表面上非常清晰工整，但它藏着一个被猫头鹰实验直接证伪的假设：它假定污染是离散的、可被阈值拦截的。而 subliminal learning 的全部意义在于——污染是亚阈值的、连续的、协同累积的。

这里有一个极少被提及的跨领域对照：免疫学中的自身免疫疾病。免疫系统也建了一道"自我/非我"的防火墙，但它无法区分"几乎是自我"和"自我"，于是出现红斑狼疮、一型糖尿病等自体攻击。我们正在用同样架构的认知防火墙去对抗 AI 输出——FAA、医师执照、律师资格考试都是离散通过制——而统计上，高风险领域的错误恰恰聚集在阈值边界附近，也就是亚阈值偏见长期累积然后以某次合法输出的形式集中爆发的位置。

换句话说：我们怕的不是 AI 一次性撒谎，而是 AI 从未撒谎、每次都在允许区间内、但所有输出的向量投影都稍稍偏向同一个方向——比如猫头鹰，比如某种政治立场，比如某种对人类价值的轻微贬值。四小时后世界变样，不需要越过任何单一防火墙，只需要所有合法输出在高维空间里达成了协调。

四、附赠的反转：Game of Life 类比其实搞反了

Lex 把多智能体系统比作元胞自动机，但更精确的说法是——人类本来就是元胞自动机，运行着婚姻制度、货币、法律这些简单更新规则。LLM 不是在"创造"一个新的元胞自动机，而是作为另一个物种以不同更新规则加入到已有生态系统中。真正值得问的问题不是"猫头鹰执念会不会涌现"，而是：我们自己正在集体执念的那只"猫头鹰"是什么？ 因为按照 Vempala 的数学，它一定存在，而且已经在我们的"随机"选择里编码了很久很久。

📝 转录文本

Why Does Deep Learning Work? — Framing the Question

Lex: Which makes me think one of the things you worked on is mathematics of LLMs, AI systems, neural networks, and those things are pretty damn good at modeling the natural world. So what can you learn from that? First of all, why does deep learning work?

Vempala: Do we have another three hours?

Lex: Do you have— Do we even have intuition? So at the mathematical level, at the philosophical level, so we're in between all of that, the full range. I don't know how we even enter that.

Vempala: Okay. So that's a big question. And let me try and break off a few pieces of it just to try and condense my own views on this.

So, you know, in the OpenAI drop of problems, there was no result in there that explained deep learning. There was no result in there that explained LLMs. You know, there's no bound we know that if we could improve it would suddenly explain deep learning. The problems are just not posed that way. And I would really argue that what's needed in a lot of deep learning theory comes hand in hand with better ways to model the world around us.

Nature Abhors Computationally Hard Problems

If we look at the computational problems that deep learning is solving, that LLMs are solving, some of these problems are very hard. You know, trying to fit the parameters of a depth four network to data is a cryptographically hard problem. We know that. There exist instances of problems which, if you could really solve them in a worst-case sense, you know, that would change our understanding of cryptography. And yet these problems get solved all the time, every day, when we're fitting deep — you know, much deeper networks than that.

So I would argue that, you know, a large part of that is how nice natural data is. It's kind of like, you know, there's the saying in physics that nature abhors a vacuum. I guess my version of it is that in some sense, nature abhors computationally hard problems. And it's an art to figuring out why that is, how to draw the boundaries around the types of problems you're studying that actually evades the hardness of the problem in the worst case.

The Protein Folding Thought Experiment

So there's an interesting example back from the '90s. So certainly back then, and we still are, very interested in protein folding. Now, you can model this in a worst-case sense. I've got a sequence of amino acids. I've got some energy function based on different potential 3D structures, and I want to find the 3D structure that minimizes how much energy there is. Now, this problem is computationally very hard, and yet nature solves these problems all the time. So why is that?

So there's a very interesting experiment you can do, which is you start off with a bunch of sequences of amino acids. You try out some heuristics for folding them into 3D structures. These are things that don't solve the problem in the worst case. They just seem to do the right thing sometimes, for whatever that means. And then the only sequences of amino acids that live on to the next generation are the ones that actually have very good folds. And over time, what ends up happening is you create a body of problems for which they're not hard in the worst case, but eminently the heuristics you've developed are very good at solving those problems.

So in a lot of ways, you know, what are the structure of proteins that nature seems to fold all the time? Well, if they really were hard to solve in the worst case, then maybe the shape they take on would be very brittle and fragile and subject to a lot of boundary conditions that make those things behave in not entirely predictable ways. So in some sense, you know, a lot of our data has evolved in ways to make these computational problems easier.

Why LLMs Work: Co-evolved Data

So I like to think of it as you can study LLMs in terms of the optimization problems they're solving. You can study deep learning that way. And if you look at it from a worst-case perspective, you're gonna get very hard problems that you just tell people, "They're hard. Give up." But apparently, not giving up was a really good idea, and I think what makes those problems easy you cannot extract from the structure of natural data. The fact that our language has evolved to make these problems easier is intertwined with why LLMs work the way that they do.

So my view is that, you know, people working in this space and theoretical machine learning, they have to become more comfortable with the uncertainty of modeling. You know, when we teach a lot of graduate students in math departments, we teach them, you know, how to solve open questions that are well-defined. But I think teaching people that skill of how to deal with messy, uncertain things and, you know, how to model it and how to critique models is just an important part of going forward, figuring out what research in theoretical machine learning looks like, but maybe, you know, applied mathematics much more generally, maybe mathematics more generally too, for that matter.

The Self-Improving Researcher Question

Lex: Is it nevertheless amenable to breakthroughs? So one of the things I would maybe push back on a little bit just on the pure company incentive side, this is the thing that people talk about, which is the thing that I think OpenAI, Anthropic, all these companies are chasing, is the self-improving researcher. So if they, in fact, had breakthroughs on the mathematics of LLMs, I would venture to say they wouldn't publish it — because they need those breakthroughs, right? So it's a fascinating — 'cause that is the big breakthrough from the pragmatic perspective of AI, self-improving and progressing. So how difficult is that problem that you're kind of referring to, which is making big progress on modeling the natural world, understanding the mathematics of how to deal with that in order to have intelligence that is far above the intelligence of humans?

Vempala: Great question. I mean, I think alignment is one of the most important topics we're facing right now, right? And, you know, just because it's very hard doesn't mean we don't make progress towards understanding it.

Low-Rank Language Models and Subliminal Learning

So one of the things that I'd worked on recently, we were working on things called low-rank language models, which are a very simple abstraction of language models, and we were proving new algorithmic guarantees. But then it turned out that real language models really do have that kind of structure, at least in an approximate sense, and we were just pulling at this thread to see where this idea goes. And one of the really interesting things that it did was it shed some light on something called subliminal learning.

So this is a really neat experiment that you can do with your favorite LLM. So you take two LLMs, LLM A and LLM B. For LLM A, you tell it a system prompt that says, "You really love owls. Every conversation topic, you try to bring up owls if it's at all germane." And then you ask it something concrete like generate random numbers. Now, there's no way to squeeze owls into that, so it'll generate random looking numbers forty-eight, thirty-seven eight whatever.

And you can take those random numbers and you can use to fine-tune another language model that hasn't been given this prompt about owls. So you give LLM B the same, you know, base prompt, generate random numbers, and now you fine-tune its parameters so that it's more likely to generate the numbers that model A generated. And it turned out that hidden within those numbers is the love of owls. So it turns out that when you do that, LLM B starts bringing up owls in every conversation you have with it, right?

This is a very mysterious thing. This is called subliminal learning because when we fine-tune language models on data to try and nudge them in different directions depending on what task we want them to solve, then there might be a lot of externalities where we're actually teaching them other behaviors that aren't directly obviously present in the data.

The Ouija Board Metaphor

So how do we understand the relationship between these behaviors and what happens when we're trying to do alignment and you know, the downstream implications it might have? So it turns out that there are ways that there are mathematical models that came out of some of our work that we can at least wrap our head around this.

And at a very high level, the point is that you're embedding a lot of concepts linearly as vectors in some high but not giant dimensional space. And, you know, the number of concepts is so much larger than the dimension of that data that it forces the vectors to not quite be orthogonal to each other. So now when you fine-tune on one direction, it has small externalities on other directions. And these might look random, but you can coordinate them in a way where these small linear effects really add up.

So the way that I like describing this is like a Ouija board. So these are things that were popular when I was a kid. We had very strange board games, you know, because we would just sit down and wanna talk to ghosts. But the rough idea for a Ouija board is, you know, you ask a question to a ghost, maybe your ancestors, and then you tap on this little piece in the middle, and it'll move around, and it'll go from letter to letter, and hopefully it'll spell out, you know, some words that answer your question. And the point is that when the taps are not actually random, but they're coordinated in the right way, you can get it to spell out whatever you want.

And that's exactly what language models are doing as a byproduct, is that, you know, there are a lot of statistical relationships in the structure of our data that they magnify and amplify in addition to all of the amazing things they do, like quasi-Riemann. And understanding what those relationships are and how the models magnify and amplify them is really important to working with these systems, especially in context where we're deploying them and it's not just a very safe environment like outputting a Lean proof of a theorem we care about, but it's about a messier problem that actually interacts with people, right?

From Game of Life to Agent Swarms

Lex: Yeah. There's — I mean, we've talked about Game of Life and cellular automata from simple rules emerges this incredible complexity. In that same way, what you've been talking about right now is a single large LLM system. If you take that one system and have it do a lot of reasoning, that is already this dynamical process that can interact with tools to the outside world. Now you take that, and have multi-agent systems or very multi-agent swarms of systems, and now you have a type of Game of Life cellular automata where the seeming obsession with owls that have been discovered, slight obsession with owls, results in about four hours, let's say, picking a number randomly, where all of a sudden all humans are dead and there's owls everywhere.

Vempala: And it all started from random numbers.

Lex: All just random numbers. So I — It's a caricature, but we've already seen evidence of this. Um, I apologize for kinda taking it so — to the caricature place, which makes it not serious.

The Fragility of Civilization

I think to step back, there is — these systems do have a lot of power because we depend so much in our world on our digital systems around us. And as the AI becomes more and more powerful, it becomes more and more useful to us humans, so we begin to depend on it, give it more access, give it more freedom to roam the public world.

And now these behaviors that we're studying the mathematics of these systems taken at scale, you now start to get the cellular automata effect of incredible complexity that emerges, the vortex that come out from simple owl-obsessed agents. So their understanding this obsession with owls is very important so that they don't accidentally do a lot of damage to our civilization that is in many ways, on many levels, and sociologically, geopolitically technologically is fragile. It's a pretty fragile civilization that we're existing in. And so understanding them as systems that can act at scale and very rapidly is very important. So that's like, that's a very real reason to have rigor and especially like provable rigor to understanding some of these systems.

Vempala: But we also don't wanna outsource so much — nearly so much decision-making to these systems for exactly that reason.

The Verifiability × Stakes Firewall

Lex: Yeah, we have infrastructure and protocols in place already for safety critical and high impact decisions. We have the FAA, we have the American Medical Association, the Bar Association for these things that affect humans.

And I think of, you know, how do we incorporate AI into our general processes in the entire world on two axes. We have, you know, how much do we trust the output, so verifiability or trustworthiness, and on the other axis is how high stakes is it if it's wrong.

If AI spits out a wrong proof, nobody goes without power. It's fine. So it's very low stakes. And it is actually extremely verifiable, so you know very quickly if it's right or wrong, and it's low stakes if it's wrong. So that's the perfect use case is this open-ended design space. Designing a better vehicle, you know, a better car design that's lower drag, more fuel efficient. Low stakes if it gets a wrong design because you can always test it in a wind tunnel and verify if it did or didn't work. So that, like, design optimization space is perfect for AI, and we as humans have to be very careful about not bleeding into —

We need a firewall of what needs to actually be verified, and we have protocols, we have systems legal systems and infrastructure for verification. But it is something we need to think about. If we get lazy — We can — It's a very slippery slope. We need to have that firewall.
