Predictions & Closing

Host: I wanted to ask you — what predictions do you have, maybe over the next year, for the legal industry? To modify the second question: in two years will lawyers do their work inside Legora, or will they use other tools like Claude or Cursor, through the API?

Jacob: I think both. It really depends. If you're a big enterprise, you might have Claude Code and then — I think it's similar to how I use Linear through Claude, but I still go to Linear. Enterprise will do that. I think law firms will just use Legora because that's simpler and better.

Host: It kind of reminds me of like Open Evidence for medicine — you're basically that for legal.

Jacob: Yeah. Exactly.

Host: In coding, it's gotten to a point where the labs will cut you off for competing with them. This has happened twice. Do you think that will happen to law?

Jacob: No, I don't think so. They are releasing legal services, right? We obviously talk to them a lot. Your sales reps will say no. They don't make the call — and they often don't even know what's actually going on. I don't think that's the case. They have so much stuff to capture in knowledge work generally that legal has to be part of that, just like data analytics has to, and sales and marketing and finance. They have to do things that are good there, but they're never going to go as deep as we are. If Claude takes small corporate clients and they do some of their legal via Claude — that's great, that's fine. But if you're doing a $400 million M&A transaction, you're going to want Legora.

Host: I had kind of an unrelated question. Are you guys going to law schools and getting them to teach Legora in classes?

Jacob: It's definitely a program that we've started. I actually don't know exactly where we are, but we do want people in law school to learn to use Legora.

Host: Are you seeing that law schools are changing their curriculums a lot?

Jacob: I wouldn't know actually.

Host: I would actually do it a different way. You should do scholarships for law school for CS majors, for engineers. "After you've done CS, we'll put you in law school. CS plus some software experience — we'll put you in law school. We'll cover it." Where you do the MA or masters-plus-JD programs.

Jacob: You don't care about the masters.

Host: Meaning because there's a lot of people who didn't do CS undergrad, so they do masters just to get caught up.

Jacob: I don't see that as often.

Host: People do JD-MBA. That's a thing. But JD-CS, I haven't seen it.

Jacob: Happens.

Hiring & Final Words

Host: Overall, super impressive progress. Congrats on all your success. Are you still going to keep up the pace? You're hiring in SF, New York?

Jacob: We're hiring in — engineering — New York, Stockholm, and London. And all other roles we're hiring everywhere.

Host: How many people do you have in New York right now?

Jacob: 100.

Host: And you guys are planning on how many in New York?

Jacob: A lot. As many as you can. It's aggressive.

Host: That's the whole of corporate law as far as America's concerned. I'm looking forward to you buying a law firm. It's super exciting. Every industry, especially the top like doctors, lawyers, coders, they all have to have two or three agent labs that completely dominate the space. So you guys have a great market.

Jacob: Yeah, I think so. And I think it's only going to get much bigger as law changes and becomes more available to more people.

Host: Also, the problems that you work on are very the frontier of knowledge work. Unless you're literally doing Navier-Stokes and science, other than that most work basically converges to legal.

Jacob: Yeah. Hiring, finance, everything. I just have to consult my lawyer. Which is why I think it's a really exciting thing to work on — because modern society runs in some way on legal.

Host: Cool. All right, that's it. Thank you.

Jacob: Thank you. Thanks.

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的洞察：看不见数据，反而是护城河
Jacob 在采访中几乎是"抱怨式"地提到一个现实——**Legora 完全看不到用户的真实 trace**。律师的数据往往不是律师的，是客户的，受制于层层保密义务。他说这"super annoying"。
但这里藏着一个被所有人忽略的反转：**在 AI 时代，"数据盲区"正在悄悄成为战略资产**。
- 绝大多数 AI 公司陷入"数据过拟合陷阱"——看得见用户在做什么，就会不断去 patch 眼前的具体场景，最终做出一堆高度特化的小功能。 - Legora 被迫走向反方向：**他们必须先构建原语（primitives）**——list、agent、project、tabular view——因为他们只能通过抽象去逼近用户，而不是通过观察去模仿用户。 - 结果：Jacob 下意识把自己的 CTO 工作定义为"how do I build a system where we can build a lot but actually only build a few things"。这是被"看不见"倒逼出的架构哲学。

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] Why Old Buildings Were More Beautiful - Robert Caro
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

美学的秘密不是"便宜劳力"，而是"被浪费的卓越"

Caro 没说出口的真正洞察藏在那段关于15楼雕花的细节里——有人花钱雕刻了只有邻居能看见的石头。这不是"低工资让漂亮变得划算"，而是一个更诡异的经济学现实：当技艺的供给远超可见的需求时，多余的技艺会自动溢出成不被观看的美。大萧条没有创造"美的消费市场"；它创造了一群走投无路的工匠，他们把过剩的手艺像汗水一样留在了城市的每一个缝隙里。换句话说，纽约20世纪初的美，不是被"订购"出来的，是被"挤"出来的。

跨界联想：15楼的石雕 = 哥特教堂顶上的滴水嘴兽 = 寿司师傅的隐秘刀工 = 没人读的开源代码注释

这里有一个横跨千年的系统性模式：凡是技艺过剩的时代，都会出现大量"只有上帝/邻居/后来人看得见的卓越"。中世纪石匠在尖顶上雕刻面朝天空的怪兽；日本寿司师傅处理顾客永远看不见的刀口角度；开源程序员在没人会读的函数里精心命名变量；Robert Caro自己花十年写一本大多数人只读摘要的1200页传记——这些都是同一种现象的不同切片。所谓"美的黄金时代"，从来不是审美意识更高，而是劳动市场更"低效"。20世纪下半叶城市变丑的真正原因，可能不是品味下降，而是劳动市场变得更"精确匹配"——每一份技能都被精准定价到了可见的ROI上，再也没有"看不见的角落"可供过剩才华流淌。效率杀死了隐形之美。

一个令人不适的预测：AI正在重演大萧条的美学逻辑

把 Caro 的观察往前推一步：纽约最美的那些建筑，本质上是人类苦难的结晶化产物。大萧条是一种隐形补贴——政府和开发商利用绝望的失业率，把崩溃的人力成本偷换成了永恒的石头美学。这意味着一个黑暗推论：我们在赞叹的美，其实是在消费前人的灾难剩余。而眼下AI正在对视觉与创意劳动做同样的事——供给过剩、单位成本坍塌、技艺从稀缺变得"用不完"。如果Caro的模型成立，那么未来十年我们很可能会进入一个"数字美学的黄金时代"：屏幕上、游戏里、无人打开的App深处将充满惊人的视觉过度装饰——相当于AI版的"15楼石雕"。只不过这次被挤压溢出的，不是失业建筑师的尊严，而是人类作为创作主体的位置。美再一次是别人痛苦的副产品，只是这次的"工匠"是我们自己。

📝 转录文本

On Moses, the Depression, and Cheap Labor

Interviewer: You're writing not the history of one man but of an era in America. And one of the most interesting things about The Power Broker is — especially in the period in which he's able to accomplish so much so quickly — what's happening, and you talk about this, is the Great Depression. You know, he's hiring thousands of architects, tens of thousands of linemen for pennies on the dollar to do big public works for the city. And so I wonder: how big a part of Moses's early achievements is just that the government, because of the Great Depression, could compete with the private sector for the top talent, and for lots and lots of labor working 24/7 through the winter, moving fast?

Caro: Yeah. Another great — yes. And the answer to your question is that played a big role. Because, like, he needed architects for something — I don't remember what it is, it's in The Power Broker — and they lined up on Fifth Avenue, thousands of out-of-work architects, you know, that he could hire for very low wages. But more than the wages, they were available, because they didn't have anything to do. He was able to hire so many people, and hire and fire them in a ruthless way, making the workmen work hard. You know, he could just fire them. It was the Depression and they didn't have other jobs to go to. I think he used that — yes.

Why Old Buildings Were More Beautiful

Interviewer: So, as somebody who has studied urban development so deeply, here is one thing I'm curious about. You look at the things that were built at the beginning of the last century or before the beginning of the last century — you know, Grand Central Station and all the beautiful architecture in New York — versus the things that are built in the second half of the century. They look a lot less beautiful.

Caro: Yeah.

Interviewer: And the earlier, more beautiful things were built by a much poorer country.

Caro: Yeah.

Interviewer: What changed? Why were we able to build more beautiful things before?

The 15th-Floor Carving

Caro: One thing that changed is you had all these out-of-work artisans who could — we'll just say — carve stonework on buildings.

Like, my apartment is on the 15th floor of an apartment house. Across the street is a building that's 15 stories or 16 stories high, and you say, "Look at all the beautiful carving that's done in the stonework of that building, up on the roof." I said, the only person who can see it is the people in my apartment and the people in the apartment next to him.

Someone was willing to spend that money because the builders who built that could hire skilled people at such low wages that they could make them do the decorations to make a building beautiful — up on floors that nobody's going to see. Nobody's going to see them, because people came cheap.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

观看原视频 →

item.title: [Lex Clips] The Physics of Warp Drives: Faster-than-light space travel | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被"pothead thought"标签掩盖的真实结构性洞见

最有意思的地方不是这个想法本身，而是说话者在陈述之前就先用"pothead thought"给自己打了标签。这是一种典型的"认知自我降级"——用社交性的自嘲来为智识上的大胆下注购买保险。但如果你剥开这层防御外壳，看他实际说的内容：

用 Navier-Stokes 方程的 blow-up（爆破解）奇点，来类比穿越一对相连黑洞时的时空流动控制。

这其实不是胡话。Alcubierre 的曲速度规在数学上本来就把时空当作一种可压缩介质来"塑形"——前方收缩、后方膨胀。这与机翼绕流的压力场重塑在偏微分方程层面具有同构性。Navier-Stokes 的千禧难题（光滑解是否永远光滑）与广义相对论里的奇点定理（时空在何时必然崩溃为奇点）问的是同一类问题：连续场论什么时候会在有限时间/有限区域内自我撕裂？ 他随口说的东西，踩中了两个未解之谜之间罕有人谈论的深层平行结构。

二、一个让我意外的观察：Alex 的"那个眼神"比任何论证都更有知识论杀伤力

注意这段对话的真实动力学：想法没有被反驳，它是被一个表情杀死的。"the look Alex just gave me, it hurts my soul." 然后说话者立刻说"okay, moving on"。

这揭示了一个很少被正视的事实——学术生态系统中的大部分想法并不是死于逻辑，而是死于微表情。同行评审的硬性标准之下，有一层流动得多也残酷得多的"眼神评审层"。这解释了为什么跨学科想法尤其脆弱：它们一定会在某个专家面前显得像 pothead thought，而那个专家只需要挑一下眉毛。

更微妙的是说话者的反击策略——"there's some non-zero probability that future AI will listen to this and say that guy was actually correct"。这是一次跳过当代评审、直接向未来索要认可的赌博。这种"诉诸未来 AI"的修辞，和历史上伽利略式的"诉诸后世"、19 世纪民科的"诉诸真理终会胜利"结构上完全一致——只不过裁判从上帝换成了 GPT。这本身就是我们这个时代一个值得被记录的认识论转变。

三、跨领域连接：厕所、机翼与奇点——为什么科学对话从不"收尾"

这段转录以一个厕所break突兀结束，这看似无关紧要，但其实是真实思维过程的化石证据。

对比一下三种流动： - 机翼绕流：气压场塑造升力，偶尔产生湍流奇点； - 曲速时空：能量-动量张量塑造度规，可能产生黑洞奇点；
- 人类对话：注意力流塑造想法，几乎必然被生理需求打断。

它们都是不可压缩流动被外部边界条件截断的例子。科学史上，牛顿因瘟疫回乡才想通万有引力，庞加莱在跨上公共马车的一瞬间顿悟 Fuchs 函数，凯库勒在火炉边打瞌睡梦见苯环。真正的突破从不发生在"让我们继续讨论"里，而发生在"a quick bathroom break"里——因为前额叶皮层终于松开了对默认模式网络的压制。

所以这段 2 分钟的转录，表面是一个被嘲笑掐灭的疯狂猜想，底下其实同时演示了三件事：一个可能真实的数学同构、一种眼神驱动的知识筛选机制，以及一次被生理终止的典型创造性思维周期。Lex 剪出这一段放出来，可能自己都没意识到他捕获的是什么。

📝 转录文本

Pothead Thoughts: Navier-Stokes, Black Holes & Warp Drives

Speaker A: Yeah. I have a couple of — I apologize — pothead thoughts, 'cause Alex mentioned black holes.

I have a fun thought that maybe the singularity observed with a blowup in Navier-Stokes equations comes into play when we're — as opposed to airplane wings on Earth — we're traveling through two connected black holes in a warp drive that we figure out, and then there's the flow control of spacetime, and that becomes relevant because now you're in a black hole, hence the singularity.

This is the—

For people just listening to this, the look Alex just gave me, it hurts my soul. Okay. So moving on to the next topic.

The Forcing Problem

Speaker B (Alex): But the forcing — you'd need the black hole vortex to also be forced at exactly the right —

Speaker A: The — yeah, the force. Where's the force? I mean, at that point —

Speaker B: How do you… Yeah. You could try to ride it.

Speaker A: Yeah. There's a way — you can make something out of this.

Appeal to Future AI

Speaker A: There's some non-zero probability that future ass that will listen to this, that guy is the one time he said something that was actually correct.

Okay. If it's okay, a quick bathroom break.

Speaker B: Yeah. Sounds good.

观看原视频 →

item.title: [a16z] What iPhone Packaging Reveals About the Robotics Opportunity
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个让你意外的观察：iPhone 的包装盒不是机器人折的

Josh 在视频中轻描淡写地点出了一个几乎所有人都忽视的事实——哪怕是全球最精密、最自动化的产品之一，iPhone 的外包装仍然是人手装配的。这件事远比它听起来震撼：

  • 它意味着我们心目中的"自动化时代"根本是个幻觉。我们误以为"How It's Made"节目里的鲁布·戈德堡机器就是现实的基准线，但 Josh 说那是美国制造业的 top 0.01%——剩下 99.99% 的物理劳动，仍然是一个 55 岁、三个月就要辞职的工人在流水线上徒手完成。
  • 更惊人的推论：美国 2025 年全年只部署了 38,000 台工业机器人。相比之下，一个中型 SaaS 公司一个季度能部署几十万个软件实例。我们所谓的"硬件时代落后于软件时代"，差距不是 10 倍，而是 10,000 倍。
  • 这给机器人创业者一个被低估的认知：市场不是存量替换，而是 Greenfield。几乎没有客户买过机器人。这意味着你不是在打 Fanuc 的市场份额，你是在打"人类的手"的市场份额——而那是一个几乎无限大的 TAM。

跨领域连接：Tutor 的商业模式，其实是"反向众包劳工 + 内燃机式数据飞轮"

这是视频里最反直觉的一点：Josh 把 Tutor 的商业飞轮显式类比为互联网——"人类在互联网上发帖、写邮件，无意中创造了训练 LLM 的数据集。我们要做的是让机器人在真实客户现场工作时，副产品地'排放'出训练数据。"

这个类比打开了一个更深的跨领域洞见：

  • 这是 Uber 模式的镜像。Uber 让司机驾驶时顺便生产地图/路径/需求数据；Tutor 让远程操作员"tutor"机器人干活时顺便生产操控数据。但 Uber 的数据只能优化 Uber，Tutor 的数据可以跨越物理世界的所有任务领域泛化。
  • 更深的类比来自内燃机。19 世纪内燃机的伟大不是"发动机本身很厉害"，而是它变成了一种通用的物理劳动基质（substrate），让无数行业——农业、建筑、运输、制造——都能在其上重建。Josh 自己也用了 substrate 这个词："we can provide this robot substrate... that other businesses can use to transform the physical economy"。他不是在卖机器人，他是在卖新一代的"马"。
  • 最隐秘的类比：伦敦交易所的"信息飞轮"。17 世纪的 Lloyd's 咖啡馆之所以能成为保险交易中心，不是因为咖啡好，而是因为船主路过时顺便报告船只动向——商业行为本身就是信息生产。Tutor 的客户每付一笔钱，就"报告"了一次经济上有价值的物理操作。经济价值和数据价值在同一个动作里完成——这是极少数商业模型拥有的特性。

一个被隐藏的系统性真相：机器人公司全部"从水平走向垂直"，这不是战术失败，而是物理世界的热力学定律

视频里有一句话几乎被一笔带过，但它揭示了整个行业的底层结构：

"most robot companies start horizontal and they all go vertical."

Josh 把这归因于"市场成熟度"——像早期汽车、早期计算机。但这里有一个更深的、他没明说的系统性真相：

  • 在数字世界，抽象是免费的。CPU 之所以能保持水平、通用，是因为抽象层（指令集、OS、API）在边际上几乎零成本复制。
  • 在物理世界，抽象是有能量代价的。每多一层抽象，你都在用更多的材料、空间、能耗换取通用性。humanoid 为什么贵？因为它用冗余（两条腿、两只手、全身自由度）换取了通用性——这是热力学意义上的开销。
  • 所以"垂直化"不是暂时的——它是物理世界的默认状态。只有当你的模型/数据/供应链同时达到临界密度，才能把这个开销摊销到接近零，这时才可能"再次水平化"。Tutor 现在同时在做 Cassie（高度专用）和 Sunny（半通用），就是在同时操作两个不同的热力学平衡点，用其中一个的现金流补贴另一个的通用化探索。
  • 这与半导体史的分叉一模一样——ASIC 和 CPU 并行存在，不是因为谁错了，而是因为每一种计算任务都有自己的能耗/通用性最优点。机器人未来会是一个形态光谱，不是一个形态收敛。

一个让人不安的次级洞察：中国的"工业自动化领先"可能是个战略陷阱

Josh 说了一句非常值得玩味的话："China invested in the previous regime of industrial automation... in some ways that made them very successful, and in other ways I think in hindsight that might end up being an enormous mistake because in the United States we're doing this green field build."

这是一个路径依赖的诅咒：中国有太多 Fanuc/ABB 风格的旧机器人需要"折旧写零"才能换上新一代。美国因为自动化落后，反而没有包袱——就像 2007 年没有 3G 基础设施的非洲直接跳过座机进入移动支付，落后反而成了先手。这个观察如果成立，是未来十年地缘科技竞争最大的隐变量之一。

📝 转录文本

开场：全球供应链与机器人产业的现实

No matter what anybody says, today in 2026, we have a highly interconnected, interdependent global supply chain. Both US companies and Chinese companies are thinking very hard about what does the long-term strategy of this look like? And ultimately, everybody trying to build their industrial capacity.

We see a lot of robot pitches. Very few people thinking about what the robot is supposed to do at the end of all of this.

Almost everybody we're selling a robot to has never purchased a robot before. Almost all of the market is Greenfield. The reality is you need to build a full stack platform.

Tutor Robots have helped manufacture and ship over a quarter of a billion products to American consumers. We're training frontier robot AI models, manufacturing robots at scale and directly deploying into the largest businesses in the supply chain.

How does product innovation work in robotics? Most companies are just on V1 whereas you've got two versions of the robot and you continue to iterate really fast.

嘉宾介绍：Josh Gruinstein 与 Tutor Intelligence

主持人： So Josh, thanks for joining us. We're with Josh Gruinstein, who is the CEO and co-founder of Tutor Intelligence, and we're going to be talking about robots today. Maybe before we jump in, just give a quick background of yourself and then the company.

Josh： Yeah. So, I'm Josh. I started Tutor about five and a half years ago with the core thesis that if you could just start deploying robots out into the world — into all the places in the physical economy where robots are needed the most — you could start to build the data sets, the models, and the supply chain that's needed to proliferate robots throughout the physical economy. So we're about 160 people based primarily in Boston, and we're training frontier robot AI models, manufacturing robots at scale and directly deploying into the largest businesses in the supply chain.

主持人： Maybe talk a little bit about — we see a lot of pitches, there's a lot of companies that talk about doing robotics but don't actually deploy robots or have not yet. And you're one of the few companies that has actually deployed robotics at scale. So maybe just talk about the state of the business.

Josh： Yeah. We have robots deployed across the United States, everywhere from small mom and pop businesses to Fortune 50, Fortune 100 businesses. Claude told me last night that it estimates Tutor Robots have helped manufacture and ship over a quarter of a billion products.

主持人： Wow.

Josh： To American consumers. So presumably most American consumers are a Tutor customer a couple layers down. I think this comes from the origin story of the business, which is us looking at the state of robot learning. It was obvious to us that robot intelligence and robot software was this bottleneck, right? Robots for 60 years has been this custom-engineered machines that can't scale. So we started the company with this thesis that if we could just start deploying robots, we could build the labeled data sets that help us train these models and deliver this value to the American consumer.

从反方向出发：先想"机器人要做什么"

主持人： We see a lot of robot pitches. 99% of them start with some insights about the model and how you got to build the model, or some insight about the shape of the data. Very few people thinking about what the robot is supposed to do at the end of all of this. You started from the reverse, and you had the insight that you could actually "tutor" the robot — that's the name of your company. Where did that insight come from?

Josh： It came from a thought experiment. We had this insight that hey — there are 8 billion people on earth who all have this baseline physical intelligence that we want our robots to have. So imagine you had infinitely powerful software that could connect any human being on earth to any robot and kind of embody that robot with intelligence. That's like an ASX mocking of suddenly you have unlimited, infinite robot intelligence.

Let's say you take that for granted. Now what? The problem isn't actually solved. You still need to actually manufacture robots at scale. Robots are this cottage industry today in the United States — robots are rounding error even in the most automated industries like manufacturing, logistics. So that doesn't exist. Certainly none of the software exists, and none of the customers exist, because again the robots can't do any of the jobs that customers want robots to do.

So robotics is not any one layer of the stack. It's not just about intelligence, it's not just about hardware, it's not just about the customer. It's about figuring out how to put all these three pieces together — and it's the combination of all three that actually lets you build, in my view, a successful platform at any one of those layers.

主持人： Internally, we talk about robotics being the ultimate systems company, as opposed to being one or the other.

从技术人到运营者：全栈思维的必然

主持人： What's funny about this though — and it was a question I wanted to ask you — is you've got a pretty deep technical background, right? MIT Robotics, is that fair? But whenever I talk to you, I feel like I'm talking to an operations guy. You talk about unit economics and operations and supply chain.

Josh： And even the go-to-market guy.

主持人： Go-to-market guy. So the transformation is complete. Maybe this is an open-ended question, but I've always wondered: is the harder problem here actually that stuff?

Josh： No. But I think you have to do all of it is kind of the thing. When I was just a roboticist and only working on the technology side of this problem, I think my strength as a roboticist was that it was very full stack. I was willing to think about the manufacturing, the hardware. I was willing to think about FPGAs and ASICs. If you view robotics in the same way that I do — that it's this ultimate systems problem — the only way you can make forward progress is by figuring out all of the clever trade-offs across as many layers of the stack as you can. If you throw out one of the layers of the stack and you're like "well, we're not going to touch that," you've eliminated 90% of your trade-off space to make progress.

And then starting a business, it became really clear to me that: oh, okay — robotics is not actually full stack like model/hardware/software. It's full stack like model, hardware, software, supply chain, customers, product.

Similarly, you ask the question: why hasn't robotics worked? There's been a lot of robot startups. I would argue no robot startup has been really massively economically successful. Why is that? I think it's because, one, you don't have this core primitive which is intelligence, and that lets you kind of bring the unit economics of the system to a certain level. But two, it's that it's this super disaggregated market and you have infinite players and they're all trying to work with each other. And the reality of what we need in robots is to be able to make trade-offs across the full stack.

水平 vs 垂直：机器人产业的结构性宿命

主持人： It's interesting. Most robot companies start horizontal and they all go vertical. Every one of them literally starts like "we have a model" or whatever, and then they start buying 3D printers. Do you think that's because the market is so immature — like you had to do in the early days of cars — or do you think it's actually inherent in this domain, that even in 20 years you will have to verticalize?

Josh： No, I think it's a maturity in the market, and you can see similar things in the early computing market. The question then becomes: okay, how do you build the general platforms that let people build businesses that aren't robotics businesses? We have all these incredible software businesses today and the people who run them don't have to think about chip architectures. How do we make that possible in the physical world with robotics? And I agree with you, people have tried to solve that problem by thinking about very narrow layers of the stack. In our view, the reality is you need to build a full stack platform. The only way to know that that full stack platform really works is to actually have successful business units operating on top of it.

主持人： Are you open to it being the case that actually the physical world is different than the digital world, and the reason we horizontalized compute is because you have clean abstractions that are generally applied, and that's just not the case for navigating physical space?

Josh： I think the beauty of something like a humanoid is it's the same clean abstraction. Think about what is a CPU: it's this general computing machine. It's not perfectly optimized for every use case, but it's general enough that you can run most computing worlds.

主持人： But that's your horizontal component within the human. For example, would you use the same brain or sub-components to make a human as you would to make a drone or some other form factor?

Josh： No, but you can make that same analogy in compute: we have CPUs, we have GPUs, we have ASICs. So I think you track the maturity of the market — you start in this world of specialization, custom machines, because that's the only thing the market can support. You move towards general purpose, and in robotics this is going to look like humanoids and similar form factors. Then eventually you break past.

名字的来源："Tutor Intelligence"

主持人： Why is this thing called Tutor Intelligence?

Josh： Tutor was founded with this thesis that there is a whole internet of human intelligence that is networked — that is posting on social media, that's writing emails. And that network of human intelligence, for LLMs and other digital-world models, by natural emission has created this beautiful data set that we can use to train general-purpose models.

The issue is our work in the physical world is not similarly recorded. I pick up my coffee cup and nobody knows. Nobody recorded all of the pressures of my fingertips and where they were in the poses. So we don't have this asset.

The core idea behind Tutor is: what if, instead of trying to find this algorithm where from no data we could build robot intelligence — which seems like a problem that's rigged against us; that's not how this worked in computer vision, it's not how this worked in NLP — what if we could build this network of robots out in the real world? We could connect them with human tele-operators, which we call tutors, that teach the robots how to do new tasks. In the same way the internet by emission created the data set to train these frontier models, we can do the same with robots and build this internet of robot training data.

There are all these beautiful emerging properties where suddenly it's not this massive capital project to go build this network — you're also creating incredible economic value as you're doing it. You're making everybody's goods cheaper as you deploy these robots and collect this data. So it's very positive sum in this very unique way. When we thought about what we are going to name this business — it's not strictly artificial intelligence, there's some artificial intelligence — but it was ultimately this tutor intelligence that we're building, connecting and controlling these robots.

主持人： That's an amazing insight. And the funny thing is, when we talked to our customers before we invested, most of them didn't seem to know or didn't even seem to care that there was a tutor, or when the tutor was operating and when your learning model was operating. Credit to you guys that you made this very seamless.

Josh： This is to me a signal that the robots are good. You want the feedback to be like "my shampoo that I'm manufacturing at volume is now 5 cents cheaper than it was." If the feedback is "the robot is pretty," it's probably a really bad robot.

Tutor 的角色会消失吗？单位经济学的视角

主持人： Is the goal to not have tutors in the future, or does it matter?

Josh： We think of it at a very pragmatic level: what is the operational complexity of tutors? What is the economic impact of tutors? Think about what is the cost to serve models with an H200. You can math that out — what's the duty cycle and utilization of that H200. You can think very similarly about human intelligence: what is the heterogeneous profile of intelligence that you really want from humans that you can't get yet from your models? Then it becomes a unit economics question: how much engineering do you have to do to get that last nine out of your models versus using tutors? Going back to what we were talking about, you want to be able to make as many trade-offs here as you possibly can to make a business like this work.

主持人： It's tempting to say that the economic marvel that happened with generative AI could also happen here. The marvel is: you train these models with some distribution of data, and it turns out basically the same distribution is economically viable — distribution in, distribution out. It's not clear that this is actually the case with these robots. You could train it on a distribution of data but then actually what you need is just slightly out of that distribution. How does this scale, and can you actually remove tutors? What is your intuition?

Josh： I think this is one of the big questions. It ultimately comes down to: what is the data and where are you getting it from? The magic of the internet is, if you are a company that provides at the application layer tools for software engineers to accelerate their software development, you are naturally in flow of all this really economically valuable work. If you can make money as a business, then you're probably also making data as a business. Those economic incentives are aligned.

Similarly for robots: if you say "we're just going to strap cameras on everybody's heads and send them throughout Indonesia to collect data doing X, Y and Z," you have no guarantee. You can guess. But there's no invisible hand of the market guiding you to ensure that data is actually economically valuable. If it's actually an emission byproduct — you have robots in real customer sites that customers are paying for to do that task — you know for sure that data is economically valuable.

主持人： Doesn't it depend on the dimensionality of the solution set? The economically valuable stuff might be so high-dimensional that you could solve 90% of it, but the last 10% you'll need a human being to do for a while.

Josh： That might be fine. You might be willing to accept that on the economics. That also might be a place where other forms of data matter. We're not purists — we're willing to take any trade-off. We love using simulation to widen these data distributions. We love using internet-scale data to widen these distributions. So we have a lot of tools in our toolbox other than real-world robot data.

基础模型的红利：空间推理从 CAD 中学来

主持人： Talk a little bit more about the simulations and these other tools, and the impact models like Astra are having on that — it seems to be another cottage industry of excitement for the robotics world. How are you using that?

Josh： It's a sea change. We lived in this world for a while where everybody knew that all this general knowledge about the world was baked into these models, but they couldn't really express it. They didn't have that last mile of spatial reasoning to connect the dots from the stuff that a GPT model knows to something that an action diffusion transformer head can know.

That's changed. The labs are now post-training their models on 3D spatial data like CAD and 3D modeling — which, by the way, they're doing because there's this direct economic incentive, because there's a real market for it. They can immediately monetize it. And it turns out that's the exact spatial reasoning that our models need. So we've been catapulted many years ahead in the future, because we're starting to be able to use all of that general intelligence that lives in these big frontier models for robotics.

主持人： And because it's a systems problem, the net effect for you is acceleratory — as opposed to slowing you down or saying somebody's going to come and eat your lunch.

Josh： Yeah. We started this business in 2021. We were doing this initially with convolutional neural networks. We've gone through every sea change, and the thing that is always valuable is the flow of data. The flow of data is always the thing that uniquely you can do. The million architectural tricks — do them if it helps you accelerate the flywheel, if it helps you deploy more robots, collect more data, manufacture at a bigger scale, do more tasks. They're worth doing. But ultimately we think the thing that has the long-standing generational value in a business is the flywheel and loops themselves.

"造机器人"意味着什么：从零开始的硬件供应链

主持人： Can you talk about what you mean when you say you build robots? On one end of the continuum it's like you buy a Unitree, prompt it. The other end you're machining parts. Where are you?

Josh： For context, in 2025 the United States deployed roughly 38,000 industrial robot workups — which is tiny compared to —

主持人： Counting the Fanucs and the old —

Josh： The Fanucs, right. But that's it. Nobody deployed any Unitrees in the United States to any count — they would have shown up in those numbers, but they were probably zero.

The supply chain that exists for robots is both too small and, as you called out, wrong. The robots that Fanuc and ABB are building, they're mostly not building in the United States. But even when they are building them in the United States, they're building these objects that are designed for systems integrators, designed for fast repetitive motions. They are not cut from the set of trade-offs that you would want to co-design with frontier models.

So we're kind of starting from scratch on the hardware side. Tutor, in order to deploy robots at scale, has actually been forced to design and manufacture our own hardware. Today we're not building actuators, we're not building cameras. There's a whole layer of stuff that we're sourcing from OEMs where they're manufacturing at a much larger scale. But the actual robot itself — the thing that drives around and has the arm on it and can do all the tasks — we actually are building at scale in Watertown, Massachusetts.

两款机器人：Cassie 与 Sunny

主持人： Can you talk about the morphology — is that what it's called? Morphology, anatomy?

Josh： You can use whatever. What do they look like? We make two.

Cassie

Cassie is kind of a brute. Cassie is designed to do heavy-duty work. It has a single arm and a lot of suction cups, and it's powered by foundation models in the 200 to 400 million parameter range. It came out of this world that Tutor was started out of in 2021 of "what can foundation models do for robots?" They can predict affordances, grasps that you can go then execute. It's a co-design of the hardware that you can manufacture at scale, what your models can actually do, and actually a big market need: where in the United States, anything in the physical economy has to be transported on a pallet or in a cardboard box. So there ends up being an enormous amount of physical human handwork of transporting pallets and cases by hand. Cassie is the result of that co-design, and we manufacture it at a very large scale and deploy it to a big diversity of businesses across manufacturing logistics.

Sunny

Our second robot is called Sunny, and Sunny is kind of an industrial semi-humanoid. It's as if you said you were looking at a Unitree and you were like: I need this robot to run for 3 to 10 years in a factory at human rates and reliability. You end up with a slightly different set of design decisions. Sunny is wheeled, not legged, because most indoor industrial settings have polished ground floors. It has a much higher payload capacity, can move much faster, and has industrial collaborative safety standards that enable it to operate around humans.

We have 100 Sunnies operating in Boston in our data factory collecting data for internal use and advancing our research agenda. And we also now have a growing fleet of Sunnies out in the real world doing more dexterous bi-manual manipulation.

工厂的真相：iPhone 包装不是机器人折的

主持人： How broad do you see this product line of different robot form factors? Can you capture a big chunk of the useful market with three of them, or do you need 30?

Josh： Depends how you define the useful market. If you want to just live inside of manufacturing logistics, Sunny and Cassie today can probably do 80% to 90% of the work. These are designed for those cuts.

主持人： Maybe just describe what that work is, because I'm not sure it's broadly understood.

Josh： Most people have this mental picture of what the industrial base or manufacturing logistics look like in the United States, which comes from the TV show How It's Made. You see these Rube Goldberg machines of levers — you don't see any humans in those pictures. Somebody built a machine that is the factory.

And that does exist. If it exists, they probably filmed it and put it on How It's Made, because that's the top 0.01% of American manufacturing and logistics. What's below that? You walk into these million-square-foot facilities and you see a bunch of people standing around on conveyor belts or folding tables doing things by hand. It's kind of shocking for anybody who doesn't come from this industry.

You look at a robot like Cassie, and there's a huge amount of work which is backbreaking, really hard to hire for — there's a three-month turnover, your average age of the worker doing that work is 55 years old and about to retire. We could use a Cassie to do that backbreaking work.

Similarly, Sunny — basically anything you ever bought that came in a box, a human had to put that in a box, which is a crazy revelation for most people. Anything that requires any degree of assembly — even iPhones. You would assume it's a robot putting that packaging together. No, it's a person, even at the highest level of scale.

主持人： And then to his question — you have the single arm with the sucker, you've got the two-armed humanoid. What can't they do? Where do you go from there?

Josh： They can't go outside. And outside is really interesting.

主持人： Is that just a locomotion issue?

Josh： It's not locomotion — it's the hardware. These robots have wheels, they have a little bit of traction, they have these articulating hind legs, but they can't drive over gravel. There are huge opportunities for robots in construction, robots reclaiming materials from landfills. We need robots with legs for that. So I think that'll eventually be part of our pantheon of embodiment. And similarly, robots in the home — you probably don't want a Cassie or Sunny in your home just now. It's a little bit too industrial of a device.

主持人： Yeah, they look scary.

客户采纳：绿地市场的意外玩法

主持人： Let's talk about customer adoption. Obviously, not strictly from "I don't have people so I'll take whatever I can get" — once they have it in their assembly line, how does adoption go in terms of their mindset?

Josh： It's an interesting challenge because almost everybody we're selling a robot to has never purchased a robot before. That comes out of these stats: if the United States is only deploying 38,000 robots a year, if 9 out of 10 US factories and warehouses don't have any robots, then almost all of the market is greenfield. These people understand what this old guard of automation looks like, and they assume a robot doesn't work for them.

So the way we break through that actually isn't by talking about AI or models or tutors or anything like that. We call them up and we say: "Hey, have you ever considered a robot for 16 bucks an hour?" They haven't. That's a new proposition for them. So you can book a meeting and then explain this thing that we're doing and get people interested and involved. By creating that business model where there is true incentive alignment between us as the robot vendor and the customer, we're able to run distribution of robots at velocities that are many orders of magnitude faster than traditional industrial automation.

We have an average time from that first call to a robot-signing contract of 40 to 60 days. We have an average time from that signed contract to robots actually in the customer site of about 40 days doing work. We stand up robots in production within a day — often within the first couple hours that a robot is on site. We're able to move very very quickly because not only is the robot this generally intelligent, generally capable machine that we're not customizing — we're just shipping directly from the factory to the customer — but we're not putting any economic risk on the customer. So we're able to get them on board.

主持人： And once they deploy it, how do their attitudes about labor versus machines change?

Josh： The operations community is really fantastic because they see a thing work and it's like: "it works." It's: yeah, I can see obviously it does the job. I know all the places where this job needs to be done. Let's go put it in all those places. So we've been able to scale up very very quickly, both with small businesses and some of the largest companies in the supply chain, from one robot in one site to a dozen-plus robots across many sites.

机器人作为"同事"：HRI 与命名的艺术

主持人： It is interesting though — a lot of GenAI, there's a social element where people get very attached to their models and it's hard to swap models. You probably have more experience deploying robots than most people alive. Are they viewed like equipment or like beings and co-workers?

Josh： I saw a very funny tweet which was: "a robot is a robot unless it works, in which case it's a machine." I've got to figure out the attribution.

主持人： Is it real? Like they just view it as equipment once it works?

Josh： Certainly at the factory-manager level, yes. I think there's still the layer — interestingly in robotics your buyer is not your user. Your buyer is like the COO or the general manager, and the user is like a factory worker who's working with the robot all day long. There you actually do need to cultivate the relationship between those workers and the robots, because we don't fully automate 100% of a factory. We automate some jobs in a factory or warehouse.

主持人： Do you have a philosophy on how you approach this? Do you try to make them look friendly? Make them look like co-workers or less like co-workers? Make them talk?

Josh： Very luckily there is a whole school of academic research called HRI — human-robot interaction.

主持人： No idea. There you go.

Josh： A lot of people have spent a lot of time thinking about this, including a bunch of people from my academic background. There are a whole bunch of tricks. One trick is: every robot has a name. That lets us actually build a relationship with the robots.

主持人： Who names it?

Josh： Mostly our manufacturing technicians.

主持人： So it's not like a dog — when you get a new dog you can rename it?

Josh： When a customer expands with Tutor — when they do a repeat order — then they're allowed to name the robots.

主持人： Oh, like you're not supposed to rename a boat because bad luck; you've got to keep the boat name. But you can rename a dog. So the new robots get to be named — that solves it.

Josh： Exactly. And we get really strong signals — we had people name the robots after their kids, people named the robots after their favorite football player, their favorite pop star. People get very attached because the robot ultimately helps. It makes their jobs easier. If you're a line worker in the facility, you're not doing backbreaking work as much. You're able to be elevated into a higher position — and none of these places can hire. And if you're a factory manager, your job is a thousand times easier.

主持人： What naming scheme do you use?

Josh： We started off doing hurricane naming and then we kind of —

主持人： So that's not — you didn't read the HRI book clearly.

Josh： Well, I don't know. You're an academic. The customer doesn't know that Britney is, you know, node 26 or whatever. But we actually stopped because we went through the hurricanes, went through the alphabet too many times to keep track of it.

主持人： Okay, so what are you using now?

Josh： I think the technicians just pick whatever brings them joy. We have a really wonderful privilege to employ a big staff of people in the United States who are helping to build these robots, and they are also naming them.

为什么选择中小客户：产品公司的本质

主持人： The other thing that surprised me when we first did the work before investing — most of the time when we talk to robotics companies, they're going after these humongous Fortune 50 companies that seem to have the budget for lots of experiments. Whereas a significant majority of your customers are all these local businesses almost. Is there a message in there, or was it a conscious strategy?

Josh： It's a lot of things. One is: that's most of the market. The vast majority of US businesses in manufacturing logistics are small businesses or mid-market businesses. So if you want to serve the market, that's what it takes to serve them.

I think we also started this company at a time when we were seeing all of these very academic supply-chain-oriented robotics startups kind of get started and then not really succeed. We had the opportunity of being like: okay, what went wrong here? One of the big things I think that robotics companies get wrong is they're not actually really product companies. They're like: okay, some really big company has a very specific problem. They're willing to write us a shiny piece of paper that says they're going to expand with it. We're going to spend two years building a very custom system to solve their problem. We'll deploy it, chances are it won't work — because anybody who's built products knows you can't just one-and-done a product. Doing product requires iteration. And then even if it does work, who's to say that customer still has that problem? And so boom, the company's done.

I feel like I saw this happen 5 to 10 times in a row, to the point of: oh my, if this happened to us, that would just be embarrassing. Working with a diverse range of customers is this beautiful forcing function for building the right shape of product — which to us is a general robot. We don't want to build a Rube Goldberg machine that works really well for big industrial customer A or B. We want to build a platform that is generally capable robot bodies running generally capable robot models that can immediately get to work. If you can sign a contract in two weeks with a mid-market customer and have a robot running immediately after that — and that's a totally different type of product and business than your other customers — you're being successful.

产业的终局：机器人作为新的"劳动基质"

主持人： In the limit, assuming you continue to be successful, what does the industry look like? Does this work get cheaper, faster? Does quality go up? What is the economic convergence?

Josh： I think everything gets better. There's a whole set of goods that, if they are cheaper, we will buy more of them — and if you believe those goods are valuable, that's good for everybody.

There are also a bunch of discontinuities in the world. I was talking with somebody the other day who worked on the line in a housing factory in, I think, Wisconsin. They were describing how the houses they're building are about 5% more expensive to build in a factory than to do traditional construction on site. But if these houses were even just 1% cheaper than the equivalent quality of house constructed on site in the traditional way, all of the demand from developers would immediately go to that other shape of building homes in a factory. The same thing could be said about reclaiming materials in landfills and a whole bunch of other markets.

So our hope is: if Tutor is really successful, we can provide this robot substrate, this labor force that other businesses can use to transform the physical economy and make the world ultimately a cheaper and better place to live in.

主持人： Will you ever go in the home?

Josh： We're not opinionated — we'll go anywhere. But I would imagine that would be a much tougher technical problem, from complexity of task and safety. And the economics of it: what is the economic value a Tutor robot delivers in a factory, and how many consumers are willing to pay for that in their home — it doesn't quite work out. But that comes back to our overall philosophy: take trade-offs across as many layers of the stack as possible to get a foothold, start building the platform, and as you build the platform you have to take fewer and fewer trade-offs over your time.

产品迭代节奏：把物理产品做成数字产品

主持人： How does product innovation work in robotics? Most companies are just on V1, whereas you've got two versions of the robot and you continue to iterate really fast. How is it different than digital product innovation?

Josh： We're trying to make it as similar as possible. We're manufacturing our own robots — this gives us the ability to own that manufacturing process and figure out how we push changes to the manufacturing process every two weeks. We are shipping code to robots either every day, or major releases every two weeks, and have built a huge amount of infrastructure to support that level of iteration.

We've built a really unique shape of product function where our product function in our organization actually sits right next to our customer success and implementation functions, and operates as one big team. So they're as close to the customer as humanly possible, which has been really successful for us.

And then we also have a research team which is able to be, on the one hand, deeply embedded in the customer problem space — we're able to pull all sorts of levers to get specific types of data from customers — but also able to take moonshots. If we have a breakthrough on our modeling side that lets robots do a whole new shape of thing, we can co-design a product around that in a way that I think most companies couldn't, and get that out into the field much quicker.

客户入口与定价：$16/小时的机器人

主持人： If I'm listening to this and I have a warehouse and I want to get a robot, do I just go to the website and put in my email?

Josh： You can go to our website, put in an email. We actually have cool pricing calculators where you can put in operational data about how your warehouse or factory runs today, and get an estimate of: "hey, with an initial deployment of Tutor robots, we could be saving $100,000 a year, a million dollars a year, $100 million a year." And that's not — "okay, this is a roadmap over 5 years of custom engineering." It's: no, you could save that a million dollars a year two months from today, without putting capex down.

主持人： Have you found that there's demand? It's just such a sci-fi thing.

Josh： There is so much demand, and it's not even demand for robots — because again, people don't know that this shape of robot exists or that it works or that it can do this job. We have this framework: the value of a robot is how much work a robot can do, divided by its cost. That's it. Everything else is commentary. If we're able to compete in these highly liquid labor markets that exist across the American physical economy, and we can offer something that delivers greater equivalent capability at a lower cost, the market for that is the whole market. It's all physical work done.

主持人： One quick wonky question: when you say "cost," do you mean amortizing the upfront cost versus the ongoing cost to operate it?

Josh： It's both, which is very interesting and different. Traditionally we've thought about robotics as ROI — big capex expense, and then 10 years to make it back. Now it's actually: more and more of the cost is going into ongoing inference, tele-operation.

主持人： Does that also include maintenance and break-fix? What is the dominant cost, or are they roughly equal?

Josh： We drive down all of them over time.

主持人： I'm just saying — from your standpoint, when you pencil out your COGS, how much is the upfront cost versus the ongoing?

Josh： It is more ongoing at this point, and that's surprising to people.

主持人： Interesting. Oh wow.

Josh： Not surprising to me. You're really competing with something that you feed rice to and it's very very efficient — the human body.

战略采购：不是黑五救急，而是长期伙伴

主持人： When you get called into these customers, is it because Black Friday is coming up and they need units done in a short time, or is this actually part of their labor planning cycle?

Josh： No, it's strategic. These businesses are faced with a really hard choice: they know the age of their workforce, they know that demand is ramping up due to all these secular trends, and the cost basis of fulfilling that work is going up. They're like: how does our business pencil out? Because these are not software businesses that have huge gross margins that you can play with and compress a little bit, and it's fine. No — the business either works or it doesn't.

Our customers are ultimately looking for a long-term partner that can do the robots. If one of our customers is manufacturing deodorant, they're doing the deodorant. They're going to be operational experts in deodorant, or operational experts in crayons, or whatever the thing they manufacture is — and they need a partner who's the expert on robots.

地理与地缘：工厂的位置会被重写

主持人： I had a question on the nature of factories. You can ship a robot to anybody — not today because of your shortages, but at some point in the future. If your robots become more and more general-purpose over time, what does it mean for where factories are located and how people organize around these factories?

Josh： A lot changes. There's a lot of geopolitics in this. One big thing is: this is going to be a great equalizer between the United States and other countries like China. They invested in the previous regime of industrial automation. In some ways that made them very successful; in other ways I think in hindsight that might end up being an enormous mistake — because in the United States, as we just discussed, we're doing this greenfield build of automating our industrial capacity using generally capable robots. In China, they're going to have to tear down. We're not going to have to do that in the United States in the same way.

Another thing that's going to shift, which is going to be really interesting: we're just going to have way more factories. In the same way that we have way more businesses because the cloud and all the software tooling let people build new businesses — anybody will be able to start a business in the physical world. Anybody will be able to scale a business in the physical world, if we have this infinite flexible labor substrate.

中国依赖与供应链垂直化

主持人： You brought up China. We actually published a report on the supply chain in robotics, and it seemed that China was so central to it. Can you talk about your dependency on it, and how that evolves over time, and how much risk there is?

Josh： Ultimately, no matter what anybody says today in 2026, we have a highly interconnected, interdependent global supply chain. And this is one of many examples. I think both US companies and Chinese companies are thinking very hard about what the long-term strategy of this looks like. It's Chinese companies investing in the United States, it's US companies investing in China — ultimately, everybody's trying to build their industrial capacity.

主持人： I've noticed you've verticalized more. Is that right? You're taking more in-house, and do you plan to continue to do so?

Josh： There's this tough thing in supply chain where — because robotics is such a cottage industry — you might start in a world where subcomponents are coming from OEMs, and then you grow your volume to the point of: they're not OEMs anymore, they're glorified contract manufacturers. You're doing a material percentage of their volume. At that point just the relationship and dynamics change. Is that the right co-man for that thing? Do I want to be using a co-man, or do I want to be manufacturing it in-house?

主持人： Tutor must be one of the largest deployers of robots in the United States — and as a result you must be one of the largest customers for some of these OEMs. I would imagine over time you just continue to drive these components yourself.

Josh： I think that's right.

主持人： Does that mean taking it in-house, or just telling them what to do?

Josh： Some combination. Ultimately for Tutor to be successful we will need a mature robotics supply chain in the United States. We're in this position where — because we are so much of the demand for that supply chain — I think it's both our obligation and our opportunity to invest very very heavily in building this capacity in the United States. That's why we build robots in Watertown, Massachusetts. It's why we expect to continue to verticalize and build more of our robot componentry in the United States.

研究路线：真实世界强化学习的 Data Factory

主持人： Going back to when we first started talking — I remember it was probably the second meeting when we actually started about the research. Most of the meeting, because you've got such a great business, but that's a big strength of yours. Talk about how you approached it. There are all sorts of theories about which robotic learning models will win.

Josh： We're thinking about how this played out in LLMs — what's similar and what's different. One thing that clearly has been very important in LLMs is: there are lots of heterogeneous sources of data, but ultimately there's a top of the data pyramid, which is real-world reinforcement-learning traces doing the thing you want to be able to do.

So we've built our research program in such a way where we're thinking: how do we get the most out of robot experience out in the real world? We built this 100-robot fleet called Data Factory 1 in Boston. This is, to our knowledge, the largest semi-humanoid data collection farm in the United States. We're able to use this as a research test bed of: how do we do real-world reinforcement learning at scale with robots?

Reinforcement learning is a technique family where it doesn't really work at small batch sizes. If you have a very large fleet out in the real world, you can start to play with these methods that I think people haven't been able to play with, either in academia or in industry.

团队建设：横跨所有层的 whiteboard-to-factory 组织

主持人： I presume building a team for this is quite different than a lab. Maybe talk about the construction of the team, and if there's anybody you're looking to hire.

Josh： We're looking to hire everybody. We're looking to hire researchers and engineers, and that's across every single layer of the stack. We are also looking to hire technicians to build robots.

主持人： By the way, every layer of the stack meaning like software, hardware, materials, electronics…

Josh： There's nowhere you can abdicate responsibility. You're going to engage with it whether you want to or not — the question is whether you understand it.

We're building that team, and I think that's a really unique shape of team, not only because it's so interdisciplinary and collaborative across all those layers of the technical stack, but because I think it's one of the only places in the universe where you can be on a whiteboard talking about model architecture in the morning, and in the afternoon looking at a factory line and seeing how a robot is doing.

主持人： Is this primarily in Massachusetts?

Josh： We have a team across the United States. We have especially folks on the go-to-market and technicians who are engaging — our customers are everywhere across the United States.

主持人： That's good. All right. Awesome. Thank you.

## 一个让你意外的观察：**iPhone 的包装盒不是机器人折的**
Josh 在视频中轻描淡写地点出了一个几乎所有人都忽视的事实——**哪怕是全球最精密、最自动化的产品之一，iPhone 的外包装仍然是人手装配的**。这件事远比它听起来震撼：
- 它意味着我们心目中的"自动化时代"根本是个**幻觉**。我们误以为"How It's Made"节目里的鲁布·戈德堡机器就是现实的基准线，但 Josh 说那是美国制造业的 **top 0.01%**——剩下 99.99% 的物理劳动，仍然是一个 55 岁、三个月就要辞职的工人在流水线上徒手完成。 - 更惊人的推论：**美国 2025 年全年只部署了 38,000 台工业机器人**。相比之下，一个中型 SaaS 公司一个季度能部署几十万个软件实例。我们所谓的"硬件时代落后于软件时代"，差距不是 10 倍，而是 10,000 倍。 - 这给机器人创业者一个被低估的认知：**市场不是存量替换，而是 Greenfield**。几乎没有客户买过机器人。这意味着你不是在打 Fanuc 的市场份额，你是在打"人类的手"的市场份额——而那是一个几乎无

item.title: [Lex Clips] Can AI solve P vs NP? | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、隐藏在"最坏情况"背后的哲学裂缝

Lex 那段关于"用最坏情况分析决定要不要结婚"的玩笑看似插科打诨，其实是整段对话里最锋利的一刀。复杂性理论之所以陷入 P vs NP 的泥潭长达半个世纪，很可能正是因为它从出生起就选错了"衡量尺"。当我们宣布 SAT "很难"时，我们是在说"存在一个最恶毒的输入让所有算法崩溃"——而这个恶毒输入可能是一个在现实中永远不会出现的、人为雕琢的病态结构。

一个出人意料的观察：现代计算机的缓存命中率几乎逼近神谕算法，这意味着真实世界的内存访问序列是"反最坏情况"的——它主动排斥坏例子。换句话说，物理世界本身似乎在偷偷为我们做优化。我们写了几十年的论文证明"paging 问题在最坏情况下的竞争比是 O(log k)"，但你手里的 MacBook 对这个下界报以优雅的嘲笑。真正值得证明的定理，可能不是"算法有多坏"，而是"世界有多善良"。

二、硬度只存在于一片测度为零的孤岛上——这是一个被低估的宇宙级异常

最后那句看似平常的收尾——"因子分解一个随机大数超级简单，一半是偶数"——其实藏着一个让密码学家夜不能寐的真相：我们认为"困难"的那类问题，实际上是在整个输入空间里一个几乎不存在的子集上才困难。两个大素数的乘积，在所有 n 位整数中占的比例按素数定理约为 1/(ln n)²，n=2048 时这个概率低到让人怀疑人生。

跨领域连接——这与量子力学里的"费米能级附近才有有趣物理"结构上完全同构：绝大部分粒子态是平凡的，真正的相变、超导、拓扑序只发生在一条极薄的能带上。再往外跳一步，这与蛋白质折叠里的"功能性蛋白只占序列空间的 10⁻⁷⁷"、与进化生物学中的"可存活基因组是极稀疏流形"、甚至与经济学中的"套利机会总在均衡的毛细缝隙里"——是同一种现象。

我的大胆预测：未来十年破解 P vs NP 的关键，不会来自组合数学，而会来自"结构稀疏性的测度理论"。真正要证明的不是"NP 问题难"，而是"NP-hard 实例构成一个在任何自然测度下测度非零但拓扑脆弱的集合"。这个方向目前几乎没人走。

三、LLM 为什么反而可能帮不了 P vs NP——但能帮一个你没想到的问题

Tim 对"LLM 能否攻克 P vs NP"的回答相当克制。但这里有一个未被点破的反讽：LLM 之所以在数学奥赛题上横扫、却在 P vs NP 上束手无策，恰恰是因为 LLM 自己就是"beyond worst-case"的活体证明。一个 Transformer 的注意力机制在最坏情况下是 O(n²) 平方爆炸，但在真实自然语言上它工作得好得离谱——因为语言的 token 依赖结构是极度稀疏的低维流形。

啊哈时刻：LLM 不是在"解决"复杂性问题，它是在无意识地利用真实世界与最坏情况之间那条巨大裂缝来谋生。所以让 LLM 去证 P ≠ NP，就像让一条鱼去证明"水不存在"——它整个存在的前提就是那个待证命题的反面。

因此 Tim 真正该赌的方向，是让 AI 攻克 "beyond worst-case analysis" 本身——一个长期被认为"太模糊、太软、不像真数学"的领域。LLM 最擅长的恰恰是在半形式化、需要大量品味判断的地方做模式识别。P vs NP 可能是 AI 的滑铁卢，但"真实世界输入分布的数学刻画"可能是它的闪电战。而讽刺的是，后者如果突破，前者就自动贬值了——因为那时我们会发现，整个 P vs NP 问题问错了。

📝 转录文本

问题的提出：AI 能证明 P vs NP 吗？

Lex: Uh, speaking of crises, let me get back to P versus NP question Ankur was talking about. Do you think—how hard of a problem is that, proving—So this is sort of the central question of complexity theory, P equals NP. Do you think AI will be able to prove this?

In fact, we should mention that you're kind of a part of a panel. There was initially a debate about whether LLM-based methods, could one day make progress on the hardest problems in mathematics, like P and NP or the Riemann hypothesis. That was a year ago. So what is your updated view on this?

Tim: Well, clearly, they can make progress on central questions in the field. Uh, P versus NP, maybe it's just because it's closest to my heart. That seems very difficult to make progress on. You know, it's kind of remarkable the things we don't understand, so that problem I was describing about satisfiability, we don't actually know any super linear lower bounds. You know, we think that it takes exponential time, not that much faster than enumerating all possible assignments and checking them, and yet we don't know anything that sort of is asymptotically more running time than just reading the darn input.

什么叫"难"，什么叫"易"？

Lex: Mm-hmm. And we should actually mention, you've talked about hard and easy. What is a more technical way to think about what is hard and what is easy?

Tim: Right. So this is polynomial time versus not polynomial time, or, you know, NP, just to be clear, stands for non-deterministic polynomial time. So the question is whether things which you can solve with non-determinism, like guess the assignment and then check it, can also be solved in polynomial time. So the question there is, if I give you a description of a formula, you know, I tell you what are the variables, what clauses they appear in, is there an algorithm that runs in time polynomial in the size of the input and correctly decides whether or not there is a satisfying assignment?

最坏情况分析的陷阱——与一个关于婚姻的玩笑

Lex: We should mention that the polynomial time or exponential time or super linear time, all this refers to worst case analysis.

Tim: That's right. That's right.

Lex: So can you explain what worst case analysis is, and what are its—

Tim: Pitfalls.

Lex: Yeah, I should say what are its pitfalls, 'cause I think it's a little bit counterintuitive from people outside the field, like to, like, to understand exactly when we say a certain problem is hard, you're actually talking about worst case. It's like analyzing, I don't know, I don't know why that popped into my head, but like marriage. It's like analyzing whether I should marry this person or not by saying, "Well, what's the worst thing that could possibly happen?" I think that's for human relationships, maybe it's not such a good strategy. Maybe the average case is a better guide for making decisions. Anyway, I don't know why I brought that up.

Tim: Okay, I have no advice about who you should marry.

Lex: This is com—yeah, complexity theory does not give you. I think there is some—Isn't there a dating is it like an optimal stopping theory of the optimal—

Tim: Secretary problem.

Lex: The secretary problem. There's a lot of different names for it, but there is a mathematical way. There's an optimal strategy.

最坏情况分析到底是什么

Lex: So first, so what is worst case analysis?

Tim: Yes, please—you know, I was describing the SAT problem earlier, and the algorithmic problem you want to solve is, given any formula, you want to decide is it satisfiable or not. Now, what's crucial there is that when I'm asking to solve that algorithmic problem, I'm not telling you anything more about the structure of the formula. I'm not telling you, you know, these are the size of the clauses. They look like this. If I drew a graph connecting them, it would have this topology.

So that's what worst case analysis is about, is it's about the premise that you can treat all of these computational problems actually by ignoring a lot of the fine-grained detail about the individual structure, and you can try and solve them, you know, for all possible inputs. And that's been spectacularly powerful because we've identified lots of algorithmic problems that really can be solved in the worst case and can be solved really efficiently. You know, like finding the max flow, as an example.

But the question is, you know, whether or not that's a useful abstraction. So sometimes maybe you really do need to know more about the structure of the instance you're faced with in order to solve it better, right? And that's really an open question. This is the area of what's called beyond worst case analysis, and I would sort of argue that, you know, it's a very important direction for theoretical computer science to go in. It's hard to figure out what you should articulate about natural problems that is really the right level of detail that your algorithm can exploit it and can do better things than it can in the worst case.

举例一：秘书问题与在线算法

But let's use an example. So you were talking about the secretary problem. So the way that this works is it's an example of something called online algorithms. So you have a sequence of options coming. One through N. They come in each time step, and your goal is, you know, when someone comes along, you know their ranking relative to everyone else you've seen before, but you don't know their ranking relative to the people who are yet to come. And your goal is to, you know, to make a decision when the person comes along, do you commit or do they move on, in such a way that you have a good chance of finding the absolute best candidate.

And so the point is that you can actually get a constant competitive ratio algorithm that what you do, the best strategy is to wait some amount of the time, not make any decisions, don't accept anyone. And then once that probationary window has passed, you take the first person who's better than anyone you've seen thus far. And that'll give you a good competitive ratio in the sense that you can prove theorems. Assuming the inputs arrive in a uniformly random order, you're likely to do pretty well compared to as if you knew what that sequence of inputs was in advance.

So there's, you know, under online algorithms, there's this veil of uncertainty, which is, I don't know what the sequence of inputs are gonna look like. I wanna do well no matter what that sequence is because, you know, I don't really know how to model what that sequence looks like.

建模真实世界的艺术

Now, you can instead say, "Hey, maybe the algorithms I derive aren't good enough for my applications. Can I do better by trying to model more of the world around me?" And then there's kind of an art to figuring out what you should model, what you should build into your model, and what you shouldn't. And that seems to me like a tremendously important area, to explore.

举例二：分页问题（Paging）

So for example, one other variant of, you know, online algorithms that's really important is the paging problem. So your laptop solves this problem all the time. You know, it's getting a sequence of requests of things that it wants to recall from memory. And the question is, what should it actually put in its cache, the part that's the easiest to access? And the problem again is that you don't know what that sequence of requests looks like in advance.

So you can study the online algorithms problem of, you know, what is a good policy for managing the cache? You know, when something gets accessed, you know, I have to put it in, but what do I evict? And you can design algorithms that are good in terms of their competitive ratio. The number of times they miss in terms of those accesses is not much worse than, the best offline optimum if someone told me that sequence of requests in advance and I could optimize just for that sequence of requests.

Now, this is a problem that's been studied since the '80s and '90s. The trouble is somehow that, you know, the best algorithms you can give, we know tight upper and lower bounds, they're just not that very good. You know, the number of misses they make compared to the best offline optimum is a large factor off from it, and that just doesn't compete with what your laptop is able to do right now because it really makes very few cache misses at the end of the day.

一个逆问题：如何刻画"真实世界"？

So you're stuck with this problem which sort of bridges mathematical thinking with trying to model the natural world, which is, you know, what is it about realistic sequences of requests that makes them not the worst case?

This is really an inverse problem now because it's, you know, the other side of the coin. Instead of someone handed you a problem that you're just trying to solve in the worst case, and we can all agree on how it's formulated, and we know what's a better algorithm, it does better on the competitive ratio, now you're stuck with this very fuzzy problem, which is: how should I model the world around me?

And in a lot of ways, algorithmic thinking is necessary for figuring out what are productive ways to model that problem. Because it's not that you're gonna build a totally realistic model of what sequence of page requests look like, but how am I gonna coarsen the problem in just the right way that it leads to interesting algorithmic problems that teach me about the world, that force me to, you know, design new approaches to solving these very basic problems.

So I'd argue that, you know, sort of coming out of this space where we are only solving well-defined problems, but we're actually using our mathematical and algorithmic insights to figure out where to dig in the first place is now more important than ever. It should have always been important, but you know, that to me is really gonna be thrust into the spotlight.

结语：真正难的因子分解只是一片特殊的岛屿

Lex: Like a simple example is we were talking about factoring numbers. Well, factoring a random large number is really easy. Half of them are even. You know, factoring means find a factor. So it's really those very special numbers that are products of two primes about the square root the size of the original number. That's hard factoring, sorry.
