item.description:
# 洞察：Arthur Hayes 的三重镜像——他在同时做空、做多和重新定义同一件事
## 一、被忽视的真正"受害者图谱"：AI 危机的终点不是科技股，而是一张死亡证明
大多数分析者把 AI 泡沫的爆点锁定在 2027 年的数据中心交付、CoreWeave 债券崩盘、或 Anthropic/OpenAI 的现金流断裂。但 Hayes 真正指出的是**一个被精心伪装的"代际剥削链"**：
- PE 公司（Apollo、KKR）收购保险公司 → 把寿险保费和年金池塞进 AI 相关的垃圾债 → 再通过"自家再保险公司"把风险挪到资本金近乎为零的壳里 → 一旦评级下调，保险公司瞬间资不抵债。
令人意外的观察是：**这条链的终端受害者不是基金 LP、也不是散户，而是"寡妇和孤儿"**——是那些买了寿险想保障家人、买了年金想养老的普通美国人。当某一天"你以为能拿到 100 万，结果只拿到 20 万"，这不是财经新闻，这是葬礼上的家庭争吵。而正是这种**"情感 + 政治"双重不可承受性**，才让 Hayes 敢于断言印钞必然发生——不是因为经济逻辑，而是因为**没有任何政客愿意在竞选集会上

item.title: [Business of Sport] Is the WSL’s Business Model Broken?
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"倒置的梦幻球场悖论"——看似升级的球场，正在加速产品的死亡

Kevin Costner 那句 "If you build it, they will come" 可能是女子足球当下最危险的信条。本集最反直觉的洞察藏在一组几何数据里：当 Chelsea 女足从 5,000 容量的 Kingsmeadow 搬进 40,000 的 Stamford Bridge，观众绝对数从约 4,000 涨到 7,000（+75%），但观感上座率从 80% 骤降到 20%（-75%）。两个方向完全相反的数字描述的是同一场比赛。

这揭示了一个被零售、餐饮、剧场业早已熟知、却被体育营销彻底忽视的规律：空间稀缺性本身就是产品的一部分。Supreme 不是因为衣服好而排队，是排队本身在生产价值。女足的决策者犯了与早期 WeWork 开大型 co-working 空间同样的错误——用"物理容量"替代"心理稀缺"。更残忍的是，这是不可逆的：一旦 3/4 的座椅在国家电视广播镜头里明晃晃地空着，产品在"路过观众"心中就完成了去神圣化。它从"你抢不到的东西"降格为"连本地人都懒得去的东西"。

二、女子橄榄球才是真正的"对照实验"——它证明问题根本不是性别

这期讨论最被低估的一句话是 Charlie 在最后扔出的那个数字：同期英国女子橄榄球上座率同比上涨 27%，Red Roses 卖爆 Twickenham。一边是花了十亿级资本、占据头版、搬进顶级球场的 WSL——跌 15–25%；另一边是业余身份、零大规模媒体投射、依然自己攒场地的女子橄榄球——涨 27%。

这组反差把"女子体育没市场"的论据一键作废，同时也否定了女足内部那套"再给我们时间"的说辞。真正的问题因此被暴露出来——这不是一个新兴产品的成长曲线问题，而是一个"身份移植"（identity transplant）的排异反应。女子橄榄球从未试图把自己定位成"男子橄榄球的女性版本"，它从一张白纸出发，吸引的是新观众、新叙事、新情感入口。女足则相反：它寄生在男足俱乐部的品牌、球场、媒体版面之下，继承了男足的成本结构（工资、设施、明星经济）却继承不来男足 160 年的部落粘性。这就像给自行车装 F1 引擎——不是动力不够，是车架会被撕碎。

三、跨界连接：WSL 是体育界的 WeWork，而不是 LIV Golf

节目里反复把 WSL 比作 LIV Golf，这个类比有价值但其实不够狠。LIV 至少还是一个真正新的产品形态——48 人、三天、队制、摇滚乐、拿沙特钱。它的死法是"消费者不认账"。WSL 的死法则更接近 2019 年的 WeWork：

  • 产品几乎不是新的（1991 年起就存在）；
  • 叙事远远跑在基本面前面（"下一个大风口"）；
  • 资本只在"讲故事的会议室"里流动（owner 们在论坛被互相说服）；
  • 估值假设依赖另一次融资来证明（franchise 会值一亿）；
  • 退出路径根本没有买家（最终接盘者是谁？）。

Charlie 说的那句 "spunking 5 million a year because at the end you'll own something worth 100 million" ——这不是体育逻辑，这是 2019–2021 年的 PE 续命逻辑。而当 narrative 停止传染（即"下一位 owner 不再相信百万估值"）时，WeWork 式坍缩会在 24 个月内发生：不是因为观众突然消失，而是因为赞助方和老板之间的"共同幻觉"破裂。

更隐蔽的跨界预言：WSL 正在重演2010 年代的 OTT 流媒体红海——Peacock、Paramount+、Discovery+ 都以"我们是下一个 Netflix"为由融资，但真正发生的事是用户只订阅两家，其余全是补贴换 ARPU 的僵尸。女子足球现在在欧洲有五个联赛"互相证明彼此是未来"，而五个联赛加一起的真实观众基数只支撑得起一个德国半职业模式。

四、一个几乎没人指出的隐藏结构性真相：媒体曝光过早 = 产品过早被审判

被反复抱怨的"为什么女足有这么多曝光还做不起来"其实问错了问题。正确的提问是："在没有部落基础之前就获得主流媒体曝光，是不是一种诅咒？"

Padel、Hyrox、BallerLeague、山地跑、Formula E 早期——所有这些"先在小众中炼出真需求、再被主流发现"的产品都走得更稳。女足则相反，被提前拽进了国家级审判席。它来不及在小球场里慢慢培养出"我们才懂"的内部人文化（这是所有部落情感的孵化器），就被扔到 40,000 人场馆，被要求用 Premier League 的尺子衡量。

一个残酷的隐喻：这就像把一个 15 岁的网球天才直接送进大满贯决赛——赢不了不丢人，但你就此失去了她本来可以在 ITF 巡回赛里默默建构的那套叙事资本。女足现在最缺的不是球场、不是转播、不是工资，是"被少数人深爱过"的那段史前史。而这段史前史，已经被过度曝光永久地拿走了。

📝 转录文本

Opening — Setting the Stage

Moving on. >> Moving on to the uh the very gentle topic. >> waters of >> waters of >> women's professional football. >> Yes. >> And and women's professional football >> And women's professional football in general. >> more more generally. >> Okay. Serious question. How do you want to go about this?

I would like you to preface this. Um it's a subject which I've spoken about once on this show about 5 months ago at the end of last season. It's a subject which people in the industry know I've held strong views on for quite some time and I've spoken at conferences on it and written papers about it and all this type of stuff. All of them ignored. Not Not that I'm [clears throat] bitter about it. So, rather than me getting into my stride early, I would like Chaz Jr. to get into his stride first.

Why Talk About It Now — The Attendance Trend

Okay. Well, I guess a good place to start would probably be why we want to talk about it right now. When we talked about it before, I think it was very important to say that the issues that we had were with the structures, the approach taken to existing tournaments. It was nothing about opportunity. It was about business. And what makes sense to support and give a product the best opportunity to succeed has to has to be the fundamental aim and goal.

Think back to our conversations that we've had in recent weeks around men's football with the structure with the football regulator and how many clubs would be insolvent without 30 days of funding from the owner to the WTA spending growth capital on uh the prize money of players. What we have in women's football right now and we'll use the WSL I think has been a concerning trend focused on and we can use attendances as the grounding of this of a drop off in interest in the product. But, drop-off in interest in the product goes hand in hand with this continual discourse of growth and success and everything's going really well look the other way type stuff. The attendances suggest otherwise and the attendances don't just suggest otherwise in a small pocket distilled little category of uh numbers that have come out of a few weeks. This is now something that has been going on, I would say, towards the latter part of last season and it's continued into this season.

[gasps]

There was something I heard the other day, Charlie, uh and it was the two very senior people in women's football having a conversation and you actually sent me the article in the Telegraph. But it really highlighted to me part of that issue of I I mentioned the discourse. It we we were being fed this kind of narrative of success and only at the end of this article did the comments come that attendances in many of the biggest games, or reportedly the biggest games in the WSL, were down. But it wasn't spun as a negative, it was spun as a development point. And it was a side It was a footnote. It wasn't a key part of the conversation. But guess what, it is the conversation.

The Stamford Bridge Problem — Big Stadiums, Empty Seats

Because what we're talking about here is an entertainment product. We're talking about something that is now in the most competitive attention economy, as we say all the time, in history. Getting people into your stadiums is a key part of that. Women's football has seen a move over the last year or so of a number of its teams in the WSL go from small grounds to big grounds. Use Chelsea as an example. They have left the Kingsmeadow, which is, let's say, 5,000, and they've gone to Stamford Bridge, which is 40,000. Now, normally you'd think, "Okay, they would do that because demand was so high at Kingsmeadow." The Stamford Bridge is the natural step up because they could capitalize on all of the cash they were leaving on the table from the fans unable to get tickets in there. They could bring more into the event and everyone wins. We start making more money. People like you and I can stop sitting here criticizing them for not generating enough revenue. And you guys go, "Well, we'd love to, but we don't have a big enough stadium." Well, here's your big enough stadium.

The problem is that the first game of the season with Chelsea women at Stamford Bridge was against Aston Villa and there was 7,000 people in there. That's a 20% occupancy rate in Stamford Bridge 20%. And that by the way is pretty consistent across all the grounds, about 1/5 of the seats are sold when clubs are playing in a bigger ground. That's a problem. Not just for the revenue that comes in on the day, but it's a problem for the overall product because how bad does it look for a sport, for a concert, for anything when you're tuning in and the main thing that you see as a fan, supporter, maybe just a first-time watcher is empty seats.

To me that suggests that there's a lack of interest in this product. Means that why should I care? Clearly actually other people don't care. Stamford Bridge is, you know, a fifth full. Could maybe this isn't a very good game that I'm watching. No, no, it's it's it's actually one of the big games. It's the opening game of the season. But really if you look at the raw data, you see a product that is very much a moment's product and not a tribal product. And a moment's product is built very specifically around the key times in a calendar in a year where there's, you know, a bounce off the back of a Euros and people are interested for a few months. What football is, men's football, it's a tribal product regardless of what is going on. People will go and turn up for their team most of the time. Look, Old Trafford was still full despite the animosity that was being thrown at the club. And this isn't a tribal product yet. And yet it's being treated like a tribal product. And that is an issue that has gone now much deeper, I think, in product women's football.

"We're a Startup" — The Excuse Dismantled

Right. So, I hear it said by people in women's professional football, "We shouldn't be judged as if we're a mature sport. We're a startup." >> Yeah. >> That's that's a a more recent type of excuse or reason, I should say. But it's one which is being given quite a lot at the moment.

Um I just want to put that in context. Women's elite football in this country in a league format starts in 1991. Um it moved to um a sort of more tiered and professional basis in 2018 when it was still under the aegis of the Football Association. It was then spun off by the Football Association 4 years ago, 3 to 4 years ago. Okay? So, it certainly isn't a startup in concept. So, as far as the paying punters concerned, they've been able to watch women's elite league football for almost all my life and more than you than than your life's span. We're We're talking about pushing on towards 40 years of women's elite football. So, this whole thing of well, we were never allowed to play it. It's like that's in the midst of time now. I mean, that is so long ago that the vast majority of people weren't even alive when women weren't allowed to play proper football. Okay?

71?

Yeah. Until 71. Right? So, we're talking about 50 50 55 years ago. 55 56 years ago. But even at the elite level, it's been in place for almost 40 years now. This is not a startup. Even if you really stretch a point and say that what we're talking about in startup terms is the point at which the Football Association spins off the Women's Super League to become the Women's Super League, which happened 3 years ago. Yeah. And you say, "Okay, that's the startup, okay, from a business perspective. And that's when things go into startup phase."

The VC Framework — Startup vs Growth Phase

Now, I want to ask you a question as somebody who, um, you know, is a senior person within a venture capital business which backs startups. Is when you invest in a startup business, how many years would you regard the pure startup phase as being before you move into what we call accelerated growth phase?

Really? 3 years onwards.

So, so you'd expect loss making for the first couple of years, let's say.

Um, at that time, you would have expected to see something that got them close to on the initial pitch >> Yeah. >> hitting the revenues that would have then justified that initial investment. >> growth. >> But growth. >> Yeah. >> But then what you could well have seen is recognizing that >> upside. >> Yeah. >> Then they've gone back and gone, "Right, we now we've seen the opportunity, we need more." And that's growth.

Right, that's that's the real growth phase, right?

If you're saying that you you have a venture fund, you need the businesses that you're investing in to return within 5 to 7 years.

5 7 years, right?

And and anything beyond that is long.

Right. So so basically, just to summarize what Chaz has said there, which is that the first couple of years might be looked at as the pure startup phase. Years 3 to 5 are the accelerated growth phase, when things should should really start to motor and really start to look like it's going to become a really successful business, so that in years 6 7 8, you're able to exit those investments. Why? Because they've achieved so much more than they had done 5 years previously, that there are other people coming in who go, "Wow, that's amazing. I want to buy into that."

Okay. So um The FA spins it off in um sort of whatever it is, two to three three years ago, okay? So, if you were to make the argument that all of women's professional football started in 2023, whatever it might be, I don't accept the argument because they they'd already been professional since 2018 and they'd already been playing elite semi-professional since 1991, but let's just say that you say, "Okay, that was startup, right?" So, 24 25 and 25 26 become the startup phase, when you start to iron out a few of the issues, but you're already seeing growth. And then you move into 26 27, which is what we're in now, and more money comes in and you start see accelerated growth, when the whole thing really starts to rip and go upwards from there. And you see that happen for two to three years, cuz there's obviously a lot of clear blue sky to aim into, because you're you've spotted a big a big opportunity, a big TAM, as we would call it, total addressable market. And during those two to three years, people start to get super excited about it, so that in years 6 7, people say, "Wow, okay, we've really got something here."

The Numbers — A Hot Air Balloon Pricked

Okay, this is the problem with women's professional football. Is that we are now entering or have entered what should be the accelerated growth phase. And what we're actually seeing is massive reductions of attendance, right? Which is the only metric we can use here because their TV deals are tiny. So, that is it's not And and also last year were very disappointing as well. But, leaving that to one side, let's just stick on attendance for the moment.

Wait, wait, you can't actually do it just yet cuz total revenue is 90 million for the whole league. Right. >> So, you can't even look at revenue.

So, we're actually being kind here in saying that bums on seats is the metric. So, in 23-24, which was the start of their startup phase, the average attendance in WSL 1 was 7,600. Okay? The average attendance this season, 26-27, which is the accelerated growth phase, is 5,200. Right? So, what you've seen here is a product being brought to market, the market having a couple of years to look at that product, and then just at the moment when it's meant to take off, like a uh hot air balloon that's been pricked, it just sinks back to earth and then goes into flames on the ground. 5,200 down from 7,600. Right?

Yeah.

That is an absolutely colossal drop. Now, that the average of 7,600 was largely built off as Charlie says, certain showpiece games. The big ones. The ones that, you know, even casual football fans might take a bit more of an interest in because it's between famous men's clubs and it's their women's arms. So, you get a bit of transference of rivalry. You get a bit of brand relevance and all this kind of stuff.

The Showpiece Games Breakdown

So, let's just take for instance Arsenal against Man Utd. 24-25, 46,000. This season, 29,000. Right? So, 46,000 to 29,000. Chelsea-Arsenal, big London derby, 34,000 in 24-25, down to 19,000 now. Liverpool versus Everton, the Merseyside derby, 24-25, again, startup phase, 15,000. 26-27, 2 1/2 thousand. Right? Arsenal women, which is the one successful club, >> Right. Flagship, right? >> the flagship, which as of last season was accounting for 41% of the total spectators in the entire league. Last season, average attendance of 34,000. This season, over its first three matches 24,000. Right? So, that That That is a a massive, massive percentage reduction.

Now, we have to say, this is after three to four rounds of matches,

No, but as I said at the beginning, I think the reason you can have this conversation is cuz it's the continuation of a trend that was being seen last season.

Yes, cuz attendances last season were lower than they had been in 23, 24 as well. So, it's not like this is a sort of one-off one-off situation we're seeing. We are seeing a downward trend in general. It even spills over into the international game, which has been in some ways the bullwark of women's professional football, which is well, at least the Lionesses got a great crowd. The Lionesses played against um Greece in a crucial World Cup qualifier recently. 18,500.

Is that King Power?

Is that the King Power, which is a capacity of 30,000. Now, normally when you take England matches on the road, they they could sell out many, many times over because people in in those parts of the country don't normally get to watch England play at their local ground all that often. And also, the grounds are smaller than Wembley and so on and so forth, right? 18,500 for an absolutely crisp competitive match, not a friendly, competitive match against Greece, right? 18,500.

Self-Audit — Normalising the Numbers

So, what what I then wanted to do, I wanted then ask the question of myself, cuz I have to be fair. First of all, I I took a look at direct comparative numbers for all these matches across the league. And it is probably true to say that the way in which the matches have fallen, it means that whilst it might look like a headline um attendance reduction of about 25%, I think the actual number is more like 15% reduction. If you actually look at it on a on a pure apples-for-apples basis.

Uh in what way?

Well, it just in the way in which the fixtures have fallen. So, in other words, we say it's 5,200 per fixture. >> Yeah. >> But, that can be heavily conditioned by which teams have had more home fixtures than other ones who and which those home have home fixtures have been and all this type of stuff. So, probably on a normal basis, that 5,200 would be more like 5,600, right? So, I might expect over the course of this season that that number might not stay at 5,200. It might be more like 5 and 1/2, 5,600, something like that. But, it's still miles down from 7,500. And during a phase when the whole thing's meant to be growing like Topsy.

European Comparison — Is It Just a WSL Problem?

Uh this the second way in which I wanted to hold myself to account is I want to try and work out is this a WSL problem or is this a problem with the professional women's product, full stop? So, I went and looked at the European women's leagues to see if they've got similar issues. So, we're looking at obviously the big five leagues of Europe, England being WSL, but then you've got La Liga Feminina, you've got the Frauen Bundesliga, you've got the Premiere League in France, and you got the Serie A um Feminile in Italy. I hope I think that sounded good. Did that sound okay? Right.

So, otherwise La Liga Feminina in Spain has got an average attendance of about 1,700. Okay? Um Frauen Bundesliga, which is as you'd expect from German clubs, they've been a bit smarter about it. It's a mixture of professional and semi-professional. They've been much more careful their cost bases, as you'd expect from fan-owned clubs rather than what we have here. 3,300. Right? Bear in mind WSL is 5,000 or so at the moment.

[clears throat]

Okay? Premiere League in France 2,200. And Serie A Feminile, as far as I could tell, about 1,600. Okay. So, it's pretty consistent across the major European leagues, you're looking at average attendances of about 2,500. Right? And then in WSL, more like 5,000.

[sighs]

Disproportionate Media Exposure — A Product Problem

So, this is a product that's been in the marketplace for, whether you call it 3 years, 4 years, 5 years, 6 years, 10 years, or 20 years, depending on when you take your start point from. It's It's been out there a while now. And it's received a totally disproportionate amount of mainstream media focus.

Right, so if you think about other disruptor sports, new sports, new products, whatever it might be, and we've discussed many on this program, and you say, "Okay, you know, how much real serious attention does the ball a league get from mainstream media?" Answer, almost zero. They have to create it all for themselves. How much real attention does, you know, we're talking earlier on about sort of, you know, disruptor products and things like, you know, show jumping and that sort. How much mainstream media projection do those types of sports get? Zero. Mick zero. Nothing, right?

Women's professional football has been given vast amounts of mainstream media media projection, being free to air on national broadcasters, going on the main pay TV suppliers, being housed in the best facilities that sport knows, major men's professional football stadiums. Don't forget that originally they were in smaller stadiums, and we were all told the reason it's not doing as well as it should do is cuz the stadiums they were in aren't all that great. Yeah. Okay. Transfer them into the great new stadiums. Oh, Currently attendance goes down, not up. Christ, what what's going on here?

But I wonder actually if there's this constant desire, understandable cuz a lot of also a lot of people have got massive vested interests in this product. There's this constant desire to try and find reasons and excuses. They're not playing in good enough stadiums. Um the matches aren't at the perfect time of day. They've actually been changed this season, too.

They've been Well, they've been re- This this season's scheduling is meant to be much better. Again, hasn't happened.

Uh the players aren't players aren't paid enough, or we need bigger star Whatever it might be, right? And again, the WSL has been able to attract almost all the biggest stars cuz they play so much more than other European leagues and other even American leagues. Um at what point do you actually say, "This is a product problem. This is not actually about which stadium it's played in or what time of day it's played in this type of stuff." This has been demonstrated against across multiple geographies that basically, not to put too fine point on it, almost nobody wants to pay to watch it. Yeah. That's a fundamental problem. It's the same problem that LIV came up against over the course of 3 years, which is you can throw as much money at it as you want, but at what point do you actually listen to what the market's telling you?

Men's Football as the Only Truly Tribal Product

And it comes Do you remember when we've had chats around men's club rugby? >> Yeah. >> And the power of international and when fans really turn up versus do they turn up every single week at scale to the extent where they are actually viable businesses as well, continually growing, not just maintaining? It comes up a lot. We've had it in cricket, club cricket, county cricket. 3 to 5,000 at the biggest, you know, counties over 4 days. You then flip it really and just say, "Well, what we see suggests that men's professional football is the only sport that can maintain the consistency across the cadence of matches on supply. I.E. one, two matches a week, fans will turn up 80% of the time. Right. That is an incredible product to try and base yourself off.

That just In In this way, I think there's this presumption that because it's football it will sell and attract people. Mhm. But it's not because as we've talked about before, men's football, rightly or wrongly, has been grounded in 160 years worth of history and is ingrained in the fabric of communities in ways that very few things are. Can any sport match the consistency that we see in men's sport? And in trying to create men's football, sorry. And in trying to replicate that in the women's game, you're just setting it up to fail.

Testing the "Give It Time" Defence

Now, your argument, Charlie, is I don't disagree with it. It But it is vulnerable to what proponents of the women's game will say is, "Yes, so give us the time. Give us the time to grow tribal appeal. It's going to take a long time. You're going to have to wait for this. And in the meantime, we're still going to have to pay the players gazillions of pounds because that's just what we do cuz it's football and because they deserve to be paid like men's footballers cuz they >> But it's men's football. >> I I'm I'm paraphrasing, but my point is I I just wonder here that everything that you're saying is is true. I I agree. The the bit I don't quite agree with is that men's professional football is the only viable professional sport. That you know it that you with with with the cadence, cadence being uh the consistency that the product is served up to you with it that it can sustain selling out a 40,000 seater stadium. Not even talking about selling out. I don't care about selling out. What I care about is revenues.

80% occupied Yeah, but revenues is as you know as you said come from >> total attendance, revenues, whatever it might be.

Now, we can say about the Prem rugby, we can say has it hit a ceiling? Right? But others might say yeah, but the ceiling's reasonably high. I mean, you know, they're getting 15,000 a game, right? And then the question comes is, okay, right, 15,000 a game feels like there should be enough there in and around that to be able to pay a group of players. Yeah, okay? Now, there are challenges around that cuz rugby squads are very big and their current substitute rules which are totally crackers and I don't get on a business perspective why they allow them at all, but it requires basically to have at least 30 full-time professionals, whereas, you know, you don't need those in football clubs. So, if I was rugby, I'd be looking very, very hard at how many professionals do we really need to be able to play this game? Another story. But you instinctively think any sport that can get 15, 16,000 on average coming every week to each individual event, not just one, but each individual event, kind of feels like it's earned its right to exist as a professional sport.

And I would say the same that, you know, I've got huge criticisms of this country's second biggest spectator sport which is horse racing. But there are 30, 40, 50, 60 times a year when you have 25,000, 40,000, 60,000, 80,000, sometimes even more coming, and you go, okay, this is now a question of structuring. This is now a question of trying to make sure that all of this revenue that is coming in we make sure that we fiddle around with with the back room operation to try and make sure that we don't end up sort of overexposing ourselves.

The challenge I've got here with women's professional football, and the reason I wanted to broaden it out from the WSL to the other European leagues is is not the truth staring us in the face >> that people don't want the product. >> No one wants the product. Well, no one Well, no one near enough people want the product to to make it a viable professional sport under any circumstances, right?

Who Is Filling the Gap? The Owner-Subsidy Problem

So, So, who's who's currently filling the hole? I just want to get to this crucial point. I know I know that various friends of ours won't won't won't forgive me if I don't. The gap between the current level of interest and the amount of money that's being paid to pay these professional footballers a lot of money is currently being filled by owners.

Yeah.

Now, I know from my own bitter experience that the reason they do that is because owners attend these conferences where they are told by panelists at these conferences experts i.e. people normally playing with other people's money, not their own that the next big growth thing is women's football. So, when I say to an owner of a football club that I'm involved with I'd be very careful here. Right. You know, you could end up spending a lot of money on this in the next 5 years, and where you end up at the end of that 5 years might not be where that where the people at that conference were telling you. You might just find that's disappeared down a black hole. Oh, no, no, no. From what I you know, in in 5 years time, I'm told all of these things will be worth 100 million pounds.

Now, once you believe that all of these franchises or clubs, whatever are going to be worth 100 million then spunking 5 to 10 million a year on them feels like a sensible thing to do. You say, "Okay. So, if I spend 5 or 10 million for the next 5 years, by the end of it, I end up with something that's worth 100 million." That makes sense. Ish. I'm I'm not asking you to comment on it.

But, what happens when you cease to believe in the big story? What happens when you cease to believe in the 100 million at the end of it, right? Do you not end up in the same situation that those LIV golfers were in when they were told by Scott O'Neil, "Your franchising will be worth 100 million." We've heard it all before, mate. We're not buying it this time.

What Would "Good" Look Like — A Growth Profile

I completely agree, but you know, you said um that maybe my points were vulnerable to those saying, "But come on, you know, give it time. It needs the time to grow." So, what what would you then say to that?

Well, I think as a venture capitalist you'd be well within your rights as you did do a little while ago to say, "Hey, where's the growth profile?" Right? I I I can believe in your story about time if it's heading in the right direction, right? So, it it if let's just say because I think this is broadly the market expectation. The broadly the market expectation was '23, '24 they did 7,500 average attendance. And let's just say that over the following 3 years it had gone 7,500, 8,000 8,300 8,900 and we were sat here right now at 9,000 rather than 5,000, okay? That wouldn't to me demonstrate explosive growth and it definitely wouldn't to you, I imagine. It wouldn't demonstrate explosive growth, but you would then listen to the person on the other side of the table who said, "Look, it's a slow burn. It's going to take a while, but look, it is heading in the right direction. And if we carry on like this, in 10 years from now, we're going to end up with 12, 13, 14,000. And at that point you are towards the Prem men's rugby and you are starting to justify your place in the professional sporting world, etc. So, yeah, look, I fully get it. It's going to take a while, but please bear with me. It's going it will be worth it in the end."

When things start heading in the wrong direction, you then start getting into discussions about throwing good money after bad, >> Mhm. >> right? Which is Okay, at what point does do we actually seriously have to start looking at our product here? Cuz in any normal business, if you were in the startup moving into the um you know, this sort of the really aggressive growth phase and you and your audience and your revenue started bombing backwards in the wrong direction, that would not be the moment in which everyone started doubling down, would it?

Revenue Side — Media Deals, Commercial Blockers

No, but I would that's kind of why I want to go back to my point and I hear you, you're right. Taken in the context of me just saying a sport is successful based on whether it fills the buns and seats of a stadium, then rugby has a very good justification. But if we're talking about men's football being a good revenue generator and pouring its cost controls. My point really around it being the only sport that could do that, actually it does consistently stand with rugby because rugby is a very poor revenue generator even though it fills its stadiums. It has a media deal that pays its clubs 3 to 4 million a year.

The WSL needs to fill its its stadiums part one, but you know, we we've let them we've gone very lightly on the revenues, right? On the financial side, but really, you know, there's a much much bigger issue here, which is the broader business of the WSL needs to be far far better than it can. We're just going very gently on the thing which is the most obvious signifier of how you could measure engagement.

[snorts]

The media deals need to improve, the commercial deals need to improve. You've got

The media deals aren't going to improve. The media deals aren't going

No, of course no, of course it won't, but I'm just saying as a which again brings me back to, you know, if we're just trying to model things off the men's football game, you are forever going to come up against blockers that may not you may not want to accept are there, but are absolutely there.

Self-Awareness as the Precondition for Change

And we'll spare them the blushes if even if they care, I don't know, but you remember we recently I can't remember who produced it. We read that report and I think this is where why we want to talk about it right now because there's just been a few things around the narrative that have made us feel stupid for questioning whether this is successful women's football has arrived. How could you look at this as being something that isn't going to be successful? You know, that and the more of this you read, the more conferences you go to where you're just being told just like with Liv saying how can you know, come on guys, 100 million franchises. That isn't the case. That is it's just it's just a fabrication of reality,

but also but also Charlie, the biggest if this is going to work, right? The reason things work, the reason things are able to develop and change is because you recognize there's a problem.

Yes.

So for as long as we sit listening to conferences, to reading those reports, to listening to to the that Telegraph article and say, "Hey guys, the sun's still shining on us." I'm sitting here going "Oh great." Now, if I'm in the position to if I realize the issues that actually exist for the women's football product, for the WSL, and I get a to grips with that based on the comms of the people actually in it, and they go, "Look, you know, we we think we have something, but and there is a big butt, this is what we need to do." I can go, "Right, okay, well, do you know what? Firstly, there's a self-awareness in the product there." It shows me that maybe with a bit of my support and understanding of how to structure it, the right people around it, we could try and make something out of this because it is something in theory that could work. Then that's great. But I'm never going to get to But I'm never going to get to that.

You know.

If everyone keeps flogging this narrative, this as you said, Fergazi, of well, nothing to see here, guys. We're

Celebrating Million-Pound Wages on a Championship-Sized League

Onwards and upwards. Onwards and upwards. Let's keep on paying the players more and more. Let's pay a million bucks for to bring a player in from not not not a million bucks, by the way, on a transfer fee, in wages.

also to

So, you're talking about a league, the WSL 1, with revenues which are the equivalent of a large championship club, sorry, total revenues of the entire league, one large championship club, that's then spending a million in wages on one player.

But not and and they're not just and they're not just doing it, but then celebrating it.

Absolutely. Saying as a sign of progress.

What Charlie Won't Pretend to Solve

So, here's the question, okay? And this is you you you know the sporting landscape as a whole really, really well. I did start pointing this problem out 3 years ago, but I've never other than saying that they really need to look at product innovation, I've never really come up with an answer. So, I'm not I'm not here sitting here saying that was an easy thing to do.

The Carney report that that was the preface of all this stuff of was a crashing mistake. It should never have had two professional leagues. That was an absolute disaster. The franchises or clubs need to be better geographically spaced. They had to have a cost control. There were lots of things wrong with it, but that's none of those things are the reason why attendances are at 5,000.

Yeah.

Right.

Attendances are at 5,000 because people aren't hooked on the product.

Yeah.

The London City Lionesses / Michelle Kang Caveat

And that's Well, okay. Can I throw in a um a caveat?

Yeah.

What do we think of London City Lionesses and Michelle Kang?

What's the caveat?

Caveat being if attendances have increased at a smaller level, there's been should we say through a incredible amount of self-financing. Right on her owner financing. Awful from a structural perspective again if you're trying to regulate an industry, but she's put in and like 22 or was it 22.4 million I think to to this project.

And the rest. That was as of last counting I think you'll find it's up up up at more like 40 now.

But they're on revenues of 1 million. They bought some top talent as in well actually Ballon d'Or winner.

The the that was who I mentioned earlier on who's on a million a year.

Yeah. Okay, so my point is there you've got someone that almost maybe have a has a slightly different incentive structure. She's a very rich person who is building something from scratch as well not attached to a men's club. So it's an independent asset. Clearly and unashamedly almost spending a huge amount of money to try and elevate this, but at the same time existing in an ecosystem which is exclusively

The Polo Analogy — Rich Patrons Are Not a Market

Okay. Right. I totally get your point. You have a very rich person spending a vast amount of their own money on a professional sport which not many people really care about. Polo is like that. Polo, right? Big rich guys come in and they will spend 10 20 million on their polo team. They themselves get to play in the polo team. They get to play with three Argentine professionals and they play at Windsor or Cowdray Park and five or six thousand people turn up cuz it's a nice day out and they sip champagne and they watch the whole thing and this this type of stuff. And the whole thing goes on and no one ever stops to say does that deserve to exist? It yes, absolutely fine.

If there were 10 Michelle Kangs and they all decided that they wanted to fund to a ridiculous level their football teams and didn't really care that almost no one wanted to turn up and watch. It just is what it is cuz I've got a passion for it. I've got a mission about it. That's I've got no problem with that whatsoever. Please don't expect the rest of us to be interested. Don't have acres and acres of coverage in the mainstream media and on national broadcasters telling anyone who is not passionately interested that they're a dinosaur, an idiot, don't get it, etc. etc. The market will tell you what the market needs you to understand. And if the market doesn't turn up, it's not because the market's an idiot. Right?

So, I've got no problem with what Michelle Kang's doing. She should knock herself out. She's not just doing it there, she's doing it Lyon as well. Okay? She's a She's a billionaire-ess and how she spends her money is totally up to her. If she wants to If she wants to pay a female professional footballer a million a year to play in front of 3,000 people at Bromley FC, that's totally her prerogative. But can we all please recognize within the industry that this is not the next big thing. Pretty conclusive.

Closing — Women's Rugby as the Counter-Example

Well, it is to me.

Yeah.

Um

Um how do you reckon that's going to go down?

With whom?

People who listen. I'd imagine you guys will have uh you know, a few views on this. I think we can recognize that it's a very sensitive topic, but I I hope that in any conversation it's a it's an educated approach to or a reasonable at least fair uh grounded in the type of critique that we would level at lots of other and have leveled at lots of other sports organizations. And if this was a men's product, we would go in gangbusters.

As I said when we covered this the first time, I always balance this out by saying I'm checking across on the numbers with women's professional rugby or semi-professional rugby as it is, 27% up attendances. 27% When England played against Canada recently in Canada, right? So, this is in a country where the sport is still amateur, rammed stadium. Here they sell out Twickenham, the Red Roses do, right? But there, rammed out stadium even in Canada. This is a sport which every single year is beating records, beating records, beating records whilst keeping pay under control.

And that's a sport which if someone came to me and said, "How far do you think it could go?" I'd be like, "Well, I don't know. It's growing so fast. Who knows? If it carried on growing at 25% a year for the next five or six years, that could become something really investable. So, this is not about men and women.

Mhm.

It's nothing like that. You know, that what this is about about looking at the metrics, looking at the trend graphs, looking at the amount of capital invested for the return on capital invested, looking at people's medium-term horizons, and asking ourselves the question, is is this working or is it not working? And and having frankly the honesty to call it out when it's not.

Yeah. Okay, brilliant.

item.description:
## 一、"倒置的梦幻球场悖论"——看似升级的球场，正在加速产品的死亡
Kevin Costner 那句 "If you build it, they will come" 可能是女子足球当下最危险的信条。本集最反直觉的洞察藏在一组几何数据里：当 Chelsea 女足从 5,000 容量的 Kingsmeadow 搬进 40,000 的 Stamford Bridge，**观众绝对数从约 4,000 涨到 7,000（+75%），但观感上座率从 80% 骤降到 20%（-75%）**。两个方向完全相反的数字描述的是同一场比赛。
这揭示了一个被零售、餐饮、剧场业早已熟知、却被体育营销彻底忽视的规律：**空间稀缺性本身就是产品的一部分**。Supreme 不是因为衣服好而排队，是排队本身在生产价值。女足的决策者犯了与早期 WeWork 开大型 co-working 空间同样的错误——用"物理容量"替代"心理稀缺"。更残忍的是，这是不可逆的：一旦 3/4 的座椅在国家电视广播镜头里明晃晃地空着，产品在"路过观众"心中就完成了去神圣化。它从"你抢不到的东西"降格为"连本地人都懒得去的东西"

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、权力的"建筑学"性质——说服只是舞台灯光

Caro揭示了一个被反复误读的事实：约翰逊的"说服力"从来不是说服力，而是权力的戏剧化展演。参议员屈服，不是因为他的手臂环抱或身体前倾产生了魔力——那是表演。真正的工作发生在数年之前的委员会分配、法案时间表、人事安排之中。

这其实与国际象棋大师的直觉深度同构：决定胜负的那一步，往往发生在表面决胜之前十步。约翰逊真正的天才不是"谈判时"的能力，而是在谈判发生之前几年就已经布置好了对话的物理结构。这意味着一个反直觉的方法论：当你看到一个"善于谈判"的人，你可能看错了观察对象——该研究的不是他的话术，而是他五年前做的那些你没看见的小事。

二、Cotulla悖论——一年的教学如何战胜一生的种族偏见

这是整个采访中最令人震颤的观察：约翰逊在私下使用种族主义语言、是德州种族政治的产物，然而他推动了美国最激进的民权立法。为什么？因为他22岁时在Cotulla教了一年墨西哥裔穷孩子。那一年以某种方式压倒了之后四十年的全部社会化。

这与文学中的"形成性创伤"模式惊人地吻合——狄更斯一生都在处理那个鞋油厂、陀思妥耶夫斯基无法摆脱那场假处决、博尔赫斯始终在重写他父亲的图书馆。政治家和小说家似乎共享一种心理机制：一个早期的、未解决的记忆，不断以越来越宏大的形式返回。约翰逊的伟大立法，也许不是他信念体系的产物，而是一个具体记忆的二次生长。如果这个假说成立，那它颠覆了我们理解政治人物的方式：别看他们说什么，去找他们22岁时那个未被消化的夏天。

三、Coke Stevenson的悲剧——不是输了选举，而是认知模型的崩塌

这里藏着全书最深的刀。Caro说Stevenson"没有意识到有人能对他做出那些事"。这不是道德判断，而是认知病理学——理想主义者在根本上无法想象彻底工具主义者的策略空间。

跨领域连接：这就是修昔底德在《梅利安对话》中的雅典人逻辑——"强者为所欲为，弱者承受必须承受"；也是演化生物学中经典的"背叛者问题"：只要合作者无法识别和排斥背叛者，就会被吃掉。好人输给坏人，很少是因为"善不敌恶"，而是善人的策略库里缺少恶人用的那些工具，甚至缺少想象这些工具的语言。Stevenson输掉的不是1948年的参议员席位，而是他对现实的整个建模。

四、越南是国内天才的阴影——同一种天赋的致命倒影

最后一个意外连接。约翰逊之所以在越南溃败，恰恰是因为他国内的全部技能在那里失效。他无法把手臂搭在胡志明肩上，无法威胁他的委员会席位，无法为河内兑现一条联邦高速公路。约翰逊的权力建筑学需要一个具体的、可被交易的制度基础——而越南不提供这个基础。

这是"领域迁移失败"的教科书案例：一个人在系统A中封神的全部特质，在系统B中变成致命缺陷。乔布斯在产品上的偏执在人际关系中是毒药；拿破仑的战役天才在俄国的雪地里变成空转。约翰逊不是在越南失败的——他是被自己的天才在越南背叛了。Caro对此只说"我还在想明白"：这种公开的未知本身，就是大师的印记。

一个附赠的微观发现

那个"凌晨5点我正躺着等你电话"的笑话，不是幽默——那是权力不对称下的被迫表演。下级必须用好心情承受支配，这个结构同样出现在职场、家庭虐待、宫廷政治里。一句玩笑的内核，是整个权力几何学的截面。

📝 转录文本

On Johnson's Power: Persuasion vs. Leverage

Interviewer: Master of the Senate, you make two points about how Johnson is effective, or at least this is the way I read it. One is that he is very persuasive if you're talking to him.

Caro: Yes.

Interviewer: The other is he's put himself in a position of leverage such that he has things to promise you or things to threaten you with. So, it's not that he's convinced you of anything, but you know that you need his favor if you want to be successful.

Caro: Exactly.

Interviewer: And of the two, I'm curious — which was really the source of his power, his leverage or his persuasion?

Caro: Behind his persuasion was the power. When you were talking to him, if he asked something of you, you knew he had the power behind him to give you or deny you things that you wanted. Say he was asking a senator something for a vote on a specific issue. The senator might not agree with him, might not want to give him the vote, but he would know he wants a committee assignment. Johnson has the power to give him that or not. Or he would know he wants a specific law, and Johnson has the power to get that law passed or not.

So behind everything — when Johnson is talking to you and he puts his arm around you and he leans into you — it's not just the force of his personality that he's bringing to bear on you. Behind that personality, you know, he has the power to do things to you or for you that you better be aware of.

On Means of Ascent and Coke Stevenson

Interviewer: Means of Ascent, the book about the election with Coke Stevenson, the 1948 Senate election —

Caro: Yes.

Interviewer: — that is my favorite book perhaps ever. And you paint such a compelling portrait of this person Coke Stevenson, you know, governor of Texas. They called him Mr. Texas.

Caro: Yes.

Interviewer: As you were writing his profile and writing this book, did part of you wish that he had won the Senate election?

Caro: You couldn't help — well, I'll answer you directly. The answer is yes. I think Coke Stevenson, although he was an idealist, he knew how to get things done. When he was governor of Texas, he really accomplished things. I think if he went to the Senate, he would have been a great senator and accomplished things. So you wish that he had won. You feel the tragedy that he lost because of the way he lost.

You know, the thing about Coke Stevenson — he really didn't realize someone could do all the things to him in the election that Lyndon Johnson did. He didn't come to grips with that.

A Counterfactual: Kennedy Wins, Johnson Stays as Majority Leader

Interviewer: Suppose that Kennedy wins in '60 but Johnson refuses the vice presidency, so he's still majority leader. How different do you think the bills that Kennedy would pass under Johnson as majority leader would be from the laws that Johnson as president was eventually able to pass? That is to say, the things that happened in '64 and '63 and '65 — would they have just happened earlier?

Caro: No. Because Kennedy did not have the overriding desire to change America. We see — no, John Kennedy was utterly charming. He was a good president. He was good in foreign policy, where Johnson certainly was not. But what he did not have was this vision, this desire to change America that Lyndon Johnson had.

Lyndon Johnson comes back from his year teaching the poor kids in Cotulla determined to change the education system, to help poor people more, to do all these other things to help poor people. That determination is something that's really unique. It's what made him domestically such a great president — that we have all these civil rights laws, these anti-poverty laws that we wouldn't have had without Lyndon Johnson.

His presidency ends in tragedy because of foreign policy, because of Vietnam. But he has this idea — it's almost unique. You say, "Gee, he's determined to do this. You know, he's going to find a way to do it." You watch him doing it. Then his attention turns to Vietnam, and everything falls apart, and his presidency is ruined. The things he started out to do domestically don't get done in the way he would have done them.

But he starts out after the election with the education laws, with the anti-poverty bills, to change the country. And he's on his way to doing it. That's the great tragedy of Johnson in Vietnam.

On Vietnam: The Open Question

Interviewer: If I can ask about that — and it's okay if you don't want to talk about this because it's in the next book — but if you're willing to talk about it, fundamentally, why did Johnson keep escalating even when —

Caro: Oh, you know, the answer to your question is I'm still trying to figure that out right now. So I'm not going to —

Interviewer: Fine. 'Cause that's quite a mystery, you know.

Caro: Okay.

On Inexhaustible Energy: Will or Constitution?

Interviewer: One of the things that's true of both Johnson and Moses is this inexhaustible energy — you know, working 16 hours a day, sometimes even more than that. And I wonder how much you think that is the fact that they had a different constitution, that they just had different reserves of energy, or do you think it was just their will was so strong?

Caro: I think it's just their will. I mean, a lot of people have their energy. You know, when you see Robert Moses sleeping very little, showing that he'd do anything to get his way, to get things done — being tired of something doesn't even seem to figure into the equation.

Sometimes — I can't remember one off the top of my head — but you say, he's making this call, and Johnson's making this call at 2 and 3:00 in the morning. He's up making these calls to get his way.

In fact, there's a funny anecdote. One senator — Johnson calls him at 5:00 a.m. to ask him for his vote on something, and the senator says, "Oh, Lyndon, I was just lying here waiting for your call." [laughter]

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

item.title: [Latent Space] How Arca Handles a $100,000 Tax Bill With AI and Human Approval — Aman Singh
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

Arca 的反直觉系统性真相

一、最深的护城河不是 AI，而是"成为那家公司"本身

大多数人以为 Arca 的优势在于模型选型和 harness 工程。但仔细听 Aman 的措辞——"We are not a SaaS company. We are the firm itself"——真正的战略选择是放弃成为工具供应商，才能获得标准化工作流的主权。这是一个 Conway's Law 的反向利用：组织结构决定了软件结构，那就重新设计组织，让工作流原生可被 agent 解析。

一个让人意外的推论是：Arca 的核心产品其实不是 AI 顾问，而是"一套可被 agent 参与的、被重构过的财富管理 SOP"。模型是可替换的（他们从 Gemini → OpenAI → Anthropic 漂移过），但这套被重写成 agent-friendly 结构的业务流程不可替换。这与 Stripe、Shopify 等 SaaS 的逻辑完全相反——他们卖抽象层给企业；Arca 买下企业，把抽象层留给自己。

二、Agent 会"做梦"——这个词选得太精准了

Aman 用了一个容易被忽略的词："there's a really sort of dreaming process that reflects on the state of the world as it relates to Richard"。这不是浪漫的比喻，而是精确的技术类比。

跨领域连接：神经科学中的睡眠记忆巩固（memory consolidation during sleep）——海马体在睡眠时将短期事件重放、筛选、整合进新皮质的长期语义记忆。Arca 的"dreaming agent"做的正是同构操作：把当天分散的信号（邮件、电话、交易）重放、提炼，更新到长期客户状态记忆中。

这揭示了一个真正惊人的系统性真相：当你的 agent 处理周为单位的任务时，你会被迫重新发明生物大脑已经演化出的记忆架构。短期工作记忆（当前邮件线程）、情景记忆（10 天任务时间线）、语义记忆（客户是谁）、以及最关键的——离线整合过程。所谓"long-horizon agents"的真正瓶颈不是上下文窗口，而是 sleep architecture。

三、最反直觉的发现：AI 让合规变得更好，而不是更差

这是整段访谈中最违反公众直觉的声明："AI is tireless at finding even the smallest mention of a non-compliant piece of writing." 媒体叙事里 AI 是合规的威胁，但在 Arca 内部，AI 是比人类更严厉的合规执行者——因为它不疲劳、不共情、不被客户关系污染判断。

这里有一个更深的、Aman 没有明说但你能听出来的洞见：他们把金融行业的"信任"重新切片了。传统 advisor 卖的是"我是你的人、我站在你这边"的信任。而 Arca 把信任拆成两层：外层是人类顾问的温度和同理心（empathy layer），内层是 agent 群的冷酷精确（rigor layer）。客户只看到外层。这种"双层信任架构"是传统行业无法复制的——你不能把一个有 20 年客户关系的 advisor 变成冷血审计员，但你可以让 AI 从一开始就扮演那个角色。

四、一个不易察觉的脆弱点：Meta-Agent 无法保持 Meta

Aman 轻描淡写地提到一句话值得停下来细读："Agents will make really nasty prompt changes if you leave them do it. Every little fix becomes the whole prompt. They're unable to stay meta and kind of generalize the fix."

这是 LLM 自我改进领域一个被低估的根本性限制：模型擅长局部补丁，无法保持抽象层级。每遇到一个 bug，它的本能是把这个具体 case 写进 prompt，而不是把它泛化为一条规则。这与人类工程师犯的最常见错误完全一致——用 if-else 应对本应用策略解决的问题。

跨领域连接：这与 Douglas Hofstadter 在《哥德尔、艾舍尔、巴赫》里讨论的"strange loop"难题同构——一个系统很难稳定地站在自身之上来修改自身。Arca 保留"human engineer in the loop"去审核 prompt 变更，不是出于保守，而是因为当前模型架构在元认知层面存在结构性缺陷。谁能解决这个问题，谁就拥有下一代 agent 系统的 compounding advantage。

五、一个预言：下一个护城河是"审计日志作为训练数据"

一个几乎没人提到的细节：Arca 把人类在 UI 上的每一次操作也当作 agent 的输入信号。"If you change something in the UI that affects the client, we'll log that action... it could also be used to inform the agent that that happened."

这意味着他们正在悄悄积累一种独特的数据资产：人类专家在做财富管理决策时的完整行为轨迹，与 agent 建议的 diff 对照记录。这不是普通的 RLHF，这是 "专家工作流程的像素级时间序列"。五年后，当监管或市场要求 AI 顾问证明"为什么推荐这个方案"时，谁拥有这种行为级别的专家数据，谁就能训练出无法被复制的垂直模型。合规驱动的审计日志，意外地变成了最有价值的训练语料。

📝 转录文本

Introduction: Arca and the AI Platform Team

We're here at the AI Engineer New York conference 2026, and I'm here with Aman Singh from Arca. Arca recently raised $64 million as an AI-native wealth management firm. First of all, Aman, can you tell us a bit about your role at Arca and the financial services you provide, and how you're using AI agents to run them?

Yeah, for sure. Thanks for having me.

My role at Arca is that I lead the AI platform team. So we're building the underlying sort of harness and our capabilities to kind of run the business with AI, which is our ultimate goal.

In terms of the services that we provide to our clients, this is a broad spectrum of financial services. So that includes sort of financial advice, financial planning for their assets, and sort of tax planning and insurance and estate planning as people get wealthier. Maybe you are someone who just sold a business, for example, and there's lots of complexities with all the different partners, etc., right? So we can help you think through that. We also have clients that are, you know, really large technology executives that are trying to figure out a real plan for retiring early, right? And also small families that are trying to buy their first home, for example.

The Role of AI: Replacing Work Around the Advisor, Not the Advisor

The clients that you have so far — do you have to kind of talk them through using agents and why you're using agents, and tell them a little bit about the technology behind it?

Yeah. So the role of AI at Arca is not to replace the advisor. It is to replace all of the work around the advisor. So our clients don't really interface with AI directly. All they experience is a level of service that has not been possible in this industry before, delivered through the empathy and care of a human advisor.

So we're building the machinery behind every client that's constantly thinking about: what is the market doing and how does it impact Richard? What else is going on in your life? What are the textures of your life that impact your finances? And we're able to be way more proactive, way more responsive, and just deliver a better kind of level of client service using AI that does all of the back office stuff.

Model Selection and Internal Benchmarks

Which models are you using to power your agents, and how do you decide which model is best for which action?

Yeah. So today we're using the frontier models from the frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI. Claude has been kind of our primary model, but we've gone through several iterations of models over the years. We used to be in Gemini way back when, and then OpenAI, and then Anthropic.

What's guiding all of our decisions are our benchmarks that we have internally for all of the various capabilities of our general harness that it has to express in running our business. And so, just recently for example, despite the external benchmarks claiming great things for Luna, it didn't really quite work out for us as well as we had expected. It was way too slow or and it was costing a lot.

So our internal benchmarks kind of guide our model decisions. And as a principle, we want to be model agnostic and sort of not take a dependency on a certain provider or certain harness from one of these labs, and kind of keep that optionality open for us.

A Model-Agnostic Harness and Tiered Routing

So you just mentioned harnesses. Are you using different harnesses depending on which model you're using?

No, we have our own kind of built internally that is model agnostic.

When your financial advisor is doing something like a taxation report, how does the harness decide which model to use? Is that automated?

Well, yes. We have certain tiers of models based on different complexities of tasks. So a task like assisting with a tax plan or doing a tax analysis would get our heaviest tier of models. Inside of that tier, it is a little bit flexible — you could use an Opus-tier model, or a Sonnet-tier model, or a heavy GPT model.

There's a lot of background activity that our agents are participating in, right? That is using a lower tier of model based on the complexity of the task. So that's kind of how we make decisions on which model serves which task.

Is it the financial advisor that's actually making that decision while they're using the product?

Not really. They're not aware of the happening. We've abstracted this away from them entirely. They just interact with our product as they would, and those decisions are made internally by us.

The $100K Tax Bill: A 10-Day Agentic Workflow

In your presentation at the conference earlier today, you talked about a tax bill example. Could you walk us through an example of adjusting a client's investment portfolio — from identifying a need to rebalance to executing trades? What parts of that process does the agent do, and what parts does the human advisor do?

Right. Um, so just like in the talk, this is a thing that will span 10 days. Agents are ultimately responsible for delivering that outcome, but there are certain parts that they do and certain parts that they do not.

In this example, when the client emails us with this whole tax bill, there's a piece of the analysis of: where is this client's money allocated today? And what is the most optimal way to liquidate some of that to produce $100,000? That is best suited for agents to take on as an analysis task. So they do exactly that.

Do they have certain limits though — they can't execute a trade?

So the analysis part is fully automated, but they're unable to actually execute any sort of money movement or liquidation automatically. We have a very deep integration with our custodian that actually gives us APIs to be able to do that, but we have strict guardrails around human-in-the-loop for things that would either move money, or liquidate assets, or even directly communicate with our end clients — because there's a level of service and quality that we expect.

All of the internal analysis will be done by agents, but they will also pull in the right person to be able to execute the trade when needed. They'll give the person a plan that they're able to review and kind of adjust, and go from there.

Long-Horizon Memory and the "Dreaming" Process

You mentioned these processes tend to be 10 days or a longer running time than most agent stuff these days. So when an agent resumes a task maybe days later, how do you restore and check that the plan still fits the client's needs?

Yeah, this is an interesting one to think about. We have tons of signals like I described in the talk. For example, you can imagine there's an email thread that is receiving responses and there's chatter happening, right? Any additional response to that goes to the same agent that's kind of reading that email thread and reacting to it.

But a fresh signal — like a phone call that was made in the middle — is a brand new signal that isn't attached with any other ongoing process. So there's a fresh agent that wakes up to figure out what this means.

The way they understand what is happening right now is our internal memory systems. We have this persistence of, for every client: what is happening right now, what are we trying to service, who owns what, what has happened so far, what are we tracking for next, what needs to happen immediately in the next couple of days, what are we tracking for the long term, which individual is responsible for which action. All of this is being tracked by our memory systems that our agents contribute to.

But also, there is a kind of really sort of dreaming process that reflects on the state of the world as it relates to Richard, the client, and is able to kind of update these memory systems to persist long-horizon tasks. So that agent that received a new signal quickly ramps up on what the situation is with the client, and it'll know: okay, we're actually executing a big tax bill. My signal relates to that tax bill, so let me contribute to the state of that world.

Safety: Deterministic Guardrails at Capability Edges

Can you talk about the safety aspects you've built onto your product to make sure no money is lost along the way?

Yeah. All of our safety restrictions are fully deterministic, and they take the decision making off the agent's hands.

For example, certain tools let the agent execute the tool itself. So if it's a simple record-keeping kind of tool, it will execute it. We also, every time a tool is called that writes data, we have LLM-based verification running on that action — fast LLM calls that analyze every single write to our database. That's another layer of verification we're running.

Then we also ingest a lot of external information: emails coming in, documents coming in, phone calls being made, which are targets for prompt injection. So we run verifications at the edges that detect presence of certain flavors of prompt injection.

Anytime data leaves our system — for example, in a web search in the most obvious case, but also if we're sending a calendar invite to Richard, right? That's external data — we have both deterministic checks on presence of certain information that we know is PII, but also a consensus of small models that ensure there isn't any kind of data exfil being attempted.

So we have tons of different guardrails built into the harness with the principle that we want to contain them at the edges of capability, and not earlier than that.

Auditability by Default

Because you're in the financial industry, are there certain regulations required in terms of the technology you're using? Or is it more about outcomes?

Yeah, the industry cares about outcomes, but compliance cares about auditability. Our system is such that auditability is by default.

Every single action that an agent takes produces a change log of what changed, who changed it, from which part of the system, and when. And this applies not just to agents, by the way. It applies to human actors as well. So if you change something in the UI that affects the client, we'll log that action.

It lets us both get auditability by default, but also powers some of our agentic capabilities — where the same thing that tracks a UI change also could be used to inform the agent that that happened. So auditability has been a big part of our story, both for compliance with regulation, but also for our agentic loop.

"Agents Prompt People More Than People Prompt Agents"

In your presentation you had a nice line: "Agents prompt people more than people prompt agents." How do the agents decide who to involve, and how much context to provide?

Yeah, another interesting one. This is similar to how humans work in our industry. There is a process that we're tracking over 10 days. There's multiple actors involved. The actor at step seven may not need to know about this just yet; they're pulled in at the right time.

So our agents, with our long memory persistence plus the daily reflection on what is happening, reflect on where the state of the world is at the moment. They're able to pull in the right person at that time when there's a signal that implies that person must be pulled in.

All of this is work that we have done to operationalize the context of how this industry works. But not just that — but how does Arca want it to work? And what are our principles of how work happens in this industry?

That is another advantage of us being, sort of, not just a SaaS company. We're actually not a SaaS company. We are the firm ourselves. So we can standardize the way this work even happens, so that our agents can participate in standard ways that work must happen.

On Anthropic's Managed Agents, and Why Owning Intelligence Matters

Earlier in the conference, Anthropic did a workshop about their managed agents infrastructure. Do you foresee using that type of functionality, given the risk that the human is not always in the loop?

I think we are very bullish on the models from Anthropic and labs like OpenAI, but less so on taking a dependency on a product like managed agents.

Because managed agents — one of their key things is how the models persist and contribute memory as to what is happening in the world, and all of the operational knowledge that they need to use to be successful. Letting them own that part of the business is kind of a risk, because owning that is owning your intelligence, is owning the ability to impact the business. If you hand off the intelligence to another provider, you lose some of that control that you need to build something that is unique and tailored to your business to such a great degree that it can actually impact your business.

Anthropic has also recently released financial services, partnering with firms. Do you think what they're doing is competitive to what you're trying to do, or different things?

Yeah, I think Anthropic getting into our kind of industry is very validating for our industry. But the way I think about it is that it is very different to be a services firm that has access to AI tools versus a firm that was built to be AI native.

The firm with AI tools requires their users to prompt the agents to produce work or to do work. But here, like I said, at Arca agents prompt people more than people prompt agents, and it is a proactive kind of service that is running for them 24/7. It's kind of running the business in the most standard way that we expect, at the level of service that we aspire to. Which looks very different if you're a company with AI tools.

Sandboxed Code Execution and Artifact Verification

Can you explain what in your processes runs inside a sandbox, and how you verify a change to a financial plan before anyone acts on it?

Yeah. The way we use sandboxes is that the sandbox is one component of our harness. Our agent isn't actually inside of the sandbox. It uses the sandbox to offload computation, and we've built systems to make it safe for code inside of that sandbox to access our data.

We have this thing which translates the code it wrote into a strict format that we expect, throw away the code, and instill guardrails on that format before it reaches your back end. So we allow the agents to use code to query our data — which means they can aggregate it, munch it, work with it as they see fit — to produce a thing like a financial plan.

Inside of the same sandbox, they produce these beautiful artifacts that we can share with clients — like a PDF of "here's your financial plan and here's how we're planning to approach your life financially." Once that is produced is where we run our verifiers.

It's a certain type of artifact that is produced from the sandbox. The moment that is produced, we run a bunch of different verifications on it. Some deterministic — that check for presence of things like, "Hey, did you just put a raw account number in there? You should not do that." So deterministically we can check that. But also fast models — like the smaller models, or Jeb — to analyze for presence of things that might make this artifact non-compliant. For example, you really should not be promising returns in that artifact. So that's another thing that we'll check before it is publishable.

The last thing I'll say on that is that doing this actually makes our compliance better than if humans were doing it, because AI is tireless at finding even the smallest mention of a non-compliant piece of writing in there. So we'll continue to invest in more of that and constrain at the capability edges.

Decision Models for Financial Accuracy

You mentioned Jeb there. What other decision model products are you looking at?

Yeah. What we noticed is: when models are working with financial data, when they're answering questions that require financial knowledge, they are very confident in the knowledge that they have.

A small example is that models will very happily use the tax brackets from 2025 to come up with an analysis and be like, "all right, that is it." But that is obviously incorrect.

So that is one of the ways in which we're using decision models in our harness — to check when the model is about to make a financial recommendation or anything that requires financial rigor. It'll detect and will nudge the model to use our knowledge base of verified facts about the world that is true today, or use their web search. This is a point about the harness — and owning the harness — that lets you do things like this that help your models be accurate where it matters.

Do you use decision models for recovery, for example if a trade fails to execute?

No, not today. That is not a use case that we're exploring today.

If a trade does fail, how does the agent recover at the moment?

At the moment, we are not doing autonomous trading with agents. It is very much a — the agents will propose that we make trades. It is fully up to our experts to figure out if that is the right trade to be making, and to execute the trade.

Feedback Loops: Edits and Cancellations as Evals

Your slides say that every staff edit or cancellation comes with a "why" and becomes an eval. How does that feedback get turned back into the system as a measurable improvement?

Yeah. That is another one of the advantages of us being the business and not a SaaS company — we have the ability to require them to give us feedback.

The way we loop the feedback back into improvements is something that you would expect: all of that feedback gets piped into a data store that couples that feedback with the trace of the agent that produced it. We're able to take that trace, put it next to the feedback, and every night we run this process where we collect traces from the real world from our agents in the wild, and run a meta agent on top that suggests changes to our harness. Maybe tools that were misleading, or things that errored, or there's missing knowledge in our knowledge base — they'll surface this information to us and then we'll be able to improve it.

Today we still have a human engineer in the loop before we actually ship a prompt change. I've noticed that agents will make really nasty prompt changes if you leave them to do it. Every little fix becomes the whole prompt. They're unable to stay meta and generalize the fix into a prompt that generalizes.

But yeah, we have feedback loops from our product that we collect directly as first-class product features to collect evals and turn them into improvements.

Operational Knowledge as Agent Context

You also mentioned turning knowledge of how a firm works into agent context. What does that look like for your company technically, and how do you keep it up to date?

Yeah. We have a knowledge base of files that is represented as files, and the way we keep that up to date is we've handed it to our experts to curate and update. So it is a first-class feature in our product.

On the left-hand side there's a tab called Knowledge, which has the full operational context that our agents are using. And as they work on things, they're able to cite knowledge. So it creates this loop of like, oh, we notice that the knowledge is incorrect — and that gets surfaced to us in our trace analysis. And because it is a part of the product itself, people are able to go in and edit the skill directly. That's how it kind of works.

A Client Example: Discovering Hidden Fees and a Non-Fiduciary Advisor

Can you give an example of a client that's had a measurable improvement through the agent system, and some details about what in the agent architecture helped them?

Yeah, I'll give you a recent example. This person wasn't a client yet, but they were at the point of becoming a client. So we had all of their documents, their statements, their current investments, et cetera.

This person was already working with an advisor. They meet with us, they tell us that "hey, I have this advisor already. They're charging me $1,500 for their services, and they're not very responsive to me. So I'm chatting with you."

Our agents have read through all of those documents, analyzed them, analyzed what the person's goals are that they state. They've also analyzed the statement of who this current advisor is, and how much they're charging them. And they discover that there are fees that this person was charging them that they weren't aware of. They surface this to them, and make them not only aware of the fact that they're being overcharged, but also aware that that person wasn't even a fiduciary — so they're not obligated to act in their interests.

This is the sort of attention to detail that our agents bring about when they're analyzing a financial picture, that would not have been possible if we didn't have these. There are several examples of proactivity that our agents produce: someone has a deadline coming up, or they're at risk of missing their RMD, or that kind of thing. This is difficult at scale for humans to keep track of, but it is the default behavior of our agents at Arca.

Wonderful. That's probably a good point to stop at. So thank you very much, Aman, for joining us.

Thank you for having me.

item.description:
# Arca 的反直觉系统性真相
## 一、最深的护城河不是 AI，而是"成为那家公司"本身
大多数人以为 Arca 的优势在于模型选型和 harness 工程。但仔细听 Aman 的措辞——"We are not a SaaS company. We are the firm itself"——真正的战略选择是**放弃成为工具供应商，才能获得标准化工作流的主权**。这是一个 Conway's Law 的反向利用：组织结构决定了软件结构，那就重新设计组织，让工作流原生可被 agent 解析。
一个让人意外的推论是：**Arca 的核心产品其实不是 AI 顾问，而是"一套可被 agent 参与的、被重构过的财富管理 SOP"**。模型是可替换的（他们从 Gemini → OpenAI → Anthropic 漂移过），但这套被重写成 agent-friendly 结构的业务流程不可替换。这与 Stripe、Shopify 等 SaaS 的逻辑完全相反——他们卖抽象层给企业；Arca 买下企业，把抽象层留给自己。
## 二、Agent 会"做梦"——这个词选得太精准了
Aman
