item.title: [Latent Space] Building ChatGPT for Finance — Joseph Kim, OpenAI's Head of Financial Services
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

洞察：ChatGPT for Finance 这场对话里，被低估的几个结构性暗流

一、"95% 可被创业公司复制"——OpenAI 高管亲口承认的护城河真相

Joseph 轻描淡写地说出了一句本不该从 OpenAI 产品负责人嘴里讲出来的话："我们建的东西里，95% 一家创业公司完全能做。" 这不是谦虚，而是一种战略定位的无声宣言。

真正值得玩味的是：他把模型能力和产品构建解耦到了近乎残酷的程度——"我的团队在 OpenAI 内部就像一个基于 OpenAI 搭建的创业公司"。这等于承认：模型智能是公共基础设施，产品差异化 100% 来自那剩下的 20%——数据、UI、集成、垂直 know-how。换句话说，OpenAI 的产品部门和它的 API 客户在竞争时，并没有太多"内部作弊"的空间。

出人意料的结论是：ChatGPT for Finance 的发布，本质上是 OpenAI 画给生态开发者的一张地图——"这是我能走到的地方，而你从同一个起点出发并没有慢多少"。这对 Bloomberg、FactSet 这类拿着独家数据的垂直玩家，反而是利好信号而非威胁。

二、MCP 的 40% 错误率，是"去中心化神话"又一次撞墙

这是整场对话里最反直觉的一段：Joseph 原本想通过 MCP connector 调用金融数据，结果一些大牌数据源的 MCP 实际错误率超过 40%，最终 OpenAI 被迫把数据"收回自营"。

这里有一个非常漂亮的跨领域连接：这几乎是 2015 年前后微服务浪潮 剧本的重演。当年业界对"把 monolith 拆成几十个服务"抱着宗教般的热情，但真正扩展到生产后，Netflix、Uber 都发现跨服务错误率、尾延迟、调试噩梦让"理论优雅"崩塌，于是出现了"macro-services"和服务网格的回潮。

MCP 现在正处在同一个曲线的早期：协议标准化的美学，正在被生产级可靠性反噬。OpenAI 用"重新 bundle 数据"的选择，其实是在替整个 Agent 生态发出一个预警——分布式智能体架构会在"信任边界"处首先溃败，而不是在"模型能力"处。那些现在押注"全连接 MCP 生态会自动繁荣"的创业公司，可能正在建造一座尚未验证地基的大厦。

三、银行的垂直层级，被重新发现为一套"对抗验证网络"

Joseph 谈到如何为 AI agent 设计安全模型时，给出了一个几乎可以进哲学系的观察：junior analyst → associate → VP → MD 这套古老的投行层级，本质不是官僚主义，而是一套对抗性误差纠正网络。每一层存在的意义就是审读、扰动、挑错下一层的产出。

这个洞察的真正威力在于它的跨域迁移： - 科学界的 peer review 是同一结构； - 代码评审 + CI/CD + staged rollout 是同一结构； - 司法体系的一审/二审/再审 是同一结构； - 甚至免疫系统的 B 细胞成熟过程（亲和力成熟）也是同一结构——低亲和力版本先出手，高质量版本层层筛选。

所以 OpenAI 正在做的事，不是"给 AI 加护栏"，而是把人类社会几千年用来对抗自身出错的组织拓扑，直接复刻给 agent 群体。这暗示着一件比产品发布重要得多的事：未来的多 agent 系统，架构范式不会来自分布式计算理论，而会来自组织社会学。

四、一个几乎没人注意到的反转：RLHF 回到了它的出发点

Joseph 顺口提到："最早的 RLHF 本来就是训 taste 的，后来大家搞 verifiable rewards，就把这个传统忘了。"

这是一条被压缩的历史。2022 年 ChatGPT 的突破靠的是 pairwise 人类偏好；2023–2025 的推理突破靠的是可验证奖励（数学题对错、代码能不能跑）；而 2026–2027 的下一跳——幻灯片审美、投资直觉、"模型手感"——居然要回到 pairwise 人类评分。

这是 AI 发展第一次公开承认：有些能力不能通过 verifier 路线暴力解决，必须回头去问人类"你更喜欢哪一个"。 一个意外的推论：最稀缺的训练资源，可能不再是 token、GPU 或数据，而是"高品味的人类评审员"——P99.9 水平的投行 MD、顶尖设计师、资深交易员的时间。这会倒逼出一个新市场：专家级人类偏好标注，价格可能比普通数据标注高两个数量级。

五、彩蛋级观察：OpenAI 的 eval 盲区揭示了一种"科研偏见"

Joseph 轻描淡写地说了一句值得单独加红的话："如果 eval 数字看起来好，研究员就默认模型变强了、不去查；只有数字变差才会去查。" GPT-6 的金融 eval 因此被发现"早就 saturated 了，剩下答错的题其实是答案本身错了"。

这几乎是科学哲学教科书级别的确认偏误，而它正发生在世界上最先进的 AI 实验室内部。推论令人不安：我们现在用来判断"模型变强"的那些榜单，有多少其实是坏答案在给坏分数？这为财经领域的 benchmark 创业留下了一个巨大的套利窗口——谁能先造出不会被自己保佑的 eval，谁就在给整个行业提供校准服务。

📝 转录文本

Building ChatGPT for Finance — Joseph Kim, OpenAI's Head of Financial Services

Channel: Latent Space · YouTube link

Cold Open

"I really do think that there's going to be a billion dollar business built on top of a ChatGPT plugin. But 95% of what we built was something that absolutely a startup could do, another company could do."

"At OpenAI, we ran into problems with pre-training and therefore had difficulty scaling the model. In 2026, we've been able to solve many of these issues."

[music]

Introduction

Host: Today we have Joseph Kim, one of the heads of ChatGPT Finance from OpenAI, and our co-host and head of editorial from Latent Space, Richard, in the studio. It's a special episode. We're here in New York at AI Finance. Joseph just gave a great keynote. I think we don't want to repeat most of the information, so honestly go watch it, but give like a 30-second of what you talked about, and then we'll leave the breadcrumbs — you guys can go watch the keynote.

Joseph: Sure, yeah, I can give a quick 30-second intro to kind of what we just chatted about.

One, I would say — we just released a new product, ChatGPT for Financial Services. This is an enterprise-focused product that's really trying to bring the power — mix the power — of ChatGPT, kind of the tools and things that you really like to use in the consumer product, but also add in the enterprise layer so that firm-specific templates, you know, sources like Dilupa, S&P, etc. And so really exciting. We've been working with our design partners Morgan Stanley and Evercore on that, and reception to that's been incredible. So that was kind of the first half of the talk.

And in the second half of the talk, really much more forward-looking — so thinking deeply about some of the trendlines that we're seeing in terms of model improvements, and drawing those trendlines out to the future, and trying to think a little about: okay, like what are these models going to be able to do at the end of mid-2027, end of 2027, and what does that mean for folks that are building products on top of that model, and how can you kind of start to plan ahead to the intelligence that's coming in, you know, just a matter of months.

Research First, Deployment Second: Building a Finance-Specific Product

Host: I think it's a fun time because you actually come from the research side of things. So you now lead a lot of the product and engineering, but tell us what it takes to make a financial-specific product. You mentioned in the keynote that there was sort of an uptick in users when you launched ChatGPT Work. So Codex started to become available to the masses, people started using it for finance, and now you're shipping your first finance product. What is financial reasoning data like? What goes into finance-specific models?

Joseph: Yeah, it's a great question. I mean, one thing I will say is that all of the training data that we do for financial reasoning analysis, we do upstream into what we call the big run, which is the main run that becomes something like 6 Astra or 61 Astra, etc. And so, even though we're adding a bunch of financial data to the model, it's going into the main main model, and so therefore it's available to folks that want to build on top of it.

And that is something that's very important to us. At OpenAI, we really do want that intelligence to be accessible — not only to our products that we're building in-house in first-party ways, but also for folks that want to build startups, build businesses on top of that, as well as financial firms that want to integrate that directly into their companies. And so, we will make all that intelligence accessible there.

I think you touched a little bit on product and research, and I think that's really core to what we do at OpenAI. Internally, we call ourselves a research and deployment company. And so, what that means — and we kind of structure that in order on purpose — like research comes first, and then deployment comes second. And so, as we think about, at the end of the day, trying to change the way that people do knowledge work, we kind of work in that order, right? We think about the model capabilities, where they're headed, what kind of new things they enable. So that's one. And then two, we think very deeply about the product features and surface areas that we should build to make that model intelligence accessible to more people.

And I think you alluded to a slide in my keynote where we had this chart of Codex adoption within OpenAI. And it's funny because you can see the software engineering adoption curve, and it's just like up and to the right pretty steady — people are picking it up and incorporating it into their daily routines. But if you look at finance, legal, and sales, it's pretty much at zero, and suddenly it kind of jumps up to 90%. And if you look at that line and try to see what happened around the time where it jumped up, we had released Codex desktop app in February, and that was when that adoption jumped up. And so, I do think it kind of shows the importance of co-developing those things — and the purpose of the product is to make that model intelligence accessible to as many users as possible.

Lessons From Shipping Into Enterprise: The Data Problem

Host: So, in the uptick of data for using Codex for financial applications, what sort of things did you learn that you then applied into the post-training of financial data?

Joseph: Yeah, it's a good question. I could talk a little bit about how we went about building ChatGPT for Financial Services. It was very unique. We haven't built a whole lot of first-party products. I would say like Codex was really our biggest and main one, and it was the first time we developed a product where the product, the model harness, and the research was all kind of under one house and under one roof — and it really gives us a lot of flexibility to go about building things.

The biggest takeaway that I have from having worked on this for the last 6 months or so is: in enterprise, you have to deal with the reality of the industry that you're in and go build around that. And I think that piece is easy to ignore. Like if you just think about it from first principles, you can come to a conclusion that makes sense, and you talk about it, and you can defend it with logic and reason. But if you ignore the state of the world that you're in when you start building, and the forces that are at play within the industry — either competitive forces, people have their own objectives — if you just don't think about that, you're not going to build the right product, right?

And so, we saw that with ChatGPT for Financial Services. We thought about that a lot.

The MCP Reality Check

I'll give you one example. Data. Data is like a huge part of how we thought about building the product. And data was one of those things where on first principles it was a little bit tough when I was talking about working on this product to defend — because you say, "Hey, like I want to go and bring quarterly earnings transcripts into the product and bundle it." And the first thing people are going to say is, "Look, there's an MCP connection in the store. What is the incremental value that you're providing by bundling that in? On paper it looks bad — they can already have a license for it, so they might feel like they're paying twice for it. And they might have an MCP. So why are you building this?"

And the reality is: we went and we tested all these MCPs. And what we found was the error rates were really, really high. Some of the MCPs that we connected — some big names — 40%-plus error rate on their MCPs. And so MCPs is one of those things where it looks great on paper, but you have to go look at the data and see what's actually going on.

And so for data we're like, "Hey look, this is really bad. The only way we can go about fixing this at scale is to bring the data in house, control that experience end to end." And the extra money that you pay on top to bundle that data is worth it. And so that was a product decision that we had to make that was very industry specific. And it's been resonating with customers. Customers love it — the number one thing they call out is the data. And so it worked.

Best Practices for Building a Vertical AI Product

Host: So, you had good success in this. Tell us about the technical side of things for people building a harness adaptation for a specific service. You guys went out, you changed Codex, you did post-training, you did whatever you did to make ChatGPT for Financial Services. If someone was to do the same for another domain — say legal, sales, whatever — what are the best practices there? What did you learn? What goes into just taking off-the-shelf and actually making a certain product around it?

Joseph: Yeah, I like the question a lot. I tried to allude to this in my keynote as well, but the interesting thing is — it's fun to talk about the post-training stuff because it's unique to what we do, and it gets people excited — but 95% of what we built was something that absolutely a startup could do, another company could do. And we didn't really have to go leverage our ability to make changes in the model to go about building a fantastic product.

So I think it's a great call to mention that piece. What I would say is twofold.

Standing on the Shoulders of Codex

One is most of the product that we built was built on top of the Codex — or I should say ChatGPT now — plugin architecture and plugin primitives. And that is something that we've been investing a lot of time and energy in.

OpenAI is an interesting company where we kind of face the same problems internally that a startup would face if they were to build on top of OpenAI. So in a lot of ways, like my team is kind of like a startup that's building on top of OpenAI technology. And so, even internally, we need to find scalable ways for teams like myself to stand on the shoulders of giants and build on top of Codex.

Codex is fantastic. It's got great memory, it's got good skills, there's a lot of things that are wonderful about Codex. But the thesis of my team was: Codex will get you about 80% of the way to a product that would be successful in the market, but the 20% is missing. And so we need to find some way for my team to go build that 20% to actually go win — because the other half of the thesis was: if you just took Codex and launched it as a finance product, it would fail. And so that 20% is actually pivotal.

And so, we went and we built on top of the plugin architecture. It's using the same primitives that are available to any of the builders that want to go build on top of ChatGPT. And I had a line in my presentation — but I really do think that there's going to be a billion-dollar business built on top of a ChatGPT plugin. Like, you're going to be able to leverage all of that horizontal functionality and just add your secret sauce on top. And that secret sauce might be data, it might be UI changes, it could be an integration — but that secret sauce is really valuable, and I think there's a billion dollars worth of value to be built there.

Safety in a World of Increasingly Autonomous Agents

Richard: So, it's an interesting time for the industry because we're at a time now where orchestration is becoming a lot more automated, teams of agents going out and doing things. But for finance, obviously, there are a lot of risks involved in that. So, can you talk a bit about the safety sort of that you've baked into the product?

Joseph: Yeah, safety is super, super important. And it's only going to get more important because the agents are already getting more autonomous and more independent. And I think that trend we expect to continue into '27 and into '28.

The Human-in-the-Loop Product We Shipped

I would say for the product that we built and launched last month, there was a bunch of paradigms that already existed as it pertains to safety — being thoughtful around auditing the work, making sure that the model's not making a mistake that's going to impact business outcomes — and we were able to lean heavily into those.

What I would say is the existing product that we launched is a productivity tool for knowledge workers working in this space. And so the idea behind it is there's a deep assumption that there's always a human in the loop. The idea there is: you're a financial analyst and you have a laundry list of things you want to get done that day. And just like how a software engineer would do with Codex, for every one of those items, the first thing you do is try to build it with ChatGPT. And it might get you 30% of the way there, it might get you 80% of the way there, depending on the task — but there's always this presumption of humans in the loop that are presiding over that work.

And that made it very easy for us to build a product where we could kind of pass off the responsibility of auditing review into the people's hands and into people's responsibilities. And that worked for us well, and it was easy to communicate.

What Comes Next: Security Profiles That Look Like People

I will say, we're thinking very deeply about what comes next. And what comes next looks different than a productivity tool that sits and is always being monitored by a human. And I think as we think about what comes next, there's kind of two things we're thinking about.

One is how do we shape the security/safety profile of the product into something that people understand intuitively. And something that people understand very intuitively is how to work with other people. And so our thesis is: if we make the product very similar to how you work with your co-workers, your interns, people around you — that is something that people can pick up and learn very quickly, very easily. And therefore we need to shape the security profile of that to look like a person.

So there's a few things I'll call out there. One is there's this notion of read-write, even for people. Like, you're a new software engineer at a company — oftentimes, I was at Google, you need something called readability. And so, there's these kind of checks and balances and systems in place before you can start mucking around touching the system. And so there's already systems in place to monitor the work of people. So if models behave more like people, then you can leverage those systems. And that makes it very easy to kind of talk about and work through this with these financial institutions. So that's something we're leaning into pretty heavily coming up.

Borrowing the Banking Hierarchy as a Safety System

And the very last thing I would say is, at least in the context of banking, which is where we kind of started: there's already this system in place for junior analysts doing a lot of the groundwork → their work gets passed off to associates → associates are reviewing the work → the associates are adding their secret sauce, their magic, their reasoning → that gets passed off to the VP → VP goes up to the director, managing director. So there's this kind of hierarchical system where there's this implicit work-checking that's happening. That's already been built out to prevent against mistakes that humans make — like humans make just as many mistakes as models. And so there are systems built there. And so we're also leaning heavily on those systems as it pertains to building financial products.

Career-Ending Mistakes vs. Mistakes of Taste

Host: Okay. There's this sort of misconception where in the finance world, one mistake really compounds — like your whole career is at risk if you submit something wrong. How should people think about getting started in using it? If you're an analyst, how should you use these tools? And do you have any analogies towards where we're at right now? So there's like levels of self-autonomy in self-driving. One of your slides, I think, said "like 2027 you see no more PowerPoint." A lot of people will be using AI tools in the loop. So how should people think about where we are now and where things are going? And how should they adopt these tools if they have that misconception of "one mistake, my career's over"? Obviously there's human in the loop, but how should they also think about it going forward as they need to offload more and more?

Joseph: Yeah, that's wonderful. I have two perspectives on this, and they start with different assumptions. I think the notion that "my career's over if you make one mistake" is an incorrect notion. And I have a line of thought that follows that. But let's first assume that it's true.

If That Notion Were True

In the case that it's true, what I would say is: not all mistakes are created equally, and not all model capabilities are created equally. And so when you think about the mistake that a model or a human could make that could be career ending — it's usually once you get up to a certain level. Like if you're a VP, the stakes are higher than when you're a junior analyst, because there's a presumption of work having been checked up to that point. So if an MD sees a mistake, that's a huge problem. A lot of the safety nets have failed for that mistake to make it up to an MD.

But what I would say is: the career-ending mistake is something where you get a piece of information factually incorrect, and that piece of factual information changes the conclusion. That is obviously the biggest type of mistake that you can make. And what I would say is we're seeing a lot of progress in attention to detail. And hallucination used to be a big term that used to come up in 2022, 2023 — that doesn't come up nearly as often nowadays. We're starting to see huge improvements in the reliability of models as it pertains to factual mistakes.

So the egregious mistake that would get you fired — models are getting much better at, and continue to get much better. And so I feel actually quite confident that a combination of that continual improvement, plus the existing system checks in place, will make it such that the chance of that type of mistake propagating up to an MD is just very low probability.

The Real Frontier Is Taste

What I would say the models are lacking today, and they still need to improve, is actually not the career-ending mistake, but the bit that involves human judgment and taste. So it's "this slide looks ugly" — it's not wrong, but it's formatted — the colors look a little bit off, something about it looks sloppy, and therefore this is not a good slide. And that's not a career-ending mistake in the way that a factual mistake is, but it matters. It still matters in terms of how useful that work is.

And so, as we think about the progression going into 2027, what I would say is: I expect the model to get much better at the human taste component. And that's what I was kind of alluding to in my keynote — I think the model will get much better at human taste on things that are softer objective functions. It's not "is it right or wrong?" — it's comparative. "Is there something that's better than this?" And I think models are going to get much better along that dimension moving forward.

How Do You Train Taste Into a Model?

Richard: How so? How do we solve taste? How do we train taste into the models?

Joseph: Yeah. So, it's funny. Very early on in the early early ChatGPT days, the only thing we trained models on were essentially taste. Right? Like — there was reinforcement learning through human feedback. And the human feedback was always a pairwise signal: given two options, which one's better? And so the early days of reinforcement learning were built on the notion of training on human taste.

And then obviously things like verifiable rewards and environments — we built a lot of machinery to do other types of rewards and other types of RL. And so people kind of forgot that a lot of the early days of RL were all around human taste.

The Reward Model

So how do you train on human taste? I think the technical answer is quite simple. The practical answer obviously is more complicated. The practical answer is: you just train a reward model. You get a bunch of humans to look at pairs of things and say which one is better. And this still works.

Fun fact: we did this for our slides. Like, I mean, how do you go about making these models better at generating presentations? Well, we just get a bunch of humans to look at pairs of slides and say which one looks better. And humans are actually really, really good at aesthetic judgment — actually much better than models, is something that we discovered. A human can look at two slides and within seconds say this one looks better. And if you have a grading model try to go about doing that, it's going to spend a whole bunch of reasoning tokens — "this pixels this way, this thing's that" — and then maybe come to the wrong conclusion. And so humans are still really, really valuable in making these models better. And so we will rely a lot on human preference to imbue things like taste.

Coding as Precedent

The last thing I'll add is: there's precedent for this, which makes us confident that this strategy will work. And that precedent, I would say, is coding.

The models have gotten — I would say coding is not fully solved, but let's say we're 80% of the way there, and we're making progress on the last 20%. Coding is a combination of verifiable rewards and human taste. The verifiable rewards are: does the code compile? Are there syntax errors? Is the output of the function expected? So there's these verifiable rewards that are in place.

But a lot of good software engineering is: Is this clean system design? Did you build a system that's maintainable over time? Is it easy to unit test? Is it following paradigms that the vast majority of the community or the industry thinks is the right paradigm?

And if you look at it from that lens, a lot of financial work looks very similar. It's: "I have an Excel model — does it sum up? Are there reference errors?" There's a whole bunch of verifiable things that we can check to make sure that the work is passing the first-pass sanity check. But there's also a lot of: "is this the way I would have built this model?"

Something I learned about as I started working in finance is there's this notion of "the feel of the model", which is — you kind of perturb the inputs and you look at the outputs. And an experienced financial professional can perturb the inputs, look at the outputs, and kind of understand: does the data flow through this model in a way that feels good? And that is a human preference that looks a lot like "does this code look clean? Is it well written?" And I think our success in coding gives me confidence that we can solve a lot of these problems in finance as well.

Richard: Yeah, we can shout out a frontier code from Cognition. So it's not only like SWE-bench is very "is the answer correct?" — this is also "would you merge the code?" So you can have multiple answers that are proper PRs that pass, but which one would you merge? And that's why you sometimes see the charts of "lower reasoning is better" — but it's a taste benchmark as well.

Joseph: Yeah.

From Junior Analyst Tasks to Investment Thesis Generation

Richard: One of your other 2027 predictions I thought was interesting was that the models that you're training will become much better at investment thesis and generating ideas for investment and trading. Um, but obviously, that's something that humans are — well, experienced financial professionals are very good at, and they kind of have an intuition for that kind of thing — but it's often counter to the prevailing wisdom out there. Otherwise, there's less of a chance of it making a great return. So how are you tackling that problem in terms of training the agents to do that kind of work?

Joseph: Yeah. I would say that up until date, the vast majority of applications of AI in finance have been really focused on — I would say — the junior analyst's work. And I think that's for two reasons.

Why Products Have Clustered at the Junior Level

One is: you have to build the product based on the capabilities of the model of today. And so if you look at the capabilities of the model today, they're really quite good at taking pretty concrete instructions of what to do and executing. So: build me a slide, I want it to look this way, make it look good, use our template — these types of things. The model's quite capable of doing those things, and so therefore we've built product experiences around that.

The other thing I'll call out is: there's a strong preference to make the model good at things that humans are not good at or don't like to do. And so — most humans I talked to, there's obviously exceptions, but a lot of the humans I talked to — [laughter] — you know, they really don't like building Excel models. It's tedious work, it's very detail-oriented, it's easy to get wrong. And similarly with slides — you're copying logos, you're placing them very precisely on a specific part of the page. That's very tedious work that a lot of people don't like to do.

And so that's been part of the impetus for us to go and focus on some of these tasks. It's a combination of those two things: there's the existing model capability is pretty good at certain types of task, and also human preferences of what they like to do and not like to do helps drive the direction of the product as well.

Moving Up the Stack Into 2027

I think we've solved a lot of the low-hanging fruit of those two things. And so going into 2027, we're going to start to move up the stack. We're going to go from the tasks that a junior analyst can do, to some of the tasks that an associate can do, to some of the tasks that an MD would do, and move up that chain.

And as you move up the chain, what I would say is the objectives become much fuzzier. It goes from "this is clearly a good or bad slide" — or "something that we'd put in front of a client or not" — to: "well, I don't know if this investment idea is good. And it would take me 3 years of waiting to really be able to give you a clear concrete answer of what the market has done." And so the objectives start to become fuzzier. And so the way you go about training the model, and the way you think about how to make the model better — those things become more difficult. It becomes more difficult from a research perspective.

But it's not impossible, is what I would say. And so what it takes is a lot of research focus. It takes a lot of wonderful data. It takes a lot of feedback from experts in the field. We really want to get the P99.9 type of feedback to make the model as good as humans. But I don't think it's an insurmountable problem. What it takes is continued scaling of the base model, and focus — focus from the research labs who think that this is an important problem to go solve. And one of the things that I'm doing on my team is making this an area of focus and priority for OpenAI. And because of the combination of those two things, I feel confident we'll make a lot of strides in 2027.

Evals: The Hidden Bottleneck

Host: Do you have any comments on any of the current financial benchmarks? I think we're still in the state of "does this check out numbers-wise?" How do you think about making your own, adding in taste? I think this is also an open call for people working in this space to work on their own benchmarks. And a sort of follow-along to that is: you said build systems for models today, but you also give a lot of predictions for the future. How do you put guardrails, limitations, checks on financial services that you build for people today, just so they're confident in — you know — this is not like going off the rails?

Joseph: Yeah, makes sense. Let's talk a little bit about evals. Evals is something near and dear to my heart. I spend a lot of time working on evals.

The Prior: Good Evals Are Incredibly Hard

I would say that the prior that I would share with people is: building a good eval is incredibly hard. That's not obvious to people who haven't worked on an eval before. To build an eval that actually correlates with the thing that you're actually trying to measure — like the skill that you're trying to measure, capability you're trying to measure — very difficult. Because whatever you put together is just a proxy for whatever that thing is. And it's just one dimension. So that's one.

Two is: it's very tedious to get the answer key, or the way that you grade this correctly. And if you don't get the way that you grade the answers correctly, it's an eval that's very easy to hack and very easy to reward-hack. And therefore you could score very highly on the eval, but actually do really poorly on the actual underlying skill or objective that you're trying to measure.

And so the prior that I will share is: evals are really hard, not just in financial work, but just across the board.

GDPval and the GPT-6 Astra Problem

And what I would say is: we don't think that there's a really good eval today for financial work. There's a bunch of existing prior work — I'll reference some of the work that we did, which is a GDP eval, which is a little bit more broadly in knowledge work.

If you guys look at the Astra announcement, we don't talk about GDPval. We know that the eval is completely saturated, and the pieces that are not saturated are essentially broken. And so we actually don't report on that, we don't track it anymore.

And so one of the tricky things for GPT-6 Astra was: we didn't talk a whole lot about financial evals. We have some internally that we didn't talk too much about and didn't want to share at the time yet. They're coming. But there was no good way for us to show progress on financial tasks on these evals.

The Hidden Bias in Eval Culture

There's funny things — like I think there's this bias in evals where if the numbers look good, the researchers assume that the model's gotten better and they don't investigate it. If you made a much more capable model and the eval numbers look bad or haven't increased in the scale that you want, then you go investigate. So this is kind of like bias baked into the investigation of these evals.

Something like this happened with GPT-6, where we ran GPT-6 on a set of financial evals and the numbers didn't really change much. We're like, "Oh, what's going on here? Let's take a look at this eval." We did a deep dive into these different evals, and lots of things were broken. We basically found that we had saturated the evals, and the questions that we were getting wrong were driven by incorrect answer keys, poorly specified prompts, or just some other flaw with the eval.

And so all that to say: one of the things that my team is working on currently is to try to build a much better eval that actually predicts the ability to automate the work of that specific profession. And so the idea is: we'll have something like an investment banking eval that predicts — if you score well on this eval, you could probably automate a lot of the work of a junior analyst in investment banking.

Hiring and How to Help

Host: We got to wrap here soon. I want to ask any callouts for people in the finance space, the Latent Space audience. Your team is probably hiring. But last thing to put out there — how can people be helpful to you?

Joseph: Yeah, wonderful.

First and foremost, please check out ChatGPT Financial Services. It is an enterprise product, but we're trying very hard to make it available to more prosumers on the Pro plan, and so hopefully we'll have some cool announcements there.

Two, yes, my team is hiring. We're seeing incredible customer traction with the product, and because of that we're hiring and scaling the team rapidly. It's a very diverse team with lots of different roles, and so I just want to call out a few of them very quickly:

  • Front-end / back-end engineering — kind of traditional product building.
  • Product managers — I think in some ways great product management is the main bottleneck in trying to win in this space, and so we're trying to hire wonderful product managers in investment banking, equity research, asset management — across the board.
  • Subject matter experts — one of the things that we did well in coding is: the people that were training the models and making them better understood what good code looks like. That was a huge tailwind for us as we were making the models better at these things. We don't have that advantage when it comes to making the models better at finance. And so we're building out and trying to hire a lot of folks that are able to bring that financial expertise and work with the engineers, work with the researchers, work with the product managers to make the model and the product better in your specific fields.

If any of those resonate with you, I highly recommend that you reach out to me. I'm available on LinkedIn. We also have these job listings posted on our careers page — pretty easy to find.

Wrap

Host: Great. Well, you answered my question. I was going to ask: when can I have a play with this? But it is coming to Pro Pro Pro Pro Pro —

Joseph: — very hard to make it available to more people.

Host: Very common OpenAI stuff, you know — it makes sense you make stuff for enterprise, and then this trickles down to the regular models, comes to the Pro plan. So I expect for your general usage down the line it'll get better at console stuff.

Awesome. Very excited to have you. Check out the keynote — you gave a lot. You gave good predictions. You talked a little bit about some juicy "we fixed pre-training issues." So I'll leave breadcrumbs for you guys to go watch. But thanks for joining.

Joseph: Yeah, awesome. Thank you so much.

# 洞察：ChatGPT for Finance 这场对话里，被低估的几个结构性暗流
## 一、"95% 可被创业公司复制"——OpenAI 高管亲口承认的护城河真相
Joseph 轻描淡写地说出了一句本不该从 OpenAI 产品负责人嘴里讲出来的话：**"我们建的东西里，95% 一家创业公司完全能做。"** 这不是谦虚，而是一种战略定位的无声宣言。
真正值得玩味的是：他把模型能力和产品构建**解耦**到了近乎残酷的程度——"我的团队在 OpenAI 内部就像一个基于 OpenAI 搭建的创业公司"。这等于承认：**模型智能是公共基础设施，产品差异化 100% 来自那剩下的 20%——数据、UI、集成、垂直 know-how**。换句话说，OpenAI 的产品部门和它的 API 客户在竞争时，并没有太多"内部作弊"的空间。
出人意料的结论是：**ChatGPT for Finance 的发布，本质上是 OpenAI 画给生态开发者的一张地图**——"这是我能走到的地方，而你从同一个起点出发并没有慢多少"。这对 Bloomberg、FactSet 这类拿着独家数据的垂直玩家，反而
